Omer Asur Cuhadar and Mohammad Sio
11 September 2026•Update: 11 September 2026
Yemeni authorities said Friday that 2,398 more families were displaced in a single day amid the latest military escalation, including 823 families in Taiz province and 1,575 in Lahj.
The figures were published by the Executive Unit for the Management of Displacement Camps and carried by the official Saba news agency.
The unit said the new displacement was recorded on Sept. 10, bringing the total number of documented displaced families to 9,746, up from 7,348 a day earlier.
It said the main areas of origin were locations affected by fighting in Taiz, Al-Hudaydah and along Yemen’s western coast, particularly the districts of Jabal Habashi, Al-Ma’afer, Maqbanah, Al-Wazi’iyah, Mawza, Mocha, Hays and Al-Khawkhah, as well as other areas.
Field teams are continuing to register displaced families, verify their data and places of arrival, assess needs and coordinate humanitarian assistance, the unit said.
It added that several schools in Al-Mudaraba district in Lahj had been opened to shelter displaced families, while local residents had also taken in some families in private homes.
The unit also held a coordination meeting Friday with the UN refugee agency to discuss assistance and the growing humanitarian needs, while maintaining contact with international and humanitarian organizations to expand the response.
Urgent needs include shelter, food, life-saving assistance, dignity kits, hygiene supplies, drinking water and water and sanitation services as families continue to arrive in reception areas.
Earlier Friday, the International Organization for Migration said at least 46,000 people had been displaced in Yemen since fighting escalated last week, warning that the number was rising “at an alarming rate.”
The organization did not specify the areas from which they had fled.
Yemen’s battlefield map has shifted in recent days as fighting between government forces and the Houthis intensified after clashes resumed in early July following years of relative calm.
The Houthis say they now control all of Al-Hudaydah province and have advanced in western Taiz, taking Mocha city and its Red Sea port and reaching areas near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s most important maritime routes.
Government forces, meanwhile, have made gains in the northern province of Al-Jawf near the Saudi border and moved closer to Al-Hazm, the provincial capital, while fighting continues on fronts in Marib, Al-Bayda and Al-Dhalea.
Yemen has been at war since the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led Arab coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

AfD files criminal complaint against Merz
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) has filed a criminal complaint against German Chancellor Friedrich Merz after he claimed that the right-wing party is calling for ethnic cleansing. Merz made the remark in a heated parliamentary debate following the AfD’s resounding victory in the regional elections in Saxony-Anhalt.
The AfD is the most popular party in Germany, according to multiple polls, enjoying the support of 28% of respondents nationally. The right-wing opposition Eurosceptic party advocates tougher immigration controls and is also highly critical of the German government’s support for Ukraine, as well as sanctions against Russia.
In a statement on Thursday, the AfD parliamentary group – the largest opposition faction in the German parliament – accused Merz of defamation that goes beyond constitutionally protected free speech in parliament.
Speaking in the Bundestag on Wednesday, the chancellor claimed that in promoting ‘remigration’ the AfD is essentially advocating “ethnic cleansing based on origin and skin color.”
Stephan Brandner, the secretary and legal counsel for the AfD parliamentary group, stated that with “his baseless and repugnant remarks” directed not only at the party itself, but also at millions of German citizens, Merz has “crossed a line… in a way that carries criminal implications.”
The concept of ‘remigration', which has been gaining traction among right-wing circles in Europe in recent years, is usually understood to mean the return of criminal and ‘non-assimilated’ immigrants and, more broadly, residents with a migrant background to their countries of origin.
Merz made the remark days after the AfD won Sunday’s regional elections in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt with 43.8% of the vote.
The chancellor’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party finished a distant second, securing just over 17.2%.
Speaking at a press conference, Merz acknowledged that the Christian Democrats, who had for years dominated Saxony-Anhalt’s political landscape, had suffered the “most serious electoral defeat in decades.”
However, the chancellor refused to change course and vowed to “strengthen our political order and our firm anchoring in Europe,” while blaming the CDU’s dismal results on poor communication with the voters.
An INSA poll published by Bild in late August indicated that support for the governing Christian Democratic CDU/CSU bloc had dipped to 20% nationwide, with 78% of respondents dissatisfied with Merz’s coalition government.
Meanwhile, Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, said on Thursday that the party does not “categorically demonize the production of defense equipment, because we will naturally need the appropriate tools for the subsequent remigration and deportation drive.”
“This is also in the interest of internal security, our own stability, and state defense,” the politician stated in response to a journalist’s question that referenced recent media reports of negotiations between Israel’s Elbit Systems and regional authorities. The arms manufacturer is reportedly seeking to set up a plant in the town of Sangerhausen.
In recent months, multiple establishment political figures have called for the opposition AfD to be banned for presumably posing a threat to Germany’s constitutional order and democracy.
In late August, Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and Baden-Wurttemberg Governor Cem Ozdemir said that the AfD should be outlawed as it supposedly calls into question the “inviolability of human dignity” enshrined in the German constitution. The politicians who represent the Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the Green Party, respectively, cited the right-wing party’s tough-on-immigration stance.
The AfD has already been placed under surveillance by the German federal authorities, which classify the party as a ‘suspected right-wing extremist’ entity. In several regions, local AfD chapters have been subjected to even wider monitoring.

From Bishkek to New Delhi, Xi advocates Global South cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11

From Bishkek to New Delhi, Xi advocates Global South cooperation
Chinese President Xi Jinping is heading to New Delhi for this year's BRICS gathering just over a week after he took part in the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in the Kyrgyz capital of Bishkek.
The two back-to-back multilateral engagements converge on a single, defining theme: galvanizing solidarity and cooperation across the Global South.
EXPANDING FAMILY
The SCO "takes root in the Global South, its heart beats with the Global South, and it is an important pillar of South-South cooperation," Xi said at the Bishkek summit on Tuesday last week, calling on the SCO to "promote the development and rise of the Global South through the SCO Wisdom."
The Chinese leader is expected to put forward further proposals on Global South cooperation at the upcoming BRICS summit, as he has noted that the BRICS is "standing at the forefront of the Global South."
This year marks the 25th founding anniversary of the SCO and the 20th anniversary of the BRICS cooperation mechanism, both milestone occasions.
Chinese President Xi Jinping chairs the "Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Plus" Meeting in Tianjin, north China, Sept. 1, 2025. (Xinhua/Huang Jingwen)
 
 
 Riding the wave of the collective rise of the Global South, BRICS and the SCO have over the years expanded their membership and broadened their networks of developing partners. Their members jointly account for more than half of the world's population and about 30 percent of the global economy. This illustrates the fact that the two groupings have evolved into major platforms for Global South cooperation.
Xi has not only joined other leaders of member countries in pushing for their respective expansions, but also put forward new ideas and initiatives like the "BRICS Plus" cooperation approach and the building of an SCO community with a shared future, opening up new vistas for win-win cooperation among Global South countries.
"China has consistently provided a clear vision and momentum for BRICS and the SCO, both conceptually and practically," said Humprey Arnaldo Russel, head of the ASEAN-China Research Center at the University of Indonesia.
Photo taken on Aug. 24, 2017 shows a flowerbed at the Xiamen International Conference and Exhibition Center in Xiamen, southeast China's Fujian Province. (Xinhua/Jiang Kehong)
"It transformed BRICS from a relatively exclusive grouping into a broader platform for cooperation among developing countries and the wider Global South," he added.
DEVELOPMENT FIRST
At the SCO summit last week, Xi called on countries to "stay committed to putting development first, and open up the prospects for shared prosperity."
Amid a turbulent and rapidly changing international landscape, development still faces severe challenges, and the road to prosperity for the Global South will not be straight.
Chinese expert Li Guiqiang (L) gives instructions on vegetable cultivation at the China-Ethiopia Addis Ababa Agricultural Technology Demonstration and Training Center in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, on Aug. 20, 2025. (Xinhua/Han Xu)
 
 "The Global South emerges for development and prospers through development. We should make ourselves the main driving force for common development," Xi said during the 2024 BRICS summit in Kazan, Russia.
For Xi, development has always been a priority. He sees it as "the master key to solving all problems," and has consistently called for countries worldwide to jointly pursue development and prosperity.
Xi has stressed repeatedly that no one should be left behind in the fight against poverty in China, and has led a formidable campaign that ended extreme poverty nationwide, which was hailed as "the greatest anti-poverty achievement in history."
His "leaving-no-one-behind" conviction also extends to his efforts to support poverty reduction and spur development across the Global South. "On the path to modernization, no one, and no country, should be left behind," Xi said.
Last week in Bishkek, Xi called for consolidating cooperation in both traditional and emerging fields, from trade, investment, connectivity and energy to artificial intelligence (AI), the digital economy and green industries.
Responding to the Global South's aspirations for common development and modernization, Xi has proposed the Global Development Initiative (GDI), which marks its fifth anniversary this year.
In the last five years, the GDI has mobilized more than 23 billion U.S. dollars, provided support for over 1,800 "small and beautiful" livelihood projects, and sponsored training programs for more than 200,000 people in different professions.
Serik Korzhumbayev, editor-in-chief of the Delovoy Kazakhstan newspaper, said: "Under Xi's leadership, the concept of development has acquired a new international dimension and become part of a broader vision for humanity's shared future."
GREATER VOICE
As the Global South rises, it deserves a bigger say in global affairs.
Last year's SCO Tianjin summit witnessed Xi's proposal of the Global Governance Initiative, a major proposition of China to advance a more just and equitable global governance system.
At the heart of this vision is the conviction that every country has a place and an equal role to play in global governance.
Xi has long argued that international affairs should not be dictated by those with more muscles. "World affairs should be discussed by all, and international norms should be set by all," he said in Bishkek last week. "The domination of international affairs by a few is an injustice left over from history, and global governance dictated by one, a few or a bloc of countries is not true multilateralism."
"As an important part of a multipolar world and a key driving force behind it, the Global South countries ought to have greater representation and voice in international affairs," Xi said.
Robotic arms work in an energy storage production workshop at the Sigenergy Nantong Smart Energy Center in Nantong, east China's Jiangsu Province, July 24, 2026. (Xinhua/Chen Yehua)
 
 
 Over the years, the SCO and BRICS have grown into vital venues for Global South countries to articulate their interests, coordinate their positions and strengthen their collective influence.
Their growing role can be seen in political coordination. The two groupings have issued statements on international and regional hotspot issues. In March this year, for example, SCO member states issued a statement expressing grave concern over developments in the Middle East and the strikes on Iran.
Xi has also pushed for improving global economic and financial governance. In 2014, Xi and other BRICS leaders formally signed an agreement establishing the New Development Bank, creating a new channel for financing infrastructure and sustainable development in emerging markets and developing countries.
At the SCO Bishkek summit, the members reaffirmed the importance of establishing the SCO Development Bank.
Now the push for a greater say is extending into emerging areas that will shape the future. In July this year, Xi announced the creation of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, and called for joint efforts to build a just and equitable system of global AI governance.
"We must carry out extensive international cooperation and help Global South countries with capacity building to bridge the AI and digital divides, promote sustainable development, and prevent creating new historical injustice in AI," Xi said.
An aerial photo taken on Oct. 22, 2025 shows wind turbines of De Aar Wind Power Project in De Aar, Northern Cape, South Africa. (Xinhua/Han Xu)
 
 
 Beyond the SCO and BRICS, China has also promoted cooperation and greater representation for the Global South through frameworks such as the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation and the China-ASEAN summit.
Xi has said on many occasions that China has always been a member of the Global South and will always belong to the developing world.
"No matter how the international landscape evolves, we in China will always keep the Global South in our heart, and maintain our roots in the Global South," he once said.

British man encouraged group chat members to abuse partners, exchange images
LONDON - A British man pleaded guilty in court on Sept 11 to encouraging other men in an online group chat to sexually abuse their unconscious partners and exchange images of the abuse.
It is the latest in a string of UK criminal cases involving men accused of abusing their partners while asleep or sedated and often going on to share images of their offences.
Darren Conway, 52, pleaded guilty to multiple charges including voyeurism, possessing an extreme pornographic image and assisting or encouraging sexual assault and the sharing of intimate images.
He admitted to messaging a man in 2025, asking the man to assault his wife while she was asleep and share images of the crime.
He also solicited images of sleeping women online at least 10 times between 2023 and 2026.
Conway was charged following an investigation by Britain’s National Crime Agency (NCA) into an online forum linked to multiple, international cases of men encouraging or committing this type of offence, known as drug-facilitated sexual abuse.
Global awareness of the crime has grown following the high-profile conviction in France of Dominique Pelicot, who drugged and raped his then-wife Gisele for nearly a decade alongside strangers.
The judge in the north London court dealing with Conway’s case said he would be sentenced on Oct 30.
“Messages found on his devices showed Conway encouraging other group chat members to engage in drug-facilitated sexual offending, alongside images and videos of a sexual nature,” London’s Metropolitan Police said in a statement.
“Conway’s actions were shocking,” Met police commander Andy Day said.
“By encouraging others to engage in sexual offending against victims who were unconscious, asleep, or otherwise stupefied, he has put women at a serious risk of harm in their own homes – all for his own sexual gratification.”
Police said while “much of the offending” on Conway’s group chat is believed to have taken place in the UK, “it is also possible that some victims are based overseas”.
In a separate case, a man in central England pleaded guilty in July to 32 sexual offences against his girlfriend while she was allegedly drugged or asleep.
In Manchester in north-west England, the husband of a woman who was allegedly drugged and sexually assaulted is set to stand trial this month alongside 12 other men accused of taking part in the abuse. AFP

The portfolio integrates services from eCloudvalley’s subsidiaries — CloudRiches Digital Technology Co (雲馥數位), Dynacloud Co (雲動力資訊), NeuroBrain Dynamics Inc (創智動能) and eCloudEdge Digital Innovation Co (雲界數位創新) — to support large-scale AI deployment.
Photo: Meryl Kau, Taipei Times
The company aims to address tool fragmentation, data silos, cybersecurity, cost and governance challenges as the use of AI agents expands, it said.
It also aims to help companies scale AI from individual proof-of-concept trials to cross-department deployment, the company said.
“As the use of AI agents expands, enterprises’ cloud consumption will also grow,” eCloudvalley founder and chairman MP Tsai (蔡佳宏) said.
Major cloud service providers are offering incentives to capture this growing demand by encouraging customers to use AI models available on their platforms, Tsai said.
As it is time-consuming and costly to build private on-premises cloud infrastructure, new enterprise cloud service adopters usually turn to public cloud services to gain quick access to AI models, he said.
As a result, eCloudvalley is gaining new customers, while existing customers are also increasing their cloud consumption as they expand AI applications, he added.
The trend is also driving recurring demand for cloud consumption, platform subscriptions, AI governance and maintenance services, Tsai said.
ECloudvalley’s customer renewal rate is about 96 percent, while one-off projects account for only a small portion of its business, he said.
Since last year, eCloudvalley has seen more enterprises adopt AI agents, eCloudvalley AI business unit head Christine Wang (王玟樺) said.
“Nearly all customers that conducted AI agent POC trials with the company over the past two to three years have moved into production environments,” she said.
Some enterprises have also expanded from adopting a single AI agent to second and third agents integrating into daily operations, she added.
Most early adopters expand AI applications to other departments, including customer service, finance, maintenance and manufacturing, after completing their first projects, Wang said.
Enterprises therefore need to track how many AI agents they have, who developed them, the models and data they use, their access permissions, costs and effectiveness, she said.
To address this, eCloudvalley introduced the Multi-AI Agent Hub and ECV AI Governance platform to integrate agents across platforms and departments, while centrally managing models, data, access rights, costs and execution records, Wang said.
Looking ahead, enterprises need AI agents to operate continuously and reliably, making the usage limits common in individual subscription services unsuitable, Tsai said.
eCloudvalley plans to discuss new collaboration models with enterprise customers, Anthropic PBC and OpenAI, leveraging its systems-integration capabilities and forward-deployed engineering team, he said.

Donovan’s Deep Dives: Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines need to face the common  threat from Beijing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:42:05 UTC
01:42:05 KST

For a time, it became popular to describe the tactics of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) in encroaching on sovereignty and militarizing islands in the South China Sea as “salami slicing.” Those slices have been getting chunkier.
The People’s Liberation Army has been increasing its navy and air force activities in the region. The Chinese Coast Guard has likewise been ramping up their activities, and the civilian paramilitary People’s Armed Forces Maritime Militia has been backing up the navy and coast guard with alarming swarming maneuvers.
The PRC claims most of the South China Sea through its U-shaped 10-dash line (formerly nine-dash line). Various neighboring states such as Taiwan, however, are much closer and have stronger historical claims.
Photo: AFP
Several neighboring coastal states such as Taiwan have competing claims to features and much stronger claims under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) to maritime zones extending from their own coasts.
In July 2016, an UNCLOS arbitral tribunal ruled that China had no legal basis for claiming historic resource rights beyond those provided by the convention within the nine-dash line.
China’s harassment of Japan over their claims to the Senkaku Islands, also known as Diaoyutai Islands (釣魚台) in Taiwan and China, is long-standing, but has intensified.
Also not new, but recently ramped up, are Chinese claims questioning Japan’s sovereignty over Okinawa Prefecture — which encompasses the Ryukyu Islands — in both state media and so-called scholarly symposiums. See Michael Turton’s “Notes from Central Taiwan: Okinawa as Taiwan” (Dec. 22, 2025) for more. Beijing has not formally laid claim to Okinawa, but there is the strong implication they might, or press for the restoration of the Ryukyu Kingdom, which had once been a Chinese tributary state.
The upgrading of the nine-dash line to 10 included a dash off the east coast of Taiwan, which presaged the recent regular “law enforcement” activities by the Chinese coast guard.
Clashes with Southeast Asian nations in the South China Sea have been ongoing for decades, but recently the Chinese navy and coast guard have been increasingly aggressive towards the Philippines. Alarmingly, there are indications that Beijing may be planning to militarize Scarborough Shoal — known as Huangyan Island (黃岩島) in China, Bajo de Masinloc in the Philippines and Democracy Reef (民主礁) in Taiwan — which would point a dagger only about 120 nautical miles from Luzon and 200 nautical miles from Manila.
Then, like a toddler pointing to whatever they want and declaring loudly “mine,” the PRC is now pushing the line through their nationalistic Global Times that “From both historical and legal perspectives, it remains questionable whether the sovereignty over Batanes Islands belongs to the Philippines” and that “the islands have longstanding historical ties with China’s Taiwan region and that relevant legal grounds exist for China to claim sovereignty.”
LAYING THE GROUNDWORK
Beijing has not yet formally laid claim to the Batanes, but is using the Global Times to apply pressure on the Philippines. The Strategist, the analysis and commentary site for the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, summed up the short-term goal: “For the moment, the manufactured claim may serve only as a flexible diplomatic and legal pressure point to advance immediate objectives: disrupting Japan–Philippines maritime boundary talks and escalating cognitive warfare against Taiwan.”
The cognitive warfare extends to the region with the intent of creating fear and strengthening the hand of those favoring appeasement towards Beijing. Appeasement has always failed over the long term with hegemonic, dictatorial regimes like the PRC’s, but fear remains a powerful motivator for some in closing one’s eyes to historical precedent and hoping somehow this time things will be different.
China is unlikely to invade Batanes or Okinawa in the immediate future, but they are creating the conditions for them to act should the opportunity arise. They are laying the groundwork for such an eventuality, such as a withdrawal of US forces, or the calculation in Beijing that their relative military advantage is worth the risk.
Recently, in joint diplomatic statements, Beijing has been increasingly pressuring other countries to strongly reaffirm their support for China’s “one China principle” that Taiwan is an “inalienable” part of China’s territory.
Watch to see if they begin to do the same with other territorial claims; it would be an important signal.
Geographically, Okinawa is north of Taiwan across the Miyako Strait, while the Batanes sit just south of Taiwan in the Bashi Channel. Both nations are treaty allies of the US, and those key geographical positions allow careful monitoring of Chinese navy activities as they traverse through the first island chain. They are also critical locations in any defense of — or attack on — Taiwan.
Military analyst Lu Wen-hao (陸文浩) recently published a piece in Storm Media entitled “China Is Quietly Signaling It Can Control the Bashi Channel.” This is based on Lu’s tracking of vessels and movements in the region, including off Taiwan’s south and southeast coasts.
If true, this is alarming. It would also dovetail with the recent Chinese propaganda on the sovereign status of the Batanes.
Beijing has also in the last few months been conducting research in these key regions, especially near Scarborough Shoal, the Bashi Channel and off the east coast of Taiwan. This may sound harmless, but they are capable of providing key military analysis and monitoring of conditions that would be very valuable in an invasion or blockade scenario, especially for the Chinese navy.
WHY THE UPTICK?
The CCP has a long-term strategy that has continued for decades — sometimes increasing or decreasing their activities.
The recent uptick in aggressiveness may be related to Washington being distracted by its war in Iran, and US President Donald Trump’s failure to stand against Beijing’s hostility towards Japan and its Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. However, there is a risk of viewing the situation through an overly US-centric lens.
A bigger factor is likely recent moves by Japan and the Philippines to both boost their individual military capabilities while simultaneously deepening their mutual cooperation and interoperability, which Beijing views with alarm, judging by their party-state media going into hyperbolic overdrive.
Though Washington remains a key partner, all of these recent moves by Beijing increase the imperative for Taiwan to closely coordinate with Japan and the Philippines. Taiwan’s problematic diplomatic status complicates matters, however.
The good news? All three nations may be aware of this. According to Reuters, Japan in 2023 appointed a serving government official to act as its de facto defence attache in Taiwan, instead of a retired official as was common previously.
The Philippines in April last year loosened restrictions on higher-level contact with Taiwan, though it still excludes the president and foreign and defense secretaries. The Philippines in July sent serving Navy spokesman Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad, Coast Guard spokesman Grand Commodore Jay Tarriela and a former Presidential Communications Office assistant secretary to attend the Taiwan International Ocean Forum in Taipei. This year, Delfin N. Lorenzana, former defense secretary for the Philippines, was a panelist at the Yushan Forum in Taipei.
Let us hope that there is more extensive cooperation among the three countries. It could be valuable on an existential level for all three nations.
Donovan’s Deep Dives is a regular column by Courtney Donovan Smith (石東文) who writes in-depth analysis on everything about Taiwan’s political scene and geopolitics. Donovan is also the central Taiwan correspondent at ICRT FM100 Radio News, co-publisher of Compass Magazine, co-founder Taiwan Report (report.tw) and former chair of the Taichung American Chamber of Commerce. Follow him on X: @donovan_smith.

The Agni-IV and India’s strategic autonomy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:42:04 UTC
01:42:04 KST

India’s test of its Agni-IV last month was not remarkable simply because another missile was launched. With a range of about 4,000km, the Agni-IV can reach Beijing and other important targets deep inside China. What the test shows more clearly is that India has a much greater capacity to deter China well beyond their disputed border.
The missile itself is only part of the story. More important is what it tells us about India’s national capabilities, and how those capabilities affect the way New Delhi deals with Beijing and the regional order.
India’s strategic autonomy is often described as a preference not to choose sides. It is also sometimes understood as an attempt to keep roughly equal distance from major powers. Neither description quite captures what India has been trying to do.
Nonalignment, multiple partnerships and selective alignment have all appeared in Indian foreign policy. They are better understood as policy choices than as the meaning of strategic autonomy itself. What India has consistently sought is the ability to protect its security and make its own decisions when the external environment changes.
That ability depends on more than diplomatic flexibility. A country might stay outside an alliance and have little autonomy if its security depends heavily on outside commitments or if critical military systems come from a single foreign supplier.
The Agni-IV is important in this sense: India has spent more than 15 years testing and improving the system. In the process, it has also accumulated experience in indigenous research and development, systems integration and the operation of strategic forces. These capabilities give substance to an idea that otherwise risks remaining little more than diplomatic language.
Autonomy is only as useful as the choices it leaves open, and Agni-IV matters, because it gives India more of those choices, especially in dealing with China.
A similar pattern can be seen in India’s approach to Beijing, a neighbor it cannot simply disengage from, and a major power that can narrow India’s security and development space.
India has reopened high-level channels with China, but that has not changed the direction of its defense policy. New Delhi is still bolstering its military capabilities, paying greater attention to the Indian Ocean and investing in technologies where dependence could become a liability.
China remains too important for India to sideline. The border dispute is still there, and trade between the two countries remains large. That helps explain why New Delhi has resumed political contact with Beijing.
However, renewed contact says little about the direction of India’s China policy. It matters more to look at the areas in which India continues to rely on China, where it is searching for alternatives and where New Delhi increasingly treats dependence as a strategic risk.
This extends beyond the bilateral relationship. On the Indian Ocean, technology and supply chains, India has been building alternatives and reducing dependence on any single major power. In doing so, it might create more room for other countries in the region as well. The result is a regional environment in which China is important, but not the only center of economic and strategic gravity.
For the Indo-Pacific region, this might be the broader significance of India’s strategic autonomy. An India with greater freedom to act and a stronger ability to withstand pressure adds another center of power to the regional order.
For Taiwan, the important question is what practical options such an India might eventually create.
Lin Hsiao-chen is an assistant professor in the Graduate Institute of International Affairs and Strategic Studies at Tamkang University.

President promulgates income tax relief measure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:42:03 UTC
01:42:03 KST

President William Lai (賴清德) yesterday promulgated amendments to the Income Tax Act (所得稅法) that would reduce the tax burden on families with children, benefiting an estimated 2.37 million people and providing about NT$8 billion (US$252.86 million) in tax relief.
The Legislative Yuan on Aug. 23 passed an amendment to the act, raising the tax exemption threshold for dependent minors and expanding itemized deductions for social insurance premiums.
Lai yesterday promulgated the amendments to articles 17 and 126 of the act, including a 50 percent increase in the personal exemption for dependent minors, from NT$101,000 to NT$151,500, the Ministry of Finance said.
Photo: CNA
The revised law, which takes effect retroactively from Jan. 1, would also allow social insurance premiums to be fully deducted as itemized deductions in the same way as National Health Insurance (NHI) premiums, it said.
Social insurance programs — including Labor Insurance, Farmers’ Health Insurance, National Pension Insurance, and insurance schemes for military personnel, civil servants and teachers — form an integral part of Taiwan’s social security system and are generally mandatory by law, making them similar in nature to NHI, the ministry said.
Premiums paid for those programs would no longer be subject to the NT$24,000 cap on itemized deductions for insurance premiums, the ministry said.
The new provisions would take effect when taxpayers file their income tax returns for this year in May next year, the ministry said.
The amendments are part of the government’s efforts to address Taiwan’s declining birthrate under the Executive Yuan’s new population strategy.
The Executive Yuan proposed the amendment on June 25 to alleviate financial pressure on families raising children and create a more family-friendly tax environment.

Daily swings being less dictated by the whims of retail investors has tempted the return of some foreign funds, which have been large sellers year to date.

Based on a blend of price-to-book and price-to-earnings valuations, “these stocks look cheap, especially compared to global peers,” he added.
Samsung trades at 2.7 times current book value and SK Hynix at five times, compared with 11 times for the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index. The South Korean memory stocks are trading at about four times forward estimated earnings, versus 19 times for the gauge of global chipmakers.
However, the two South Korean memory stocks remain more than 25 percent below their all-time highs, with investors still spooked by wild swings on daily news and position adjustments.
“These names are going to be volatile. For most investors, there are ways to get the same returns with a lot less volatility,” Tuttle Capital Management chief executive officer Matthew Tuttle said.
Despite the decrease in leverage and measures implemented by regulators to restore calm, daily moves of 5 percent or more are still common for Samsung and SK Hynix. EDITORIAL: Taiwan would not give up easily
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:42:00 UTC
01:42:00 KST

In an article published on Tuesday in The Atlantic, titled “Will Taiwan Just Give Up?”, journalist Simon Shuster emphasizes the unpredictability of the US as an ally under US President Donald Trump and cites diminishing faith in the US as a contributor to what he sees as waning determination to resist China.
As the title suggests, Shuster views a deal between Taiwan and China as an increasingly inevitable alternative to a costly war — one that Taiwan, lacking reliable allies and military capabilities, would eventually be destined to lose.
He focuses on Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) — her meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) in April, her party’s ties with the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and her optimism that Taiwan could strike a deal with China while preserving its freedom.
However, one major flaw with Shuster’s argument is that it risks conflating the KMT’s abandonment of its once staunchly anti-communist position and Cheng’s increasingly shameless capitulation toward China with the views of the Taiwanese population as a whole.
To be fair, he acknowledges that Cheng’s election as KMT chair was decided by only about 65,000 KMT members — a tiny fraction of Taiwan’s 23 million people.
Her influence primarily stems from her position as party leader given its legislative control, particularly over defense spending, he said.
Yet the article attributes Cheng’s delusionally optimistic vision for cross-strait relations, the positions of several KMT figures and retired military officers, and comments of others he interviewed to an apparent uncertainty among Taiwanese over whether a deal with China is the right choice — a conclusion that is not supported by broader public evidence.
A June survey by the Taoyuan National Development Education Foundation found that support for cross-strait political negotiations in Taiwan has fallen by more than 16 percent since 2018, while only 3.2 percent of Taiwanese favor unification with China.
The Mainland Affairs Council found that more than 80 percent of Taiwanese reject Beijing’s “one country, two systems” framework, while 88 percent believe Taiwan’s future should be decided by its 23 million people — a right that would disappear were the nation to come under China’s control.
An Academia Sinica survey found that nearly 60 percent of Taiwanese would be willing to resist a Chinese invasion “at all costs” regardless of US assistance.
These figures do not paint the picture of a nation preparing to quietly surrender, but one that understands the risks of war, recognizes uncertainty and refuses to regard surrender to China as a solution.
Diminishing confidence in the US and distrust of China are not mutually exclusive. Taiwanese can recognize Washington’s volatility while acknowledging that Beijing has repeatedly denied its sovereignty and openly sought to sabotage its democratic system.
Shuster rightly points out that many Taiwanese would prefer to maintain the “status quo,” but it is important to understand what “status quo” means in this context. It means maintaining democracy, freedom of speech and the press, the ability to trade freely with the rest of the world and the right to go about life without interference from Beijing.
Most Taiwanese are well aware that a political deal with China would mean waving goodbye to that “status quo.” They see what has happened to democratic institutions and political freedoms in Hong Kong, and there is little reason to assume Taiwan would receive a fundamentally different bargain.
History further illustrates why Taiwanese should not be mistaken for a passive population. The democratization movement of the late 20th century, the Sunflower movement in 2014 and more recent mass demonstrations over issues such as food safety are proof of a society accustomed to holding those in power accountable, organizing and demanding change.
Shuster’s article identifies genuine concerns. Gone are the days that Taiwan could assume that the US would automatically come to its defense. The nation’s military preparedness, defense procurement and societal resilience require serious attention, but acknowledging these vulnerabilities and admitting defeat are two different things.
Taiwanese might be uncertain about Washington’s response in a cross-strait crisis. They might disagree on arms procurements or deterrence strategies. However, those debates are evidence of a society grappling with how to preserve its way of life.
It would be foolish to ignore these issues; but it would be equally foolish to conclude that the only alternatives are an unwinnable war or submission to Beijing.
The choice Taiwanese face is not whether to trust the US or China, but how to defend their democratic way of life — something history has proven they would not give up so easily.

Energy-saving posters draw teachers’ ire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:42:00 UTC
01:42:00 KST

The National Teachers’ Association yesterday demanded that the government recall manga-style posters about electricity conservation from elementary and junior-high schools over concerns about their portrayal of “intimate interaction.”
The Energy Administration’s public information poster consists of three panels, with each showing a character pinning another against a wall and whispering an electricity-saving tip in their ear.
The association said in a statement that it had no issue with the agency’s effort to reduce energy waste, but the artwork was inappropriate for the intended audience.
Photo courtesy of the National Teachers’ Association
The pose struck by the characters in the poster was “provocative and intimate,” and inspired by a manga trope that has sexual connotations, it said.
The eyes of the students would more likely be drawn to the depiction of intimacy instead of the public service message, the association said.
The government should not treat public information posters displayed at schools as for-profit commercial advertisements in public spaces aimed at a general audience, it said.
The government should have checked the content of the posters, and ensured that they were safe and appropriate for minors before ordering teachers to put them up in places with high foot traffic on campus, it said.
“A school is a place of education, not a free bulletin board for government agencies to pin their advertisements,” association chairman Yeh Ching-chi (葉青?) said.
Multiple government agencies have been bothering teachers with their public information campaigns, demanding that educators put up posters, take pictures of the posters and provide written reports on the material’s impact, he said.
These reports are sometimes detailed and require educators to estimate the number of students who have seen the posters, Yeh said.
Such demands come from public functionaries who want to boost their performance indicators without doing the footwork, he said.
Schools are willing to assist the government in educating the public about important matters, but government agencies do not have an unlimited mandate to treat teachers as part of their staff to command, he said.
In response, the Energy Administration said the poster used manga-style artwork to attract attention, as the general public would likely find energy savings an overly serious topic.
However, it said it would reflect on criticism that the posters were unsuitable for minors and adjusts its public information campaign.

====================================================================================================

US trial remains elusive for top terror suspect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:41:59 UTC
01:41:59 KST

Two decades after US authorities locked Khalid Sheikh Mohammed away at a military detention center in Cuba, the purported mastermind of the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks sometimes seems barely any closer to being put on trial than the day he arrived.
A judge recently set a 2028 date for Mohammed to finally be tried before a military tribunal, but some lawyers predict it will never happen — not that year or any other year.
They say the maze of legal issues that arose because Mohammed was tortured following his 2003 capture in Pakistan is too twisted to ever be straightened out.
Photo: Reuters
A fleeting bid to put him on trial in a civilian court in New York City was shouted down years ago over security concerns.
A plea agreement that would have kept Mohammed imprisoned for life, but spared him from a possible execution, began to collapse shortly after it was announced in 2024 and finally died for good last year.
“It’s all contaminated by politics and the lack of accountability on torture,” said Joshua Dratel, an attorney who played a part in assuring that Mohammed has proper legal representation.
Late last month, the US military judge who set a June 5, 2028, trial date for Mohammed and three others charged in the 2001 attacks ruled that prosecutors could not use an alleged confession he made to the FBI in 2007.
Those statements were deemed tainted because Mohammed was subjected to “enhanced interrogation techniques” overseas, including the simulated drowning technique called waterboarding.
While the ruling was a blow to the prosecution, the US government decided not to appeal, in part because doing so could have further delayed a possible trial.
Meanwhile, Mohammed remains jailed in Guantanamo Bay, where he was taken on Sept. 5, 2006, following more than three years in secret prisons in other countries.
Terry Strada, whose husband, Tom, died at the World Trade Center in the 2001 attacks, said that she and other people who lost family members still hope a trial will someday happen.
“We very much want to see this come to an end at some point. We do want to see justice served. It’s just as important as 25 years ago,” she said.
However, Terry Strada, the national chair of the group 9/11 Families United, also said she would rather have Mohammed rot at Guantanamo Bay indefinitely than get behind a resolution that would involve dropping the death penalty as a possibility.
She said she worries that if Mohammed is not executed, future US leaders might someday be tempted to swap him for Americans held prisoner elsewhere in the world.
The death penalty “fits the crime and it would prevent that from ever happening,” she said. “And that’s important to me.”
Mohammed was captured in Pakistan in 2003, accused of developing and directing the attacks, as a leader of the Islamic militant group al-Qaeda. Some of the delays in his legal proceedings have stemmed from his treatment after he fell into US control.
A US Senate report pointed to his extended torture in CIA custody, including 183 sessions of waterboarding.
For a time in 2009, it seemed Mohammed was headed to New York after then-US attorney general Eric Holder announced plans to try him and four other men charged in the 2001 attacks in a Manhattan courthouse just blocks from the World Trade Center site.
Then-US president Barack Obama, who had pledged to close the Guantanamo detention center, said Mohammed would face “the most exacting demands of justice.”
Almost immediately, opposition arose. Some critics predicted Mohammed would use a trial as a platform to spread hateful views of the US and its allies. Others cited security concerns, saying it could again make New York a terrorist target.
Former New York City mayor Rudy Giuliani called the plan unwise and said it showed “a lack of concern for the rights of the public.”
“It was a charade in many respects,” Dratel said.
The military tribunal system has proven itself to be a worse solution, unable to function efficiently, without a proper structure and without fidelity to federal courts, he said.
“Each time you reach an impasse, no one knows what to do,” he said.

01:41:58 KST

I was in Taichung at a large family gathering when President William Lai (賴清德) spoke to members of the Lions Clubs International. He discussed everything from economic growth, wages and tax cuts to child care, housing rentals and long-term care. He also quoted the Book of Rites (禮記), which says: “When the Great Way prevails, the world belongs to all the people; the worthy and capable are selected, and trust and harmony are cultivated.”
There is work well on its way in Taiwan toward realizing the ideals that the passage laid out: “the old are cared for until death, the able-bodied are gainfully employed, and the children may grow and flourish.” However, the preceding line, being concerned with selecting the worthy and capable, and fostering trust and harmony, might prove to be even more difficult.
What does it mean to be “capable”?
A good academic background and being well versed in the law is certainly important for a minister, but real governance is not about sitting in an office, reading reports and listening to briefings; it is about going out into the community, listening to people, identifying problems, understanding them and solving them.
Former Singaporean prime minister Lee Kuan Yew (李光耀) governed under a different system from Taiwan’s. While we certainly need not copy it as a whole, his emphasis on developing talent, meritocracy and practical results is worth considering. Someone’s true capabilities are not shown in their resume, but in how they handle responsibility and difficult situations. For example, when encountering a policy setback, can they identify what went wrong, listen to different viewpoints, correct their mistakes and get the job done properly?
The construction project at Daan Forest Park is one such test of governing ability.
I have previously raised concerns about the Taipei City Government’s public works in the park (“Public works reflect governance,” May 30, page 8).
The city government said that although an on-site inspection had been conducted before construction began, the age of the infrastructure and insufficient records meant that it was only after excavation began that fire mains from 1988, unidentified power lines and Chunghwa Telecom Co (中華電信) cables were discovered on site. Other factors included changes in regulations governing the handling of excavated soil, underground water seepage and heavy rain.
Perhaps not all of these issues were foreseeable, but the question of how many among them could have been caught in advance is still worth asking.
A rule of thumb for good governance could be three years of planning, one year of renovations and 10 years of use.
This is not to suggest that all projects need three years of planning, but to emphasize a philosophy of governance: It is better to spend the time before construction begins than to leave the costs to be paid afterward.
Elections can determine who receives the people’s mandate, but they do not guarantee that the right people end up in the right jobs. True virtue is not loyalty to one’s leader, but responsibility to the people. True capability is not about giving good presentations, but solving people’s problems.
Cultivating trust and harmony is equally important. Trust is earned, and politicians must be accountable for their promises; political parties may compete and debate with each other, but must still cooperate for the good of the country. Democracy is not about eliminating differences in opinions, but building the trust needed to live together despite those differences.
The Book of Rites proposed these ideals more than 2,000 years ago. Today, they remain one of the most important tests for Taiwan’s democracy.
“The world belongs to all people” asks whom the government serves; “select the worthy and capable” asks who should govern; and “foster trust and harmony” asks how society can build cohesion.
True commitment to these ideas means putting the best people in the positions best suited to them, and ensuring that power is genuinely used to listen, serve and solve the problems of everyday people.
Hsiao Hsi-huei is a freelancer.

Taiwan and Paraguay are to cooperate in environmental governance with a pilot carbon credit project covering five hectares of woodland in Paraguay, the Climate Change Administration said yesterday.
Deputy Minister of Environment Hsieh Yein-rui (謝燕儒) led a delegation to visit Paraguay’s Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development from Monday to yesterday, during which they exchanged views on environmental governance.
Minister of Environment Peng Chi-ming (彭啟明) and Paraguayan Minister of Environment and Sustainable Development Rolando de Barros Barreto in October last year signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) on carbon credits.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Environment
Administration Director-General Tsai Ling-yi (蔡玲儀) said the project aims to explore feasible carbon credit cooperation mechanisms.
The ministry commissioned the Industrial Technology Research Institute, which collaborated with a Paraguayan company, for an “afforestation, reforestation and revegetation” project in the Chaco region, she said.
The project is more of a pilot study to help develop methods to verify and transfer carbon credits, she added.
Hsieh said the cooperation goes beyond the exchange of systems and policies.
What matters more is integrating resources and practical experiences to establish an implementable and sustainable model, he said.
The administration said Taiwan’s main focus is not the total amount of verifiable carbon credits, but the project’s environmental integrity, scientific foundation and information transparency.
Taiwan expects to bring tangible benefits for sustainable development in Paraguay, it said.
Tsai said Taiwan and Paraguay have reached a consensus on environmental governance via the carbon credit MOU.
That effort is being deepened through bilateral cooperation on talent development, with the National Tsing Hua University (NTHU) and the National University of Asuncion on Wednesday signing another MOU.
Ten Taiwanese students traveled with the delegation to Paraguay to attend learning exchanges under the Taiwan Global Pathfinders Initiative, Tsai said.
The Climate Change Administration said the MOU signed by the universities focuses on promoting sustainable innovation, entrepreneurship and talent training in terms of sustainable production, ecosystem conservation and climate resilience.
NTHU College of Sustainability dean Fan Chien-te (范建得) said the schools’ MOU helps leverage Taiwan’s training resources to meet Paraguay’s needs.
It is expected to incorporate knowledge of climate change, greenhouse gas management and sustainability into bilateral exchanges to assist Paraguay in developing local green-collar professionals, he added.

Thai police yesterday said that they arrested a senior Buddhist monk on suspicion of embezzling US$2.8 million intended for his monastery, alongside a suspected female accomplice he was having sex with.
The case is the latest scandal to hit the clergy in Buddhist-majority Thailand after a sex and extortion case involving senior monks last year prompted public outrage and calls for greater scrutiny of temple finances.
Phra Wachirayan Wi, the 66-year-old abbot of the 14th-century Wat Phutthaisawan in the ancient capital of Ayutthaya, was arrested on Thursday on charges including embezzlement and money laundering, lead police investigator Pattanasak Bupphasuwan said.
Photo: AFP
A 47-year-old woman accused of helping convert and conceal the money was also arrested.
Leaked security camera footage of the pair having sex on a table in the monk’s residence was widely broadcast on Thai media.
In Thailand, Buddhist monks take a vow of celibacy and also renounce material possessions.
Police began investigating Phra Wachirayan in the middle of July after receiving an anonymous tip alleging him of misconduct and misuse of temple funds.
Pattanasak, commander of the police Crime Suppression Division, said investigators identified two streams of money linked to donation receipts issued in the temple’s name.
About 89 million baht (US$2.69 million) was donated for temple renovations, with another 2.8 million baht in payments for Buddhist amulets and other sacred objects, he said.
However, “the money from both streams did not enter the temple’s account — not a single baht,” Pattanasak told a news conference yesterday.
Authorities had seized assets worth about 215 million baht, including 16kg of gold bars and jewelery, and 28 land title deeds, he said.
Police are investigating which were personal property and which belonged to the temple.
“We will expand the investigation to identify other people involved and restore public confidence in Buddhism,” Central Investigation Bureau commissioner Nattasak Chaowanasai said.
Wat Phutthaisawan is a prominent royal monastery with a large following that includes government officials, businesspeople, police and military personnel.

The transformation of Taipei City
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:41:52 UTC
01:41:52 KST

During the Japanese colonial period, Taipei was the seat of Taihoku Prefecture, “taihoku” being the Japanese transliteration of “Taipei.” The Governor-General’s Office, Taipei Prefectural Government and Taipei City Hall — today the Presidential Office, Control Yuan and Executive Yuan respectively — along with other colonial institutions laid the foundations for the city’s development into Taiwan’s premier urban area.
After the Republic of China (ROC) fled from China — or, as some would put it, relocated to Taiwan and occupied it — Taipei became its capital. Power was inherited from the Japanese, and rewritten under ROC rule.
Taipei became the heart of the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) party-state-military establishment. Its status fostered a sense of detachment from the rest of Taiwan. It was insisted that then-Taipei County be upgraded to a special municipality named New Taipei City, ignoring the reality that the area had consisted of several medium-sized cities surrounding Taipei.
The resulting system bears a certain resemblance to Tokyo, where 23 central special wards are bordered to the west by 26 cities also contained within the metropolitan government. New Taipei City emerged as an awkward administrative configuration, a product of a local government rushing to secure municipal upgrades.
In the 1994 direct elections for Taipei mayor, the KMT nominated Huang Ta-chou (黃大洲) while Jaw Shaw-kong (趙少康) broke away from the party to run as an independant. The split vote led to the victory of Chen Shui-bian (陳水扁) of the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP). At the time, raucous chants and yellow flags bearing slogans saying “Defend the ROC” filled Taipei’s streets, creating widespread anxiety.
However, prior to full democratization, there was another period in which Taipei elected its own mayors, and candidates outside the KMT establishment were often successful.
Henry Kao (高玉樹), an independent, enjoyed considerable popularity as mayor, serving in two periods: from 1954 to 1957 (as an elected provincial city mayor) and 1964 to 1972. He was elected in 1964 and remained in office as an appointed mayor after Taipei in 1967 was upgraded by the KMT into a special municipality. At that point, the mayorship was no longer an elected office, it was appointed by the party.
Many still regard Chen as the best Taipei mayor since the full restoration of direct elections. His administration’s approval ratings exceeded 70 percent, yet was defeated by the KMT’s Ma Ying-jeou (馬英九) when he sought re-election 1998. What does this tell us about the civic identity of the people of “Chinese” Taipei? One may draw one’s own conclusions.
What followed was Taiwan’s first democratic transfer of power in 2000 when Chen, having lost the Taipei mayoral race, went on to become president. The quiet revolution of Taiwan’s democratization had taken shape.
During the 1998 Taipei mayoral election, Chen’s campaign headquarters was directly across the street from where I lived. I watched the vote count from my home alongside German sinologist Helmut Martin. When Chen lost, Martin found the result so incomprehensible that he cried.
How could this have happened? My answer would be that this is Chinese Taipei, haunted by the ghost of a consciousness shaped by exile and colonialism.
Apart from the oldest Taipei natives, there are at least three other types of Taipei people.
The first is represented in When the Flowers Bloom (花咲季節), a short novel published in Japanese by Yang Chian-ho (楊千鶴) in 1942, depicting the awakening consciousness of Taiwanese women under Japanese colonial rule. The story was later reimagined by Yang Shuang-zi (楊双子) in her 2017 novel.
The second comes from the community of exiled government officials, merchants and businessmen who arrived in Taiwan in 1949, as depicted in author Pai Hsien-yung’s (白先勇) 1971 collection of short stories titled Taipei People.
The third are the Taiwanese who moved to Taipei from other parts of the nation, as depicted in novelist Wang Chen-ho’s (王禎和) short story Little Lin Comes to Taipei (小林來台北).
Nevertheless, the yoke of Chinese Taipei has continued to hold Taiwan’s premier city politically hostage.
Since the reinstatement of direct elections, Taipei has gone through one term under Chen, two each under the KMT’s Ma and Hau Lung-bin (郝龍斌), then-independent Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) and one under Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安).
Chiang entered the world as Chang Wan-an (章萬安), but claims that he is a descendant of the Chiang family, the great grandson and grandson of former presidents Chiang Kai-shek (蔣介石) and Chiang Ching-kuo (蔣經國). Whether his surname is Chang or Chiang, the incumbent mayor has certainly leveraged the family name of the former presidents to his advantage.
We once again approach elections. Now, perhaps because of recurring questions about special privilege, he faces the younger, more talented and more perceptive Puma Shen (沈伯洋) of the DPP as an electoral rival. It is a test for the oft-repeated, but inconsistently practiced political idiom: “Choose the worthy and the capable.”
The KMT’s grip on the ROC’s exilic and colonial consciousness in Taiwan must change. Those who have become rooted here must emerge as members of a collective that still bears the name ROC, but exists in Taiwan. Transforming “Chinese” Taipei into Taiwan’s Taipei is a cultural question and a political project for the rebuilding of Taiwan. We must stop clinging to the dream of exiled, colonial China in arrogance and self-importance. Taiwan belongs to all Taiwanese, regardless of who arrived first or later, and Taipei belongs to Taiwan. Transformation toward a new, locally rooted identity must begin with Taiwanese consciousness in the city.
Lee Min-yung is a poet.

Taiwan to mark Disaster Prevention Day with drills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:41:52 UTC
01:41:52 KST

A large-scale earthquake drill in eastern Taiwan, nationwide emergency alarm tests and the mobilization of more than 176,000 civilian disaster responders are among the activities scheduled for National Disaster Prevention Day, with the government yesterday launching the annual campaign.
The Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Education announced the disaster response exercises at an event in New Taipei City to promote public preparedness for national emergencies.
On Sept. 21, emergency broadcast systems, as well as earthquake, tsunami and air raid sirens, are to be tested, a spokesperson told the event.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of the Interior
Broadcasts to mobile phones, television and radio would also be tested, as they could become the only source of accurate information for the public during a crisis, the spokesperson said.
The tsunami siren would be sounded twice in five-second alerts, with a five-second interval before a recorded message ordering an evacuation is played, they said.
First responders are to be mobilized from Wednesday to Friday next week to conduct simulated search and rescue operations, and establish mock mass-casualty medical aid stations, they said, adding that foreign groups would participate in the drills.
The exercises would test key capabilities, as well as the government’s ability to control its emergency response assets efficiently, the spokesperson said.
The Ministry of the Interior has helped establish 275 Taiwan Community Emergency Response Teams, comprising 5,000 volunteer first responders and 176,000 certified disaster relief volunteers, including security guards, drivers and other people with critical skills, they said.
The public is urged to download the Readiness TW e-APP on their mobile devices, and prepare three days of supplies and go-bags in every household, the spokesperson said.
Taiwan’s disaster response capabilities have come a long way since the devastating Jiji earthquake on Sept. 21, 1999, the date on which National Disaster Prevention Day is held, Minister of the Interior Liu Shyh-fang (劉世芳) said.
The interior ministry’s goal is to have a force of 200,000 certified disaster relief volunteers by the end of the year, Liu said.
The certified disaster relief volunteer concept revolves around training people who already work in communities, enterprises, schools and large buildings using their first aid and other skills to protect others, she added.

Pomelo harvest affected by water shortages, typhoons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:41:51 UTC
01:41:51 KST

Pomelo production in eastern Taiwan is not expected to be much more than 14,000 tonnes this year, 20 percent less than the average of the previous years, due to typhoons and water shortages, the Agriculture and Food Agency’s eastern region branch said yesterday.
Pomeloes are in season as the Mid-Autumn Festival approaches.
Eastern Taiwan is a key pomelo production region with 1,066 hectares of planting area, accounting for nearly one-third of the 3,626 hectares used to grow pomeloes nationwide.
Photo: Wang Chun-chi, Taipei Times
Yilan County’s Dongshan Township (冬山), Hualien County’s Rueisuei (瑞穗) and Yuli (玉里) townships, and Taitung County’s Donghe Township (東河) are the region’s primary pomelo producing areas, branch Deputy Director Chen Chi-tsun (陳吉村) said.
The region’s pomelo production is projected to be 14,334 tonnes this year, Chen said.
That is 20 to 30 percent less than the average of the previous years, as production was affected by water shortages in March and typhoons last year, he said.
Harvesting has been completed in Taitung, and is 90 percent done in Yilan and Hualien, he said.
The harvest would be completed by the end of this week to meet surging demand ahead of the Mid-Autumn Festival, Chen said.
Pomeloes from the east coast have varied cultivation methods, and tastes dependent on the environment they are grown in, he said.
Pomeloes in Donghe must tolerate sharper day-night temperature changes and strong winds due to their coastal location, while those in Rueisuei and Yuli townships are on hillsides with well-drained soil, Chen said.
Yilan pomeloes are more tender and sweet, while Hualien pomeloes are juicy and springy with a hint of tartness, he said, adding that Taitung pomeloes are soft and naturally refreshing.
The Dongshan Township Farmers’ Association yesterday loaded 2.4 tonnes of red pomeloes into containers and shipped them to Singapore, Chen said.
That marked the association’s first ever pomelo shipment to Singapore, he said, adding that the association would export 8 tonnes of pomeloes to the country.
While Taiwanese pomelo consumption is highly concentrated around the Mid-Autumn Festival, most people in Singapore regard it as a regular fruit and purchase it more frequently, he said.
Consumers should buy more pomeloes and store them to enhance the richness of their flavor, he said.
Freshly picked pomeloes are crisp, but they become tender five to 10 days after harvest when left in a cool, well-ventilated place, he said, adding that the method boosts the fruit’s fragrance and sweetness.

Madring to bring chaos to Formula One weekend
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:41:48 UTC
01:41:48 KST

Formula One rolls into Madrid this weekend for a first look at the Madring, a new Spanish Grand Prix venue with a banked beast of a corner and enough unknowns to have drivers reaching for the word of the day: challenging.
Spain is hosting two races this season, with Madrid’s street circuit around the IFEMA exhibition center following Barcelona’s Catalunya Grand Prix on the calendar. The Madring is the first new circuit since Las Vegas three years ago and brings down the curtain on the regular European leg of the season.
The Madring’s signature comes at Turn 12, where “La Monumental” slings the cars around a long, banked arc before spitting them over a crest, leaving drivers momentarily aiming at grandstands built to hold up to 45,000 fans — and the blue sky — rather than tarmac.
Photo: Reuters
Until now, most of the field have only met the circuit in the simulator, leaving teams to untangle set-ups and racing lines on a layout whose pecking order remains guesswork.
“It looks different. It looks that the track has character, that is charismatic, with a lot of different kinds of corners,” Madrid-born Williams driver Carlos Sainz, an ambassador for the track, told a news conference on Thursday.
Sainz has driven a few laps in a road car on an unfinished version of the track, but said that was “nowhere as representative as the laps that I did in the simulator.”
Ferrari pair Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton are the only other drivers with some prior experience of the Madring after driving there during a filming day in July, when the circuit was still more building site than Grand Prix theatre.
Hamilton, the seven-time world champion, was quick to pour cold water on any suggestion of an advantage.
“I think it’s hardly any,” he told reporters. “It was dusty, super, super dusty. There was zero grip. We couldn’t change the car because it’s not a test. It was filming,” he said.
“We weren’t even flat out in many of the corners. We were low, just low power, low grip. The benefit, the only one thing is I’ve seen which way the track goes. So honestly, I don’t think we have any advantage,” he added.
The circuit is built partly inside Madrid’s convention center and partly on the streets of Valdebebas, across from soccer side Real Madrid’s training ground. Its mix of enclosed sections, tight walls and sweeping spectacle has intrigued drivers, though overtaking might be at a premium.
La Monumental, with its diagonal banking and vast grandstand backdrop, carries echoes of US oval racing and has the potential to feel more like a stadium than a conventional circuit.
Hamilton said the layout reminded him partly of Montreal’s kerbs, but compared the difficulty of learning it to Saudi Arabia’s Jeddah circuit, introduced in 2021.
“It’s a massively challenging circuit,” he said. “Of all the new tracks that I’ve gone to, this one, maybe Saudi, I like the two closest in terms of how difficult it was to get on top of the car and find the right lines.”
Leclerc also expects qualifying to take on extra weight.
“It looked like a very challenging track, and I think exactly the kind of track that I enjoy as a driver,” he said.
“It’s true to say as well that I think coming Sunday the amount of overtaking opportunities there will be will be very little,” he said.
That could make today the weekend’s main act.

President promulgates defense autonomy legislation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:41:48 UTC
01:41:48 KST

President William Lai (賴清德) yesterday promulgated a Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT)-led bill aimed at promoting defense autonomy and the uncrewed vehicle industry, following its passage by the legislature last month.
The Legislative Yuan on Aug. 27 passed the Act on Strengthening Defense Autonomy and Developing the Unmanned Vehicles Industry (強化國防自主暨無人載具產業發展條例), which in principle provides NT$240 billion (US$7.59 billion) over six years, while allowing additional funding subject to legislative approval.
The act directs the Ministry of National Defense to prioritize the procurement of domestically produced “low-cost, high-performance” uncrewed systems.
Photo: Wu Chun-feng, Taipei Times
It requires the central government to, in principle, earmark NT$40 billion annually for six consecutive years, using its general budget to procure uncrewed vehicles to reinforce national defense and drive industrial growth.
The Ministry of Economic Affairs is designated as the competent authority, while the defense ministry is required to oversee matters involving military procurement, the act says.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) countersigned the bill, as national security and industrial upgrading could not wait, Presidential Office Deputy Secretary-General Xavier Chang (張惇涵) said.
There had been speculation that Cho would not countersign it, as the government had argued that the mandated spending requirements unconstitutionally infringed upon the Executive Yuan’s exclusive prerogative to compile and allocate the national budget.
Taiwan’s uncrewed vehicle industry is taking off, supply chains are beginning to take shape and democratic partners around the world are seeking trusted “non-red supply chains,” Chang said.
At a time when uncrewed vehicle technologies are evolving rapidly, the government must use national demand to create markets, use markets to support research and development, use innovation to drive industrial growth, and ultimately use industrial strength to bolster national defense and safeguard national security, he said.
While the Executive Yuan countersigned the bill, it would uphold two key principles, Chang said.
First, while Article 4 of the act establishes a funding principle, it does not impose a spending cap, he said.
The Executive Yuan will continue to uphold its constitutional authority over budget preparation, allocate funding based on the actual needs of defense force-building and industrial development, and accept legislative oversight, he said.
Second, Article 2 designates the defense ministry as the lead agency for defense-related matters, while Article 12 places the “National Uncrewed Vehicle Industry Development Strategy Special Committee” under the economic ministry, Chang said.
The committee will focus primarily on industrial development, while matters requiring military expertise will remain under the jurisdiction of defense professionals, he said.
The Executive Yuan last week submitted an additional budget proposal for this year that includes NT$55.9 billion for uncrewed vehicle programs, Chang said.
He urged lawmakers to expedite review of the supplementary budget and next year’s central government budget, as the funding is critical to Taiwan’s asymmetric warfare capabilities.
Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) caucus secretary-general Fan Yun (范雲) said the party regrets that the Executive Yuan’s proposal was not the one promulgated, but respects the Executive Yuan’s decision to countersign the bill given the urgency of Taiwan’s defense needs.
The legislation demonstrates Taiwan’s support for the uncrewed vehicle industry and would reinforce international confidence in the feasibility of developing non-China supply chains here, Fan said.
KMT Culture and Communications Committee Director Chen I-hsin (陳以信) said that the act allocates NT$240 billion over six years, exceeding the Executive Yuan’s original proposal of NT$210 billion over five years.
All three military drone procurement programs proposed by the Executive Yuan were incorporated into the legislation, Chen said.
The Executive Yuan’s decision to countersign shows that the KMT’s version does not weaken national defense, but instead provides greater resources and flexibility, while exposing earlier government criticism of the proposal as unfounded, he said.
The premier’s countersignature and the president’s promulgation of legislation passed by the Legislative Yuan are constitutional obligations, Taiwan People’s Party caucus whip Jacky Chen (陳清龍) said, accusing the government of undermining democratic governance and the rule of law by portraying a routine constitutional process as a political favor.
As uncrewed vehicle technologies evolve rapidly, relying on special budgets tied to long-term procurement contracts would leave the military unable to keep pace with operational requirements, and would ultimately weaken, rather than strengthen, the armed forces’ combat capabilities, he said.
Additional reporting by Chen Chih-cheng

Silicon photonics are emerging as a mainstream optical communications technology and is seen as key to overcoming bottlenecks in AI computing power. The technology is a key project under the government’s New 10 Major AI Infrastructure Projects, with industry, government, academia and research institutions working to overcome critical technological hurdles and build a self-reliant silicon photonics supply chain, the ministry said. Iran seeks end to blockade of Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:41:41 UTC
01:41:41 KST

The Iranian government yesterday called for an end to Saudi Arabia’s blockade of Yemen and the immediate resumption of talks, in its first public statement since Iran-backed Houthi rebels entered a key Yemeni port and intensified their threat to a key global shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
In a statement carried by the state-run Islamic Republic News Agency, the Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said that Yemen’s sovereignty must be respected and its problems cannot be resolved through a blockade or military alliances.
Iran said it was ready to help support negotiations.
Photo: AP
Meanwhile, experts say the developments in Yemen could give Tehran more leverage in any negotiations with the US after more than six months of war.
The Houthis’ entry into the Red Sea port of Mokha on Thursday brought the group within 80km of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, an important alternative for global shipping as Iran targets vessels on the Strait of Hormuz.
It is the rebels’ biggest territorial gain in years.
The Bab el-Mandeb at the southern end of the Red Sea is especially important to neighboring Saudi Arabia, a key US ally, with its blockade of the Houthis feeding into the rebels’ escalating attacks on Saudi Arabian shipping as the kingdom tries to get its oil out of the region.
Saudi Arabia, which earlier this week said it had always offered “opportunities for negotiation,” also has said it has the right to defend itself in response to the Houthis’ actions under the blockade they declared on the kingdom in July.
The National Defense Council of Yemen’s Saudi Arabian-backed and internationally recognized government on Thursday condemned the Houthis’ renewed attacks on Saudi Arabia, saying it would respond to threats.
It said a military operation by Yemeni forces would not be limited to a single front.
The sharply escalating fighting threatens to end a fragile truce that had largely halted Yemen’s civil war since 2022.
At stake are the 40 million people in the Arab world’s poorest country who fear a return to the conflict that killed 150,000 and brought many others to the brink of famine.
The Houthis have been at war with Yemen’s government since 2014, when the rebels swept from their mountainous heartland and seized much of northern and central Yemen.
Saudi Arabia entered the war the following year on behalf of the government.
Hans Grundberg, the UN’s envoy to Yemen, warned that the nation now faces the “harsh reality” of a return to war.
Grundberg told an emergency meeting of the UN Security Council on Thursday afternoon that the international community must address this “new and more dangerous phase — one whose consequences, if left unchecked, will not stay within Yemen’s borders.”
