Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford, the reigning NFL MVP, had no touchdowns and was pulled late in the fourth quarter, the Super Bowl favorites outclassed by their division rivals in front of a massive crowd of 100,021 at the Melbourne Cricket Ground.
The attendance on a local workday — the morning kick-off suiting a US prime-time audience — was the seventh largest for a regular-season NFL game, and second only to the 49ers-Cardinals match-up at Mexico City’s Azteca in 2005 among international games.
Photo: Kirby Lee, Imagn Images
“What an atmosphere to get a win in,” 49ers tight end George Kittle said. “The boys played well. The juice was there all day, and I mean, anytime you get a win versus division opponent is always a great thing,” he said.
The 49ers had landed in Melbourne a week before the game to overcome jet lag and adjust for the time-zone difference with the US West Coast.
And their players were cheered warmly as they ran out onto the sprawling, oval-shaped playing field having endeared themselves to locals with their high praise for Melbourne’s coffee and food scene.
There were loud boos for the Rams, though, who arrived only the day before the game and stuck to their normal US routines, and that strategy might come under the microscope after they were dominated for much of the game.
Rams coach Scott McVay defended their preparations, saying his team fell short in multiple departments.
“Today was humbling, but sometimes life can do that to you,” he said.
“We’ve got a lot of football left and we’re not going to allow this one game to do anything other than help us learn and grow,” he added.
It was a painful Rams debut for Myles Garrett, the league’s Defensive Player of the Year last season, who could not lay a glove on Purdy after a record 23 sacks with Cleveland last year.
He said he was still troubled by a knee problem from the off-season.
“This was the worst version of myself that I’ve put out there,” Garrett said.
“I have to be better. I have to recover and get back to being the player I know I can be and that I’ve shown I can be before,” he added.
49ers kicker Eddy Pineiro opened the scoring with a field goal with six minutes 15 seconds remaining in the first quarter, but the Rams hit back in the second.
Stafford found receiver Puka Nacua with a 41-yard pass to set up a five-yard touchdown run from Kyren Williams.
Both teams were moving the ball well on the ground, but interceptions prevented any further scores until Demarcus Robinson caught a 39-yard pass from Purdy to put the 49ers 10-7 up with four minutes 28 seconds left in the half.
With Stafford struggling to get his passing game going under pressure from the 49ers’ defensive line, San Francisco ramped up the intensity early in the third.
Wide receiver Mike Evans celebrated his first touchdown for his new team when he connected with Purdy on a two-yard pass as the 49ers went ahead 17-7.
The San Francisco defense then denied Nacua and Stafford, on a quarterback sneak, touchdowns by inches on consecutive plays late in the quarter.
Purdy took the 49ers straight up the other end for another touchdown on a 15-yard pass to Deebo Samuel early in the fourth.
There was no way back from there for the Rams, and Kyle Shanahan extended his winning record to 12-7 in his coaching rivalry with McVay.

Taiwan drafting travel advisory on PRC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:41:41 UTC
01:41:41 KST

The government is preparing guidelines to help Taiwanese mitigate risks when traveling to China as Beijing prepares to implement new border rules that could extend inspections to mobile phones and other electronic devices, National Security Council adviser Alex Huang (黃重諺) told the Chinese-language Liberty Times (the Taipei Times’ sister newspaper) in an interview published yesterday.
Beijing’s revised entry and exit regulations are scheduled to take effect on Tuesday next week, raising international concern and prompting the US to update its travel advisory for China.
As China is to begin conducting random inspections of personal communication devices from next month, many Taiwanese have expressed concern that business secrets could be exposed or that their past social media comments could be used against them, Huang said.
Photo: Chang Chia-jui, Taipei Times
The Mainland Affairs Council, the Ministry of Economic Affairs and other agencies are drafting guidelines to advise Taiwanese on how to protect themselves when traveling to China, he said, urging three groups of people in particular to exercise heightened caution.
First, civil servants at all levels — whether serving in local, central or security-related roles — could become targets for intelligence gathering, Huang said.
Recent cases have included police officers being questioned about critical infrastructure protection measures and judicial personnel being asked about internal operations, he said.
Village wardens and local civil affairs officials could also be targeted for information regarding air-raid shelters, emergency supplies and distribution channels, he added.
The second risk group is religious workers, he said.
As China does not have genuine religious freedom, religious activities such as missionary work, ordinations and baptisms must be conducted in the presence of officials from religious affairs bodies overseen by the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) United Front Work Department, he said.
Gatherings of believers and religious study sessions are also treated as matters of national security, he added.
Some followers of the I-Kuan Tao religious group who traveled to China for sightseeing have reportedly been arbitrarily detained and remain in custody, he said.
Third, professionals working in sensitive sectors such as semiconductors, quantum science, advanced materials and defense, as well as employees of key foreign companies and firms connected to entities sanctioned by Beijing, could be at particularly high risk of having their personal freedom restricted, he said.
With the new border rules, China is tightening domestic controls in an attempt to retain talent and technology and discourage citizens from seeking opportunities abroad, he said.
The country’s economic slowdown has created a situation in which only a small number of people benefit while many others struggle, he said, adding that global supply chains are accelerating efforts to reduce reliance on China.
The introduction of a series of regulations since the so-called “22 guidelines to penalize Taiwanese independence separatists” were implemented demonstrates Beijing’s efforts to extend its jurisdiction beyond its borders and reflects a deep distrust of its own people, he said.
Using China’s Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress as an example, Huang said it elevates Han Chinese culture above others, prioritizes the use of standard Chinese language and characters, and even requires parents to teach their children to “love the CCP.”
Such provisions demonstrate a distortion of constitutional principles and governance, he said.
Amendments to China’s National Defense Mobilization Law would broaden the scope of mobilization to include supply chains and other matters linked to China’s development, Huang said.
The legislation also changes the treatment of civilian resources from temporary requisition to expropriation involving the transfer of property rights, he said.
Foreign companies, including Taiwanese businesses, have already begun paying closer attention to the risks posed to intellectual property and human resources, Huang said.
He urged the international community to remain vigilant regarding the CCP’s attempts to challenge the world order and bring all assets under its control.

Micron to give engineers NT$1m, equity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:41:40 UTC
01:41:40 KST

Micron Technology Inc is to provide its engineers in Taiwan a cash bonus of NT$1 million (US$31,600) plus equity rewards, as the company’s local unions are demanding an additional payout to reflect their contribution to the chipmaker’s blowout profits.
The Idaho-based chipmaker said in a statement yesterday that its entry-level, Taiwan-based engineers’ average compensation would reach NT$3.4 million for the past fiscal year after the cash and equities awards. All employees in Taiwan would receive equities as part of the annual merit grants, the company added.
Before the announcement, Micron’s unions asked for a one-time cash payout equal to about seven years of an employee’s base salary. That would translate into an average payment of about US$170,000 per worker, based on Bloomberg calculations off data the unions provided. They are also demanding the company allocate a portion of its profit to be shared with global employees as bonuses going forward.
Photo: Ritchie B. Tongo, EPA
The row over Micron’s payouts coincides with a global debate about who deserves a cut of the sudden wealth generated by booming investment in artificial intelligence (AI)-related data centers and other infrastructure.
That has spurred Micron’s South Korean rivals Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix Inc to promise employees a share of the profits in their bonuses. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co has also vowed to set aside 30 percent more in profit-sharing payouts for employees.
However, the size of some of the bonuses has created rifts within companies and communities, with growing calls that users who supply AI with the data it needs also get a cut.
Micron has been handed a major boost from the AI boom. Its cutting-edge high-bandwidth memory is required to make AI accelerators from the likes of Nvidia Corp. The US chipmaker reported a 15-fold gain in net income in the third quarter, while its share price has risen more than 500 percent over the past year.
Micron employs about 15,000 people in Taiwan, which serves as a key manufacturing hub for the chipmaker.
At the same time, it still relies on the US for the bulk of its research and development operations and some production, while it also runs plants in Japan and Singapore.
The US memory maker and the Taoyuan union failed to reach an agreement during a mediation meeting last week, with a second round of mediation scheduled.
Micron is looking to avoid being dragged into a crisis similar to what Samsung Electronics faced in May, when a planned 18-day strike was called off after last-minute negotiations and a successful deal that created a special bonus pool worth 10.5 percent of the chip division’s operating profit, subject to profitability targets.

Russian screening of film on Japan raises questions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:41:38 UTC
01:41:38 KST

In a small meeting room in a downtown Taipei office building, Russian officials hosted an unusual screening of an old Soviet documentary called Smashing Militarist Japan for about 20 Taiwanese guests.
Despite the small audience, the screening of the 81-year-old film has alarmed the Taiwanese government.
Russia is helping China push its narrative of a rising military threat from Japan, and is seeking to sow discord over Taipei’s relations with Tokyo and other Western partners, it said.
Photo: Reuters
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi last year suggested a hypothetical Chinese attack on Taiwan could trigger a Japanese military response, causing a diplomatic crisis between Tokyo and Beijing and prompting repeated warnings from Beijing that Japan is seeking a return to its aggressive past.
Officials in Taiwan say they believe the closed-door screening last week of the film by the de facto Russian embassy in Taipei is part of a new effort to spread and bolster China’s “new militarism” line against Japan.
The Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not respond to a request for comment. The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it was unaware of the screening.
It added that Allied powers, including China, Russia and the US, had defeated Japanese militarism, and that “upholding and promoting a correct historical view of World War II is the shared responsibility of the international community.”
The film shown was 1945’s black-and-white The Defeat of Militarist Japan, which the Russian office translated into Chinese on Facebook as Smashing Militarist Japan. The film, available on YouTube under the name “The defeat of Japan,” shows images of the Soviet attack on Japanese-occupied Manchuria and the Kuril Islands.
A voiceover denounces the “robber philosophy of the divine superiority of the Japanese race” and shows footage of Japanese atrocities against Chinese civilians.
The showing of the film sits in a sensitive area for Taiwan. Freedom of speech is constitutionally protected, but it also has laws, including the 2019 Anti-Infiltration Act (反滲透法), aimed at preventing hostile foreign forces — chiefly China — from covertly influencing its politics.
There was no police presence outside the screening and no effort was made to shut it down.
The National Security Council said it was “closely monitoring” Chinese-Russian military and “cognitive warfare” cooperation when asked about the screening.
“The two countries are attempting to amplify specific topics and distort historical facts and political issues,” it said.
Taiwanese officials said Russia posed a new challenge, as Moscow could approach some Taiwan contacts with less immediate legal scrutiny than if Chinese officials were to do so, as their activities are subject to Taiwan’s security laws.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said that about 20 people from the “academic world” had been invited to the screening.
While Taiwan respects the “lawful conduct of normal exchanges,” activities held by the Russian office “should also respect historical facts and conform to universal values such as democracy and freedom,” the ministry added.
Staff from the Russian office, including Deputy Representative Sergey Chudodeev, declined entry to Reuters reporters, saying it was an invitation-only event.
After the screening, Russian Representative Pavel Lapin said Moscow’s Taipei office hoped to organize similar events in the future, a person who attended the event said.
“The Soviet Union and the Chinese people endured the heaviest casualties in that war. The contributions they made toward crushing German fascism and Japanese militarism are indisputable and cannot be diminished,” the Russian office said in a Facebook post about the screening.
A person who attended said those present included former journalists, business figures, academics and other public-facing figures.
Last month, China and Russia issued a joint statement warning against remilitarization in the Asia-Pacific region.
Russian diplomats in Taipei have generally kept a very low profile since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, diplomatic sources said.
The Russian office in Taipei opened in 1996, and it has always had a more understated presence in Taiwan compared with the de facto embassies of the US, the EU, the UK and others, diplomatic sources say.
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office dismissed Taiwan’s concerns about the film as “another ploy to manipulate anti-China sentiment for political gain.”
Taiwan has been on Russia’s “unfriendly” countries and territories list since it joined other Western allies in sanctioning the country following its invasion of Ukraine, and senior Russian officials have openly backed China’s claims to Taiwan.
Moscow and Tokyo have their own long-running dispute over Russia’s seizing four Kuril Islands off northern Japan at the end of World War II, one of which Russian President Vladimir Putin visited last month, drawing condemnation from Tokyo.

Subsidies to aid religious exchanges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:41:37 UTC
01:41:37 KST

The Ministry of the Interior has unveiled religious exchange subsidies of up to NT$3 million (US$94,823) to encourage religious groups to diversify their international partnerships.
Although the ministry did not mention China by name, the policy appears to be geared toward steering religious groups away from that country, as infiltration of cultural exchanges is deemed a national security risk.
The initiative, which started on Friday last week, is intended to encourage religious groups to develop global relationships and raise Taiwan’s international profile while adhering to a Taiwanese perspective, the ministry said in a statement.
Photo: Wang Yi-sung, Taipei Times
The subsidies are to facilitate religious exchanges with foreign countries, the globalization of Taiwanese religions, religious cultural development, training of clergy, cultural heritage transmission and cooperation to reduce the carbon footprint of religious sites, it said.
The program applies to temples engaging in global exchanges, accredited academics participating in international seminars and faith groups inviting their foreign counterparts to Taiwan for religious purposes, it said.
The subsidies also apply to events aimed at ensuring the continuity and transmission of folk religious rituals, and conferences promoting sustainable practices in religious rites and temples, it said.
The regulations surrounding religious exchange subsidies were rewritten to broaden the eligibility requirements for beneficiaries and the types of activities that qualify, the ministry said.
Temples, religious groups, privately established religious research associations, universities and colleges and non-profit groups that have been legally registered for at least a year can apply, it said.
Groups are encouraged to make use of the subsidies to facilitate religious exchanges between the nation and the global community, it said.
The religious and cultural exchange subsidies application guidelines have been published by the National Religion Information Network and are accessible at https://religion.moi.gov.tw/.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:41:37 UTC
01:41:37 KST

Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) is visiting Italy to attend an international conference on freedom and democracy, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said yesterday, confirming a previously unannounced trip.
The organizers invited Hsiao to attend the Second Ventotene European Conference for Freedom and Democracy, which is being held on the Italian island of Ventotene from Thursday to today, the ministry said in a statement.
She was accompanied by Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍), it said.
Photo: Wang Wen-lin, Taipei Times
The Presidential Office would provide more information about the trip after Hsiao returns to Taiwan, it said, without saying when she departed Taiwan or when she would return.
The confirmation came after European Parliament Vice President Pina Picierno, the main initiator of the conference, late on Thursday announced during the event that Hsiao had arrived in Italy, despite Beijing’s attempt to prevent the trip from happening.
Hsiao’s participation had not been announced beforehand.
“No one can dictate who may be hosted on European soil, which voices may be heard, or who must be kept hidden,” Picierno said in an Italian-language social media post late on Thursday.
“That is why today we welcomed the vice president of Taiwan, Hsiao Bi-khim, to Ventotene — her presence was kept confidential until her arrival to safeguard her participation in the Second European Ventotene Conference for Freedom and Democracy,” she wrote.
“The message is simple and crystal clear: Intimidation cannot determine who takes part in our democratic debate,” she said. “Freedom of dialogue is not up for negotiation with autocracies. And Ventotene, today more than ever, must remain a place where freedom and democracy are defended without fear.”
Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China (IPAC) executive director Luke de Pulford backed Hsiao’s participation at the event.
“The only response to Beijing’s attempt to shrink the world for Taiwanese people is to show that Taiwan is welcome,” De Pulford said.
This is “not simply because it is in our national interest to do so, but because it is wholly wrong to allow a democracy like Taiwan to be persecuted and outcast on the international stage,” he said.
The ministry also pushed back against Beijing’s criticism of Hsiao’s visit.
China has no right to dictate Hsiao’s participation in events she was invited to by the European Parliament, ministry spokesperson Hsiao Kuang-wei (蕭光偉) said.
Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokeswoman Mao Ning (毛寧) earlier yesterday said that Beijing had lodged solemn representations with Italy and the EU over the visit.
China consistently opposes any form of official contact between Taiwan and countries that have diplomatic relations with China, Mao said, calling Beijing’s “one China” principle the political foundation of China-Italy and China-EU relations.
The trip to Italy marks the second time Hsiao has visited Europe since taking office in May 2024.
She last visited Europe in November last year to deliver an address at an IPAC meeting in Brussels.

====================================================================================================

Miliband overturns decades of inertia on illegal Israel settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:41:33 UTC
01:41:33 KST

The indefatigable ability of British Foreign Office ministers over decades to issue boilerplate statements of concern about the extension of illegal settlements in Israel has long been a matter of ridicule.
Even some of the Conservative ministers who issued them, notably Alan Duncan and Alistair Burt, have agreed. Duncan described the UK stance toward settlements as weak and naive, while Burt wondered at the ability of the Foreign Office to find new forms of diplomatic condemnation that never amounted to any specific action. Margaret Thatcher, often torn as prime minister between her natural sympathy for Israel and her fear of the Gulf states falling under the sway of the Soviet Union, similarly expressed her anger at the settlements.
However, in the face of the Israeli disillusionment with a two-state solution — to which the UK had been committed at the UN since 1946, if not before — the UK produced little practical policy to prevent the spread of Israel’s illegal settlements.
The UK-Israel trade agreement prevented preferential tariffs applying to goods coming from territories brought under Israeli administration after June 1967. The business department also advised companies not to trade with the settlements — but many simply ignored the advice or, to secure the preferential tariff, relabeled their goods as from Israel. Then-minister for trade Chris Bryant told the business select committee in June it was very difficult to be certain of the origin of goods.
At the same time, the legal advice was that the UK regime could place sanctions on entities only if they were linked to settler violence, but could not put a contractor under sanctions simply for working on settlements.
It was this unhappy moral and legal mess that Ed Miliband inherited. As soon as he took office as foreign secretary, he said he refused to be a bystander to further suffering and the destruction of the two-state solution that settlement expansion represented. In this he had the support of British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Above all, Miliband felt that the UK could not feign powerlessness, and to do so, or pay lip service to action, would prove disastrous to Israel’s own future. He was perhaps the only front-rank Labour politician who could push this argument through at such pace, overturning the inertia and caution built into Foreign Office legal advice.
His Jewish heritage — his mother, Marion Kozak, was a Holocaust survivor who fled to Israel — his life growing up with the Palestinian question and empathy for those subjected to anti-Semitism put him in a near unimpeachable position to adopt the role of Israel’s critical friend.
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee might this week say the Labour government is gripped by Jew-hatred, a charge he laid at Miliband’s door knowing he is Jewish, but Miliband’s riposte is simple. The best route to Israel’s security lay in Palestinian self-determination and the introduction of the two-state solution in its fullest form. To equate Israel only with the current Likud-led government as too many Conservatives have been prone to do, was a category error, he said.
“Holding Jewish people responsible for the actions of the Israeli government is anti-Semitism, plain and simple,” Miliband said.
He is thus the first UK foreign secretary to describe what is happening in the West Bank as ethnic cleansing, and in so doing to in effect to accuse Israel of turning a blind eye to acts that amount to war crimes.
Miliband also ended the two years of delay in responding to the International Court of Justice (ICJ) advisory opinion in June 2024 that the occupation is unlawful. In what he admitted was an overdue statement of reality, he accepted the ICJ opinion that the occupation, and not just the settlements, were so designated. Accepting the ICJ opinion arguably places stronger obligations on the UK government to not assist the occupation. It might help to explain why the trade ban extends into services such as providing insurance for illegal settlements.
The biggest diplomatic rabbit Miliband pulled from the hat was the agreement of France and Canada to impose similar trade bans. France took the lead last year on recognition of Palestine; this year, it is the turn of the UK to lead on following through on the consequences of that recognition.
Paris appears to have been persuaded by the UK to stop waiting for the EU to reach an agreement on collective action, since it seemed unlikely the opposition in Germany and indifference in parts of the European Commission would end. A group of countries imposing the trade ban together of course makes Israeli reprisals harder, and serves to underline Israel’s isolation.
The perceived weaknesses are obvious.
Miliband still left it to the international courts to determine whether a genocide occurred in Gaza, something that might not be adjudicated for at least five years. There was mounting evidence of ethnic cleansing in Gaza, he said, but again it was for the courts to determine if that was so.
There is no pledge to protect the ICJ or the International Criminal Court from the US drive to render them inoperable. As to a UK arms sales ban, an exemption continues for the sale of parts for F-35 jet planes to the main US spares pool — all on the basis the F-35 jets “do not materially support the occupation” — the criteria the foreign secretary has set.
Miliband specifically condemned the Boycott, Disinvestment and Sanctions movement because it targets the whole Israeli economy and not just the occupied territories. The secondary legislation required to make sanctions as wide as envisaged might take as long as nine months, contrasting with the speed with which sanctions were enforced against Russia over the annexation of Crimea.
However, to focus solely on what is absent is to miss the moment.
Duncan, for instance, said: “At last, in the face of state-backed terrorism by illegal settlers, the British government has shown unprecedented moral courage.”
There is a risk of a cascading backlash from the White House — but US President Donald Trump, trapped in a political labyrinth after he was persuaded to attack Iran, has little reason to come to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s aid. Miliband has taken a risk, but after more than 70,000 deaths in Gaza, and the two-state solution on life support, it might be time to dare.

Article 2(b) of the Treaty reads: “Japan renounces all right, title and claim to Formosa and the Pescadores.” So, tomorrow would be the Diamond Jubilee of Formosa’s freedom from Japanese sovereignty. As my good friend and former Examination Yuan President Yao Chia-wen (姚嘉文) voiced in these pages last year (“San Francisco treaty should be taught: adviser”, Sept. 7, 2025), the Japan peace treaty should be taught in all Taiwan schools to

DEFENSE
CSBC, Havoc team up
CSBC Corp yesterday announced that it has teamed up with US-based all-domain collaborative autonomy firm Havoc to develop autonomous surface vessels (ASVs) in Taiwan. The shipbuilder said in a statement that it had signed a partnership agreement with Havoc at the firm’s headquarters in Rhode Island on Thursday to pursue licensed coproduction of ASVs for Taiwan’s maritime security. Under the agreement, the two companies are to leverage their respective capabilities to integrate Havoc’s industry-leading autonomy software into CSBC-built platforms produced and maintained in Taiwan, it said. The cooperation is in line with Section 1266 of the US National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 on joint US-Taiwan production of uncrewed systems, as well as Taiwan’s policy goal of promoting defense autonomy and domestic production of uncrewed vehicles, the shipbuilder said. The two firms hope to establish a scalable cooperation model that combines Taiwan’s industrial base with US autonomous technology to further enhance capabilities for producing and deploying autonomous maritime systems, it added.

A panel of representatives from government, labor, management and academia meets annually in the third quarter to review minimum wage levels for the coming year. Fast-paced dance takes off on streets in Ivory Coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:41:30 UTC
01:41:30 KST

On the streets of a working-class Abidjan neighborhood, hundreds of young people gather every week after class to dance the biama, a high-tempo combo of acrobatic twists, frenetic footwork and funny facial expressions.
The craze has gripped Ivory Coast — where nearly two-thirds of the population is aged under 25 — since it evolved from the country’s popular coupe-decale dance music a few years ago.
In Yopougon, the district where it all began, so-called biamasseurs organize the outdoor events where one DJ after another takes to the stage, which is little more than a vacant sandy piece of ground with some plastic chairs for spectators.
Photo: AFP
Dancers take part for free, while it costs between 1,000 and 2,000 CFA francs (between US$1.70 and US$3.50) to watch.
From 5pm, boys and girls in their teens don colorful sportswear of jogging pants and T-shirts to perform the high-energy moves of the quick-pace street dance.
“Biama means fun” in Nouchi, Ivorian slang, said 29-year-old Junior Koffi, known as “God of War,” who organizes the Wednesday evening events. “It’s danced to different rhythms, from zouk to zouglou and afrobeat.”
The music is often a mix of styles created by arrangers, who take their inspiration from the dance steps.
“It’s quite a funny dance,” said “le Pere Rogodogo” (“Father Rogodogo”), who was one of the first organizers of the regular street gatherings.
Young people “let their imagination run free to create their moves, dance with their eyes, pull faces,” he said.
Fans join Parfait Fidele Kposser, known as “Agbalais le Mystique” (“Agbalais the Mystic”) for dance practice in the street at the weekend.
On an afternoon last month, four boys aged 15 to 17, who call themselves the Daltons, worked on choreography with him as locals watched, some stopping to film.
With the tips they earn dancing in the evening they buy clothes and school supplies in a city with a cost of living that is one of the highest in Africa.
Biama was created by accident in 2021 in a video gaming room when a jubilant young man jumped up and started improvising dance moves to celebrate winning some money, filmed by his friend.
Today, Karl Guei, whose nickname is “Kalomaman,” has 2 million TikTok subscribers, according to culture journalist Toussaint Konan.
Since then, the dance has taken Abidjan, the country’s economic capital, and other cities by storm, with weekly events undeterred by the risk of the late-night noise disturbing nearby residents, who sometimes do complain.
They serve as a springboard for beginners and a showcase for the more accomplished whose rising fame and popularity is amplified by social media.
Videos by dancer and singer Dydy Yeman, one of the movement’s leading figures, have racked up tens of millions of views on YouTube.
The artist has already performed outside of Ivory Coast, elsewhere in Africa and in Europe, but his beginnings were humble.
He expressed “pride” in coming from Yopougon, the birthplace of biama, before going on stage in front of thousands at a festival in the fashionable neighborhood of Cocody, where entry prices were considerably higher at between 10,000 and 15,000 CFA francs.
The crowd, wearing fluorescent bracelets, their faces and T-shirts covered in paint, followed the steps led by Yeman and sang along to the lyrics of his songs.
“Even when I’m sitting, my legs start moving,” said Jean, 22, a first-year student.
Curiosity prompted Maimouna Tinta, 19, who has just graduated from high school, “to see if what’s on TV is true.”
Biama even has its own television program, a news bulletin about the dance broadcast on a private channel.
Sociologist Stephane Babo said the trend “fully deserves to exist” and might “last over time.”
“Beyond the passion ... there’s a whole economic side to it,” notably by creating jobs and even careers, Babo said.
“The dancers, during their performance, are paid after all,” he said, also pointing to other associated businesses such as the sale of clothing.
Arranger Elie-Michel Assie Diou sees “a market” in the biama movement’s success.
He said his studio had recorded more than 50 artists in just a few years.

Three Hong Kong rights advocates who organized annual vigils in remembrance of China’s 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown yesterday were sentenced to about five to seven years in prison, with officials in Taiwan calling the punishment “harsh.”
Lee Cheuk-yan (李卓人), Chow Hang-tung (鄒幸彤) and Albert Ho (何俊仁) were convicted of inciting subversion earlier this year under a national security law.
Lee received a seven-year prison term and Chow was sentenced to seven years and three months. Both pleaded not guilty. Ho was given a lower sentence of five years and two months, partly because he pleaded guilty.
Photo: Chiang Ying-ying, AP
The trio of defendants was charged in September 2021 and has been held in custody for years.
Hong Kong once had a vibrant civil society marked by protests and a freewheeling press, but after a 2019 protest movement rocked the territory, authorities reduced public choice in elections and prosecuted leaders of news firms.
After the sentencing, Lee’s wife, Elizabeth Tang (鄧燕娥), told reporters that Lee had been prepared for the worst and looked calm.
Tang said that he would appeal against the results.
Chow’s mother, Medina Chow Lau Wah-chun (劉華珍), joked that she had to thank those who had prosecuted Chow for helping to write the truth of the 1989 crackdown into the court records.
“Many years ago, my daughter already said that she wants to have a proper debate with them in court one day,” she said.
Chow’s friend Lau Ka-yee said Chow also would appeal.
In Taipei, the Mainland Affairs Council condemned the “heavy sentences” handed to the three.
“The pursuit of democracy and human rights is not a crime,” the council said in a statement, adding that authorities have “fabricated charges and conducted political trials in the name of national security to shield an authoritarian regime.”

為什麼人們坐著時會蹺二郎腿？對許多人來說，翹二郎腿是一種舒適且習慣性的動作。多年來，人們一直在思考這種姿勢是否對健康有害。有些人認為，這可能會導致高血壓或循環問題。另一些人則擔心這可能會影響姿勢，尤其是脊椎與骨盆部分。
研究顯示，雖然蹺二郎腿時血壓可能會略微上升，但在改變姿勢後很快就會恢復正常。將雙腿緊緊交叉可能會暫時減少抬起的那條腿的血流，但影響極小。如果你蹺二郎腿坐太久，你的小腿或腳可能會發麻。然而，這可以藉由經常調整坐姿來避免。
另一個常見的看法是，蹺二郎腿可能會導致靜脈曲張，也就是呈現藍色或深紫色的腫脹靜脈。然而，這種姿勢並不被認為是主要原因。生活型態因素，如長時間坐著或站著、缺乏運動，以及肥胖等疾病，扮演更關鍵的角色。研究也指出，遺傳可能會增加罹患靜脈曲張的風險。
與其對血壓或靜脈曲張的影響不同，對姿勢的影響（尤其是在脊椎與骨盆區域）更為複雜。雖然蹺二郎腿可以伸展髖部周圍的肌肉，但長時間這樣坐著可能會導致骨盆旋轉或傾斜。這可能會造成下背不適，甚至導致脊椎錯位。此外，長時間維持蹺二郎腿姿勢的人，在坐著時也更可能會向前傾或駝背。
整體而言，蹺二郎腿坐著不太可能會造成嚴重的健康風險。其影響反而與姿勢和身體排列更緊密相關。對大多數人來說，這通常是一個無害的習慣──只要記得經常換邊，並避免維持同一個姿勢太久。

習慣性暴飲暴食可能會導致長期健康問題。
2. circulation n. （血液）循環
Regular exercise improves circulation and keeps the body healthy.
規律運動能促進血液循環、維持身體健康。
3. slightly adv. 略微，稍微
The temperature dropped slightly after sunset.
日落後，氣溫稍微下降了。
4. temporarily adv. 暫時地
The employee was temporarily assigned to another department.
這位員工被暫時調到另一個部門。
5. swollen a. （身體部位）腫脹的∕腫起的
David couldn’t walk properly because of his swollen knee.
大衛因為膝蓋腫脹而無法正常走路。
Practical Phrases
1. go numb 發麻
numb a.（身體部位）發麻的∕失去感覺的
My feet started to go numb after sitting on the floor for too long.
坐在地板上太久後，我的腳開始發麻。
2. be likely to V 可能會……
be unlikely to V 不可能會……
This machine is likely to break down if it is not maintained regularly.
這臺機器如果沒有定期維護，很可能會故障。
This plan is unlikely to succeed without careful preparation.
這個計畫若沒有周全準備，不太可能會成功。
3. pose a risk 造成風險
pose vt. 造成（威脅、問題等）
Driving while tired poses a serious risk to others on the road.
疲勞駕駛會對其他用路人造成嚴重風險。

Several European cities are replacing traditional white streetlights with red lighting to reduce light pollution and protect wildlife. In Copenhagen’s suburb of Gladsaxe, red LED lights have been installed along roads and cycle paths near bat habitats. The lights are placed at intervals that create darker gaps, allowing light-sensitive animals to cross safely without being exposed to predators and still providing enough visibility for people. Studies have shown that white and green light can reduce bat activity, whereas red light has little to no effect. Studies conducted in the Netherlands found that light-sensitive bats remain active under red lighting.

Tax revenue surges amid boom in stock market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:41:27 UTC
01:41:27 KST

Tax revenue surged last month as a stock market boom drove a sharp increase in securities transaction taxes, helping push government tax collections to a record pace in the first eight months of the year.
Tax revenue rose 28.9 percent from a year earlier to NT$198.2 billion (US$6.26 billion) last month, the Ministry of Finance said yesterday. Securities transaction tax revenue jumped 94.5 percent to NT$54 billion, its 13th consecutive month of annual growth.
The increase reflects the growing contribution of Taiwan’s buoyant stock market to government coffers, as demand for artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks has lifted trading activity and generated more tax revenue.
Photo: CNA
Liu Shun-rong (劉訓蓉), Department of Statistics Deputy Director, said the increase was driven by a sharp rise in stock trading activity.
Average daily stock-market turnover reached NT$1.09 trillion last month, nearly doubling from a year earlier, as domestic and overseas investors increased their exposure to local shares benefiting from the AI boom, Liu said.
For the first eight months, average daily turnover climbed 1.7-fold from a year earlier, providing a major boost to securities transaction tax revenue and helping strengthen government finances.
Housing-related tax revenue also improved last month. Property-related income tax revenue rose 33.2 percent from a year earlier, while land value increment tax increased 22.7 percent and deed tax gained 15.3 percent.
Liu said the gains reflected a broad improvement in housing-related tax collections.
However, for the first eight months property-related income tax revenue was still down 1.1 percent from a year earlier, although the decline narrowed significantly.
Not all tax categories benefited from broader economic recovery.
Commodity tax revenue fell 20.2 percent in the first eight months to NT$77.4 billion, Liu said. The decline was mainly due to tax cuts on gasoline and diesel, lower tax collections on imported vehicles and increased tax refunds for newly purchased vehicles.
Total tax revenue for the first eight months reached NT$3.75 trillion, up 25.2 percent from a year earlier. The sharp increase underscores how the stock-market rally, fueled in part by Taiwan’s central role in the global AI supply chain, has become an increasingly important source of government revenue.

The US’ Iran war forgot about nukes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:41:27 UTC
01:41:27 KST

When was the last time you heard a meaningful proposal to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear arsenal?
There has been nothing on the subject since the June Memorandum of Understanding between the US and Iran; the promised 60 days of talks to settle questions around Tehran’s uranium-enrichment program never began and have long since expired.
When the war was launched, on Feb. 28, a resolution of the nuclear dispute was prominent among the dizzying array of US and Israeli aims to explain the attack. But as should be clear by now, the attempt was entirely reliant on achieving regime change. That was always a Hail Mary pass, and from the moment it became clear that the Islamic republic would survive, there has been no nuclear strategy whatsoever.
Illustration: Ting Louise
Arguably, it was only before the war began that this issue was at the center of attention, where it belonged. That was back when US-Iran nuclear negotiations in Geneva got cut short by the surprise airstrike that killed then-Iranian supreme leader Ali Khamenei and set the conflict in motion, with all the unintended — if widely predicted — consequences that have followed.
Wherever one chooses to stick that pin, it is undeniable that the existential nuclear question that this war was supposedly launched to address has been forgotten, drowned out by the more immediate need to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
“There may not be a nuclear agreement,” US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright told ABC’s This Week on Sunday, adding that the administration might just destroy capabilities instead. “An agreement may await the next administration in Iran. We simply don’t know that.”
Wright went on to say how important it is to stop Iran getting a bomb; I agree. First, a nuclear deterrent would provide immunity to a dangerous regime that is repressive and totalitarian with an Islamist twist that is anti-Semitic, sectarian and expansionist. Such a combination leads to a second reason: Others in the Middle East — including Saudi Arabia, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates — would feel obliged to follow or even race to get there first.
The proliferation threat here is so significant that, despite the late supreme leader’s fatwa pledging not to develop a weapon, the suspicion that he was lying warranted the decade-plus of economic and diplomatic pressure that culminated in the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA). That deal ensured intrusive nuclear inspections and the reduction of Iran’s enriched-uranium output and stockpiles to near-zero.
The JCPOA was flawed in that it sunset those limitations over a 10 to 15-year horizon. I would argue that this failing was big enough to have justified demanding a renegotiation and extension of the deal’s restrictions once it was due to expire, with a return to sanctions and other forms of pressure as necessary.
In fact, the prospect of a nuclear Iran was bad enough that it might also have warranted US President Donald Trump’s premature decision to renege on the deal in 2018 — but only if he had had the ability to force a better one. Unfortunately, and again predictably, he did not. His rejection of the agreement allowed Tehran to abandon its terms as well, enriching uranium in larger quantities and to higher, near-weapons-grade levels than ever before.
Given this state of affairs, the airstrikes that the US and Israel carried out last year could also be justified as a measure of last resort, if credible evidence had emerged that the Iranians were weaponizing their fuel stocks. However that caveat, which was not met, is crucial. The risk of partial success — of showing Iran that it lacked the defenses to prevent the destruction of nuclear assets, without the land war needed to ensure they were not rebuilt — was that it would simply drive Iran to build the nuclear deterrent it did not yet have.
This is precisely how events appear to be unfolding. It is why Israel wanted to finish the job just six months after Trump had declared the Iranian-enrichment program “obliterated.” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took his argument for a mass strike that would trigger regime change all the way to the White House. This was not necessarily wrong because it was immoral or illegal: Who would seriously have complained if February’s airstrikes had indeed succeeded in toppling the regime, freeing a desperate population and ending Iran’s destabilizing pursuit of both its nuclear program and its proxy wars across the region
Instead, the strikes were unjustifiable because it was evident that they would not succeed. They were considered and avoided by all previous US presidents since 1979, because Iran’s first step would, inevitably, be to block Hormuz to international shipping, with the immediate impact on the global economy that this implied.
Through their disruption of Hormuz, Iran’s leaders now have international leverage and a deterrent power that they never before possessed. And because the ever-present question of whether the US and Israel were willing to take Iran on in open warfare has now been answered, the Islamic republic has more reason to build its own nuclear arsenal. Israel, the country that so often cried wolf on this subject, is now probably right about its urgency.
“Iranians are clever. They are diverting all of the discussions to the Straits of Hormuz,” Major General Tamir Hayman, a former Israeli military intelligence chief, said in a podcast on Wednesday last week for Tel Aviv’s Institute for National Security Studies, where he is now executive director.
The US “is cooperating with that and focusing on the Straits of Hormuz, and while we are doing that we are losing eye contact to the ball — and the ball is the nuclear aspect,” he added.
I have seen no proof that the Iranians are currently seeking to weaponize their nuclear program, or that they are knowingly using Hormuz as a decoy to achieve that — I suspect control of the strait is valuable enough to be a goal in its own right. However, the debate within Iran’s elite over whether to develop a nuclear deterrent has now spilled into the public domain, and why not? What else to conclude but that North Korea is untouched, while Ukraine and Iran lie in ruins, because only Kim Jong-un has a working nuclear arsenal.
Indeed, Iran’s new supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, can only believe he is in hiding, wounded and mourning the deaths of his father and family because Iran did not have one. Either he capitulates to the US, or he survives long enough to achieve a nuclear breakout, but seen from the vantage point of Khamenei’s bunker, nothing in between is likely to make much sense.
Hormuz is a problem that will have to be managed. That will be the cost of the mistake Trump made by going to war in February. However, the net result of his actions since 2018 is that the Iranian nuclear question is less resolved, more dangerous and more likely to result in a nuclear arms race than it was when he destroyed the JCPOA. He needs to put the issue back at the heart of his Iran agenda.
Marc Champion is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Europe, Russia and the Middle East. He was previously Istanbul bureau chief for the Wall Street Journal. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

China’s 13-year-old swimming prodigy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:41:24 UTC
01:41:24 KST

Yu Zidi made history last year aged 12 when she became the youngest-ever medalist at the swimming world championships. Now a teenager, she headlines China’s bid for Asian Games domination and has Olympic glory in her sights.
The 13-year-old school girl with a pixie hair cut stunned the sporting world last year with a series of eye-popping times.
At the last year’s World Aquatics Championships in Singapore she helped China reach the 4x200m women’s freestyle relay final. She did not swim in the final, but China came third, earning Yu a historic bronze for swimming in the heats.
Photo: AFP
Yu just missed out on medals in the 200m and 400m individual medley events and the 200m butterfly, coming fourth in all three races.
In November last year at China’s National Games, having just turned 13, she clocked a blistering 2:07.41 in the women’s 200m medley for what was then an Asian record.
While training with the China team in Beijing, she told local media this month she was “excited” for her Asian Games debut.
“Train well, don’t slack off. Demonstrate the level of your training and work hard to break past yourself,” she said, according to state news agency Xinhua.
The Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan open on Saturday next week.
A coach, Ha Sinan, once described Yu with a Chinese saying that translates as “a newborn calf is fearless of tigers.”
However, the teenager has spoken of struggling to deal with the heavy load placed on her.
Yu grew up in the city of Baoding, about 150km south of Beijing.
She started swimming aged six and since then has juggled schoolwork with training.
“Being in class all day and still having to train was really tiring,” she said in January.
“Sometimes I was so tired I could fall asleep even while eating,” she said at an event celebrating Hebei province’s National Games wins.
Yu said she “never considered quitting” and always dreamed of being a national champion.
Yet during the tune-up to last year’s National Games she said the pressure of wanting to win the 400m medley nearly became too much.
“It was like a big stone that weighed on me and made it hard to breathe,” she said.
Yu eventually told her coach she wanted to do anything other than train.
Her coach told her to persevere and “believe in yourself,” she said. Yu went on to win four medals at the National Games.
Some in the swimming world have questioned the mental and physical impact of high-level training and competing on Yu at such a young age.
It seems certain that Yu would compete at the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics, when she will be 15, and on current trajectory would be a major medal threat.
She is aware that her success for someone so young has made international headlines, but she knows hard work outweighs innate talent.
In June she won the women’s 400m medley in 4:30.79 at China’s national championships, a time which would easily have earned her silver at the Paris Games in 2024.
“There is still a long road ahead,” she added.
“I will keep holding fast to my original dream, drawing strength from my team, to stand on the Olympic podium,” she said.

Rybakina to play Sabalenka for US title
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:41:20 UTC
01:41:20 KST

Aryna Sabalenka realized she was probably going to lose the No. 1 ranking to Elena Rybakina. There was not much she could do about that.
The US Open trophy is a different story.
Rybakina can only take that away from Sabalenka by winning it on the court today, and the two-time defending champion showed in an overpowering display in the semi-finals how serious she is about a three-peat — which would be the first at Flushing Meadows since Serena Williams from 2012-14.
Photo: Getty Images via AFP
“I wanted badly to go to the finals, and of course I want to go all the way,” Sabalenka said.
Rybakina set up a matchup between the top two players in women’s tennis by rallying past Coco Gauff 3-6, 6-4, 6-4.
Sabalenka beat Jessica Pegula 7-5, 6-2 in the first semi-final, running away with the second set after they played largely even in the first.
Sabalenka is currently No. 1 and Rybakina No. 2 in the WTA rankings, but that changes on Monday after Sabalenka held the top spot for 99 consecutive weeks.
Rybakina won the Australian Open to start the season, beating Sabalenka, then kept on closing after the four-time Grand Slam champion had a poor summer by her standards.
Rybakina needed only to reach the semi-finals in New York to clinch the No. 1 ranking.
The second semi-final was more a battle, with Gauff trying to fight from behind in the final two sets, but Rybakina not letting her come all the way back.
Gauff jumped on Rybakina with a strong start — she had four aces to one for Rybakina, who leads the WTA Tour in that category — in a first set that she took in 38 minutes.
Gauff trailed 4-1 in the second set and battled back to 4-all before Rybakina won the next two games. Rybakina went ahead 5-3 and served for the match, but Gauff broke to give herself one more chance while being cheered by a crowd that included former first lady Michelle Obama.
Gauff won her first major title as a teenager when she rallied past Sabalenka in the 2023 US Open final, but nobody has been able to knock off the Belarussian in Flushing Meadows since. Pegula put up a good fight in the 2024 final and last year’s semi-finals, but she could not keep it close the way Sabalenka played on Thursday — and was not sure anybody else would have, either.
“I think that’s definitely — you can ask her — probably the best match she’s played this year,” Pegula said. “I mean, I thought her level was insanely high.”
Sabalenka pounded 29 winners to Pegula’s 12. She has won 19 straight matches at the US Open since losing to Gauff in the 2023 final.
The top four seeds made it to the women’s semi-finals at the US Open for the first time since 1975. Sabalenka, Rybakina and Gauff have all won multiple major titles, while Pegula is still looking for her first.

01:41:19 KST

The Taipei Department of Education yesterday said it is terminating contracts with a school lunch caterer after dozens of students at two separate schools reported suspected food poisoning symptoms after eating meals provided by the vendor this week.
On Tuesday, Chengyuan High School told the Taipei Department of Health that 87 students had experienced diarrhea and displayed symptoms suspected to be food poisoning from 10pm on Monday.
Another school with the same contractor has been linked to a suspected food poisoning outbreak, after Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Taipei City Councilor Hung Wan-chen (洪婉臻) said students at Da Li Senior High School had complained of physical discomfort after eating school lunches.
Photo courtesy of the Taipei Department of Health
Taipei Department of Education Director-General Tang Chih-min (湯志民) said they had received reports of more than 10 students from Da Li feeling unwell this week and are investigating whether their symptoms were linked to the lunches.
Students who reported their illness on Thursday were diagnosed with acute gastroenteritis, the department said.
City officials investigated the schools on Tuesday and have been monitoring the students’ conditions, it said.
The health department said that after the first school’s report, it had asked schools to step up disinfection and said they would conduct surprise inspections to ensure food preparation environments and catering quality meet standards.
The catering company has terminated its contract with Chengyuan, and the Department of Education is discussing the termination of the caterer’s contract with Dali, Tang said.
Hung said the contractor continues to provide meals to other schools, including Da Li’s junior-high division, where students reported gastrointestinal discomfort from Monday to Thursday.
The city has expanded inspections and would require immediate improvements when deficiencies are found, Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) said, adding that follow-up inspections would cover ingredients, cooking and catering procedures, and sanitation.
DPP Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋) said the problem might not be the caterer, but the food supplier.
Authorities should investigate as soon as a contractor begins showing problems, he added.

ISU withdraws Russian skater’s neutral status
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:41:12 UTC
01:41:12 KST

Russian figure skater Kamila Valieva would be unable to compete internationally after the International Skating Union (ISU) revoked her neutral athlete status, the sport’s governing body said on Thursday.
Valieva was 15 when she became the center of a global controversy at the 2022 Olympics after a sample collected two months earlier tested positive for the banned heart medication trimetazidine.
The failed test emerged after she helped Russia win team gold, a result from which she was later disqualified, elevating the US to the top of the podium.
Photo: AP
Valieva, 20, returned to competition in January at the Russian Jumping Championships after completing a four-year doping ban, but remained ineligible for the Milano Cortina Winter Olympics.
Russian men’s skater Mark Kondratiuk, a teammate of Valieva’s at the 2022 Winter Olympics, also had his neutral status revoked, as did ice dancers Alexandra Stepanova and Ivan Bukin.
Russian state news agency TASS quoted Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev as saying that all the skaters affected by the ruling would appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).
“The Russian Figure Skating Federation and our skaters, who have been unfairly deprived of the right to compete in the ISU’s international competitions, will soon file a claim with the CAS against the ISU,” Degtyarev, who is also the president of the Russian Olympic Committee, told TASS.
“Our athletes and federations will receive legal support, including the provision of qualified lawyers,” he said.
Russian athletes have been barred from competing under their national flag since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The ISU subsequently established a pathway for selected competitors from Russia and Belarus to participate as Individual Neutral Athletes, subject to a rigorous vetting process.
Under the ISU’s neutrality criteria, athletes can be denied neutral status if they are deemed to be serving in the Russian or Belarusian military or security services, have taken part in military operations against Ukraine since February 2022, or have publicly expressed support for the war.
“Each determination is subject to the applicable appeal rights under the ISU Constitution and Regulations,” the governing body said in a statement.
The ISU did not specify which criteria Valieva had not met.
Reuters has contacted the Russian figure skating federation and there has been no immediate comment from Valieva or the federation.
The governing body added that 234 individuals affiliated with member federations in Russia and Belarus had submitted neutrality declarations for potential participation in ISU events and international competitions during the 2026-27 season.

Gymnastics official fired over non-issuance of invites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:41:12 UTC
01:41:12 KST

The Ministry of Sports yesterday dismissed the secretary-general of the Chinese Taipei Gymnastics Association (CTGA) after the organization unilaterally rejected an invitation for two gymnasts to compete at next month’s Artistic Gymnastics World Championships in the Netherlands without informing the athletes or their coaches.
CTGA secretary-general Chiang Chien-tung (江建東) failed to comment on or apologize for the association’s decision to deprive two gymnasts of the opportunity to compete in the competition in Rotterdam next month, the ministry said in a statement.
Gymnasts Lee Chia-wei (李佳蔚) and Pan Cai-chen (潘采宸) earned reserve qualification spots for the uneven bars and floor exercise events respectively.
Photo: Lo Hsin-chen, Taipei Times
The CTGA on Tuesday apologized. It said it received an e-mail on Aug. 20 offering reserve spots, with a confirmation deadline of Aug. 21.
Administrative procedures are that the matter be reviewed via the governing body’s athlete selection and training committee, which would have meant compiling attendance and other records, it said in a separate statement.
As a result, it failed to promptly inform the athletes and their coaches, the CTGA said, adding that it would conduct an internal review and implement measures to prevent similar incidents.
The ministry said that it contacted the CTGA on Thursday, demanding an immediate investigation and public apology, but received no response.
Chiang was also absent when the ministry convened yesterday, it said.
The CTGA mishandled the issue and its explanations show it failed to fulfill its administrative duties, the ministry said, adding that it ordered the governing body to submit a comprehensive review, clarify its decisionmaking process and determine responsibility.
It also dismissed Chiang from his post in accordance with Article 43 of the National Sports Act (國民體育法), the ministry said.
Clear mechanisms are needed to fill vacancies in international competitions and issue emergency notifications, it said.
Notifications about an athlete’s eligibility must be relayed immediately to athletes and their coaches, it added.
Gymnasts must not be deprived of opportunities due to internal administrative delays, the ministry said, adding that those responsible for infringing upon athletes’ rights would be held accountable.
Democratic Progressive Party Legislator Hsu Fu-kuei (徐富癸), who has been advocating for the athletes, welcomed the ministry’s decisions, saying they would better protect gymnasts.
The ministry and sports associations should establish clear rules governing competition eligibility and ensure that the athletes who were affected are compensated.
Tsai Yu-hua (蔡玉華), Pan’s grandmother, thanked Pingtung County Commissioner Chou Chun-mi (周春米) for her support and called for the full decisionmaking process to be made public.

INTERVIEW: AI pushes banks beyond traditional processing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:41:08 UTC
01:41:08 KST

Artificial intelligence (AI), real-time payments and digital assets are pushing corporate treasury management beyond traditional transaction processing, giving companies faster visibility over cash and liquidity while enabling more automated and programmable payments, Standard Chartered Bank said.
The shift is creating new opportunities for Taiwan as it builds a regulatory framework for digital assets, with clearer rules for tokenized securities and stablecoins needed to support the development of the market, according to Standard Chartered Financing and Securities Services regional head Pierre Mengal.
“The rise of digital assets and tokenized securities is reshaping traditional custodians from passive asset holders into trusted providers of digital market infrastructure,” Mengal said during an one-on-one interview on Wednesday after attending the bank’s treasury forum in Taipei.
Photo: courtesy of Standard Chartered
Standard Chartered identified six trends shaping the future of corporate treasury: real-time treasury management, programmable liquidity, the use of AI in treasury operations, and the growing commercial use of tokenization and digital assets.
These technologies are allowing companies to extract more value from payment data while making resilience a competitive advantage, the bank said.
Digital assets are gradually moving from an emerging financial technology toward practical applications in payments, custody and treasury management, Mengal said.
Their integration with real-time payments and new financial infrastructure could further accelerate the move toward more automated and connected financial operations, he said.
Taiwan took a step toward developing its digital-asset market in June when the legislature passed the Virtual Asset Services Act (虛擬資產服務法), establishing a legal framework covering virtual-asset service providers, custody, cybersecurity, asset segregation and internal controls.
The next priority should be regulatory clarity for tokenized securities and stablecoins, including rules governing ownership, custody, settlement, taxation and accounting, Mengal said.
Taiwan’s established capital-market infrastructure could provide a strong foundation for banks, custodians and securities firms to support the issuance, custody and settlement of tokenized assets, he said.
The market could also explore the use of stablecoins and tokenized deposits for cross-border payments, securities settlement and corporate treasury management, Mengal said.
“Digital financial transformation is redefining the growth path of companies, allowing them to gain more flexible ways to manage cross-border funds,” he said.
Such tools could help Taiwanese companies expanding overseas manage cross-border funds more efficiently while strengthening operational resilience, he said.
The growing use of AI, real-time data and digital assets is also changing how companies view resilience. Rather than being limited to risk management, resilience is increasingly becoming a strategic advantage as businesses seek to respond more quickly to changes in liquidity, payments and operating conditions, he said.
Standard Chartered has expanded its digital-asset capabilities in the past few years, covering custody, trading, tokenization and stablecoins, he said.

Ex-Colombian president urges peace push with FARC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:41:07 UTC
01:41:07 KST

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella should fully implement the peace accord signed with Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) guerrillas a decade ago to help unite a divided country, former Colombian president Juan Manuel Santos said.
Santos — who led the Latin American country from 2010 to 2018 — negotiated the peace deal with the FARC and won the 2016 Nobel Peace Prize for his efforts.
“The elections have greatly polarized the country,” Santos told reporters during a visit to Oslo to mark the 10-year anniversary of the signing of the pact, which diplomats from Norway and Cuba helped broker.
Photo: Reuters
“This [the full implementation of the deal] could be a way for the country to find common ground and at the same time be the solution to many of the problems Colombia faces today,” he said, citing poverty among farmers, drug trafficking and security in conflict areas.
Santos is an influential figure in Colombian politics and a well-known international campaigner for peace-related causes.
Colombia’s conflict — originally begun over land rights and other social issues — has dragged on for more than six decades, as guerrilla groups, paramilitary squads and drug traffickers have fought the government and each other.
Although funding for armed groups has traditionally come largely from drug trafficking, illegal mining of gold is now a major source of their income.
The wide-ranging deal with FARC was built into the country’s constitution, but the ways many of its provisions are rolled out — everything from support for demobilized rebels to land reform to benefit poor farmers — are subject to government changes in strategy and focus.
Santos’ successors — who have not always supported the entire accord — have struggled to fully enact it amid fiscal constraints, the COVID-19 pandemic and other political concerns.
De La Espriella, a lawyer who has legally represented people with ties to paramilitary groups, criticized aspects of the deal during his election campaign, especially the Special Jurisdiction for Peace, the transitional justice court tasked with investigating crimes committed during the conflict.
He said he would dismantle the court, which he characterized as ineffective and expensive.
However, in his inauguration speech, De La Espriella said that he would respect the special court’s place in Colombia’s judicial system, but that there would be rigorous oversight over the tribunal.
Santos said that his successors, Ivan Duque and Gustavo Petro, did not fully implement the peace accord — which was designed to be rolled out over 15 years — and that Petro’s “total peace” policy, where he sought deals with additional armed groups, delayed implementation of the FARC deal.
Petro “concentrated on what he called ‘total peace,’ that is, trying to negotiate with criminal groups dispersed throughout the country, at the expense of the deal with the FARC,” Santos said.
“That’s why I hope [De La Espriella] understands that implementing the peace accord is perhaps one of the best programs of government that he could put into action.”

France joins Slovakia in demanding delisting of Russian oligarch Usmanov ahead of sanctions deadline in sensitive talks held among EU ambassadors.
The French government has joined Slovakia in seeking the delisting of Russian-Uzbek businessman Alisher Usmanov, causing “huge frustration” among other EU countries, four EU diplomats told Euronews.
Slovakia has long pushed for Usmanov and another Russian oligarch, Mikhail Fridman, to be removed from the EU's sanctions list targeting individuals close to Vladimir Putin's regime and the military-industrial complex sustaining the war in Ukraine.
But Bratislava is no longer alone. Paris has also called for Usmanov, who has been under EU sanctions since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, to be delisted.
Usmanov is an Uzbek-born Russian billionaire who built his fortune through investments in metals, mining, telecommunications and technology and is considered close to the Kremlin.
Usmanov denies this.
The French move has caused “huge frustration” among other member states, particularly against the backdrop of escalating hybrid threats in Europe, including the latest case of an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport in Germany.
“It raised a lot of questions about the motivation — seems mostly economic reasons at play here. Not a lot of understanding on the side of other member states,” an EU diplomat told Euronews, speaking on condition of anonymity given the sensitivity of the talks.
The EU sanctions regime currently targets more than 3,000 individuals and entities linked to Russia's military-industrial complex and its contribution to the invasion of Ukraine. The regime is due for renewal on 15 September, with member states under pressure to reach an agreement by then.
Individual listings have so far been renewed every six months, but a 12-month renewal is now on the table. Sectoral sanctions already shifted from six-month to 12-month renewal cycles in July.
In several meetings of EU ambassadors, Slovakia has opposed the renewal, pushing for both oligarchs to be delisted and the six-month timeframe to remain in place.
The Slovak demands are not new. Bratislava has repeatedly called for the delisting of the two high-profile Russian oligarchs, including when the sanctions were last extended in March.
EU sanctions require unanimous approval for renewal, meaning a single country can veto an extension. Slovakia's opposition has already caused frustration among member states, but France's new position is likely to complicate the talks further.
Paris presented Usmanov's delisting as a political compromise, betting that Slovakia would not abandon its two delisting demands as it did last time.
EU ambassadors are due to meet again on Monday to discuss the renewal and will be under pressure to reach a political agreement before the 15 September deadline.
A French official said Paris supported the renewal of sanctions, but declined to comment on the discussions, citing confidentiality.

More than 30 handguns, M-16 rifles seized in smuggling attempt from Jordan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:35:41 UTC
01:35:41 KST

An attempt to smuggle dozens of weapons from Jordan into Israel was foiled Thursday night after IDF surveillance soldiers spotted two suspects crossing eastward from Israeli territory into Jordan. They later returned carrying bags. Forces dispatched to the area following the sighting arrested the two and found 35 weapons in their possession.
Pvt. A., a surveillance soldier in the 909th Combat Intelligence Battalion, began her shift at the Tirza operations room at 8 p.m. About two hours into her shift, she noticed two people whose behavior aroused her suspicion.
“I spotted two people inside the enclave, moving east toward Jordan. It looked suspicious to me, and I immediately notified the company operations room, which was unaware of anyone who was supposed to be there,” she said. “Within less than 10 minutes of the sighting, the forces arrived in the area.”
Following the report, troops from the Jordan Valley and Valleys Brigade, officers from the Israel Police’s Jordan Border Unit in the Judea and Samaria District and Border Police officers in the West Bank arrived at the scene and set up ambushes in the area.
After the suspects crossed into Jordan, the surveillance soldiers lost visual contact with them but continued scanning the area for hours.
“The soldier who took over after me spotted them returning from the direction of Jordan, and they were caught by the forces we had dispatched to the location,” A. said. “They were caught with two bags, and all the weapons were found inside. If not for the surveillance soldier sitting at the post, they would have found out about it only after the fact.”
She added: “We were awake all night. I heard as soon as they were caught, and I’m proud to have played a part in thwarting a mission by people who were apparently planning to use the weapons in a terrorist attack. We’re staying here on guard. I wish everyone a happy and peaceful holiday, and I hope we also get to have a peaceful holiday meal.”
The two suspects are Jericho residents in their 50s. According to police, they attempted to smuggle more than 30 handguns and two M-16 rifles. The suspects and the seized weapons were transferred to the Judea and Samaria District’s Central Unit for further investigation.
Sgt. N., A.’s commander, also began her shift at 8 p.m. It ended at 4 a.m. Friday. The two serve in the 909th Combat Intelligence Battalion, which was established in April and operates under the 96th Division. The battalion is composed entirely of women.
Following the initial sighting, Capt. B., a company commander in the battalion, was also called to the scene.
“The sector is usually quiet, so we train a lot for a situation in which something does happen. Complacency is our enemy,” N. said. “We handled the incident very quickly. As soon as A. spotted something suspicious, and after checking we understood that no one was supposed to be there, we declared ‘Turki Parash’” — a military term referring to a suspicious approach from Israeli territory toward the border.
“When they entered the enclave, we lost visual contact with them, but we continued scanning for three hours until they returned to Israeli territory with the bags on them,” N. added. “As soon as they crossed, they were caught by the forces that had arrived at the location. They were excellent. The company commander who led the operation called me immediately.”
N. said the incident demonstrated the importance of the surveillance soldiers’ work in the sector.
“The significance of our role is incredible. You are the eyes, the one protecting all the people, the communities and the farms. We protect them, and if we don’t do it, there is no one else who will.”
N., who will remain in the sector with her fellow soldiers during the holiday, added: “We know how important it is for us to be here on Shabbat and holidays. We have a sense of family here. We’re far from home, but it feels as much like home as anywhere. We’ll hold the holiday meal in a way that allows everyone to take part.”
