Extra fishy: your tinned mackerel may not be what you think it is
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:59:37 UTC
00:59:37 KST

If you’ve recently opened a tin of mackerel and thought there was something fishy going on, you may have been right. An overfishing crisis means that instead of traditional mackerel, some now contain a different fish with a similar name, prompting concerns that shoppers are being short-changed.
Over the past year big brands such as Princes, as well as some supermarket own labels, have replaced traditional tinned mackerel fillets with jack mackerel fillets.
Although clearly labelled, food experts say jack mackerel is a poor replacement for the oily fish, because it is a different species with a different flavour and different nutritional values. They also say shoppers may not realise a product has changed until they get it home.
The new products are being sold at a similar price despite the fact that it is a much cheaper fish, leading the consumer group Which? to describe it as another example of “skimpflation”.
Tinned fish is an “affordable and convenient way for households to add important nutrients to their diets”, said Sue Davies, the head of food policy at Which?.
“While manufacturers face genuine supply chain pressures and sustainability challenges, they have a responsibility to shoppers to be completely upfront when they change a product’s recipe.
“Skimpflation can feel particularly sneaky as shoppers may not realise a product has changed until they get it home and eat it,” she said.
Lidl is the latest retailer to switch and, in a recent video by the viral canned seafood reviewer Marcus Ansell, he rates its original mackerel fillets eight out of 10 while the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC)-certified replacement scores a lowly 3.5 out of 10.
“Jack mackerel is of significantly lower quality,” said Ansell. “It is quite a bad tinned fish really. I’ve had a lot of messages and some comments on my videos from people who thought they were buying real mackerel and were very disappointed when they tried it.”
Ansell added: “It’s not a substitute at all. . It’s a completely different species and is nothing like mackerel in its taste, texture, or smell … and there’s the health aspect, which is important to some people.”
Compared with traditional mackerel, jack mackerel has roughly half as much omega-3, a fatty acid that it is recommended people have twice a week as part of a healthy balanced diet.
“So they’re scamming us on mackerel now,” said one poster under the review. “Can’t even get some tinned fish without being legged over.”
Chilean jack mackerel costs about a third of the price of Atlantic true mackerel, according to the Financial Times, which first reported the story.
Last year the labelling rules were changed by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs to allow the species to be marketed as “jack mackerel”. Previously it could only be sold as “horse mackerel”, “jack”, “scad” or “trevally”.
The Marine Conservation Society (MCS) warned last year that mackerel stocks were at breaking point owing to overfishing. Its Good Fish Guide, which ranks choices using a traffic-light system, rates north-east Atlantic mackerel “red”, making it a “fish to avoid”.
Princes said it had taken the decision to move its branded range away from north-east Atlantic mackerel following years of concern over unsustainable catch levels.
It added that the “species is clearly identified on our products, and we would consider sourcing north-east Atlantic mackerel again if sustainable management is restored and MSC certification regained”.
Lidl said it was moving its tinned mackerel over to MSC-certified Chilean jack mackerel. “Before our next purchasing window for smoked mackerel, we will review if north-east Atlantic mackerel continues to comply with our sourcing policies and scientific advice.”
Earlier this year Waitrose suspended the sale of mackerel because of overfishing and instead directed its customers to buy herring and other species.

An “Alliance of New Forces”: Why the International Criminal Court Could Face Existential Threats
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
18:58:56 EEST
00:58:56 KST

Oleksii Shevchuk, advocate, Finalist for Ukraine’s nomination to the International Criminal Court (ICC) as a Judge
The International Criminal Court is facing more than yet another institutional crisis. What is at stake is a challenge that may determine the future of the entire system of international criminal justice — a system that emerged from the post-Second World War legal order as a response to mass atrocities, wars of aggression, and the impunity of political and military leaders.
If the International Criminal Court is politically isolated, financially weakened, and deprived of any meaningful capacity to secure compliance with its decisions, the international community may find itself facing a profound accountability vacuum. International treaties will, formally, remain in force. The Geneva Conventions, the Rome Statute, and the numerous resolutions and instruments adopted by international institutions will not simply disappear. Yet without effective mechanisms of enforcement and accountability, they risk becoming normative declarations increasingly detached from practical consequences.
This is the central danger of the present moment.
A Court Established to Confront Impunity
The International Criminal Court was established under the 1998 Rome Statute as a permanent international judicial institution entrusted with prosecuting individuals responsible for the most serious crimes of concern to the international community as a whole.
Its jurisdiction encompasses four categories of international crimes:
• genocide;
• crimes against humanity;
• war crimes; and
• the crime of aggression.
The fundamental significance of the ICC lies in the fact that it does not replace national criminal justice systems. Rather, it operates on the principle of complementarity. The Court intervenes where a state is unwilling or genuinely unable to carry out a genuine investigation or prosecution.
This principle is of fundamental importance. In many situations, a state whose senior officials, military commanders, or political leadership may themselves be implicated in international crimes cannot ensure impartial justice in relation to its own conduct. Authoritarian regimes do not ordinarily investigate their own systemic abuses. Aggressor states do not readily prosecute those who made the decision to launch a war. Military establishments implicated in systematic violations of international humanitarian law cannot always be effectively held to account through domestic institutions alone.
International criminal justice is therefore necessary not as a symbolic supranational layer imposed upon national courts, but as an essential safeguard for circumstances in which domestic justice is unable to function effectively or is deliberately obstructed.
The Ukrainian Dimension: Accountability for Aggression
For Ukraine, the institutional capacity of the ICC is not a theoretical question. It has immediate and profound practical consequences. The Russian Federation’s full-scale aggression against Ukraine has forced international law to confront questions that, for decades, remained largely doctrinal: Can the highest political and military leadership of an aggressor state genuinely be held criminally accountable? Can international institutions respond effectively to mass atrocities while an armed conflict is still ongoing? And can law retain its authority when it is violated by a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council?
Russia’s aggression has been accompanied by extensive allegations and documented incidents potentially falling within the scope of international criminal law: killings of civilians, deportations and forcible transfers, torture, unlawful deprivation of liberty, attacks against civilian objects and infrastructure, the unlawful transfer of children, persecution in occupied territories, and other serious violations of the laws and customs of war.
In these circumstances, the work of the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICC is not an abstract international procedure.
It is one of the few mechanisms capable of individualising criminal responsibility at the level of those who make decisions, issue orders, organise or coordinate criminal conduct, or fail to prevent or punish international crimes where the applicable legal requirements for responsibility are met.
Yet it is precisely here that the fundamental structural weakness of the Court becomes apparent. The ICC may investigate crimes, collect and preserve evidence, issue arrest warrants, and bring charges. It does not, however, possess its own police force, coercive apparatus, or independent mechanism for physically apprehending suspects.
The enforcement of its decisions therefore depends upon state cooperation, diplomatic resolve, and the willingness of States Parties to the Rome Statute to place their international legal obligations above short-term political expediency.
The Political Erosion of the Court
The contemporary assault on the ICC does not necessarily require a formal decision to abolish it. A more plausible — and potentially more dangerous — scenario is the gradual political, financial, and operational erosion of the institution.
Such a process can unfold through several interconnected mechanisms.
First, through the systematic delegitimisation of the Court. The ICC is variously portrayed as “politicised”, “selective”, “anti-Western”, or, conversely, as an “instrument of the West”. These mutually contradictory narratives nevertheless serve a common objective: to undermine confidence in the very idea of independent international criminal justice.
Second, through financial pressure. The ICC is a complex judicial institution conducting long-term investigations across multiple jurisdictions. It must process vast quantities of digital, documentary, forensic, satellite, and testimonial evidence while simultaneously protecting victims and witnesses. Such work requires stable and adequate funding.
Resource constraints therefore mean far more than reductions in staffing. They translate into slower investigations, weaker witness-protection mechanisms, diminished operational capacity in conflict zones, and a reduced ability to withstand sophisticated disinformation and interference campaigns.
Third, through pressure directed against officials of the Court. Sanctions, political intimidation, media campaigns, and personal attacks targeting ICC prosecutors, judges, and staff create a profoundly dangerous precedent: any state or coalition of states threatened by the prospect of criminal accountability may seek to punish not those suspected of committing international crimes, but those responsible for investigating them.
Fourth, through the non-execution of arrest warrants. An ICC arrest warrant is not a symbolic political statement. It is a judicial decision carrying legal consequences and engaging the cooperation obligations of States Parties under the Rome Statute.
If states begin to determine selectively which warrants they will execute and which they will disregard on grounds of political convenience, the architecture of international legal obligation itself begins to erode.
Law cannot function according to the principle of geopolitical convenience. It is either binding or, progressively, it ceases to operate as law in the substantive sense.
An “Alliance of New Forces”: A Community of Impunity
An increasingly visible feature of the contemporary international order is the convergence of states and political regimes for which international criminal justice is perceived not as a safeguard of international order, but as a direct threat to their model of governance.
This does not necessarily take the form of a formal military or political bloc governed by a common treaty, secretariat, or command structure.
Rather, it may be understood as an ad hoc convergence of regimes sharing a common interest: reducing the influence of international accountability mechanisms, delegitimising universal standards of human rights and international humanitarian law, and constructing political immunity for individuals implicated in the most serious international crimes.
Russia, Iran, North Korea, military regimes, and authoritarian political systems in different parts of the world may have profoundly different histories, ideologies, economic structures, and geopolitical objectives. What may nevertheless unite them is their hostility towards international mechanisms capable of individualising criminal responsibility at the highest levels of state power.
Of particular concern is that this emerging community of impunity operates not only in the military and diplomatic domains. It also relies upon information operations, legal manipulation, state-controlled media, economic leverage, bilateral arrangements, obstruction within international organisations, and coordinated efforts to delegitimise international institutions.
Its strategic logic is straightforward: if an international court cannot be abolished outright, it can instead be rendered sufficiently weak, slow, dependent, and politically toxic that states gradually cease to regard its decisions as authoritative and binding.
From this perspective, the ICC is not attacked because it is institutionally irrelevant. On the contrary, it is attacked precisely because it possesses the potential to establish a precedent that is profoundly threatening to authoritarian systems of power: that even the highest political and military leadership is not beyond the reach of criminal law.
Why the Collapse of the ICC Would Be Catastrophic
The abolition, paralysis, or effective marginalisation of the ICC would have consequences extending far beyond the fate of a single international institution.
First, it would severely undermine the principle of accountability for the gravest international crimes. This does not mean that national courts would entirely lose their ability to investigate war crimes or crimes against humanity. The deeper problem is that the international system would lose its permanent judicial mechanism designed to operate precisely where a state is itself implicated in criminal conduct or is unable or unwilling to provide genuine justice.
Second, force would increasingly displace law as the organising principle of international relations. States possessing significant military, economic, or informational power might conclude that international prohibitions are ultimately declaratory rather than consequential. If aggression, mass deportations, systematic violence, or attacks against civilian populations carry no realistic prospect of individual criminal accountability, such practices risk becoming normalised instruments of state policy.
Third, the broader system of international humanitarian law would be weakened. The Geneva Conventions, their Additional Protocols, customary international humanitarian law, and the Rome Statute do not operate in isolation. They form part of an interconnected normative architecture in which substantive prohibitions must be reinforced by mechanisms of investigation, evidence preservation, adjudication, and punishment.
Without mechanisms capable of translating norms into consequences, legal rules gradually lose their regulatory force. They may continue to exist in treaty texts while exercising progressively less influence over actors sufficiently powerful to violate them.
Fourth, victims would lose not only an avenue towards justice, but also an international mechanism for recognition of their experience. International criminal justice performs more than a punitive function. It establishes an authoritative evidentiary record, contributes to historical memory, counters denial and revisionism, and recognises victims as subjects of law rather than anonymous components of casualty statistics.
International Law Requires Enforcement
International law is frequently criticised for lacking a “world government” or a global police force. There is some validity to this criticism: the international legal order does not possess a single centralised coercive authority comparable to the enforcement apparatus of a sovereign state.
Yet this does not mean that international law is fictitious.
Its effectiveness depends upon the interaction of treaty obligations, domestic implementation, mutual legal assistance, sanctions regimes, diplomatic pressure, international reputation, and — ultimately — the political will of states to comply with the rules they have accepted.
The ICC constitutes one of the central components of precisely this kind of legal architecture. It cannot independently arrest a suspect. What it can do, however, is fundamentally important: determine that an individual must answer not to political convenience but to law; collect and preserve evidence; issue judicial warrants; restrict the international mobility of suspects; and create conditions in which impunity can no longer be assumed to be permanent.
The history of international criminal justice demonstrates that accountability often arrives late. Political regimes change. Alliances dissolve. Governments reconsider their positions. Individuals once considered politically untouchable lose protection. Properly collected and preserved evidence, however, remains.
This is precisely why weakening the ICC today is so dangerous. Such efforts are directed not merely against particular investigations or individual arrest warrants. They threaten the future capacity of the international community to establish the truth and secure accountability when political circumstances eventually make justice possible.
The Court Must Be Strengthened, Not Merely Defended
Support for the ICC cannot be confined to political declarations affirming a commitment to international law. Preserving the Court’s capacity requires concrete institutional action.
First and foremost, States Parties to the Rome Statute must comply with their obligations to cooperate with the Court, including obligations concerning the arrest and surrender of persons subject to ICC warrants. Selective compliance with international legal obligations directly undermines the credibility of the entire system.
Equally important are stable and adequate funding, protection of prosecutorial and judicial independence, stronger national mechanisms for investigating international crimes, the development of joint investigative teams, effective evidence-sharing arrangements, and sustained support for victims and witnesses.
For Ukraine, this also requires the continued development of a robust domestic system of accountability for international crimes. The existence of the ICC does not relieve national authorities of their obligation to document, investigate, and prosecute war crimes effectively. On the contrary, the principle of complementarity presupposes strong national institutions capable of operating in accordance with international standards.
At the same time, national justice alone cannot fully substitute for international mechanisms in cases involving the highest political and military leadership of an aggressor state, transnational networks of participation and support, international arrest and surrender mechanisms, and the global judicial recognition of international crimes.
Conclusion
The International Criminal Court is not a perfect institution. It faces procedural constraints, depends heavily upon state cooperation, and often operates more slowly than societies experiencing war and mass atrocities understandably expect.
Yet the Court’s imperfections are not an argument for dismantling it.
They are an argument for reforming it, strengthening it, and providing it with the institutional capacity necessary to fulfil its mandate.
What is being decided today is therefore not merely the future of one international court.
At stake is whether the international order will preserve the principle that aggression, genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity cannot be legitimised by sovereignty, military power, political expediency, or membership in the “right” geopolitical camp.
If the international community allows the ICC to become powerless, isolated, and systematically delegitimised, the resulting vacuum in international criminal justice could persist for decades.
And that vacuum will not remain empty.
If law retreats, power will take its place.

Hungary plans diesel subsidy for car owners amid rising fuel prices
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
23:57:25 CST
00:57:25 KST

BUDAPEST, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- The Hungarian government will provide a monthly subsidy of 5,000 forints (about 16 U.S. dollars) to nearly one million diesel car owners through December to compensate for rising fuel prices, Prime Minister Peter Magyar announced on Friday.
The measure will apply to owners of diesel-powered vehicles with a maximum engine output of 150 horsepower, including individual entrepreneurs and agricultural producers.
Magyar said eligible motorists would receive a total of 20,000 forints (63.97 dollars) over the four-month period, corresponding to 5,000 forints per month.
According to Magyar, the amount reflects the approximate difference between current market prices and the previously protected fuel price for a typical refueling. The subsidy will be paid automatically, without requiring an application.
He said the measure was designed to help motorists most affected by the diesel price rises while excluding high-performance and expensive vehicles from taxpayer-funded support.
Magyar also announced additional assistance for the agricultural sector. Agricultural users will be allowed to reclaim the full amount of excise duty included in the diesel price until the end of the year.
The government aims to prevent higher global oil prices from significantly increasing agricultural production costs and subsequently feeding into food prices, Magyar said.
Diesel prices in Hungary have risen sharply in recent weeks amid higher global oil prices, reaching 701 forints (2.24 dollars) per liter, the highest level in four years.
The government of former Prime Minister Viktor Orban introduced a temporary fuel price cap in March amid surging crude oil prices, limiting petrol prices to 595 forints (1.90 dollars) per liter and diesel to 615 forints (1.97 dollars) per liter.
After taking office, Magyar's government decided in June to phase out the cap as international oil prices eased following a framework agreement between the United States and Iran. ■

Ukraine: Russian strike on Kyiv gas station kills 2

Ukraine: Russian strike on Kyiv gas station kills 2
September 11, 2026
At least two people were killed in Kyiv after Russian jet-powered drones struck a petrol station on Friday.
A 12-year-old boy was among 12 people who were injured by the attack, Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said one of the injured was a first responder who was "wounded in a double-tap strike."
Russia increasingly targeting petrol stations with new, faster drones
Friday's drone strikes come a day after what is thought to be the first Russian attack on a Kyiv gas station during the war.
Russia has struck around 300 petrol stations in Ukraine in recent months, most of which were in or near frontline areas.
The attacks on petrol stations come amid a spike in Russian assaults using new, faster and harder-to-intercept jet-powered drones to strike logistics centers, warehouses and commercial supply chains.
Ukraine condemns escalating Russian 'terror'
Zelenskyy said Russia was escalating these strikes on civilian energy infrastructure, calling them "increasingly terrorist in nature."
"Maximum attention must be focused on protecting the skies, finding solutions to protect people, and scaling up countermeasures against Russian drones," the Ukrainian leader said in a post on X.
The CEO of Ukrainian oil giant Ukrnafta, which owns the gas station and one other that was also struck on Friday morning, condemned Russia for "yet another deliberate strike on civilian facilities."
"There is no military objective in such attacks. This is terror against the civilian population," Bogdan Kukura said.
Russia has not publicly commented on the latest attacks, but has consistently denied targeting civilians.
Ukraine, Russia striking logistics, energy targets
More than four and a half years since Russia launched its full-scale invasion and with the fighting on the front lines in eastern Ukraine mostly stalled, Russia and Ukraine have been increasingly hitting logistics, energy and other economic targets in a bid to dent the other's war effort.
Ukraine has also stepped up its own drone attacks inside Russia. Overnight, two people were killed in Russia's Tula region, while one person was killed in Kursk on Friday, officials said.
Tula's regional governor Dmitry Milyayev added that three people were injured in the attacks.
Ozon, Russia's second-largest e-commerce platform, said a Ukrainian drone had struck a logistics hub in the city of Saratov, starting a fire.
More than 20 warehouses belonging to Ozon and Wildberries, Russia's other leading online retailer, have been hit in Ukrainian attacks in recent weeks.
Kyiv says the strikes are justified as part of its campaign to undermine Russia's war effort, which has also seen Ukraine target Russian oil refineries and other energy infrastructure.

Your Taxes: Israeli property flip ends with a costly VAT lesson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:52:34 UTC
00:52:34 KST

There has been a recent flurry of important real estate tax cases in Israel. They relate to hotel companies, property flips, and transparent house property companies. Below, we review a problematic VAT case involving a property flip (quick onward sale of the property).
VAT case:
The Israeli District Court recently ruled that a taxpaying entity could not change its mind. The taxpayer wanted to refund VAT it incorrectly recovered on the purchase of a residential property in order to avoid a much higher VAT bill on the sale of that property. This case is potentially relevant to many investors in Israeli homes. (Twenty Four Seven International Holdings LLC v. Central Tel Aviv VAT Director 18654-10-22 of 25.6.26, Judge H. Kirsch).
Background:
The taxpayer was an American limited liability company (LLC) which was an Igud Mekarka-in (Hebrew legal term for a real estate association or entity) for Israeli tax purposes. This is an entity in which all the assets are rights to Israeli real estate. Taxes potentially include corporate income tax and sometimes VAT.
The LLC in this case owned an old building in Tel Aviv, consisting of residential apartments (89% of the floor space) and shops (11% of the floor space). The taxpayer purchased its interest in 2008 for NIS 3.7 million plus VAT at 15.5% (then around NIS 574,000).
The VAT office allowed the taxpayer to recover the input VAT on the purchase, as it said it intended to do a flip.
Subsequently, the taxpayer retained and rented out the apartments and shops for a good rent. It only sold the property eight years later, in 2016, for the much higher amount of NIS 33.34m.
So did VAT of around NIS 5.7 million apply to the sale price at the prevailing rate (then 17%, now 18%) as the taxpayer waited eight years before selling?
The taxpayer claimed it had incorrectly recovered VAT on the purchase and should be allowed to change its mind in order to avoid VAT on the sale. The Court disagreed.
Court judgment:
The Court ruled that full VAT applied to the sale price of NIS 33.4m. and the taxpayer could not change its mind.
What are Israel’s VAT rules for real estate?
A business can recover VAT on its purchases but only if the purchases are used to generate sales liable to VAT (VAT Law Sec. 41).
In the case of Israeli residential real estate, a VAT exemption applies to rental income if the lease does not exceed 25 years (VAT Law Sec 31(1)). Therefore, people who rent their homes in Israel do not pay VAT to their landlord.
And when selling a home in Israel, a VAT exemption applies to the sale if, “by law,” it was not possible to recover input VAT applicable at the time of the purchase.
However, if it was determined that part or all the input VAT on the purchase was recoverable, a pro rata VAT charge then applies upon sale (VAT Law Sec 31(4)).
In this case, the taxpayer had purchased the property and recovered all the VAT on the purchase price in order to limit its immediate cash outlay.
Eight years later, in 2016, the taxpayer sold the property and wanted a full exemption on the entire NIS 33.4m. sale price in order to reinvest in US real estate. The taxpayer claimed that “by law” the VAT office should never have allowed it to recover input VAT on 89% of the purchase price of NIS 3.7m. in 2008.
The Court ruled you can’t have it both ways by changing your mind. The residential apartments were rented out for eight years, and input VAT on the purchase should not have been recovered. But since the input VAT on the purchase was recovered, full VAT applied to the sale.
The Court denied the taxpayer permission to pay back the input VAT on the purchase to the Tax Authority.
Comment:
If you are contemplating investment in Israeli real estate, it is critical to check out the long-term implications in all countries. That includes checking out the structure and anticipated VAT implications upon purchase, upon renting out, and upon eventual sale of the real estate concerned. And if you commit to a quick flip, check the consequences if you change your mind and keep the property for a few years.
Wishing readers a happy and prosperous new year.
As always, consult experienced professional advisors in each country concerned at an early stage in specific cases.
leon@hcat.co
The writer is a certified public accountant and tax specialist at Harris Consulting & Tax Ltd.

Your Investments: Turning Rosh Hashanah reflection into financial action
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:52:33 UTC
00:52:33 KST

The summer is over, the children are back in school, and suddenly we are confronted with the reality that another year has passed.
For many, Rosh Hashanah is primarily about honey cake, apples and honey, synagogue, and family. But there is also another theme that runs through the day and deserves our attention: accountability.
Rosh Hashanah is the Day of Judgment. One of the most powerful descriptions of this appears in the Unetaneh Tokef prayer that we recite during the Musaf service.
The prayer describes God as reviewing the actions of every individual: “You cause to pass, count, reckon, and are mindful of” every living soul.
It then famously declares: “On Rosh Hashanah it is inscribed, and on Yom Kippur it is sealed.”
Count, reckon, mindful
The prayer goes on to ask who will live and who will die, who will be wealthy and who will be poor, who will enjoy tranquility and who will suffer.
The language is striking. “Count.” “Reckon.” “Mindful.” There is an accounting taking place. That should sound familiar to anyone who has ever sat down to review a financial plan.
At the end of each year, businesses analyze what occurred over the previous 12 months. They look at revenue, expenses, profits, losses, assets, and liabilities. Investors review their portfolios. They examine what worked, what didn’t, and whether their investments are still aligned with their goals.
Why shouldn’t individuals do the same with their personal finances? The run-up to Rosh Hashanah provides a perfect opportunity for financial reckoning.
The Rambam makes the connection between Rosh Hashanah and accounting even more explicit. In Hilchot Teshuvah 3:4, he explains that a person should view himself throughout the year as if his merits and sins are equally balanced. One additional sin can tip the balance toward guilt, while one mitzvah can tip it toward merit. The Rambam describes the shofar as calling to “inspect your deeds, repent, remember your Creator” and improve our ways.
Of course, Judaism’s accounting system is not the same as a brokerage account. We can’t put our acts of kindness into an Excel spreadsheet and assign them a dollar value. But the underlying message is powerful: We are expected to take stock.
Before making financial resolutions for the coming year, take a few minutes to look backward.
What was your income? Expenses? Did you take on debt? Did you save enough for retirement? Did you invest according to a plan, or just chase hot stocks? And perhaps most importantly: Did your money actually help you accomplish what matters most to you?
That last question is often overlooked.
Money as a tool
Financial planning isn’t simply about making as much money as is humanly possible. Money is a tool. It is supposed to help us provide for our families, educate our children, retire with dignity, give charity, and live according to our values.
Think about someone who has a great salary but spends every dollar. On paper, the income looks impressive. In reality, the person may be moving backward. Conversely, someone who earns less but consistently saves, avoids unnecessary debt, invests prudently, and gives generously may be building a much stronger financial future.
That is why an annual financial review is so important. These are the financial equivalents of examining our deeds.
There is another important lesson in the Rosh Hashanah message. The purpose of the accounting is not simply to look backward. It is to change the future.
The Unetaneh Tokef concludes its frightening description of judgment with the famous words: “But repentance, prayer, and charity avert the severity of the decree.”
That is a remarkably optimistic message. We are not being told that the past is irrelevant. Rather, we are being reminded that the future is still in our hands. The same is true with our finances. Maybe, last year, we spent too much, didn’t save enough, and took way too much investment risk. The good news is that we can change. Financial accountability isn’t about beating ourselves up over past mistakes. It is about learning from them.
Let’s use the opportunity of the new year to get back on track financially. Take out statements. Look at the numbers. Review the goals. Examine the spending. Check the investments. Discuss the coming year’s major expenses. Decide how much will be saved and how much will be given to charity. And then make a plan.
Rosh Hashanah reminds us that every year matters. We don’t know what the coming year will bring. But we do have an obligation to make responsible decisions with the opportunities and resources we have.
The goal of an annual financial review isn’t to predict exactly what will happen in the markets or in life. Nobody can do that. The goal is to make sure that when we look back a year from now, we can say that we made thoughtful decisions, followed our plan, and used our resources wisely. That may be one of the most practical ways to translate the message of Rosh Hashanah into our everyday lives.
Shana tova! May we all be blessed with a year of health and happiness, and may our prayers be answered with mercy and favor.
The information in this article reflects the writer’s opinion and not necessarily that of Portfolio Resources Group Inc. or affiliates.
The writer is author of Retirement GPS: How to Navigate Your Way to A Secure Financial Future with Global Investing and a licensed financial professional in the US and Israel. For more information: (02) 624-0995, www.aaronkatsman.com, aaron@lighthousecapital.co.il.

What remains of America’s 9/11 memory - and what is disappearing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:52:21 UTC
00:52:21 KST

History, as Israelis know all too well from our own challenged historical accounts, is fungible. As politics change and stories pass from one generation to the next, and feelings are considered, even the basic facts can be reinterpreted. The story of 9/11 is no different.
And while September 11 is not being scrubbed from the record, demography, schoolhouse inconsistency, partisan fights over marking the anniversary, and a shift in public language all point to fading lived memory – and, in some institutions, a softer or redirected story. Memorials still stand, names are still read, and most adults still say the day remade the country. What has changed is the kind of memory. In some circles, the retelling of the event has shifted from shared shock to contested history.
The initial reason 9/11 may feel different 25 years later is because of who is alive to remember it. More than 100 million Americans were born after 2001 or were too young to form a memory of that morning.
History vs lived experience
“We’re teaching a generation of students now for whom 9/11 is history, and for some, it’s ancient history like the Vietnam War or the Korean War or World War II,” Joshua Rovner, an associate professor of foreign policy and global security at American University’s School of International Service in Washington, who has taught courses on 9/11 since 2001, said in USA Today in September 2025.
YouGov, a British-founded public-opinion and market-research firm that runs online polls, conducted an August 2026 survey of 1,098 US adults and found that 46% first learned of 9/11 from the news – but among 18- to 29-year-olds, 37% learned it in school, and 6% said they had not heard anything about it. Older Americans still carry “where I was” memories. Younger ones often do not. For many, it is an annual date, not a constant presence.
Politics and war have taken a toll on 9/11 memories. The attacks are now bound up with two long wars, trillions of dollars, thousands of soldiers dead, and security that was never totally achieved. Pew’s 2021 review found 69% saying the US mostly failed to achieve its goals in Afghanistan. A Washington Post-ABC poll that same anniversary year found more Americans saying 9/11 changed the country for the worse (46% ) than for the better (33% ). The brief post-attack unity, “trust in government at 60% in October 2001,” per Pew, collapsed to 24% by 2021.
On the 20th anniversary of 9/11, Newsweek quoted University of Florida political scientist Stephen Craig. “Today, 9/11 is ‘a source of substantial political tensions,’ not the rally it was when [president George] Bush hit ~90% approval,” Craig said. “The post-9/11 ‘rally round the flag’ was short; the longer polarization predates and outlasted it.”
Schools have not filled the gap with a national story. There is no uniform curriculum assigned to teach about 9/11. Only 14 states, including New York, Texas, Illinois, and California, explicitly require September 11 in social-studies standards. In the other 36, the topic is discretionary – left to districts and teachers. An article by Jeremy Stoddard and Diana Hess, professors at the University of Wisconsin, Madison, in The Conversation’s September 2021 issue, describes an “anniversary-only” pattern.
“Teaching 9/11 as a memorializing event on the anniversary also generally avoids deeper inquiry into the historic US role in the Middle East and Afghanistan. This includes, for example, arming mujahedeen fighters against the Soviets in Afghanistan in the 1980s and aiding Iraqi president Saddam Hussein in the war against Iran also in the ’80s.”
They suggest teachers take a more “in-depth approach to explore how US actions contributed to the formation of al-Qaeda, which bombed the World Trade Center in 1993 and later carried out attacks on US embassies in East Africa as well as on the USS Cole, a Navy ship fueling in Yemen, in the years leading up to 9/11.”
In some schools, 9/11 lessons have taken a progressive spin, tilting towards Islamophobia, the Patriot Act, and American foreign-policy guilt. The result is inconsistency – and a vacuum in which conspiracy content and social-media fragments can stand in for a shared account.
Changed media reporting
Anniversary journalism in 2026 illustrates the same split over emphasis. While most high-profile news still calls 9/11 a terrorist attack and still cites the death toll, a smaller set of prominent pieces treats the attacks mainly as the opening of a story about Muslims, surveillance, and civil liberties.
Asma Khalid’s August 18 Atlantic essay, “Islamophobia has corroded American values,” links the 25th anniversary to America’s 250th and moves quickly from 2,977 dead to the Transportation Security Administration, watchlists, and current anti-Muslim rhetoric. PBS NewsHour’s September 1 “Settle In” episode with Rozina Ali, timed to the anniversary, centers on the FBI and post-9/11 surveillance of Muslim families.
The Washington Post reported on August 28 that Canada’s CBC had a policy of not labeling specific attacks as terrorism and made an exception for 9/11 only after public criticism. USA Today’s Susan Page package still named 9/11 the worst terrorist attack in US history, then devoted a major section to liberty versus security – the Patriot Act, Section 702, Snowden.
The New York Daily News asked whether the country is safer and quoted critics of a sprawling surveillance architecture. CNN’s coverage of the fight over Mayor Zohran Mamdani at Ground Zero put families’ objections beside the mayor’s account of post-9/11 surveillance of Arab American communities. While none of these pieces deny the dead, some “soft-soap” the language, referencing “those who lost their lives” versus “those who were killed.” Several relocate the moral center of the anniversary from the hijackings to the response.
Agreement that the day mattered does not produce agreement about how to mark it. Thirteen percent of Democrats said Americans focus too much on 9/11; 43% of Republicans said the country focuses too little. Republicans backed a national 9/11 holiday 62-43 over Democrats. Democrats said Muslims have been treated worse than people of other religions since 9/11 by 72-28 over Republicans.
Threat perception has cooled even while the “changed us completely” number holds. Gallup’s October 2025 crime poll finds Americans worry about identity theft (69%) and scams (53%), while 41% of parents in August 2025 feared for a child’s safety at school, numbers well above the 36% who in 2021 said they worried about becoming a terror victim (down from 58% recorded in a Gallup flash poll on the night of September 11, 2001) and unlike fall 2001, when nearly half said they were less likely to fly and about a third were less willing to enter skyscrapers or large crowds.
Language and media play a huge part in how this story is told. Commemorative and official speech often prefers “lost their lives,” “died,” or “lives were stolen” to “killed in attacks.” King Charles and Queen Camilla’s April 2026 note at the New York memorial, as quoted by the BBC, read: “We honour the memory for those who so tragically lost their lives on 11th September 2001. We stand in enduring solidarity with the American people and in the face of their profound loss.” Mamdani, quoted in USA Today’s August 25 identification story, said, “We honor the nearly 3,000 people whose lives were stolen that day.”
Memorial English is not a conspiracy, but over time, using only the softer verbs, plus curricula that skip perpetrators and ideology, can leave students with tragedy without agency: a disaster that “happened,” not an attack that was planned.
Outsourcing memory
So, the accurate charge is not that America has erased 9/11; it is that the country is outsourcing memory to an anniversary ritual while arguing over the caption. The dead are still named. The towers have been rebuilt. What is at risk is the harder sentence: that nearly 3,000 people were murdered in a terrorist attack by al-Qaeda, that the ideology did not vanish, and that remembering the victims and ensuring that America remains vigilant and secure are lessons we can’t afford to forget, erase, or hijack with conspiracy theories.
What is worthy of a school assembly in September, what gets a curriculum unit on wars and the dangers of unchecked and well-funded terror, and which verb a generation hears first – that’s what will keep the memory intact. As will telling our personal memories, which you, our readers, have shared to help preserve the history of that infamous day.
The writer’s memories of that tragic day: America must never forget
Tears streaming down our faces, my friend Anita and I met at the supermarket in Dobbs Ferry, New York. Food shopping seemed like the logical thing to do on a bright September morning with the sky so blue it looked like a painting and your world was falling apart.
The only planes overhead were teams of fighter jets – an unlikely sight in the Westchester suburb north of Manhattan. We shopped as though we were expecting a winter storm, but in truth we didn’t know what we were expecting. Communications were down – we couldn’t reach our husbands who worked in lower Manhattan by phone, and we were worried.
Anita’s husband worked on Wall Street near the Trade Center. Mine was an accountant at St. Vincent’s hospital. The newscasters on TV and radio were no help, being at a loss for putting the news puzzle together. We only knew that it appeared someone was attacking America using large jetliners as missiles.
At first it seemed like an accident – a plane somehow flew into a building, but by the time the second Trade Center building had been struck, it was clearly something more. The building of the World Trade Center, where I had once worked on the 62nd floor in the New York State Tax Department, was burning top-down like a cigarette.
Were our husbands alive? Were we to be the next target?
I filled my tank with gas in case I needed to drive to Canada with the two younger children. I spent time saying Psalms. It soothed my soul just enough to try and think clearly. My eldest son, at Yeshiva University High School in Manhattan, managed to get an open line. He told me he was stuck in New York. Public transportation, trains, buses, everything had stopped. Cars were gridlocked. Ash was blowing across the East River and into the Hudson, and as we watched, the news went from horrific to horrendous.
The first building came down, shooting debris through the streets, sending chunks of building into revolving doors of lower Manhattan, trapping my brother and many others in buildings nearby and covering everyone within miles with ash. Firefighters stood helplessly at the scene.
Like most news stories, the attacks on 9/11 unfolded in layers. Layers that affected every person in the US. But especially those of us in New York. Life simply stopped.
My ex-husband got stuck overnight on emergency duty in the hospital, an accountant on emergency duty, waiting for victims of the mass casualty, victims that never came. We were scheduled to sell our house – the closing set for September 13. The buyer, Rodolfo (Rudy) Hermano, was the catering manager for Windows on the World, the famous restaurant on top of Tower One.
It took a day or two to get the courage (and the phone lines) to call our lawyer. How does one even ask the question – did our buyer survive the blast that killed approximately 170 staff and patrons reported to be in the restaurant that day? His story is below.
On Friday, I baked challah and brought some to the shiva home of Rena Speisman, the mom of Hayley, who was in my son’s class. Her husband, Bob, a 48-year-old diamond industry executive, was a passenger aboard American Airlines Flight 77, the hijacked aircraft that was flown into the Pentagon.
While I was not directly affected, there were very few degrees of separation for my family from the tragedy that hit America just 23 miles down the Hudson from where we lived. My school chum Devorah suffered the loss of her uncle Abraham Zelmanowitz, known by the family as Avreymel.
Although he worked in the North Tower on Floor 27 for Blue Cross/Blue Shield and could have made it out alive with the rest of his colleagues, he chose to stay behind and try to help his co-worker and friend Ed Beyea, a paraplegic confined to a wheelchair. He sent Ed’s aide Irma Fuller out of the building to safety and assumed his care. FDNY Capt. William Francis Burke Jr. stayed to try to help the men in the stairwell, but the three men perished together when the building collapsed.
Abe Zelmanowitz’s DNA was identified in August 2002 – almost a year after 9/11. I attended the funeral on August 5, 2002. The casket, covered by a small parochet, was the size of a shoebox. Avreymel was buried in the Mount of Olives Jewish Cemetery, near his parents’ graves.
This selfless man, Avreymal Zelmanowitz is just one of so many who are being remembered on this 25th anniversary.
The morning the windows went dark: Rudy’s story
Rodolfo “Rudy” Hermano and his wife, Cathy, both worked busy jobs in hospitality. Rudy was in catering sales at Windows on the World, the acclaimed restaurant on floors 106 and 107 of the World Trade Center. Cathy was assistant director of catering at Hilton New York.
Parents of two young children, the dual-career couple had a “commuter date” each morning on the 6 a.m. Metro-North train from Irvington to Grand Central Station, where they caught up on events of the week. But on September 11, 2001, Rudy – usually perpetually early – was late.
He skipped the commute that would have put him on the 107th floor with his catering team and drove instead, planning to visit his mother in a Brooklyn hospital after work.
Jackie Sayegh, a bubbly colleague one desk away, used to tease him: “Rudy, this is not a hotel. Stop coming early.” That day she came in early anyway, so she could take Friday off to see her new husband in Atlanta.
Driving down the West Side Highway, Rudy reached the 168th Street exit when traffic stopped dead, and cars were forced off the road. Only emergency vehicles were waved through. He pulled into a neighborhood coffee shop and stood at the counter as a television behind it showed the first tower fall.
“To my left was a postman,” Rudy recalls. “He was in uniform, and I was in a suit. People were dressed casually, and I wasn’t. Then when I saw the towers on fire, and the first one collapsed, the man looked me up and down and said, ‘Do you know anyone there?’ And I said, ‘That’s where I work. Up there.’ The postman just looked at me with big eyes, and I really didn’t know what to say. We were buying a house. Did I still have a job?”
He tried to reach Cathy, who had taken their usual train, and left a voicemail she saved until very recently: “Something’s happening in the World Trade Center. I’m listening to 1010 WINS news. Airplane hit. I’m calling the office, it’s busy. It must be my building. I am not there.”
Hermano had been at Windows only about 10 months.
“The office was a family,” he said in a recent interview with the Magazine. Jennie Emil – whose brother David’s company, Night Sky, operated Windows and other restaurants – was not there that day. Jay Magazine, the catering sales manager, had booked that morning’s risk management client seminar for 100 attendees and was upstairs. An NYU nutrition intern, Orasri Liangthanasarn, newly hired as a second assistant, had come in early to catch up on her work. The captain, banquet manager Jupiter Yambem, and two or three servers were on the floor.
“Within our catering family, Jay, Jackie, Orasri, Jupiter, our servers, and so many others did not make it out. They were among some 75 staff who were trapped.”
A YouTube video, “Windows on the World, 9/11 Untold Story,” tells the behind-the-scenes story of that day. According to the video, around 8,000 people were inside the North Tower when the plane struck. The vast majority managed to escape, but not the 1,344 people above the impact zone.
Ken Womack, author of The Restaurant at the End of the World, said, “One of the great miracles of 9/11 is how many people survived and were able to get out of the Trade Center. But that wasn’t the case if you were on the 92nd floor or above in the North Tower. During the initial attack, sheetrock and other wreckage collapsed in the stairwells, virtually cutting them off.”
In one heartbreaking scene in the video, using real audio from that day, assistant general manager Christine Olendar begs the police for help. “What are we going to do for air?” she cries. The police assured her help was on the way. It wasn’t.
According to Rudy, within a week the small group of Windows on the World survivors gathered at Jennie’s apartment and hugged everyone who walked in the door. Rudy went to memorials and house prayers for immigrant families he had barely had time to know.
Greg Hein, who had referred Rudy for the job and was director of catering, was on his way in. When he came up from the subway into the concourse, people were running out, shouting, “Go out!” He didn’t know what was happening. He ran outside, looked up, saw the fire – and then the explosion as the second plane hit. Debris came down. He ran across the street to St. Peter’s [church] and huddled by the fence with his briefcase over his head, watching pieces of the aircraft fall around him.
He kept going back to Ground Zero to help. The dust wrecked his lungs. He died two years ago of those breathing complications. He was younger than Rudy.
“Fortunately, within a few months, I was working again,” Rudy recalls. “At the time, if you remember, the world stopped. There were no jobs in New York. I was lucky. In January, I bumped into an executive chef at the Regency I used to work with. He said, ‘So what are you doing?’ I said, ‘I really don’t know.’ Then he said, ‘I’m going to arrange for you to work with us at the Marriott in Stamford.’”
The Hermanos are moving again – this time to Santa Fe. Before Rudy left New York, he extended his stay for a reunion on September 11 with the surviving catering staff of Windows on the World. Twenty-five years later.
The ‘Magazine’ shares: Where were YOU when America was attacked?
No matter what country they lived in, people who lived through September 11, 2001, have deep and disturbing memories of exactly where they were and what they were doing on that crisp, beautiful morning when America was attacked.
Jennifer Abrahamsen, teacher, Sloatsburg, New York:
“I left school on my prep period to make a deposit at the bank. When I got to the bank, there was video of the towers burning on the television screen. I returned to school, and nobody in the building knew what was happening. You would be surprised how cut off from the outside world schools can be. I told the women in the main office what I had seen on TV. A television was turned on in the school library.
More and more teachers found out, and finally children of parents who worked in the Trade Center were called individually to the guidance office, and a family member was located to bring them home. Once all of those students were with family, an announcement was finally made during the last period of the day to tell the students about the attack on the World Trade Center. The principal at the time likened it to when US president John F. Kennedy was shot (on November 22, 1963).
One of my eighth-grade students raised his hand at the end of the announcement and told me he was scheduled to be at a party at Windows on the World that weekend. He asked if there would still be a party.”
Major “A.” in the IDF combat reserves, drafted since Oct. 7 (aliyah in 1984):
“I was working in Rochester, New York, at a tech firm, sitting at my desk. Every single person in the office got up from their desk and went into the break room to watch it on television. I saw it was a terrorist attack, watched for about 15 minutes, and went back to work. Because as an Israeli and an IDF veteran, I knew the only way to deal with terrorism on a community level is to clean up and get back to work; otherwise, the entire society is permanently paralyzed in trauma.
Meanwhile, for the next several months, people came to work and watched television all day long and didn’t get anything done; then they would rush home and sit in front of the television and watch… Exactly the opposite of what we are trained to do here in Israel. I ended up having to do the jobs of most of my coworkers while they sat in the break room all day long for months on end. They were frozen and addicted to witnessing the trauma over and over again. This is why we Israelis continue to thrive despite the horrific things that our enemies do to us.
Rachelle Ben David, Karnei Shomron resident (aliyah in 1982):
“I had been teaching in Kedumim, and when I got home, my friend called me and told me to turn on the TV. I watched as the second plane flew into the World Trade Center Tower. I knew people who lost friends and neighbors in the towers. A friend I taught with in Kedumim had a brother who was in the towers on the 70th floor when he heard a boom. Being Israeli, as soon as he heard a boom, he ran for the stairwell and flew down all the stairs. He survived.”
Edna Krausz, Jerusalem (aliyah in 2025)
“I had no idea anything had happened at 9:30 a.m. on September 11. Before opening my gift store in New Rochelle/Scarsdale, New York, I ran to grab a coffee at Starbucks. The grim faces around me told the story that was unfolding on the radio, and I listened with horror to what was transpiring. As I opened my shop, Inspiration Gallery, suddenly streams of people came through the door – apparently looking for inspiration… and hugs.”
Edna summarized, saying she gave out a lot of hugs that day. “It was solid comfort,” she continued. “I was amazed at how people reach out to other people. We don’t know what to do – so we seek God’s comfort in whichever way we can get it.”
She recalled, “A friend of mine had a daughter working on a high floor in the towers. The employees were told to stay in place. This girl, Lisa, said, no. She was familiar with terrorism and had been in the building during the first World Trade Center bombing. She ran for the stairwell and made her way out. I believe that people like this were getting a message. God communicated directly to their souls. As we say each day in the Amida (silent prayer) – ‘You grant our soul knowledge.’”
Elaine Strasberg, Karnei Shomron (aliyah in 2013):
“Tuesday morning, heading to my Israeli dance class on the Lower East Side, I was driving into Manhattan from Queens, going over the Williamsburg Bridge at 8:45 a.m., listening to the Nachum Segal music show on the radio. Traffic was exceptionally slow. When the program ended at 9 a.m., I switched to the WINS news station and heard about an explosion at one of the Twin Towers. I looked out the window and saw the smoke coming out of the tower. As I kept listening to the theories of what was happening, I saw the second plane hit the second tower!
Then I understood why traffic was hardly moving. We were not allowed to enter Manhattan and were diverted back into Brooklyn. When I got home and turned on the TV, I saw the collapse of the second tower. Of course, we stayed glued to the TV, hearing of the Pentagon and the plane crash in Pennsylvania.
My friends who had already gotten into Manhattan for the class were stuck there for the entire day and didn’t get home until late that night.”
Nahum Zak, Boca Raton, Florida:
“I was at the post office in Kew Gardens Hills, New York City, picking up the Palm Pilot I bought on eBay when I heard the radio report behind the teller saying a small plane (that was the first report) flew into one of the towers. The teller and reports seemed to think it was an accident.
“I remember thinking there’s no way someone flies by accident over NYC airspace into the No. 1 terrorist target in the state.
“It was the worst day of my life.
Yael Harris Resnick, Karnei Shomron (aliyah in 2013):
“Everyone has their own memories of that tragic day 25 years ago. Mine started early that morning around 6:45 a.m. when I woke up to my own tower falling, an eerie foreboding of what was about to happen in NYC about two hours later. I was very newly pregnant with my first baby, and I was bleeding. A lot.
“It was also my first day as a kindergarten teacher in New Jersey, just across the bridge from NYC, in a new school. There were kids counting on me. Little did I know at the time just how much they would need the loving support of their teachers. I put my own dread aside and promised that as soon as my obstetrician’s office opened, I would call to make an emergency appointment.
“You know how the rest of the day went for NYC and the world. I don’t need to describe the horror, the confusion, the relief, the pain. Despite the urgency of global catastrophe, personal catastrophes do not cease to exist. It was difficult due to traffic jams and the chaos of the day, but I managed to be squeezed in for an appointment. It was my first. The one where they check for a heartbeat. Miraculously, there was one. There was also one extra sac that was empty. No heartbeat. One tower down.
“I cannot describe the emotions of a moment like that. Lumped together with that devastating day, all I could do was be thankful, so thankful for that one strong little heartbeat fluttering inside me.
“Twenty-five years later, that little heartbeat has grown into a beautiful young lady. This summer she married the love of her life and was the most beautiful bride. It can’t be a coincidence that she is obsessively connected to all things 9/11 (especially the musical Come from Away) even though she hadn’t yet been born. And that she is now studying on the mother/baby and ultrasound ward at Shaare Zedek hospital to be a nurse, a gentle, old soul, present and nurturing when mothers receive news just like I did on that September 11, 25 years ago.”
Tsivya Fox-Dobuler, Ramat Beit Shemesh (aliyah in 2002):
“We lived in Far Rockaway, Queens. My ex-husband was on a train heading into Manhattan when he saw the first plane hit the Twin Towers. After years in Israel, he knew instantly it was terror, not an accident, so he got off, crossed the platform, and came straight home.
“I was teaching five-year-old boys at yeshiva that morning. My assistant walked in late and white as a ghost; a few minutes later the vice principal canceled playground on the most beautiful day of the year. I still didn’t understand until Mrs. Katz, whose kohanim sons were members of Hatzalah, looked like she’d seen death itself. After school I walked to the bay in Bayswater. People were lined up watching the towers burning in the distance, and Israelis who had lived nearby for years were suddenly saying they wanted to go home to Israel.
“The silence for weeks afterwards was almost worse. We lived 15 minutes from JFK Airport; for five days no civilian planes moved, only F-16s circling. My ex-husband had always said one day we would want to leave America and wouldn’t be able to. That week we believed him. A week later, we walked through Ground Zero. Clothes in a Gap store were still perfectly folded under thick ash. The smoke rose in straight pillars for months.
“A neighbor was saved because her elderly father, who never asked her to stay home, begged her not to go to work that morning. Our hazan (cantor) from shul was in Tower Two – obediently staying in place as he was advised to do – when a coworker grabbed his hand and forced him down hundreds of steps; they stepped outside seconds before the tower collapsed.
“On Yom Kippur, when he reached the words ‘who by fire,’ he collapsed on the floor, and the whole shul stood in silence, sobbing with him. For weeks, no one in Far Rockaway left their houses until NYC mayor Rudy Giuliani got on television and said it was time to start living again.”
Matti Led, Fair Lawn, New Jersey:
“I was at my desk in Brooklyn, a high school student, staring out the window, wondering why the clouds over Manhattan were so dark. Our principal interrupted class to break the news to us. We thought he was pranking us. A bunch of students ran down to the pay phone to call their parents who worked at the World Trade Center. Lots of kids were crying as they waited and tried to call their parents.
Later, as I took the B68 home through “Little Pakistan” (a Muslim neighborhood on Brooklyn’s Coney Island Avenue), I looked at the passengers on the bus and wondered if any of them were terrorists. Walking home from the bus stop, there were tiny shreds of paper (from the WTC blast) all around me.
“The reality only hit me when I actually saw videos of the planes hitting the towers.”
Tania Hammer, Talpiot, Jerusalem (aliyah 10 years ago):
“I was living in Far Rockaway and could see the Twin Towers across the way. I taught at Hebrew Academy of the Five Towns, and ran to a shop to pick up some supplies when I saw the first plane hit. We thought it was a terrible accident, so I went back to school. When the second plane hit, parents went berserk and converged on the school to grab their children. It was very chaotic, but the teachers couldn’t leave, and we tried to do some therapy with the children that stayed.
“Then we heard the Pentagon was hit, and I became anxious. My sister, a tax lawyer, was scheduled to work at the Pentagon that week. I had to call my sister. I tried and I tried but I couldn’t reach her. Nobody knew what exactly was happening. Eventually my sister picked up. I asked if she was okay, and she said, ‘Yes, why?’ She said she had stayed home to let a plumber in. That’s when I burst into tears.
“She said, ‘Why are you crying?’ and I said, ‘Turn on the radio.’ She turned on the radio and screamed, ‘Oh my gosh.’ There was no way she would have stayed home ordinarily. I told her, ‘Do you know what’s happening? Hashem saved you by sending a faulty toilet!’
“I had a cousin who worked on Wall Street, but every road was closed. He was covered in asbestos and dust from head to toe. He lived in Queens and couldn’t reach his wife or children, so he just followed the crowd and ended up on the Staten Island Ferry to his wife’s cousin’s home. She opened the door and screamed when she saw him. He told her, ‘It’s me, Jeff!’ She thought he was a monster. She was able to reach his wife. And then he had to find his way home. On foot. He must have walked a billion miles that day.
“Last time I went to New York, I visited the Ground Zero Memorial. It’s very well protected, and it offers different things to view, to see, a place to pray.”
Chaim Lauer, Arnona, Jerusalem (aliyah in 2021):
“I was getting on a bus to come into Manhattan. I heard about the first crash while waiting for the bus. On the bus, another passenger had a radio and said the second tower was hit. I said out loud, ‘We are at war!’ The other passengers looked at me as if I were crazy. Most did not understand that we were… and still are… at war.”
Florence Schleifer, Karnei Shomron (aliyah in 2011):
“I lived in Baltimore, Maryland, and was working as a kindergarten teacher in a boys’ yeshiva. My daughter Chanina lived on the Lower East Side. She was taking her two- and three-year-old to play group when they heard a huge boom. They were able to see the Twin Towers from where they were standing – the smoke, the fire, everything.
“My daughter stood on the street as people looked in shock, screaming, ‘Oh my God, a plane just accidentally flew into the World Trade Center!’ Chanina looked at the crowd and exclaimed, ‘That’s no accident. That’s terrorism.’
“Chanina called my husband, who contacted me at school, and then we found out about the plane that flew into the Pentagon. The principal announced, ‘Everybody’s getting picked up.’ As far as we knew, we were sitting ducks. Planes are flying, we’re near Washington, and we’re a boys’ school with hundreds of little Jewish boys.
“Meanwhile, in Israel, our daughter Shira, who lives in Jerusalem’s Har Nof, was having her first baby and was in the hospital. Suddenly the medical staff came into their room and said, ‘You’re American?’ They said, ‘Yeah. They said, “There’s an attack in America,” and they turned on the TV. Our grandson was born after a while. His birthday is 9/11.
“My two granddaughters, after witnessing the crashes firsthand in New York, worked with therapists to process what they had seen. They had them drawing pictures of big buildings on fire and planes flying into buildings.”
Schleifer ends her recollection on a positive note: “And after they made aliyah and grew up – both girls became soldiers in the IDF!”
