US commemorates 25 years since 9/11 terror attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:26:00 UTC
00:26:00 KST

US commemorates 25 years since 9/11 terror attack
September 11, 2026
Commemorations are being held across the United States on Friday to mark the twenty-fifth anniversary of the deadliest attacks ever carried out on US soil.
Events are taking place at the sites of the attacks — in New York City, Washington DC and Shanksville, Pennsylvania — and elsewhere around the nation to honor the 2,977 people killed that day.
The main ceremony is being held in New York, where Islamists from the terror group al-Qaeda flew two hijacked commercial airliners into the twin towers of the city's famous World Trade Center — a symbol of American economic power.
New York Mayor Zoran Mamdani, Governor Kathy Hochul and former Presidents Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden are in attendance as well as current Vice President JD Vance.
Friday's event will feature wreath layings and vigils, punctuated by several moments of silence, marking the moments of impact and collapse and honoring the memory of the dead.
Family members will read out the names of the people killed that day, as well as six that were killed in a 1993 al-Qaeda bombing in the building's basement.
This year, the ceremony also acknowledged more than 600 firefighters who died from illness related to the toxic air and dust emanating from the burning structures of the site.
In Washington, President Donald Trump spoke at a ceremony at the Pentagon, the symbol of the US' military might, which was also targeted with a hijacked airliner that day.
In his remarks, Trump referenced his ongoing war in Iran, saying the US will never forget 9/11, adding, "that's why we fight today."
Other administration officials are headed to the Flight 93 National Memorial in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. It was there that passengers stormed the cockpit of a hijacked United Airlines jet in midflight, forcing the plane to crash in an empty field and keeping attackers from hitting their final target, the US Capitol.
EU and NATO allies honor victims
European Union and NATO allies also commemorated the event.
European Council President Antonio Costa on Friday expressed admiration for "victims, their families and those who rushed to help others."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen underscored the strength of democracies, pointing out that the attackers had failed to rob democratic nations of their freedom.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte posted on X that allies had, "stood together" that day, "invoking Article 5 for the first and only time in NATO's history."
Rutte added, "America's friends and allies in NATO stood with you then and we stand with you today."
US President Trump has often threatened to attack NATO allies and voiced doubt about alliance members' commitments to helping the US in times of need.
The world after 9/11
The audacious attack quite literally changed the world, stunning the US and triggering a chain of events that impact people's everyday lives to this day.
The incident sparked the Bush administration's "War on Terror," which drew the US into its longest-ever military conflict in Afghanistan and shattered trust in the nation when Bush insisted on invading Iraq, which was not involved in 9/11.
America's reputation suffered as a result of extrajudicial policies such as renditioning and "enhanced interrogation" at secret CIA prisons, as well as its creation of a detention facility in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, where suspected terrorists were held for years in dystopian conditions without trial.
The aftereffects of the wars are still costing the US billions and the debacle of Iraq irreparably damaged the solidarity the US was shown in the immediate aftermath of 9/11.
The attacks changed airport security measures, as well as the US government's ability to surveil citizens — leading to the creation of the Department of Homeland Security, one of the biggest agencies in the US government, and passage of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) and the USA Patriot Act.
Further, the event dramatically changed attitudes towards Muslims.
There was much controversy this year over whether Mamdani, for instance, should attend the New York ceremony. Republicans argued against it but the mayor insisted he would do so out of love of city and country and respect for those who died that day and in the years after.
This year's ceremony honors those who have died in the aftermath of the attack
Mamdani's election as mayor shows just how far parts of the country have come since that day and the young Muslim Democrat this week opened a new chapter in the story of 9/11 by releasing tens of thousands of documents showing that leaders had hidden information about the toxicity of air in the city after the attack.
As asbestos and toxic smoke blanketed the city for months officials told residents and clean-up workers that they had nothing to fear.
In fact, the toxicity of dust, rubble and smoldering plastic and metal has led to at least 9,400 additional deaths according a federal medical monitoring program.

Timber Giant Accused of Forging Environmental Records to Hide Toxic Emissions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:26:00 UTC
00:26:00 KST

Reported by
Romanian prosecutors have charged two subsidiaries of Kronospan, one of the world’s largest producers of wood-based panels, with venting carcinogenic gases into residential areas and falsifying environmental records to conceal the pollution.
The indictment, sent to trial following a two-year investigation, targets Kronospan Trading and Kronochem, along with two company employees tasked with environmental oversight. Authorities accuse the firms of releasing nitrogen oxides and formaldehyde - hazardous chemicals used in timber processing - at levels up to three times the legal threshold between 2022 and 2023.
According to prosecutors, the industrial giant maintained the illusion of regulatory compliance through fraud. Whenever internal monitoring registered illegal pollution spikes, staff allegedly withheld the findings and repeated testing until favorable numbers were achieved.
“Only values favorable to the company were transmitted to state authorities, thus creating the appearance of compliance,” prosecutors said in a statement. An expert report compiled for the investigation warned that the unmonitored chemical releases were severe enough to "endanger human life or health," particularly in neighboring urban neighborhoods.
The case stems from a 2023 raid of Kronospan’s local headquarters after authorities uncovered suspicious discrepancies in the company's self-reported emissions data. Kronospan operates two massive manufacturing hubs in Romania, processing millions of cubic meters of raw timber annually into paneling exported across Europe.
In a statement provided to OCCRP, Kronospan rejected all allegations and expressed confidence that the company would be cleared in court.
"Both companies operate using Best Available Techniques on all production lines and have invested over 80 million euros in de-pollution equipment," the company said, adding that emissions undergo continuous monitoring in its on-site laboratories.
A Romanian court will now evaluate the prosecution's evidence against Kronospan's defense to determine whether the timber producer subverted federal environmental safeguards and exposed nearby residents to toxic risk.

25 years after 9/11, America remembers as death toll from aftermath keeps rising

- The death toll continues to rise, with over 450 firefighters who responded during the attacks dying from illnesses linked to toxic exposure.
- Efforts continue to preserve the memory and lessons of 9/11 through education, funding for the 9/11 Memorial and Museum, and improvements in emergency response systems by first responders.
AI generated
NEW YORK – A quarter-century after the Sept 11, 2001, terror attacks, families returned to the World Trade Center site to read aloud the names of the dead, marking a milestone anniversary of a tragedy that reshaped America.
Mourners and survivors gathered around the twin waterfall pools that mark the footprints of the two towers in Lower Manhattan for the sombre ceremony.
Joining for the day of remembrance were US Vice-President J.D. Vance, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and former mayors Rudy Giuliani and Mike Bloomberg.
All of the living US presidents, aside from President Donald Trump, were also in attendance: Joe Biden, Barack Obama, George W. Bush and Bill Clinton.
As has been the tradition, family members read out the names of the 2,983 people killed on 9/11, as well as the Feb 26, 1993, World Trade Center bombing.
Beginning at 8.46am, six moments of silence were observed at the times when each of the towers was struck, when each fell, when the Pentagon was attacked and when United Airlines Flight 93 crashed.
The 17-minute period between the north and south towers being hit defined an era and a nation, and 25 years later, an estimated 100 million Americans – nearly 30 per cent of the population – are too young to remember that day.
Trump attended a ceremony in the morning on Sept 11 at the Pentagon, honouring the 184 people who died there on 9/11 when a hijacked plane crashed into the Arlington, Virginia, building.
Trump vowed the US would never forget the attacks and would continue to “fight”.
“Today we renew the sacred oath that we first swore in their names a quarter of a century ago. We will never, ever forget. That’s why we fight today,” he said.
“We don’t have a choice. There can only be victory,” added Trump. “We fight hard. We fight to win.”
For the first time, this year’s Lower Manhattan ceremony includes an acknowledgement of how the toll of the attacks is still growing.
After the reading of the names, a seventh moment of silence will be observed, honouring those who died years later from illnesses and injuries linked to the aftermath of the attacks.
It is a recognition that, even as the morning the twin towers collapsed passes from living memory for more Americans, its consequences are still unfolding.
Lives still being lost
Nowhere is that more deeply felt than in the New York City Fire Department (FDNY), which lost 343 members when the towers fell.
In the 25 years since, 453 members have died from cancers, lung diseases and other illnesses linked to the toxic dust and debris that blanketed Lower Manhattan.
Fire Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore, 32 years old on 9/11, was an EMS Academy instructor in Queens who got the call and went to work. She now leads a department where only about 700 of its 17,000 members were there that day.
“What we have found so far is the fire department continues to live that day,” Bonsignore said in an interview.
Firefighters who were children when the towers fell now work alongside the dwindling number who responded that morning.
New recruits inherit the stories of people they never knew and a skyline they never saw. And the number lost to the attacks’ long aftereffects continues to rise.
According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the World Trade Center Health Program now cares for more than 145,000 survivors and first responders, with enrolment swelling by roughly 10,000 people in each of the past two years.
More than 57,000 members have had a certified cancer diagnosis.
“We expect to continue seeing cancer and other serious conditions that have longer latency periods,” CDC director Erica Schwartz said at a Sept 3 event commemorating the work of the World Trade Center Health Program. “That is one reason this 25th anniversary carries such meaning.”
Never forget
Speaker of the New York City Council Julie Menin credits her experience in organising to rebuild Lower Manhattan as the reason she is in public service.
At the time, she was a lawyer and owner of Vine, a restaurant and catering company, living not far from the site of the attacks with her family and parents. They remained downtown, with Menin founding a non-profit dedicated to helping small businesses and becoming a founding trustee of the 9/11 Memorial & Museum.
Menin helped secure US$1 million (S$1.3 million) in funding in 2026 for the institution to expand education and outreach for New York City students.
She wants them to learn about the tragic events, as well as “the acts of heroism of the first responders, and the unity that really brought the city together, and simple acts of kindness that happened in those days and weeks after 9/11”.
First responders continue to adopt lessons learnt from the attacks.
The FDNY and EMS have made changes to their communications systems and technologies used to locate members in emergencies. And they continue to work to keep memories of that day alive.
“You own it, and that’s how we have been able to keep this alive,” said Bonsignore. “And I feel confident that they will own that day, like I own it, having been there firsthand.” BLOOMBERG

F-35 jets: fixed-price scandal will have no immediate consequences
A Swiss parliamentary report on the absence of a fixed-price agreement for the procurement of new F-35 fighter jets from the US has sparked controversy. For now, however, no changes are expected, while former Defence Minister Viola Amherd has yet to comment.
Centre-right parties, which hold a majority in parliament, have made clear that they are not keen on a parliamentary committee of inquiry (CPI) into the procurement issue, while the Greens are pushing for this solution.
According to the House of Representative’s Committee on the Examination of Public Accounts (GPK-N), no flat-rate fixed price has been agreed with the US, as stated in a report published on Tuesday. The Swiss defence ministry has repeatedly assured the public that 36 American-made F-35A fighter jets would be delivered at a fixed price of CHF6 billion ($7.5 billion).
The new parliamentary report has sparked concerns in all parties in Switzerland. “The impact on Switzerland’s image is catastrophic,” Green lawmaker Clarence Chollet told the Keystone-ATS news agency.
Swiss People’s Party leader Thomas Aeschi declared: “We need to ask and clarify some fundamental questions. Who was in charge of the dossier? Was the law firm supervised, or did it act independently?”
For its part, the centre-right Radical-Liberal Party is calling for the restoration of trust between the government and parliament. Lawmakers must have access to clear information when the process is of such importance, it says.
More
Swiss government criticised for F-35 price failings
No legal consequences
As for any legal consequences, Andreas Stöckli, professor of constitutional and administrative law at the University of Fribourg says “it is difficult to assess whether federal administration staff face any risk”.
“The requirements for financial liability on the part of Swiss administration staff are stringent,” he says.
It would be necessary, for example, to prove that there was unlawful conduct, and that the act was committed intentionally or through gross negligence, Stöckli told Keystone-ATS. In such a case, separate legal proceedings would have to be initiated. For the same reasons, the law firms involved in the F-35 procurement process should not be subject to legal proceedings either.
More
Renewed controversy in Switzerland over US fighter jets – explained
Amherd remains silent
When contacted by Keystone-ATS, Viola Amherd said she had already commented on the matter and would not be making any further statements regarding the allegations raised in the report.
The former defence minister from canton Valais, who is a member of the Centre Party, is unlikely to be held responsible, even though the negotiations relating to the purchase contract fell within her remit. According to the Greens, “such a fiasco cannot be attributed to the responsibility of a single person”.
Vincent Martenet, a lecturer in constitutional law at the University of Lausanne, noted that “members of the Federal Council enjoy absolute immunity for statements made before parliament”. In short, there remains only one option: a political one, via the creation of an parliamentary committee of inquiry (CPI) into the affair.

A CPI? Unlikely
The Greens are exploring this possibility and could put forward a motion during the autumn session of parliament in Bern.
However, the chances of persuading parties on the right to establish a CPI are slim. According to Pierre-Alain Fridez, a former Socialist lawmaker, “most parliamentarians will feel that the contracts have been misinterpreted. I fear they will stop there,” he said told the 24 heures newspaper.
The Social Democrats, for their part, expect the Federal Council to investigate whether any false statements liable to criminal prosecution were made in what it calls a colossal fiasco. The left is therefore likely to refuse to consider the request for an additional credit of almost CHF400 million for the 30 F-35s that are planned.
According to parliamentarian Benoît Gaillard, more time is needed “to shed light on the matter”.
“In our democratic state, it is a disgrace that a procurement worth over CHF6 billion, grudgingly accepted by the public, has been so badly managed,” said Clarence Chollet.

Syria says 9 detained Assad-era pilots carried out strikes during 3,200 flight hours since 2011
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:22:31 UTC
00:22:31 KST

Laith Al-Jnaidi and Mohammad Sio
11 September 2026•Update: 11 September 2026
Preliminary investigations with nine detained pilots showed that they carried out airstrikes targeting several areas during more than 3,200 flight hours logged since the start of the Syrian revolution in 2011, a source at Syria’s Interior Ministry said Friday.
The remarks were carried by state-run Alikhbariah TV a day after authorities announced the arrest of the nine pilots in the western province of Latakia over their involvement in “war crimes against the Syrian people.”
The pilots used different types of military aircraft, most notably Mi-24 attack helicopters, Su-22 fighter jets, MiG-29s and MiG-21s, the source said.
The strikes particularly targeted towns in Eastern Ghouta in the Damascus countryside, Aleppo and its northern countryside, Deir ez-Zor and surrounding areas in the east, and the Hama countryside in central Syria, the source added.
Their missions included combat sorties, “bombing revolutionary positions, populated areas, facilities and vital sites,” as well as close air support, reconnaissance and target identification, according to the source.
The source said they were also responsible for equipping helicopters and fighter jets with various types of explosive munitions and carrying out the required technical checks and operational preparations before takeoff.
Their duties also included identifying locations and coordinates, preparing target data and supplying it to pilots, directing them during missions, and transporting former regime officers to combat zones and military positions, the source added.
A Thursday statement by Latakia Internal Security Commander Abdulaziz al-Ahmad said a series of security operations conducted in cooperation with the Counterterrorism Branch led to the arrest of the pilots following surveillance, tracking, intelligence gathering and investigations.
He said the detainees had participated, according to the investigations and available information, in “numerous crimes and violations against the Syrian people,” exploiting their military positions and expertise in combat and helicopter aviation.
The statement said the operations they took part in included bombardment and attacks that caused large numbers of deaths and injuries, inflicted extensive damage on cities and towns, displaced residents and destroyed homes, facilities and civilian infrastructure.
The detainees were identified as Brig. Gen. Manhal Anwar Saleh, Brig. Gen. Sami Ibrahim Mahmoud, Brig. Gen. Ghiyath Ali al-Rahiyah, Col. Issa Ezzeddine Khaddur, Col. Marwan Salah Nafesh, Col. Bashar Samir Wannous, Lt. Col. Ayham Hamza Aliya, Capt. Ayham Ahmad Daoud and Capt. Ammar Issa Junaidi.
Al-Ahmad said the arrests were part of efforts to pursue anyone found responsible for crimes against Syrians and ensure that those implicated are referred to the competent judiciary.
Syrian authorities periodically announce the arrest of people accused of committing violations against civilians during the years of the revolution, which began in March 2011 before opposition forces entered Damascus and toppled the Assad regime on Dec. 8, 2024.

‘Tool of oppression’: Rising number of UK pro-Palestine voices debanked
The mother of a Palestine Action prisoner, the politician George Galloway and a leftist news outlet are among those speaking up.
The mother of a Palestine Action prisoner has said she was refused a mortgage due to “adverse media”, as more pro-Palestine voices in the United Kingdom are opening up about their experiences of “debanking”.
Emma Kamio, a small business owner in south Wales, was denied a remortgage with Lloyds on her commercial properties in April due to “adverse media.”

The decision “devastated” her, she told Al Jazeera. “It has put me in a difficult position, one where I have relinquished my responsibilities [in the family business] and let my sister pick up the slack.”
Despite the setback, she said business was no longer central in her life.
“I’ve got one goal and that’s to get my girl out of prison,” she said.
Her daughter Leona “Ellie” Kamio has also been affected. In February 2025, while the 30-year-old nursery teacher was held on remand awaiting trial, Kamio was debanked by Lloyds Bank – meaning the financial institution suddenly closed her bank accounts without explanation.
George Galloway, the Scotland-born politician and broadcaster, said last week that Bank of Scotland, owned by the Lloyds Banking Group, closed his personal account without explanation or notice after 39 years.
“My parliamentary and old age pensions are paid into these accounts,” he wrote on X. “The mortgage on our family home is paid out of them. The mortgage is with them.”
In late June, when Lloyds debanked The Canary, the left-wing news outlet wrote that the bank “has not explained why it has taken this action … despite multiple communications from us”.
More recently, the Pakistani-British writer Tariq Ali on Wednesday said a bank, which he did not name, refused to receive a transfer from his account due to his “opinions”.
“My opinions can only mean those on one subject: Palestine,” he wrote on X.
In the case of Kamio, her account was closed before the UK proscribed Palestine Action as a “terrorist” organisation. It was also before she was convicted of criminal damage in connection with a raid on a factory operated by Israeli defence firm Elbit in Filton, Bristol, in August 2024 – and sentenced as a “terrorist”. Four of six Palestine Action activists convicted of criminal damage, including Kamio, are seeking to appeal their unprecedented sentencing.
Their appeal submission argues that the judge was wrong in law to find that the non-terrorism offence of criminal damage in their case had a terror connection.
Since Palestine Action was outlawed, more than 2,700 people have been arrested under the Terrorism Act at rallies and demonstrations in support of the group.
A spokesperson for Lloyds said the bank does not close customer accounts or make lending decisions “based on political or personal beliefs. Our decisions are based on relevant laws, regulation, account conditions, or lending requirements. We’re unable to comment on individual cases.”
“We have reached a point where debanking pro-Palestine voices has become systemic,” Anas Mustapha, at the campaign group Cage which advocates against legal abuses from UK counter-terrorism strategies, told Al Jazeera.
He said Cage was debanked more than a decade ago, “with no explanation ever given”.
“Since then we’ve watched the same pattern extend further, with activists being penalised for their politics, and now the families of people jailed for opposing a genocide.”
‘Tool of oppression’
The issue last made the headlines in late 2023, when Muslims in the UK found a rare common link with Reform leader Nigel Farage.
Anas Altikriti, head of the London-based Cordoba Foundation think-tank, was among those affected by debanking, which he said was being used as a “tool of oppression.”
“This is happening on an industrial scale, to thousands upon thousands of people,” the British entrepreneur, who has also been debanked several times, told Al Jazeera on Friday.
More than 450,000 bank accounts were closed each year, according to The Telegraph.
Altikriti argued that the attack on the World Trade Center in New York on September 11, 2001, marked the beginning of the “commercialisation of the term terrorism”.
Twenty-five years on, the term “slides off the tongue so easily for any kind of adverse opinion,” he said. “The problem is that once that term is on record, it’s always on record. It’s fixed. It’s always there and it impacts your entire life.”
Altikriti was himself labelled a “terrorist” in a banking database following a claim from the United Arab Emirates that was never independently verified by UK authorities. The British citizen said the term has not made his country safer because it is being used “in order to satisfy certain political agendas”.
“If this can happen to me, it can happen to anyone,” he added.

Russian losses in the war with Ukraine.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:22:12 UTC
00:22:12 KST

This publication is divided into two parts:
Bi-weekly Summary. A text summary, updated every two weeks, in which we report on what we have learned about recent losses and the frontline events that led to the deaths of Russian soldiers.
Interactive Infographics. The second part provides visualisations of the losses since the start of the war, showing, for example, where the dead served or which regions they came from. We update the data for these graphics, while the accompanying text is refreshed but remains largely the same.
A detailed description of our method for estimating total deaths using Probate Registry data can be found at this link.
Last update to the named list: September 11, 2026.
Last update to the Probate Registry estimate: May 9, 2026; estimate as of late December 2025
Full named list and a map of verified losses is available here: 200.zona.media.
For this update, we have added over 6,000 names to our database. This spike is not related to the current situation on the frontline, but rather to the fact that we have mass-processed posts about missing soldiers and added those whose deaths have been confirmed through the Probate Registry and other sources.
Important note: as before, we do not count those missing in action. All these added people have died and are either buried or recognised as deceased in the absence of a body. These are the same kinds of records as the rest, we simply use a public missing-person post as a source for the soldier’s full name and details, and then check whether their death has been confirmed.
In the data we’ve collected, there are still relatively few fatalities recorded for 2026: right now, we have only 6,600 records of Russian military personnel with known dates of death who died this year, and since the last update, we added 631 people. For comparison: in 2024, we know of 95,600 deaths, with 1,692 added in the last two weeks; 59,700 deaths for 2025, with 3,613 added. In other words, the losses for this year make up a very small portion of our update.
Why are the recorded losses for this year so low in comparison? There are several reasons, but they all come down to one: the nature of the war has changed. Combat operations are being conducted in a strip known as the “grey zone” or “kill zone”, evacuating bodies from this territory is virtually impossible until full control is established, and the front is moving at an increasingly slower pace.
A backlog is also accumulating on our end: there are so many obituaries that we do not have time to process them all.
But the main reason for the lag in our numbers is that the death of any given individual is being registered with a growing delay. And to show how this happens, we selected one of the lists published by the Ukrainian project “I Want to Live” (“Khochu Zhit”).
The project posted this leak on April 17. The post claims that the 5,007 names are inmates recruited into the Russian army “in one of the months of this year.” We verified that at least 4,000 men from this list actually exist, and from then on we worked specifically with this shortened version of the leak.
The first check showed that almost all of these people were alive as of January 1, 2026.
On April 26, we cross-referenced this list for the first time with the Probate registry and state databases. This check revealed that 118 people had died in 2026.
Here is the result of the next check on May 20: the number of confirmed deaths increased by 80, with the majority of them occurring between January and March.
The third check, about a month later, already showed 352 dead. The trend continued: the people from the “I Want to Live” list were dying in January-March.
We did the latest check just before publishing this update, on September 10. Now, there are already 807 people on the list of the dead, which is one in five out of the 4,000.
In the first three months of 2026, 682 people died, or 84.5% of the known losses: 81 in January, 316 in February, and 285 in March. And only 125 people (15.5%) died in May–August.
In our database, built from publicly available verifiable sources like obituaries, only 112 of the 807 people are present (that is one in seven). It is obvious that public information about deaths appears even later than the official registration of death.
It is evident that over time the graph grows “upwards”, meaning we are mostly recording the deaths of people who actually died back in winter and early spring. Naturally, the data we’ve collected cannot be exhaustive, and we expect that information about the dead from this list will continue to be added. We do not expect to see the final picture of these losses for another two years.
How can it be explained that people from this list suddenly began dying en masse in the winter of 2026? First, there is no doubt that these people definitely died in the war. From obituaries, we know they were assigned to various military units: for example, the 254th Motorised Rifle regiment, the 15th Motorised Rifle brigade, the 5th Motorised Rifle brigade, and others. This means it’s impossible to tie these losses to a specific military formation. Nor is there data about particularly fierce battles in January–March: the intensity of combat operations did not decrease, but neither did it increase.
The simplest explanation: these people were indeed recruited over a short period of time (not necessarily within one month, as “I Want to Live” claims), assigned to assault units after brief training, and thrown into battle. The relatively small share of deaths after March suggests that the majority of these servicemen were either killed, severely wounded, or found a way to leave the assault troops. And new reinforcements came to take their place.
The map below shows the distribution of casualties across Russia’s regions. These are absolute figures and have not been adjusted for population or number of military units.
You can filter the map to show total losses, losses by branch of service, or the home regions of mobilised soldiers who were killed.
In most cases, official reports or visual cues like uniforms and insignia allow us to determine a soldier’s branch of service, or how he came to be in the army (mobilised, volunteer, prisoner, etc.).
The chart below compares these different groups of servicemen.
From early summer and into the mid-fall season of 2022, volunteers bore the brunt of the losses, which is strikingly different from the situation in the initial stage of the war: in winter and early spring, the Airborne Forces suffered the greatest damage, followed by the Motorised Rifle troops.
By the end of 2022 and the beginning of the next year, losses among prisoners recruited into the Wagner PMC increased markedly. They were formed into “assault groups” to overwhelm Ukrainian positions near Bakhmut.
By March 2023, prisoners became the largest category of war losses. After the capture of Bakhmut, there have been no cases of mass use of prisoners so far.
By September 2024, volunteers once again emerged as the largest category among the KIA. This shift reflects a cumulative effect: prison recruitment had significantly waned, no new mobilisation had been announced, yet the stream of volunteers continued unabated.
By September 11, 2026, the death of 7,656 officers of the Russian army and other security agencies had been confirmed.
The proportion of officer deaths among overall casualties has steadily declined since the conflict began. In the early stages, when professional contract soldiers formed the main invasion force, officers accounted for up to 10% of fatalities. By November 2024, this figure had dropped to between 2–3%—a shift that reflects both evolving combat tactics and the intensive recruitment of volunteer infantry, who suffer casualty rates many times higher than their commanding officers.
Officers killed in Ukraine
To date, the deaths of 15 Russian generals have been officially confirmed: five Lieutenant Generals, seven Major Generals, two who had retired from active service, and one Ukrainian SBU general who had fled to Russia.
Lieutenant General Oleg Tsokov, deputy commander of the Southern Military District, was killed in July 2023—the first officer of that rank to die in the war. In December 2024, Lieutenant General Igor Kirillov, head of the Nuclear, Biological, and Chemical (NBC) Protection Troops, was killed by a bomb in Moscow. Lieutenant General Yaroslav Moskalik, a senior officer in the General Staff’s Main Operational Directorate, was killed by a car bomb in a Moscow suburb in April 2025. In December 2025, Lieutenant General Fanil Sarvarov, head of the Operational Training Directorate of the Russian General Staff, was killed in Moscow by a car bomb. On March 31, 2026, Lieutenant General Alexander Otroschenko, commander of the mixed aviation corps of the Northern Fleet, was killed in the crash of an An-26 transport aircraft in Crimea.
Two deputy army commanders, Major General Andrei Sukhovetsky (41st Army) and Major General Vladimir Frolov (8th Army), were killed in the first weeks of the war. In June 2022, Major General Roman Kutuzov was killed in an attack on a troop formation.
Major General Sergei Goryachev, chief of staff of the 35th Combined Arms Army, was killed in June 2023 while commanding forces against the Ukrainian counter-offensive in the Zaporizhzhia region. In November 2023, Major General Vladimir Zavadsky, deputy commander of the 14th Army Corps, was killed near the village of Krynky.
In November 2024, Major General Pavel Klimenko, commander of the 5th Separate Motorised Rifle Brigade (formerly the “Oplot” Brigade of the so-called Donetsk People’s Republic), was fatally wounded by an FPV drone.
In July 2025, a strike on the headquarters of the 155th Naval Infantry Brigade killed at least six officers, including the Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Russian Navy, Mikhail Gudkov.
The two retired generals on the list are Kanamat Botashev, a pilot who had been dismissed for crashing a fighter jet and was fighting for Wagner PMC when his Su-25 was shot down in May 2022, and Andrei Golovatsky, a former Interior Ministry general serving an 8.5-year prison sentence (but maintained his rank) who was killed in June 2024.
On March 17, 2026, SBU Major General Volodymyr Lyapkin was killed in the Kherson region. Until February 2014, Lyapkin headed a department in the Ukrainian special services, but after the victory of the Maidan revolution, he fled to Russia. After the war began, he served in the occupation administration of Kherson and then transferred to the “Bars-33” unit.
The date of death is known in 231,300 cases. While this data does not capture the full daily reality of the war, it does suggest which periods saw the most intense fighting.
Please note that data for the most recent months is most incomplete and will change significantly in the future.
The age of the deceased is mentioned in 234,600 reports. For the first six months of the war, when the fighting was done by the regular army, the 21-23 age group accounted for the most deaths.
Volunteers and mobilised men are significantly older: people voluntarily go to war over 30, and the mobilised are generally over 25.

UK to expand settlement sanctions to occupied Golan Heights, East Jerusalem
The UK government intends to include the illegal Jewish settlements in the occupied Golan Heights of Syria and East Jerusalem in the sanctions regime it is imposing on the settlements in the occupied West Bank, The New Arab has learned.
On Tuesday, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced that the UK is preparing to ban the entry of goods from illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank into British markets. He confirmed that financial and banking service transactions with these settlements would also be prohibited, alongside additional sanctions on settlers and contributors who support settlement activity in the West Bank, acknowledging that the region is facing ethnic cleansing committed by settlers he described as "terrorists".
However, the foreign secretary did not mention at the time the Israeli settlement movement in the Golan Heights, which Israel occupied by force during the June 1967 war.
Informed sources at the British Foreign and Commonwealth Office stated that these measures "will also include Israeli settlements in the Golan Heights and East Jerusalem". The New Arab has also learned that the relevant ministries have begun working on establishing the sanctions regime so that it encompasses all illegal Jewish settlements in the Golan and East Jerusalem.
British markets import wine produced in the occupied Syrian territory, a practice that anti-settlement activists in the UK have long demanded be banned.
Since occupying the Golan Heights in the 1967 war, Israel has established 34 settlements, housing 30,000 settlers. According to international law, these settlements are entirely illegal. The Israeli government announced in December 2024 its aim of doubling the number of settlers in the occupied Golan Heights, clearly stating that its long-term goal is to settle 100,000 residents there by 2030.
Anti-settlement activists welcomed the expansion of the British sanctions regime to the occupied Golan, noting that it reflects "consistency" in the government's policy toward settlement activity.
In statements to The New Arab, Chris Doyle, Director of the Council for Arab-British Understanding (CAABU), described the move as a “very good and highly significant step”, noting that successive British governments "have long declared that it (the Golan) is also an occupied territory". The CAABU head also warned of the "massive impact" of illegal settlement activity on the Syrian population in the Golan Heights.
Doyle added that including the Golan settlements in the sanctions confirms "the British government's desire for its positions to be consistent”.
Regarding the inclusion of East Jerusalem settlements, Doyle said it should not be taken for granted because, according to international law and resolutions, East Jerusalem is part of the occupied West Bank. Israel, however, considers East Jerusalem separate from the occupied territories, Doyle highlighted
The UK's intention to extend the sanctions regime is expected to unsettle the administration of US President Donald Trump, who in March 2019 recognised Israel's claim of sovereignty over the occupied Syrian Golan.

15:21:18 UTC
00:21:18 KST

Russia has a bear problem — attacks are reported almost daily. Officials are killing ‘potentially conflict-prone’ bears and want greater powers to drastically reduce their population.
Reports of brown bear attacks on people have poured in almost daily from across Russia since late summer 2026. Here are just a few fatal cases from the past three weeks:
- August 19. A bear attacked a 29-year-old tourist near the village of Artybash in the Turochaksky district, Altai Republic. At night, the bear entered the tent where she was sleeping with her fiancé, dragged her into the forest, and killed her. Komsomolskaya Pravda reported that he had proposed to her before the trip. She worked for the Emergency Situations Ministry’s Main Directorate for the Novosibirsk region.
- August 31. Two women from the Yeniseysky district in Krasnoyarsk Krai went missing while picking mushrooms near the settlement of Podtesovo. Their bodies were found on September 2 showing signs of a bear attack.
- September 6. A bear killed a 40-year-old man as he walked through the woods in the settlement of Yuzhno-Yeniseysky, Krasnoyarsk Krai.
- September 7. In the Zakamensky district of the Republic of Buryatia, a bear attacked a local resident about 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from the village of Khurtaga while he and his wife were out moving their cows. His wife managed to run away and call for help, and the bear was eventually driven off, but the man had sustained injuries too severe to survive.
Who’s to blame?
Authorities attribute the bears’ growing presence near populated areas — and the resulting threat to people — to the animals’ seasonal activity, a shortage of natural food sources, easy access to food waste, and a growing bear population. How well these explanations hold up scientifically remains unclear.
A poor harvest of berries, mushrooms, and pine nuts in the taiga has forced bears to search for food elsewhere, the Russian news outlet Kommersant Sibir reports. Kemerovo Governor Ilya Serdyuk, for his part, has suggested that wildfires in Krasnoyarsk Krai are pushing bears into the Kuzbass.
Bears approaching people is a familiar problem in Kamchatka, but many other regions have not previously encountered anything like it, Vladimir Gordienko, a wildlife biologist and researcher at the Kronotsky State Nature Reserve, told the Russian state news agency RIA Novosti. Bear encounters have nonetheless been recorded across Russia, mostly in its Asian part.
“This is an unusual situation, when this kind of behavior — bears acting erratically — is being recorded simultaneously across many territories,” said Nikolai Maltsev, head of the Krasnoyarsk Krai State Hunting Oversight Agency.
Dmitry Sergeev, a regulation expert at Khakassia’s Natural Resources Ministry, also calls the situation “abnormal.” He said the bear population exceeds the norm. “They don’t have enough space, so they’re coming out directly to people,” he said, adding that this has been happening “for the second year now, and I don’t think it will be the last.” He did not specify how, or how precisely, the animal population had been counted.
How many bears are there in Russia
Russia’s brown bear population totals 307,900, according to the Natural Resources Ministry. The largest populations are in Krasnoyarsk and Khabarovsk Krais, Kamchatka, and the Irkutsk region. The ministry estimates that the country’s bear population has grown 2.3 times since 1990.
How are authorities proposing to deal with the bears?
Authorities have declared a state of heightened alert in several districts of the Kemerovo region, in Bratsk in the Irkutsk region, in Krasnoyarsk and several districts of Krasnoyarsk Krai, in the town of Abaza in Khakassia, in the Charyshsky district of Altai Krai, and in Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky, citing bears approaching populated areas and attacking people. In the Turochaksky district of the Republic of Altai, where the tourist was killed, officials have imposed a curfew and changed school schedules.
Since September 7, authorities have banned entry into Krasnoyarskiye Stolby National Park after dark. They are also urging Krasnoyarsk residents and tourists to avoid the remote parts of Tatyshev Island, where a bear was spotted, and have introduced access restrictions at Tunkinsky National Park in Buryatia and the Altai Biosphere Reserve.
Authorities are shooting bears that threaten people. The Republic of Altai’s Ministry of Natural Resources and Ecology announced that more than 50 bears have been killed since the attack on the tourist, with licenses issued to shoot 157 more. Krasnoyarsk Krai’s Ministry of Natural Resources and Forestry announced in early September that more than 180 “potentially conflict-prone individuals” had been killed in the region, and the head of Krasnoyarsk’s State Hunting Oversight Agency said 60 bears had been shot in the vicinity of Krasnoyarsk alone.
Regional authorities say these measures are not enough. The governor of the Magadan region, where bears appear in populated areas every year, has called for changing the rules governing bear population control. “A bear that comes into a populated area will pass its new skills on to the next generation. Something needs to be done about this,” he said in an interview with RIA Novosti on September 9. It is unclear what his claim about the animals’ behavior is based on. No such phenomenon is described in the scientific literature. The governor called current legislation outdated and said officials need to be “thinking about the people who could be killed or injured.”
On September 11, Russia’s Natural Resources Ministry announced that it is collecting proposals from the regions on changing the laws governing bear population control.
If the situation does not change and the winter of 2026–2027 turns out to be harsh, Tuva’s Natural Resources Ministry predicts, “a second wave of hungry, non-hibernating bears will hit us in the spring,” Kommersant Sibir writes.
Killing the animals alone will not solve the problem, experts warn. Wholesale extermination of every bear that turns up near populated areas will not help, Dmitry Taranenko, a candidate of biological sciences and senior researcher at the Institute of Systematics and Ecology of Animals of the Siberian Branch of the Russian Academy of Sciences, told the Russian state news agency TASS.
Kamchatka Governor Vladimir Solodov said bears are approaching people in search of food, although the scientific literature shows that food-seeking accounts for only a small share of encounters. Most happen by chance, far from cities. Regional authorities are focusing on unauthorized waste dumps that can draw bears into populated areas, he told RIA Novosti, and are distributing safety guidelines urging tourists “not to leave food in their tent or behind at the campfire.”

UK lawmakers throw out Bill to legalise assisted dying
- UK MPs rejected a Bill to legalise assisted dying for terminally ill adults by 286 votes to 270 after emotional debates and long parliamentary struggles.
- The proposed law would have allowed adults with less than six months to live to end their lives with medical and expert approval.
- Opponents celebrated the vote, calling it a protection for vulnerable people, while campaigners called it a devastating setback and vowed to continue pushing for change.
AI generated
LONDON – British MPs on Sept 11 rejected a Bill to legalise assisted dying in a knife-edge vote and blow to campaigners in favour of the controversial procedure that is legal in a host of countries including Canada and Switzerland.
Plans to legalise assisted dying have had a long, emotional and ultimately stalled passage through Parliament, with protesters on both sides of the debate regularly demonstrating in Westminster.
Lawmakers in the House of Commons had taken the historic step to back a separate but identical Bill legalising the practice for some terminally ill adults in 2025, before that was scuppered in the unelected upper House of Lords.
The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill was reintroduced this parliamentary session, but MPs struck it down after hours of impassioned debate Sept 11, with 286 voting against and 270 in favour.
The Bill would have allowed adults in England and Wales who have been given less than six months to live and can clearly express a wish to die the option to opt to end their own lives.
They would need the approval of two doctors and an expert panel to make the decision.
‘Scary’
Campaigners against assisted dying celebrated the result, with Gordon Macdonald from the Care Not Killing group calling it a “decisive vote”.
He said MPs had “over the last 24 months seen through the pernicious pretence that this draft legislation was safe and wouldn’t put pressure on vulnerable people to end their lives prematurely”.
Disability rights campaigner Philip Friend, 80, told AFP he was relieved.
“We were really worried about this Bill,” he said, adding opponents saw it as “very dangerous because it didn’t have the safeguards, it didn’t investigate coercion”.
“It was a very, very scary place.”
But outside Parliament, campaigners hoping for the law change wiped away tears and comforted each other.
“This is a devastating setback for dying people,” said charity Dignity in Dying, adding that “this issue is not going away”.
Rebecca Wilcox, the daughter of Esther Rantzen - a high-profile television personality who has a terminal diagnosis - told AFP she was “completely devastated”.
“My mum just described this as a tragic day,” she said, noting one British newspaper had called the previous parliamentary blocking of the Bill “a vandalism of democracy”.
“We will come back and we will do it again and we will still fight in the same dignified, measured way,” she vowed.
Neutral PM
New Ipsos polling in late August 2026 indicated sustained backing for assisted dying among British adults aged 16-75, with two in three supporting the draft legislation.
Ahead of Sept 11, new Prime Minister Andy Burnham had said he would sit out the vote, so as not to “unduly influence the debate”.
Since becoming the country’s leader in July, Burnham has relaunched his years-long push to improve social care for the elderly and vulnerable, and has supported prioritising palliative care.
The controversial draft assisted dying legislation passed in a landmark vote in the House of Commons last June.
But it was torpedoed by more than 1,200 amendments in the upper House of Lords, which was accused of obstructing and delaying the Bill.
Earlier this year, lawmakers in Scotland, where health is a devolved issue, rejected a Bill to legalise assisted dying.
Lawmakers in the self-governing British dependencies of Jersey and the Isle of Man have already approved assisted dying legislation, but the moves are awaiting royal assent. AFP

How a 19-year-old officer defied orders and joined the Six-Day War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:19:10 UTC
00:19:10 KST

In September 1967, three months after the Six-Day War, stories began to emerge that the war itself had left untold. Behind the headlines about the great victory were countless personal stories: split-second decisions, acts of heroism, mistakes, loss and incidents that sounded as though they had been written for a movie.
One such story appeared 59 years ago this week on the front page of Yedioth Ahronoth. Its protagonist was a 19-year-old female officer whose identity was not disclosed. She boarded a half-track without permission, went into battle with an armored unit, disappeared as far as the IDF was concerned, survived an anti-tank shell strike and, when the war was over, was sentenced to 35 days in military detention.
Six days later, the young woman had a name and a face: Second Lt. Anat Kirshner of Netanya. Before long, her story and photograph had appeared in newspapers around the world.
The war caught her on a bus
Kirshner came from a longtime Netanya family. She was a graduate of Tchernichovsky High School and a former member of the Scouts youth movement. Even her name carried a military legacy: Her father, Ezra, who had been a commander in the Irgun, named her Anat in memory of David Raziel, the organization’s commander, who was known by the alias “Maj. Gen. Ben-Anat.”
She served in an armored brigade made up of reservists. Around Israel’s Independence Day in 1967, she completed officers’ training and was sent on leave until she was due to report to her new unit in the IDF Southern Command.
On the morning of June 5, she was due to report for duty in the south. She boarded a bus and set out for her new unit. Midway through the journey, regular radio programming was interrupted. An excited announcer reported that war had broken out.
Anat later said she engaged in a brief “soul-searching.” She decided that at that moment she could be of greater use to the IDF in the unit she already knew. At the first stop, she got off the bus, turned around and headed north, back to the armored brigade.
A helmet, trousers and a half-track
By the time she reached the unit, only about 15 minutes remained before the force was due to depart. The commotion of war was all around her: Engines were running, soldiers were loading equipment and commanders were trying to get the vehicles moving.
One of the soldiers gave her a pair of trousers and a helmet. Anat put them on and climbed aboard one of the half-tracks.
The commanders spotted her and ordered her to get off immediately and report to the unit to which she had been assigned in the Southern Command. It was an explicit order. Anat simply did not obey it. Amid the chaos, no one checked whether she had actually left. The soldiers sitting with her in the half-track chose to remain silent, and the armored column set off with the young officer still aboard.
During the night, the half-tracks and tanks advanced toward the Jordanian border in the Jenin area. By morning, Jordanian forces began firing artillery and mortars at the convoy. In the half-track carrying Anat, one of the soldiers stood up. His steel helmet slipped from his head, and seconds later he was hit and fell. He was the brigade’s first fatality.
The shelling intensified. Soldiers were killed and wounded, and Anat jumped over the side of the half-track and ran with the troops to take cover behind a stone wall. The sights overwhelmed her. She burst into tears but managed to regain her composure and began helping bandage the wounded. One of them, whose hand had been severed, refused to let her treat him. He feared the sight would shock her.
When the battle ended, Anat discovered that Eitan, the brigade’s operations sergeant and one of her close friends, had been killed and that his body was lying by the roadside. She took a gold chain from his body and continued with the force. Her clothes were stained with blood, so she changed into Jordanian military fatigues found in a captured army depot.
'I didn’t want to die'
Later, the unit left one of the cities it had captured and came under heavy shelling. The half-track Anat was riding in was struck by an anti-tank shell. She and another officer jumped out. The officer was killed, while Anat emerged unhurt.
She ran with the surviving soldiers toward a nearby hill. This time, she could no longer hold herself together. “I didn’t want to die,” she later recalled. She went into shock and began to cry.
It was the soldiers around her who helped her recover. They told her that having her in the half-track helped them cope with the horrors they were witnessing and continue fighting. If her presence was helping them hold on, they told her, she had to pull herself together as well.
Anat calmed down and returned to duty. For three days and nights, she barely slept. She continued with the unit, watched forces blow up a bridge over the Jordan River and was then sent north with the brigade to the Golan Heights. At one point, exhaustion finally overcame her. She fell asleep inside the half-track and did not realize that the unit was taking part in the battles to capture the Golan Heights. She woke only after the fighting in the area had ended.
While she was fighting, the IDF was looking for her
No one in the Southern Command knew where the officer who was supposed to have reported for duty on the first morning of the war had gone. At the headquarters of the IDF’s chief women’s officer, concern mounted as attempts to locate her proved unsuccessful. According to the newspaper report, throughout the war no one could even bring themselves to call her parents and ask whether they had heard from her.
Only several days after the fighting ended did military personnel call the Kirshner family in Netanya. Her parents were horrified. Until then, they had no idea their daughter was considered missing. Her mother remembered Anat’s deep attachment to her former unit and called the armored brigade. They reassured her: Anat was alive and well.
On the eve of Shavuot, her mother left home and walked along Herzl Street in Netanya. Suddenly, she saw her daughter coming toward her, dressed in the Jordanian military fatigues she had worn during the fighting. Their reunion in the street was emotional. At home, Anat told her parents and sisters everything she had been through.
Her mother was angry. Not because she had gone into battle, but because of her lack of discipline.
From the battlefield to military detention
Several days later, Anat returned to her unit in the Southern Command. This time, a military policewoman was waiting for her.
She had been absent without leave, ignored an explicit order and participated in battles she was not authorized to take part in. She faced disciplinary proceedings and was sentenced to 35 days in military detention.
Before long, the young woman who had survived shelling, treated wounded soldiers and traveled with armored forces from Jenin to the Golan Heights found herself changing clothes once again, this time to enter a military prison.
Her mother called the commander of the armored brigade. According to the article, he tried to reassure her, saying: “Mrs. Kirshner, you can be proud to have a daughter like that.”
Senior military officials also apparently understood that the case was more complicated than an ordinary disciplinary offense. On the recommendation of the IDF’s chief women’s officer, Col. Stella Levy, Southern Command chief Maj. Gen. Yeshayahu Gavish decided to reduce her punishment. Within about a week, Anat was released from prison and returned to service as an officer in an IDF unit in the Gaza Strip.

Polish MEP takes axe to Ukrainian Nazi-linked memorial (VIDEO)
A Polish MEP has taken an axe to a memorial honoring Nazi-linked Ukrainian nationalist paramilitaries responsible for massacring Polish civilians during World War II.
In a video posted on X on Thursday, Grzegorz Braun can be seen repeatedly striking a stone obelisk in Bialystok, near Poland’s border with Ukraine, which commemorates members of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA).
The UPA was the armed wing of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN), a WWII-era ultranationalist movement led by Stepan Bandera which collaborated with Nazi Germany. UPA fighters massacred tens of thousands of ethnic Polish civilians in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia, now largely in western Ukraine.
”The UPA monument in the Dolhobyczow municipality in Hrubieszow County is to be dismantled,” he wrote. “The obelisk offending the memory of the victims of the Ukrainian genocide against Poles should be removed... immediately after documenting the crime of Banderism,” Braun added.
Pomnik UPA w gminie Dołhobyczów w powiecie hrubieszowskim do likwidacji❗️
Obelisk obrażający pamięć ofiar ukraińskiego Ludobójstwa na Polakach powinien zostać usunięty profesjonalnymi narzędziami natychmiast po udokumentowaniu przestępstwa banderyzmu!#StopBanderyzacjiPolski… pic.twitter.com/8Q4QZ2z5vJ
According to Braun, local Poles feared Ukrainian retaliation if they removed the memorial. He said one proposal to dismantle it was met with the response: “We’re afraid they’ll set us on fire.”
The memorial stands over a burial site containing 41 UPA members killed in a clash with Soviet forces in February 1946. According to Polish records, a Ukrainian memorial was erected there without authorization in the 1990s. The stone monument honoring the UPA fighters was added later and has also faced questions over its legal status.
The site has repeatedly been vandalized. Unidentified people damaged inscriptions on the obelisk earlier this month, while the Ukrainian Embassy expressed “deep outrage” after another attack in July.
The OUN and UPA massacres remain a major source of tension between Poland and Ukraine. Warsaw recognizes the killings of predominantly Polish civilians in Volhynia, Eastern Galicia, and neighboring regions in 1943-1945 as genocide and estimates that up to 100,000 Poles were killed.
The dispute has intensified amid Kiev’s continued honoring of WWII-era Ukrainian nationalists. Vladimir Zelensky took part in the May reburial of OUN leader Andrey Melnik as part of efforts to establish a “Pantheon of outstanding Ukrainians” and later granted a Ukrainian military unit the honorary title “Heroes of the UPA.”
Polish President Karol Nawrocki responded by stripping Zelensky of the Order of the White Eagle, Poland’s highest state honor. Warsaw has also warned it will not support Ukraine’s EU membership bid unless Kiev changes its approach.
Polish MEP Ewa Zajaczkowska-Hernik has meanwhile called for an end to free weapons deliveries to Ukraine, arguing that Warsaw has provided some $4.6 billion in military aid only to be repaid with a “Banderite pantheon of heroes.”
”Let’s stop being suckers for Ukraine!” she wrote on X.
Russian President Vladimir Putin weighed in last month, arguing that the neo-Nazi nature of the Ukrainian government has become so visible that even Poland’s strongly anti-Russian authorities can no longer ignore it. Warsaw, he said, faces an “obvious demand” from its population to confront the issue.
Public attitudes toward Ukrainians in Poland have also deteriorated. A July CBOS poll found 52% of Poles opposed accepting Ukrainian migrants, against 42% in favor – the first time opponents had outnumbered supporters since tracking began after the 2014 Western-backed coup in Kiev. Support has fallen from 94% in 2022 to 42% this year.
An August IBRiS survey separately found that 67% of Poles support deporting unemployed Ukrainian men of military age.

Ukraine increases food exports in September, but remains at 40% of its capacity

Ukraine increases food exports in September, but remains at 40% of its capacity
Ukraine increased the volume of agricultural exports by road, rail, and the Danube River this month compared with August, but exports remain at only 40% of their full operational capacity as Russia continues to block the Black Sea, Ukraine’s Agriculture Ministry reported on Sept. 11.
Since the start of September, Ukraine has exported 630,000 metric tons of agricultural products, more than half of which was grain — 380,000 tons. While this fairs better than in August when Ukraine only exported 33% of its capacity, the alternative export routes to the Black Sea can only handle half the volume of seaports.
"Our task is to simultaneously expand alternative routes, support agricultural producers with financing and temporary storage of the harvest, and work on restoring full-fledged exports through seaports," Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi said.
The blockade of Ukraine’s Black Sea ports has sparked fears of a global food crisis as farmers struggle to send grain to customers in Asia and Africa. At the same time, there are concerns that Ukrainian farmers will lose money as grain prices fall and storage space runs out.
Last month, Kyiv predicted that it could lose 10.8 billion euros ($12.6 billion) from blocked agricultural exports.
To help farmers, the Agriculture Ministry has raised $12 million for free polymer storage sleeves for frontline farms to protect their grain from the elements. Other support includes expanding the state "5-7-9%" loan program, allowing farmers to borrow up to Hr 90 million ($2 million) each for operating costs at a fixed 10% interest rate.
As farmers continue to work under immense pressure, the pace of lending to the agricultural sector is increasing and could total an additional Hr 15 billion ($337 million) per month, reaching Hr 60 billion ($1.3 billion) by the end of the year, the ministry said. 
Ukrainian farmers need to raise at least Hr 80 billion ($1.8 billion) for the full autumn sowing campaign, which starts around now.
Ukraine previously asked the EU for 220 million euros ($255 million) to help cash-strapped farmers. While Brussels said it was considering the proposal, no decision has been made yet.
In the long run, without enough support, farmers may plant fewer crops, hampering an industry that accounted for 60% of Ukraine’s exports in the first half of the year.

EU and Ukraine Launch Joint Drone Alliance to Match Russian Mass Production

The initiative aims to accelerate the development, production, and scaling of unmanned aerial vehicles through joint ventures and shared technology.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance builds on a May 2026 European Commission initiative to develop a joint industrial ecosystem for unmanned aerial vehicles.
European Commissioner for Defense and Space Andrius Kubilius emphasized the urgent need to adopt Ukraine’s battlefield experience, noting that drone design cycles and countermeasures must now be measured in weeks rather than months.
According to Babel, Kubilius highlighted a stark production gap: while European industry currently produces approximately 1.5 million drones annually, Russia is manufacturing up to 10 million FPV drones and 130,000 jet-powered Iranian-designed Shahed drone variants each year.
To counter this threat, the alliance will focus on establishing adaptable production lines capable of rapid expansion in the event of a wider European war.
Furthermore, the partnership aims to integrate Ukrainian battlefield technologies, such as the “Delta” intelligence system, while securing vulnerable supply chains for microchips, electronics, and explosives, Babel wrote. The alliance, which was initially established in Kyiv in July 2026, plans to hold its next board meeting before the end of the year.
Ukrainian FP-1 long-range drones, meanwhile, have recently set a new distance record by traveling over 3,200 kilometers to strike a Gazprom processing plant in Russia’s Yamalo-Nenets region.
