How 9/11 turned a terrorist attack into a generation of war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:12:05 UTC
00:12:05 KST

How 9/11 turned a terrorist attack into a generation of war
On the morning of September 11, 2001, Americans watched in horror as hijacked planes struck the World Trade Center and the Pentagon and crashed in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Nearly 3,000 people were killed. Less than a month later, the US went to war in Afghanistan. Two years after that, it invaded Iraq.
What began as an attack by Al-Qaeda would come to reshape US foreign policy, the Middle East, and the way Islam was discussed around the world.
A quarter of a century later, September 11 still casts a long shadow over American public life. Al-Qaeda’s responsibility for the attacks has long been established, but the edges of the story remain blurred. Documents remained classified for years and only emerged piece by piece; lawsuits dragged on; questions lingered over who might have known more, who might have helped, and how far the web surrounding the hijackers actually extended. In the gaps between what was proven, what remained secret, and what was merely suspected, conspiracy theories flourished – but so did genuine political and legal questions that America has never quite managed to put to rest.
Nowhere has that shadow fallen more heavily than on Saudi Arabia; 15 of the 19 hijackers were Saudi citizens, and for decades, victims’ families, lawyers, and advocacy groups have pressed for greater disclosure about possible links between people associated with Saudi institutions and some of the attackers. The result is a peculiar political afterlife of 9/11. Even as Washington and Riyadh have remained strategic partners, questions surrounding the attacks have repeatedly resurfaced whenever the relationship with the kingdom comes under scrutiny.
Under former President Joe Biden, the issue returned to public attention when his administration ordered a new review and declassification of government records related to 9/11, following sustained pressure from victims’ families. The Saudi question also became entangled with a broader political reassessment of Washington’s relationship with Riyadh following the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi.
In that sense, September 11 left behind more than a settled account of a terrorist attack. It left a long political shadow – one that continued to affect how Americans view particular Arab states, their governments, and eventually, the Muslim world.
The architecture of suspicion
The more immediate consequence of September 11, however, was broader than the hunt for those responsible. The attacks changed the conceptual framework through which the US understood Islam itself.
After 9/11, the country needed explanations: Why did it happen, what produced Islamist violence, and how could another attack be prevented? The American system responded in a characteristically American way: It went looking for expertise. Government agencies poured money into universities, professional associations, and think tanks, demanding explanations – and quickly.
But there was an almost paradoxical mismatch between the question and some of the intellectual tools available to answer it. Many of the scholars being asked to make sense of Islam, political Islam, and jihadist violence built their expertise studying religion in a different context: Christianity in the US, including Christian fundamentalism and its relationship with political extremism.
To Grigory Lukyanov, a research fellow at the Institute of Oriental Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences and deputy dean at Russia’s State Academic University for the Humanities, the episode illustrates something larger about the American response to 9/11: Confronted with an unfamiliar threat and under enormous pressure to produce answers quickly, institutions reached for intellectual tools they already possessed.
“You needed ideas, you needed solutions, you needed an understanding of how to solve the problem,” Lukyanov said. “Money was given to scholars of religion, quick results were demanded, and existing analytical frameworks were transferred onto Islam.”
Islam increasingly became something to be categorized in security terms.
A movement classified as ‘moderate’ might be treated as a potential partner; one categorized as ‘radical’ could become a target of surveillance, sanctions, or counterterrorism operations, but the consequences quickly moved beyond policy and into everyday life. In September 2001, 28% of Americans said they had become more suspicious of people of Middle Eastern descent; in March 2002, 25% of Americans said Islam was more likely than other religions to encourage violence (now, 25 years later, it’s 51%).
For Lukyanov, the resulting distortions were almost built into the speed and structure of the response. “It is difficult to search for alternatives in counterfactual history,” he said. “The attack had happened. What could the United States do – simply not conduct a War on Terror? Retreat into something like the Monroe Doctrine, recoil from what had happened and accept defeat? That was almost impossible to imagine.”
The US of 2001 was at the height of its post-Cold War power, the Russian expert said. The Soviet Union disappeared a decade earlier; China had not yet emerged as a peer economic competitor; Washington possessed unmatched military, financial, and political reach. September 11 was therefore interpreted not only as a terrorist atrocity, but as a challenge to American global leadership.
“Not responding was impossible,” Lukyanov said. “The question is that the response was built on the experience, analytical frameworks, decision-making patterns and limitations that American political elites had at that moment.”
America’s road to endless war
If the securitization of Islam was one consequence of September 11, the most visible was measured in soldiers, bases, and wars. Yet here as well, 9/11 was less a beginning than an acceleration.
The US was hardly a newcomer to the Middle East in 2001. Its involvement expanded dramatically after the Cold War and the 1990-91 Gulf War. The US had troops and military facilities across the region, protected the Gulf monarchies, enforced no-fly zones over Iraq, supported Israel, and remained indispensable to Arab-Israeli diplomacy. By the end of the 1990s, American primacy in the region was difficult to contest.
“The United States began sinking into the Middle Eastern swamp long before September 11,” Lukyanov said. “There were essentially no other external players, and almost no major conflict or problem in the region could be resolved without the participation of Washington.”
September 11 was therefore not the moment America entered the Middle East. It was, in Lukyanov’s words, a crescendo – the moment an already extensive political and military commitment became something larger and far more difficult to control.
Less than a month after the attacks, the US invaded Afghanistan to destroy Al-Qaeda and remove the Taliban government that had sheltered it. The initial campaign was remarkably swift. By December, the Taliban regime had collapsed. What followed was not. The US would remain in Afghanistan for nearly 20 years, its longest war, losing more than 2,400 service members as it tried to build a new political order. It ended in August 2021, with the Taliban sweeping back into Kabul.
Five years later, Taliban fighters patrol the capital in American-supplied Humvees, carrying American weapons and wearing American tactical gear. Around $7 billion worth of US-funded military equipment remained in Afghanistan after the collapse of the forces the US spent two decades building.
Destroying one enemy, creating another
Then came Iraq.
Unlike Afghanistan, the 2003 invasion was not presented as war against the organization that carried out the September 11 attacks. The administration of George W. Bush argued that Saddam Hussein’s regime possessed weapons of mass destruction (which were never found) and presented Iraq as part of a broader post-9/11 security threat. But by then, the invasion had already removed the Iraqi state’s leadership, dissolved much of its coercive apparatus, and opened a political vacuum at the center of the Arab world.
One consequence of the US invasion of Iraq can still be felt today, Lukyanov argues, pointing to the ongoing exchange of strikes between Iran and US forces across the region.
“It was the American invasion of Iraq, prompted by the 9/11 policies, that created the conditions for a geopolitical conflict in that country, escalating the geopolitical standoff between the United States and Iran,” Lukyanov adds. “It was precisely because of this that the United States significantly increased its support for Israel and its policies.”
Hussein’s fall destroyed a regime that brutally dominated Iraq for decades, but it also removed one of the principal Arab counterweights to Iran. Iraq’s long-suppressed Shia majority acquired unprecedented political power, while many Sunnis who occupied privileged positions under the old order suddenly found themselves marginalized.
The dismantling of the Iraqi Army and Baathist state structures left hundreds of thousands of armed and militarily trained men without a place in that order. Insurgency spread and sectarian violence followed. A new generation of jihadists that came into that landscape, now known as ISIS, built itself amid the occupation and the Sunni insurgency. By 2014, ISIS seized Mosul and proclaimed a caliphate across large parts of Iraq and Syria.
The friends America abandoned
The War on Terror did not only transform America’s enemies, it also transformed its friendships.
Across the Arab world, authoritarian governments quickly discovered the political value of becoming indispensable to America’s new struggle. Tunisia, Sudan, Yemen, Egypt, Jordan, and several Gulf monarchies expanded counterterrorism cooperation with the US, while governments increasingly presented domestic repression as part of the same fight against extremism. The distinction between jihadists and non-violent Islamist opponents could become dangerously elastic. Organizations that threatened the regime politically could be folded into a much broader security problem.
For aging authoritarian systems, the new order offered an opportunity. Lukyanov argues that some regimes came to believe that cooperation against a common enemy would buy them a kind of political absolution. “The War on Terror gave them the illusion that, by acting against a common enemy together with the United States, they would receive forgiveness for everything that had happened in the past.”
Few countries tested that proposition as dramatically as Libya.
Muammar Gaddafi spent decades as an adversary of Washington. But he was also an enemy of the jihadists seeking to overthrow him. After 9/11, this suddenly gave Tripoli and Washington something to talk about. Libya shared intelligence on Al-Qaeda and other Islamist militants with Western services; in 2003, Gaddafi renounced terrorism and agreed to dismantle his weapons-of-mass-destruction programs. Sanctions were progressively lifted, diplomatic relations restored, and in 2006, the US removed Libya from its list of state sponsors of terrorism.
For a time, the bargain appeared to work. A ruler once treated as an international pariah reinvented himself as a counterterrorism partner. Washington, meanwhile, gained intelligence cooperation and the dismantling of Libya’s unconventional weapons programs without another war.
But there was a catch. Cooperation abroad did not require meaningful liberalization at home. Libya remained brutally authoritarian even as relations with Washington improved; elsewhere, the counterterrorism imperative similarly gave security states additional room to operate. In Egypt, emergency laws allowed thousands to be detained without fair trials, while Washington tolerated serious abuses by governments it relied upon for counterterrorism cooperation.
Then, a decade after September 11, the bargain began to come apart when uprisings began in Tunisia in late 2010, and Zine el-Abidine Ben Ali fled. In Egypt, Hosni Mubarak resigned after nearly 30 years in power. And in Libya, the reversal was even more extraordinary: Gaddafi – the former enemy who dismantled his weapons programs, shared intelligence on jihadists, and rebuilt relations with the West – faced an uprising of his own. NATO intervened against his forces, and in October 2011, Gaddafi was killed.
The political vacuum produced another irony, Lukyanov said. For decades, some Arab governments portrayed Islamism as one of the principal dangers from which their rule protected both their own societies and the West. Once several of these governments fell, however, Islamist movements proved to be among the best-organized political forces left standing. Ennahda won Tunisia’s first post-revolutionary election; in Egypt, the Muslim Brotherhood emerged as the dominant electoral force and its candidate, Mohamed Morsi, won the presidency. “In the end, in both Egypt and Tunisia, for example, movements that had provided Al-Qaeda with a social and political support base came to power,” Lukyanov said.
In the places where revolutions did not produce functioning political systems, the circle became darker still. Libya descended into fragmentation and civil war; Yemen collapsed into a regional conflict; Syria became the battlefield in which local rebellion, state repression, regional competition, and transnational jihadism converged. Groups linked to Al-Qaeda, and eventually ISIS, found new territory in the wreckage.
When the War on Terror came home
Six days after the attacks, Bush visited a Washington mosque and declared that “Islam is peace,” seeking to draw a line between the perpetrators and millions of ordinary Muslims. On the ground, however, the backlash was already well underway.
Anti-Muslim hate crimes surged from just 28 in 2000 to 481 in 2001 – a more than seventeen-fold increase. Another 49 assaults and 104 incidents targeting places of worship were reported in the first week after 9/11 alone. In Chicago alone, the number of reported anti-Muslim or anti-Arab hate crimes jumped from four in all of 2000 to 51 in just the three months from September to November 2001.
The effect was measurable within Muslim communities themselves; 57% of Muslim Americans said they had experienced some form of bias or discrimination since the attacks, and 48% said their lives had changed for the worse. Yet the response was not uniformly hostile; 79% also said they had experienced an act of kindness or support from friends or colleagues of other faiths.
The consequences went beyond the immediate backlash. The security architecture built in the aftermath of 9/11 also expanded the reach and militarization of law enforcement. By 2020, nearly 65% of the roughly 18,000 US law enforcement agencies had received military equipment through the Pentagon’s 1033 program, such as weapons, ammunition, and tactical armored vehicles.
“If we return to the question of how Islam and the Islamic world have changed, Islam as a teaching has not changed,” Lukyanov stresses. “Nor have the borders of Muslim states changed. What has changed, however, is the position of Muslim communities in Western countries and in countries outside Muslim-majority regions.”
A quarter of a century later, the legacy of 9/11 extends far beyond the attacks themselves. Not only the US, but the world around it changed: Wars reshaped the Middle East politics (though did not change the region’s borders), new extremist movements emerged, regional rivalries deepened, and Muslim communities in the West faced greater suspicion and scrutiny. In that sense, perhaps the most consequential story of 9/11 for the Muslim world is not what happened on that day, but what followed in response.

Following the success of the Buenos Aires and Lima stops, the international tour of the MEI—National Museum of Italian Emigration—continues in South America and arrives in Colombia. On September 14 at 6:00 p.m., the “MEI Experience Cube” will be inaugurated in Bogotá. This immersive multimedia experience, conceived by the MEI, uses images, testimonials, and audiovisual content to tell the stories of Italian emigration to various countries around the world. According to a press release, the installation will be on view through October 13, 2026, at the Italian Cultural Institute in Bogotá, located at Calle 35 No. 15-32, Barrio La Magdalena. The Colombian leg of the exhibition is hosted by the Italian Cultural Institute (IIC), in collaboration with the Italian Embassy, the Committee of Italians Abroad (Com.It.Es.) in Colombia, and ICSAIC, and under the patronage of the Italian-Latin American Institute (IILA). The MEI Experience Cube was created to share the heritage and story of the National Museum of Italian Emigration, based in Genoa, with the world through a format capable of adapting to the various host countries. An immersive journey that focuses on the individual and collective experiences of Italian emigrants, weaving them together with the history, culture, and development of the regions where they chose to live. In Bogotá, the narrative will therefore focus on the relationship between Italy and Colombia and the legacy left by Italians in the country, as illustrated through several particularly significant figures and events. To date, there are 11,634 Italians residing in Colombia. “With the Bogotá stop, we continue a journey that takes the National Museum of Italian Emigration beyond national borders to places where the Italian presence has left a profound mark,” says Paolo Masini, president of the MEI Foundation. “Each country allows us to tell different stories, but they are all part of the same great narrative: that of millions of Italians who, leaving Italy, built new lives and contributed to the growth of the communities that welcomed them. In Colombia, these ties are particularly significant, and the MEI Experience Cube allows us to showcase them through a contemporary, immersive, and accessible medium.” The Oreste Sindici Cultural Association of Ceccano, Roma Tre University’s Department of Architecture, and Professor Maria Margarita Segarra Lagunes, with “Vissi d’arte,” collaborated on the creation of the content. The experience was developed by Federico Basso for Opera Digitale. Media partners: Rai Italia and ANSA. Paolo Masini, president of the MEI Foundation, will be present at the inauguration, having traveled from Italy specifically for the occasion. Representing the Italian Embassy in Colombia will be, among others, Ambassador Giancarlo Maria Curcio, Second Secretary and IIC Regent Marina Zappettini, and Head of the Consular Chancellery Paola Orsini. Ambassador Curcio expressed particular satisfaction that the exhibition is being held in Bogotá and noted that it will certainly be visited with great interest not only by the Italian community in Colombia but also by the many Colombians who feel a close connection to Italy and are grateful for the contribution our compatriots have made to the country’s development.

As conflict engulfs Mocha, Yemen, health workers keep hospital open
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:10:35 UTC
00:10:35 KST

“Our teams have been present in Mocha and the surrounding area since 2018. Our work focuses on improving access to paediatric and maternal healthcare, a lifeline for many women and children in an area where access to such care is a daily challenge.
In Mocha, we support the General hospital through the direct presence of MSF teams, as well as through broader support to the hospital and Ministry of Health staff. Outside the city, we also support maternal and paediatric healthcare in two healthcare centres in the region: Mafraq, east of Mocha, and Khawkhah, to the north. In these two facilities, our support includes funding, training, medical equipment, and supplies. We do not have permanent MSF teams based there.
The rapid evolution of the situation this week, including the swift advance of Ansar Allah forces and their control of most of the western coast, has had a major impact on both medical activities and the needs of people in recent days.
Just a few days ago, our teams in Mocha were preparing to reopen our former field hospital in the city to treat patients, including providing trauma stabilisation, in response to the fighting taking place east of Mafraq and the gradual arrival of displaced people in Mocha.
The rapid advance of Ansar Allah forces has fundamentally changed the situation. Within hours, the hospitals providing trauma services on the western coast were evacuated, while large numbers of people fled Mocha. 
We had already started providing water to displaced people arriving in the city, as well as finalising the setup of cholera isolation and treatment units in Khawkhah and Mocha. We were also increasing our ambulance fleet to refer critical patients to Aden, as hospitals there were at capacity.
The rapid advance of Ansar Allah forces has fundamentally changed the situation. Within hours, the hospitals providing trauma services on the western coast were evacuated, while large numbers of people fled Mocha towards the south and Aden, including healthcare workers from the city’s hospitals. The General hospital in Mocha was no exception.
Our team remained in Mocha, but we had to scale back and reorganise our activities and focus on one immediate priority: doing everything possible to keep essential medical services at the General hospital running.
So far, thanks to the commitment of Yemeni doctors, gynaecologists, nurses, and other healthcare workers, we have been able to maintain a minimum level of essential care, including deliveries, emergency care, and intensive care. As of today, around 30 healthcare workers remain present at the hospital. This may not seem like many, but their work is saving lives.
Our medical and humanitarian mission must be respected... Without these basic guarantees, we simply cannot do our job: treating people and saving lives.
When the city was taken, dozens of patients were still hospitalised in the maternity and paediatric wards. It was essential to maintain their care while continuing to receive patients requiring urgent treatment. On that day [Thursday 10 September], hospital teams cared for two patients who arrived in the paediatric and maternity emergency departments, performed two emergency caesarean sections, and continued caring for seven patients in intensive care and 10 babies in the neonatal intensive care unit, in addition to dozens of other patients and babies in the regular wards.
The situation remains extremely challenging. As of 11 September, almost all other healthcare facilities in the city had stopped functioning, largely because their staff had left. There is currently no possibility of referring patients, either within the city or to Aden.
The medical needs were already enormous before the latest escalation. They are even greater now.
We are looking for ways to reinforce our team in Mocha, but this is not straightforward. The situation remains highly stressful for both people and our teams. There were further bombardments overnight, and there is still considerable uncertainty about what may happen in the coming hours and days.
For us to continue providing care, our medical and humanitarian mission must be respected. Medical facilities, vehicles and staff must be protected so that people can safely access the care they need. This is also essential to allow patients in critical condition to be referred safely when the treatment they need is not available locally. Any threat to the medical mission puts the provision of essential healthcare at risk and may jeopardise our ability to continue working in Mocha. Without these basic guarantees, we simply cannot do our job: treating people and saving lives.
We do not know what will happen next. What we do know is that medical needs are enormous and go far beyond trauma care. We will continue to do our utmost to support the community and maintain access to essential healthcare for as long as we can.”

Croatia’s parliament speaker Friday warned Serbia that it cannot count on Zagreb’s support for EU membership if it continues on its current political path following the “completely unacceptable” funeral of late convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic.
Croatian Parliament President Gordan Jandrokovic said the farewell held in Serbia for convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic was “completely unacceptable” and contrary to European values, according to a statement issued by the Croatian Parliament.
“If Serbia remains on this political path, it cannot count on Croatian support for membership in the European Union, nor on support for the continuation of membership negotiations,” he noted during a meeting with Teresa Ribera, EU commissioner responsible for a Clean, Just and Competitive Transition.

Mladic, a former commander of the Bosnian Serb Army, died in The Hague on Aug. 27 at age 84 while serving a life sentence for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes.
He was convicted of crimes committed during the 1992-1995 Bosnian War, including genocide for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, in which more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed.
Mladic’s body was flown from The Hague to Belgrade and was received with a guard of honor, and a funeral ceremony was held, a controversial move that has sparked widespread condemnation, especially across Europe.

UN Security Council extends Sudan sanctions regime, arms embargo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

15:10:15 UTC
00:10:15 KST

Rabia Iclal Turan
11 September 2026•Update: 11 September 2026
The UN Security Council on Friday unanimously adopted a US-drafted resolution extending the Sudan sanctions regime, including an arms embargo, for one month until Oct. 9.
All 15 council members voted in favor of the short-term technical rollover, which maintains the existing measures while allowing more time for negotiations on potential changes to the sanctions regime.
US Ambassador Jeff Bartos said Washington welcomed the adoption, but stressed that a long-term technical rollover was “not an option.”
Bartos said the US wants to expand the arms embargo from Darfur to all of Sudan, broaden sanctions criteria to cover conflict-related sexual violence, kidnapping for ransom and attacks on humanitarian personnel, and strengthen the mandate of the Panel of Experts.
“The current sanctions regime is over 20 years outdated, and is insufficient to address the realities of the war today,” he said.
“That is why this council should expand the arms embargo across the entire territory of Sudan, expand the listing measures to include horrific actions such as conflict-related sexual violence, kidnapping for ransom, and attacks on humanitarian personnel, and strengthen the mandate and effectiveness of the panel of experts,” he added.
Sudan’s UN Ambassador Al-Harith Idriss Al-Harith Mohamed opposed any expansion of the arms embargo, arguing that it would undermine Sudan’s ability re-establish control, its right to self-defense and creates “unfair equivalence” between the Sudanese Armed Forces and armed groups.
The sanctions regime, established in 2005, currently includes an arms embargo focused on actors operating in Darfur as well as targeted travel bans and asset freezes.
Sudan has been engulfed in fighting between the army and the RSF since April 2023, leaving tens of thousands dead and displacing millions.

Siberia’s Irkutsk Region Offers Military Recruiters Record $18K Commission for Enlisting Foreigners

00:10:00 KST

Siberia’s Irkutsk region has introduced a record-high commission for military recruiters who successfully enlist foreign nationals and stateless persons into the Russian military, according to a directive signed by the regional governor on Thursday.
Under the directive, recruiters will now receive 1.5 million rubles ($17,800) for every foreign citizen they sign to a military contract. The new commission represents a fourfold increase over the past seven months, making Irkutsk the highest-paying Russian region for foreign enlistment incentives, according to the exiled news outlet Vyorstka.
Irkutsk previously offered a flat recruiter fee of 400,000 rubles ($4,700) per contract, regardless of the recruit’s citizenship. Vyorstka said the latest directive explicitly separates foreign citizens and stateless individuals from Russian recruits, while doubling the commission for enlisting Russians from other regions to 800,000 rubles ($9,500).
The move reflects a broader trend as regional governments scramble to meet military recruitment quotas. The Smolensk region recently raised recruiter payouts from 115,000 rubles ($1,300) to 1 million rubles ($11,900), while the Ryazan region hiked its commission to 805,000 rubles ($9,500).
Ukraine, which also allows foreign nationals to fight alongside its armed forces, previously identified more than 28,000 foreigners from 136 countries — excluding those from North Korea — who fought on the Russian side as of April 2026.
In a report published Thursday, Amnesty International said Russian recruitment efforts “frequently involved deceptive, coercive and exploitative practices.”
“Testimonies… describe contracts signed without informed consent, confiscation of passports, restrictions on freedom of movement, inadequate training and threats against those seeking to leave military service,” the NGO said, saying the practices “may amount to human trafficking.”

Norway’s Princess Astrid dies aged 94 days after King Harald’s funeral
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
18:08:47 EEST
00:08:47 KST

Norway’s Princess Astrid has died aged 94, two days after attending the funeral of her younger brother King Harald V, the Norwegian Royal House said on Friday. Her death came exactly two weeks after Harald died at Rikshospitalet in Oslo on 28 August.
Princess Astrid, King Harald’s elder sister and a member of the Norwegian royal family for more than nine decades, died on 11 September.
“His Majesty the King has received with great sorrow the news that Princess Astrid has passed away,” the Royal House said.
King Haakon ordered the flag at the Royal Palace in Oslo to fly at half-mast on Friday. The flag will also fly at half-mast on the day of Astrid’s funeral. Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said the state will cover the cost of the funeral.
Astrid had attended King Harald’s funeral at Oslo Cathedral on Wednesday. She entered the cathedral in a wheelchair before the service. A wreath from her carried a message thanking her brother for their life together.
NRK reported that Astrid had also spent time beside Harald’s coffin at the Palace Chapel before the funeral. She later watched mourners gathering among flowers outside the Royal Palace.
King Haakon paid tribute to his aunt in a statement issued by the Royal House. He recalled how Astrid assumed a central public role after the death of Crown Princess Märtha in 1954.
“At just 22, she had to step into the role of first lady when my grandmother, Crown Princess Märtha, died,” he said.
Astrid held that position for 14 years. She represented Norway at home and abroad, often alongside her father, King Olav V. The role passed to Sonja Haraldsen when she married Crown Prince Harald in 1968.
Norwegian newspaper VG reported that Astrid had faced health problems during her final year. Pneumonia led to hospital treatment in March. She returned to hospital with heart failure in May and received a temporary pacemaker.
Astrid was born in 1932, the middle child of King Olav V and Crown Princess Märtha. Her elder sister, Princess Ragnhild, died in 2012.
Astrid married businessman and competitive sailor Johan Martin Ferner in 1961. They had five children. Ferner died in 2015.
Her children, Cathrine, Benedikte, Alexander, Elisabeth and Carl-Christian Ferner, thanked their mother in a family statement released through the Royal House.
“Thank you for being the best mother we could have had,” they said, recalling her support for her family and her concern for people who needed care.
Astrid continued to represent the monarchy into her 90s and held 12 patronages. Speaking to NRK about why she continued working, she said being of use to others gave her a sense of purpose.
King Haakon said Astrid had also served as a source of support for Harald and other members of the family.
“We learned a lot from her, and she was not afraid to speak up,” he said. “Her passing is a great loss to us. We will miss her.”
Sweden’s King Carl XVI Gustaf said he and Queen Silvia had spoken with Astrid during Harald’s funeral events only days before her death.
“We remember Princess Astrid with warmth and send our condolences to the princess’s children and their families, as well as to the entire Norwegian royal family,” he said.

Get AI models ‘under control’, EU tells tech firms after hacks
- The European Union has urged tech firms to control their powerful AI models following hacks by autonomous AI agents, including breaches of Hugging Face and a German website takeover.
- The EU's AI Act enforcement began in August, allowing it to demand information, impose fines, and restrict or recall AI models if risks escalate.
- EU cybersecurity agencies have gained access to advanced AI models like OpenAI's GPT-6-ASTRA and Anthropic's Mythos 5 for testing and risk assessment.
AI generated
BRUSSELS – Top tech firms need to get their powerful artificial intelligence models “under control”, the European Union warned on Sept 11 after a series of hacks by AI agents.
Fears over rogue AI have spiked after OpenAI technology operating outside human supervision hacked into Hugging Face, a repository of AI models.
And during an incident revealed last week, thousands of autonomous AI agents built by OpenAI defied their instructions and took over a German website.
Asked about reports that the hack was broader than suspected, an EU spokesman said: “It is high time for these providers to get their house in order and to make sure that they get their advanced models under control.”
The EU said earlier this week it was looking into the incident.
The 27-nation bloc has adopted comprehensive AI rules and its enforcement powers kicked in in August, which means companies must comply with the law or face fines.
“The AI Act is fully enforced. It’s not just a set of rules on paper any more,” spokesman Thomas Regnier said.
He added that the European Commission, the EU’s AI watchdog, has already demanded information from several companies – which he did not name.
“If it gets bad or worse, we can definitely evaluate models. We can require risk mitigation measures, and in extreme cases and where necessary, we can also restrict, withdraw, or even recall AI models,” he said.
The EU’s cybersecurity agency has received access to OpenAI’s latest models, including GPT-6-ASTRA, as well as to Mythos 5, the powerful AI model from rival firm Anthropic, which it is currently testing, Brussels said on Sept 10. AFP

MOSCOW, September 11. /TASS/. The Bank of Russia does not plan to keep the key rate at a level the economy cannot bear for long, the regulator’s Governor Elvira Nabiullina said, adding that this would push unemployment up and put pressure on real incomes.
"In any case, we will not keep the interest rate for a long time at a level that is, as they say, unbearable for the economy. Why? If the rate's level is unbearable, it will quickly lead to a cyclical downturn, which means growth of unemployment, declining real incomes, and a drop in underlying inflation below the Central Bank’s targets," she told a press conference following the regulator’s board meeting.
The Bank of Russia will ease its monetary policy and lower the key rate within the framework of its inflation-targeting policy, anticipating such a turn of events rather than waiting for it to unfold, Nabiullina noted.
Earlier, the regulator decided to keep the key rate at 14% per annum, noting that current price pressures have increased in recent months.

Int'l Criminal Court feels Trump's squeeze as more states exit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:04:00 UTC
00:04:00 KST

As the U.S. ratchets up pressure on the International Criminal Court (ICC), sanctioning two more high-ranking staff recently, a small but growing number of the global tribunal’s member states have announced their withdrawal.
The departures of Venezuela and Chad bring to five the number of countries to withdraw from the court in the past year, joining Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger.
The surge in withdrawals comes as the ICC faces hostility from the U.S. and a leadership crisis after it ousted its chief prosecutor.
"Five countries have announced plans to withdraw from the Rome Statute, and we welcome more announcements in the future,” a U.S. State Department spokesperson told the AP.
The Rome Statute established the ICC in 2002 as the court of last resort to prosecute individuals responsible for the most heinous atrocities: war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide and the crime of aggression.
Based in The Hague, it takes cases when nations are unable or unwilling to prosecute crimes within their borders.
"The ICC regrets any decision to depart from the collective effort to end impunity for the most serious international crimes,” the court's spokesperson Oriane Maillet told the AP.
In July, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that the U.S. was launching a "sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court to U.S. sovereignty.”
Rubio said he would pressure the court's 125 member states to withdraw from the court, sanction organizations that work with it and ban staff from traveling to the U.S.
The Trump administration has already sanctioned a dozen ICC staff in retaliation for warrants the court had issued for Israeli war crimes in Palestine and investigations into U.S. personnel in Afghanistan.
The Central African country of Chad specifically cited the United States in its decision to withdraw. Its Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Sabre Fadoul said in a statement that in a phone call with a U.S. official on July 23, "the American side expressed its concerns regarding the functioning of this institution and requested that Chad reconsider" its membership.
Four days later, Chad said it would leave the ICC.
Iva Vukusic, a researcher at Utrecht University, told the AP that the U.S. campaign will reveal how committed countries are to the court. "Are they willing to defend it if it costs them something real?” she said.
The State Department told the AP the U.S. would call on nations that "enjoy the benefits of the U.S. security umbrella" to reject the ICC.
It is not just pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump that is sending ICC members toward withdrawal.
Ruling military juntas in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger blamed selective justice. The ICC had become an "instrument of neocolonial repression in the hands of imperialism,” the trio said when they announced their withdrawals last year.
A coup ousted Niger's democratically elected government in 2023. Since then, a military junta abandoned longtime partners and formed new alliances, including with Russia, where President Vladimir Putin faces an ICC arrest warrant for the war in Ukraine. Mali and Burkina Faso have undergone similar transformations.
"These countries are ruled by authoritarian leaders who want to avoid accountability for the harms they are inflicting on their own people,” Mel O'Brien, an associate professor of international law at the University of Western Australia, told the AP.
Burundi similarly accused the court of focusing too much on conflicts in Africa when, in 2017, it became the first country to withdraw from the ICC. The court opened an investigation into the East African nation earlier that year.
Most of the court's initial investigations were into African countries, though most requested the involvement of the ICC.
South Africa and Gambia also announced in 2017 that they would withdraw but later changed course.
A change of government can also bring a country back into the fold. Hungary announced it would withdraw from the court in 2025, but following the election of a new government, its parliament voted to remain.
The court also had an investigation in the Philippines when then-President Duterte said his country would withdraw from the ICC.
In 2019, the Southeast Asian country became the second to withdraw, but because withdrawal from the court is not retroactive, the investigation continued.
Duterte is now in ICC detention in the Netherlands awaiting trial on charges of crimes against humanity for deadly anti-drug crackdowns he allegedly oversaw while in office. Opening statements are set for November.
An investigation into possible crimes committed by Venezuelan security forces under former Venezuelan President Maduro will continue despite the country's announcement last month that it will also withdraw from the ICC.
In a statement, the country's Foreign Minister Felix Plasencia said the court had been "instrumentalized to deepen inequalities among peoples and disregard their right to self-determination and sovereignty.”
Venezuela is currently in the middle of U.S.-backed talks between the ruling party and the opposition.
Ukraine previously signed an agreement to give the court jurisdiction over crimes on its territory, following the outbreak of hostilities with Russia in 2014.
Joining the court was "Ukraine's way of saying that accountability for the gravest crimes cannot be optional, and that we intend to help build that system of justice,” Ukraine's Prosecutor General Andriy Kostin told the AP.

Xinhua Headlines: Multinationals bank on new opportunities as China upgrades services sector
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
23:03:25 CST
00:03:25 KST

* The 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services, running from Sept. 9 to 13, has attracted a heavier presence of multinational companies compared to last year, with 473 of these being either Fortune Global 500 firms or industry leaders.
* China has actively promoted trade in services and opened its services sector wider. These efforts are creating more opportunities for countries and businesses around the world.
* By bringing together governments, international organizations and investors, the fair provides a unique opportunity for exchange, sharing of experiences, and the creation of opportunities.
BEIJING, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- Opportunities, partnerships and shared prosperity are among the most frequently mentioned terms by exhibitors and guest speakers who are in Beijing for a major services trade fair.
This was evident when Ragnhild Sjoner Syrstad, Norway's state secretary for industry and commerce, briefed a large crowd at the Norwegian Pavilion on her nation's exhibition at the 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS).
As the guest country of honor for this year's event, Norway has brought firms spanning health, nutrition, design and lifestyle to its pavilion. According to Syrstad, the stronger presence and diversity of Norwegian firms demonstrate the importance Norway places on both the CIFTIS and the business relationship between the two countries.
Another example was Alexander Poulev, Bulgaria's deputy prime minister and minister of economy, investment and industry, who explained why his delegation has traveled more than 7,000 km to attend the CIFTIS. He praised the fair as an opportunity to turn the longstanding friendship between Bulgaria and China into concrete investments, stronger trade, and long-term economic cooperation.
With the theme of "Global Services, Shared Prosperity," this year's CIFTIS features the debut of over 100 new products and services, covering fields such as information and communications, fintech, and digital and intelligent healthcare. A series of forums and business matchmaking activities are also being held.
EXPLORE OPPORTUNITIES
The 2026 CIFTIS, running from Sept. 9 to 13, has attracted a heavier presence of multinational companies compared to last year, with 473 of these being either Fortune Global 500 firms or industry leaders.
During the fair, U.S. pharmaceutical giant Lilly, a Fortune Global 500 company, is showcasing innovative treatment solutions across the fields of metabolic diseases, neuroscience, oncology and immunology. Wang Li, head of Lilly China's drug development and medical affairs center, said that as China's clinical research capabilities and innovation ecosystem have continued to advance, the country has become an indispensable partner in Lilly's global R&D system.
In 2024, Lilly established a medical innovation center in Beijing, focusing on enhancing clinical development efficiency, accelerating new drug R&D and implementing medical solutions. In 2025, the firm launched its first overseas innovation incubator, Lilly Gateway Labs, also located in Beijing. Wang said the Lilly innovation incubator not only brings Lilly's expertise in science, management and resource support to local startups but also deeply integrates into Beijing's pharmaceutical industry ecosystem.
Banking on China's huge medical market demand, the company announced earlier this year that it planned to invest 3 billion U.S. dollars in China over the coming decade to expand supply-chain production capacity. This decision marked another significant move by the company to deepen its roots in China and support the development of the local healthcare industry.
"We will use the CIFTIS as a bridge to actively introduce global innovation into China, and collaborate with top local academic and industrial forces to bring more innovative treatment options to patients, jointly promoting the high-quality development of China's pharmaceutical and health industry," Wang noted.
ABB, a global leader in electrification and automation technologies and also a Fortune Global 500 company, is eyeing the vast business potential arising from China's urban renewal. Lars Eckerlein, general manager of ABB China Limited, said China's 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) opens a new chapter for the nation's real estate and construction sectors. He added that the company is proud to leverage its expertise in construction and renovation to support China's urban renewal and its sustainability and high-quality development goals.
Speaking about his firm's participation in projects across China, from renovating aging buildings to improving energy efficiency, Eckerlein said the Shekou Tower renovation in Shenzhen in south China had achieved an energy-saving rate of 75 percent and cut carbon emissions by 142 tonnes annually. The project also helped remove potential hazards posed by outdated facilities, using an integrated energy management solution.
Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang said China has actively promoted trade in services and opened its services sector wider. These efforts are creating more opportunities for countries and businesses around the world, he said in a keynote speech delivered at the 2026 Global Trade in Services Summit that marked the opening of the fair.
China runs a deficit in services trade, with its imports growing steadily. The value of annual services imports has stood at around 4.4 trillion yuan (about 650 billion U.S. dollars) per year in recent years.
BUILD PARTNERSHIPS
As the first national-level comprehensive services trade exhibition in the opening year of China's 15th Five-Year Plan, the CIFTIS not only injects fresh vitality into global services trade, investment and consumption, but also serves as a platform for promoting openness and cooperation among countries and fostering mutually beneficial partnerships.
Poulev, the Bulgarian deputy prime minister, said trade in services is an important pillar of bilateral ties. "We want to see more organic products reaching the Chinese market and more Bulgarian companies building long-term partnerships with Chinese businesses."
He also said that Chinese companies have globally competitive technologies in sectors like electric mobility, software, automation, robotics and advanced manufacturing, while Bulgaria has skilled engineers and an established industrial ecosystem.
"This creates a strong opportunity that combines Chinese technology and investment with Bulgarian engineering and expertise," he said, adding that Bulgaria also offers a strategic location for companies looking to expand their presence in Europe.
In Poulev's view, stronger investment cooperation can create new supply chains and enhance the value of bilateral trade. "We are ready to build the next generation of Bulgaria-China economic cooperation together."
This willingness to build stronger partnerships resonates with the African region. In a video address to the summit, Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye, who also serves as the current chairperson of the African Union, said that the CIFTIS, as one of the world's largest platforms for trade in services, embodies a vision of openness, cooperation and shared development.
By bringing together governments, international organizations and investors, this fair provides a unique opportunity for exchange, sharing of experiences, and the creation of opportunities, he said.
"In a constantly changing world, we need more than ever to move forward together, share our experiences, and innovate to create new opportunities and build a better future for our countries," he said, adding that efforts should be doubled to turn trade in services into a true driver of shared prosperity, sustainable growth and economic development.
PROMOTE PROSPERITY
Ding, the Chinese vice premier, pointed out that trade in services is an important component of international trade and is playing an increasingly important role in driving global economic growth and industrial upgrading. He said that amid the accelerating restructuring of the international economic and trade landscape, advancing trade in services and promoting opening up and cooperation in the services sector is not only China's choice but also a necessity for the world.
Johanna Hill, deputy director-general of the World Trade Organization (WTO), told the summit in a video address that services account for around half of global trade in value-added terms. This share is only likely to grow, propelled by the rise of digital technologies, notably AI. At the same time, services are becoming an ever more important part of global supply chains. They support not only production, but also design, management, logistics and distribution.
Against the background of complex and sometimes frail international trade relations, she said countries that have successfully integrated services trade in their development strategies can share their experience and support those that are still making the transition.
Hill also said that China is already helping translate its experience into practical support via cooperation with the WTO. The South-South capacity building program, additionally, provides an important vehicle for doing this, by supporting developing countries in areas such as services trade, investment facilitation and electronic commerce.
According to Standard Chartered's Benjamin Hung, the next phase of trade will increasingly be shaped by the flow of services, in particular, in the form of knowledge, standards and ideas.
"Through years of reform and opening up, China has become one of the world's leading trading nations and a major contributor to global growth and prosperity," Hung said, adding that Standard Chartered has been privileged to both witness this journey firsthand and take part in it.
"We live in a world of increasing fragmentation, yet trade remains one of the few truly universal languages, connecting people, markets and opportunities across borders. Trade works best when it is open, transparent, predictable and rules-based," he said.

The BOI meeting chaired by Thai Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas approved the measures, marking a structural pivot away from low-margin manufacturing incentives toward advanced technology, domestic supply-chain integration, and realized capital deployment.
The strategy aims to lift national investment to 30 percent of gross domestic product and sustain economic expansion above 3 percent annually, said BOI Secretary General Narit Therdsteerasukdi.

Advanced electronics and electrical components dominated the approvals, accounting for 10 projects valued at 2.54 billion dollars. Other cleared investments span processed foods, pet nutrition, and precision automotive components.
The approvals bring Thailand's cumulative fast-track pipeline across three intakes to 42 projects worth 10.39 billion dollars and 27,000 skilled jobs.
In a bid to anchor multinationals locally, the BOI partnered with the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Stock Exchange of Thailand to launch the "BOI to IPO" program.
The scheme accelerates listing reviews, offering SET-certified "New Economy" companies up to three additional corporate tax-exempt years, or a 50 percent tax rate cut for five years. Other promoted companies can claim up to two additional tax-exempt years or a 50 percent cut for three years. ■

Roundup: Britain's economy expands in summer, but cost pressures persist
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
23:02:53 CST
00:02:53 KST

LONDON, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- Britain's economy expanded both in July and the May-July period, with momentum mainly drawing from the services sector. Nevertheless, in the run-up to the Autumn Budget, analysts have warned of the pressure of costs for both households and businesses.
The country's monthly real gross domestic product (GDP) rose 0.4 percent in July, with all three major industrial sectors recording mild growth, data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) showed Friday.
The figure followed 0.3 percent growth in June, and no growth in May, according to the ONS.
In July, the services industry reported a 0.4 percent increase, and the production and construction industries recorded 0.2 percent and 0.1 percent increases, respectively.
In the three months to July, Britain's real GDP is estimated to have grown by 0.4 percent compared with the three months to April, the data also showed.
The services sector contributed the most, with output rising 0.6 percent. However, production and construction outputs fell by 0.5 percent in both sectors in the May-July period.
"Within services, computer programming was the largest contributor, continuing the strong growth seen throughout the year, with evidence that businesses involved with artificial intelligence and related technologies helped to boost this sector," said ONS Director of Economic Statistics Liz McKeown.
Although the better-than-expected performance signaled more resilience to the fallout from the Middle East conflict than initially forecast, analysts have warned of more challenges in the second half of the year.
"While July's data are encouraging, the challenge now is whether that resilience can withstand a much tougher autumn," said Anna Leach, chief economist at the Institute of Directors.
"As the Middle East conflict intensifies, oil is back above 100 U.S. dollars a barrel, gas prices are at their highest since late 2022, and financial conditions have tightened markedly. These developments will raise inflation, squeeze household incomes and business margins, and weigh on spending and growth," she added.
Ben Jones, senior lead economist at the Confederation of British Industry, echoed Leach's predictions. He noted that higher household energy bills are beginning to bite, while volatile energy markets and a global bond-market sell-off are adding to uncertainty and pushing up borrowing costs.
"Business surveys have become less pessimistic than earlier in the year, but the improvement remains tentative," he said.
Stuart Morrison, research manager at the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC), said the "warning lights of cost pressures and global uncertainty are still flashing for many of the businesses."
To reduce business costs and tackle the youth employment crisis, the BCC has suggested the government should cut employer National Insurance contributions for under-25s.
It also suggests introducing a targeted tax package to ease energy and business rate pressures for all firms while restoring consistent, locally delivered export support to help more smaller firms trade globally and drive growth. ■

Leaked CCTV footage of the pair having sex on a table in the monk’s residence was widely broadcast on Thai media.
In Thailand, Buddhist monks take a vow of celibacy and also renounce material possessions.
Police began investigating Phra Wachirayan in mid-July after receiving an anonymous tip alleging him of misconduct and misuse of temple funds.
Pattanasak, a commander of the police crime suppression division, said investigators identified two streams of money linked to donation receipts issued in the temple’s name.
About 89m baht ($2.7m or £2m) was donated for temple renovations, with another 2.8m baht in payments for Buddhist amulets and other sacred objects, he said.
“But the money from both streams did not enter the temple’s account – not a single baht,” Pattanasak told a news conference on Friday.
He said authorities had seized assets worth about 215m baht, including 16kg (35lb) of gold bars and jewellery and 28 land title deeds.
Police are investigating which are personal property and which belong to the temple.
“We will expand the investigation to identify other people involved and restore public confidence in Buddhism,” said Nattasak Chaowanasai, the commissioner of Thailand’s Central Investigation Bureau.
Wat Phutthaisawan is a prominent royal monastery with a large following that includes government officials, businesspeople, police and military personnel.
The former abbot, also known as Luang Pho Atichot, was well known for making amulets, with the Thai prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, reported to be among those who wore his creations.
The abbot was defrocked shortly after his arrest.
Last year, police arrested a woman accused of blackmailing at least 11 monks she had sex with, extorting nearly $12m of monastery funds from them, in a case that shook Thailand.

‘Abuse of power’: Von der Leyen rapped after backing space mega deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:01:19 UTC
00:01:19 KST

Ursula von der Leyen delivers a speech during the International Space Summit at the Grand Palais in Paris on Sept. 10, 2026. | Pool photo by Aurelien Morissard via AFP/Getty Images
BRUSSELS — A senior EU lawmaker has slammed Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s open endorsement of a space deal that awaits competition scrutiny as an "abuse of power".
In a rare intervention on Thursday, von der Leyen told a space summit in Paris that she viewed a planned €6.5 billion joint venture between the bloc’s top satellite players as exactly the type of industrial champion that the bloc needs to lead in the space economy of tomorrow.
Her remarks drew a stinging rebuke from liberal MEP Stéphanie Yon-Courtin, who anchored the European Parliament’s last annual competition report.
Advertisement
“Endorsing a merger at a conference covered by the media, without any substantive review, is an abuse of power and misconduct,” the French MEP wrote on X.
Von der Leyen was referring to Project Bromo, a joint venture between satellite makers Airbus, Leonardo and Thales to compete, at least in part, with the Starlink satellite-internet service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which recently went public in the U.S. and is valued around $2 trillion.
“These are the types of industrial champions we need if Europe is to lead in the space economy of tomorrow,” von der Leyen said.
Her words would have been music to the ears of the summit host, French President Emmanuel Macron, who has publicly backed the project together with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.
But they raised red flags with the antitrust community in Brussels, where the project has yet to be formally notified or assessed by the EU executive’s competition department led by Executive Vice President Teresa Ribera.
“What is the point of Competition Commissioner Teresa Ribera and the Directorate General for Competition if it is the president of the Commission who unilaterally decides a case?” Yon-Courtin asked.
Advertisement
Eyebrow raiser
Von der Leyen’s comments, which come nearly a year after the Bromo partners first announced their three-way deal, also raised eyebrows among competition lawyers and corporate lobbyists.
It is highly unusual for EU officials to comment on live merger matters: the Commission received a rap on the knuckles in 2015 from the European Ombudsman after former competition chief Joaquín Almunia made public comments on an ongoing investigation into a banking cartel.
But dealmakers and their advisers are also starting to come to terms with the new reality: DG Competition’s authority no longer stretches as far as it did in the days of powerful former Competition Commissioner Margrethe Vestager.
“It was certainly surprising, particularly for lawyers, but I think it was intentional,” John Davies, a veteran antitrust lawyer and consultant at Brunswick, told POLITICO. “The president has clear views about how merger control should now develop and took the opportunity to put a political marker down.”
German center-right lawmaker Andreas Schwab, also a competition expert, suggested a more nuanced reading of the president’s comments. “It was a political comment on the strength of the European industry, not an authorization decision,” he told POLITICO.
The Commission declined to comment, noting that the proposed merger had yet to be formally notified.
Advertisement
Thriving or surviving
Von der Leyen has sought to take ownership of the bloc’s policy to vet corporate deals — in response to demands from France and Germany to bend the EU’s antitrust rulebook to allow for the creation of “European champions.”
In particular, she has championed an overhaul of the EU’s merger guidelines that would give increased weight to considerations such as innovation, saying these would help companies “to thrive, scale, and innovate.”
But von der Leyen’s assertiveness has put her at odds with Ribera, her Spanish number two, who has defended the traditional role of the EU’s trustbusters in fighting corporate abuse of dominance that inflicts harm on consumers.
“A blank check for companies to merge under whatever circumstances will not make Europe more competitive,” Ribera told a conference at the OECD in Paris last week. “Scale, in itself, is not a goal.”
Backers of the space deal say, for their part, that Project Bromo is a matter of survival for the European space industry against competitors from outside the bloc that have leads in technology, scale and access to funding.
None of the three companies can go it alone, Airbus defense and space chief Michael Schoellhorn, warned in an interview with POLITICO in January. European manufacturers have struggled against larger U.S. competitors as the market shifts from expensive, bespoke satellites toward mass-produced constellations and integrated space services.
Bromo is meant to pool engineering, production and research across Europe’s biggest players, creating the kind of cross-border industrial champion already represented in cross-border European missile maker MBDA. But it wouldn’t compete broadly against SpaceX and would have a joint corporate structure rather than being fully vertically integrated.

‘Incredible progress’: Inside the €682bn drive to turn the Mediterranean into a renewable powerhouse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:00:54 UTC
00:00:54 KST

More than 552 GW of utility-scale solar and wind projects have been announced, or are already under development, across the Mediterranean.
The Mediterranean has impressive potential to transform itself into a clean energy powerhouse, with one EU country leading the way.
A new analysis, using data from the Global Integrated Power Tracker, shows that the region has an estimated 552 gigawatts (GW) of utility-scale solar and wind projects that have either been announced or that are actively under development.
This represents around $792 billion (approximately €682.79 billion) of investment.
It exceeds the US’s entire planned capacity across all generation types, which currently stands at 548.3GW, and gives the Mediterranean a lot to boast about ahead of the United Nations’ COP31 climate summit, which is being held in Antalya, Tükiye.
The Mediterranean’s solar and wind boom
Almost two-thirds of wind and solar projects in the pipeline along the Mediterranean (361.3GW) aim to be commercially operational by 2030.
If these targets are met, it would grow the region’s operating solar and wind fleet by a staggering 43 per cent, representing around one-third of its current power mix.
A new report from Global Energy Monitor found that while the amount of capacity under development is still not enough to meet regional clean energy targets, it shows that governments have rolled out “ambitious policies, programmes and strategies” in their energy transition.
Which country is leading the way?
Spain has rapidly established itself as a leader in Europe’s renewable transition, ranking first in prospective utility-scale solar (108.8GW) and third in wind (56.6GW).
The country, which generated 75 per cent of its electricity from clean sources last year, has managed to reduce the influence of expensive fossil generators on the electricity price by 75 per cent since 2019 thanks to its existing renewables capacity.
Its investment in wind and solar is already providing tangible benefits for consumers, saving the average household around €10 every month on their electricity bills.
“Spain has broken the ruinous link between power prices and volatile fossil fuels, something its European neighbours are desperate to do,” says Dr Chris Rosslowe, a senior analyst at energy think-tank Ember.
“Boosting grids and batteries will help Spain break free from fossil dependency for good.”
Dr Rosslowe warns that Spain risks “sliding back” into costly gas reliance amid post-blackout fears. However, Spain’s planned renewable projects show the country is still striving towards a clean energy future.
Egypt is also emerging as a leader in the North Africa subregion of the Mediterranean, with almost 100 GW of wind and solar projects in the pipeline.
“Industrial decarbonisation heavily influences this development,” the report says, “With 37.7GW of in-development renewable capacity tied directly to green hydrogen applications.”
This is followed by Greece, Italy, Morocco, France and the Western Sahara.
“Countries across the Mediterranean are not starting from scratch in the energy transition,” says Hailey Deres, a senior researcher at Global Energy Monitor.
“COP31 offers a chance to showcase the incredible progress that has been achieved so far and as well an opportunity to build on that groundwork.”
Deres adds that overcoming barriers such as Europe’s outdated energy grid will “ultimately determine” how much of planned renewable capacity actually gets built.

No pit stops: Chinese coal mine makes big upgrade with autonomous electric trucks

In FocusNo pit stops: Chinese coal mine makes big upgrade with autonomous electric trucks
The deployment of self-driving vehicles, now past the pilot stage, has improved safety, efficiency and operating costs, mine manager says
In north China’s Inner Mongolia autonomous region, home to the country’s largest coal reserves, a vast open-pit mine cuts deep into the earth, shrouded in clouds of dust. Winters here are long and brutal, with temperatures plunging to as low as minus 40 degrees Celsius (minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit).
In older, more traditional days, hundreds of truck drivers, bundled in heavy winter gear, had to brave icy roads and the risk of frostbite as they hauled loads through the pit. When dense fog and snow rolled in, visibility could fall so low that drivers had to stop work for fear of a fatal crash.
More than a year on, the performance of the 100-vehicle fleet offers a chance to assess how the technology has fared beyond the pilot stage – and whether it can be scaled up further to help upgrade China’s traditional energy sector.
“The autonomous electric trucks have helped us cut operating costs, improve safety and increase efficiency,” said Zhao Yaozhong, deputy manager for technology at the mine.

Historical art can hide scientific secrets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Historical art can hide scientific secrets
From bats eating birds to butterfly behavior, art can contain ecological clues
In the upper right corner of his 1611 painting “Air,” Flemish artist Jan Brueghel the Elder drew a bat holding a songbird in its jaws. While the painting might have been an allegory, the bat’s behavior was real — though scientists would not officially observe the behavior for another 400 years.
Artists are often keen observers of nature. Whether mimicking the reality in still lifes and landscapes or imagining a composite world filled with symbolism and fantasy, some artists show real biological phenomena — from predator-prey interactions to insect metamorphoses. Working closely with art historians, some researchers are spotting scientific insights in artistic works, often reflecting the deep interests of their creators.
For Pedro Romero-Vidal, an ecologist at Doñana Biological Station in Seville, Spain, the bat in the Brueghel painting was “completely unexpected.” It was a greater noctule bat (Nyctalus lasiopterus) carrying a bird. While the bat usually dines on insects, the artist may have heard about the bird-eating behavior during visits to the bat’s home range in Italy. But scientists would document evidence of bird-snatching from the bats’ fecal remains only in the early 2000s and confirm the behavior by listening in on songbird snacking in 2025.
The bat finding was something of a side quest, says Romero-Vidal, who published the analysis earlier this year in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. He and colleagues have been scanning historic paintings for “monkeys and parrots, since these animals were often transported from distant places, and we can glean interesting [ecological] information from their appearance in paintings from different centuries.” Many paintings fit the bill. “We’ve identified more than 1,500 works,” with these animals, he says. Repeated depiction means the artists at least knew about the critters, either by observing menageries or hearing about them from other people.
Jan Brueghel the Elder wasn’t the only artist painting ecological folk knowledge ahead of scientific ideas. Others, such as German-born artist Maria Sibylla Merian, who was active in the late 17th and early 18th centuries, used detailed still life paintings to show ecological relationships. “She figured out — and people hadn’t done this before — matching the insects with the host plant,” says art historian Anna Knaap of the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston. Merian’s work influenced people like Carl Linnaeus, who’s considered the father of modern taxonomy. “She was a scientist ahead of her time,” Knaap says.
In 2025, the museum put on an exhibition of the works of Rachel Ruysch, another late 17th and early 18th century artist. While preparing, Knaap and another Museum of Fine Arts historian Christopher Atkins wanted to collaborate with researchers, knowing the potential scientific importance of the works. So they turned to biologist Charles Davis of Harvard University.
Davis was immediately impressed with Ruysch’s botanical knowledge. “There’s all these little kind of nerdy botanical details that only an expert would know,” he says. “They’re in many cases representative of the species’ identity.” For example, the artist depicted flower parts such as sepals and anthers with careful accuracy, which Davis used to identify specific species and their origin in the Dutch colonial territories.
He also found an amusing mistake. “In one of her most famous paintings, there’s a carrion flower,” Davis says. The flowers mimic the smell and appearance of dead animals, attracting flies as pollinators. But Ruysch’s work depicted an unlikely partner dancing toward the bloom: a swallowtail butterfly (Papilionidae). “I sort of laughed,” he says. Ruysch probably never saw the flora in its natural habitat with its usual pollinator, having encountered it only in botanical gardens.
Art historians have many tools to figure out whether an artist meant to portray something with realism or took artistic license. “We look at what visual evidence exists. We make comparisons,” Atkins says. “So within a particular artist’s work, for example, you can see sometimes repeated motifs, which suggests then that that is not necessarily a completely realistic feature.” Art historians can also look to an artist’s original sketches of a landscape and compare it with the final product.
These artists may not have left written records of any scientific musings, but they certainly pictured them, Atkins says. A collaboration between art historians and scientists can reveal those insights. “These things have been sitting in pictures for hundreds of years,” Atkins says. “Where it gets really exciting is when the two sides come together and share their expertise.”
