Sean Penn-Produced Ukraine Documentary “Black Sunflowers” Premieres at Toronto International Film Festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:25:23 UTC
23:25:23 KST

- Category
- Culture
Sean Penn-Produced Ukraine Documentary “Black Sunflowers” Premieres at Toronto International Film Festival
Ukrainian-focused documentary Black Sunflowers, exploring the lives of a young generation navigating adulthood amid Russia’s full-scale war, will have its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF) on September 11.
Directed by James Marcus Haney, the 95-minute documentary will screen as part of TIFF’s Docs program. Hollywood actor and activist Sean Penn, who has been an active supporter of Ukraine, serves as one of the project’s executive producers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Black Sunflowers portrays a generation of young Ukrainians whose lives have been radically transformed by the full-scale war, balancing the experiences of youth with the realities of the frontline.
The documentary follows ravers, street racers, artists, photographers, and soldiers, including a DJ who joined the military but continues to perform while on leave, a nature photographer who became a war journalist, young soldiers with combat experience, and couples separated by deployments to different sections of the frontline. Their lives move between underground parties, high-speed car races, relationships, plans for the future, and military service.
Through these individual stories, the filmmakers present the war not as an abstract geopolitical conflict but as an experience embedded in the everyday lives of an entire generation.
Haney first traveled to Ukraine in 2022 on assignment for the international organization War Child UK. During that visit, he learned about Ukraine’s underground rave, street-racing, and drifting communities, which continued to exist despite the war.
Over the following three years, Haney divided his time between Kyiv and Los Angeles, immersing himself in these communities while working on the film.
According to the director, the project centers on the experiences of a generation forced to come of age amid the realities of war. He said Western media coverage largely focuses on destruction and combat, often leaving less attention for Ukrainians’ everyday lives and what they continue to fight for.
“Wars aren’t just fought by soldiers, but by entire generations. The film is both a generational portrait and an exploration of war,” Haney said.
Music plays a prominent role in the film, with its soundtrack bringing together Ukrainian, European, and American artists to reflect the musical world of its subjects. The documentary features tracks by Fred Again, Brian Eno, IDLES, Morphine, Sega Bodega, Nastia Vogan, Koloah, and other performers.
The film was created in collaboration with Ukrainian production company Limelite, with Volodymyr Yatsenko, Anna Yatsenko, and Vlad Bolelov among its Ukrainian producers.
Penn’s involvement in Black Sunflowers comes as he is also attached to another film project connected to Ukraine. The American actor is set to appear alongside Adrien Brody in Snake Island, an upcoming film directed by Hollywood filmmaker Doug Liman.
For the production, parts of central Zagreb have been transformed into a wartime setting. Barricades and military equipment were installed near the Esplanade Hotel, while extras wearing Ukrainian military uniforms were also seen during filming.

25 years after 9/11, al Qaeda remains a threat – even as Washington looks away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:24:25 UTC
23:24:25 KST

25 years after 9/11, al Qaeda remains a threat – even as Washington looks away
A quarter of a century after the deadliest terrorist attacks in US history, al Qaeda’s various branches have moved away from the global jihad advocated by Osama bin Laden, focusing instead on regional insurgencies. Their actions continue to destabilise swathes of the world, from the Sahel to Afghanistan, neglected by a US administration that critics say has unlearned the lessons of 9/11.
Twenty-five years after 9/11, al Qaeda is a very different force from the one that struck at the heart of America. But it is far from spent.
The global jihadist network has suffered major blows over the past two decades and a half, notably losing its leader Osama bin Laden in a US raid in Pakistan in 2011 and his successor Ayman al-Zawahiri in a strike on Kabul just over a decade later.
WatchLive: New York marks 25 years since 9/11 attacks
It was last able to mount an attack on US soil in December 2019, when three people were killed and eight injured at the Pensacola Naval Air Station in Florida, in an attack claimed by AQAP, the al Qaeda branch based in the Arabian Peninsula.
While its ability to strike on Western soil appears diminished, the jihadist network remains a deeply destabilising force in several parts of the world, including the Sahel, Somalia, Yemen, Afghanistan and Pakistan.
“It is not the same organisation that existed on 9/11. But that does not mean it has disappeared completely,” Bruce Hoffman, a counterterrorism expert at the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), told a roundtable discussion at George Washington University earlier this month.
A less centralised organisation than in bin Laden’s days, al Qaeda “has adopted a strategy of devolving authority to its franchises and affiliates, and there’s at least two dozen of them throughout the world”, Hoffman added.
WatchTen years after Paris attacks, West Africa has become world's terrorism hotspot
Among its regional branches, those based in Africa are currently the most active, particularly in the semi-arid Sahel region stretching across Western and north-central Africa, according to FRANCE 24’s Wassim Nasr, an expert on jihadist networks.
Nasr said the recent withdrawal of French and other international troops from the Sahel had “paved the way for a lasting and interconnected presence of jihadist groups throughout the region”. He pointed to the JNIM (Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims), “al Qaeda’s most active affiliate in the region, which extends across Mali and Burkina Faso, as well as Niger, Togo, Benin and Nigeria”.
Regional outfits, global reach
In the eastern Horn of Africa, the al Qaeda-aligned al Shabaab is another active and potent force. It now controls vast swathes of territory in Somalia, having undone years of painstaking efforts to stabilise the war-torn country.
Across the Gulf of Aden, in the Arabian Peninsula, years of conflict have weakened AQAP militarily, though it has managed to replenish its financial resources and resume its propaganda campaigns in both Arabic and English, aimed at Western audiences.
Al Qaeda also remains active in Afghanistan, five years after the withdrawal of US forces and 25 years after bin Laden directed the 9/11 attacks from his Afghan lair. Despite the Taliban’s denials, “al Qaeda continues to enjoy a permissive operative environment” in the country, wrote South Asia specialist Pearl Pandya in a study published by Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), a US-based research centre on armed conflicts.
The organisation’s various branches and affiliates have retained an ability to plan and think on a global scale, said Colin Smith, the UN coordinator responsible for monitoring sanctions regimes targeting al Qaeda, the Islamic State (IS) group and the Taliban. He highlighted al Shabab’s role as a strategic hub between Africa and branches in the Middle East and Asia.
According to a report released by his team last month, part of a $50 million ransom paid to free a hostage seized by JNIM in Mali in late 2025 was channelled to affiliates including al Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb (AQIM), al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula and the organisation’s senior leadership, believed to be in Afghanistan or Iran.
“This demonstrates just how global the organisation is,” Smith told the roundtable at George Washington University.
Threat downgraded
Analysts say the resilience shown by al Qaeda-linked groups is cause for concern at a time when the threat from Islamist terrorism is no longer at the heart of US strategic thinking.
When the White House unveiled a much-anticipated US Counter-terrorism Strategy earlier this year, the first since 2018, many experts were stunned to discover that transnational cartels and criminal gangs – newly designated as foreign terrorist organisations – topped the list of terror threats.
Listed in second place, jihadist organisations were limited to a handful of groups deemed capable of carrying out external operations against US territory and its interests abroad.
“To a reader of official government documentation regarding the terrorism threat landscape twenty-five years after 9/11, it would appear that the story that began with the attacks has largely concluded and that jihadism no longer presents an urgent and lethal threat to the West,” wrote Colin P. Clarke and Clara Broekaert, executive director and researcher respectively at the Soufan Centre, in a study on the future of the global jihadist.
Watch more9/11 then and now: Do September 2001 attacks still shape our world?
As a result of Washington’s shifting priorities, many analysts and officers highly specialised in international jihadism have been transferred to other units. They are now tasked with monitoring threats posed by drug cartels and far-left groups, which the Trump administration regards as the third highest ‘terror’ threat.
In testimony to the US House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence in June, CFR’s Hoffman warned that “the counter-terrorism architecture built after 9/11 is eroding – through budget cuts, personnel losses, and the diminution of terrorism as a national security priority – recreating the conditions of under-resourcing and institutional neglect that preceded the 2001 attacks”.
Speaking at a conference in Dallas on Wednesday to mark the anniversary of those attacks, former president George W. Bush lamented a return to isolationism in the US. In a thinly veiled dig at the Trump administration, he criticised those who “don’t pay attention to the lesson of 9/11, because what happens overseas mattered to our national security at home”.
Homegrown menace
The fight against Islamist terrorism remains a priority in much of Europe, even though the outbreak of war on the continent’s eastern border means it is no longer perceived as the most pressing security threat.
“Right now, the greatest threat to Western European countries is not Islamist terrorism, but rather Russian interference and the war in Ukraine,” said FRANCE 24’s Nasr. “This is because jihadist groups no longer have the same capacity to operate across borders, as was the case when the Islamic State group could mount attacks from territories it controlled in the Middle East.”
Nasr said security services monitoring jihadist activity were mainly focused on the homegrown threat: people already based in the West carrying out attacks in response to calls from terrorist organisations abroad.
“This does not mean intelligence services have lost sight of foreign-based groups. It does not necessarily involve the same services or the same resources,” he cautioned.
Earlier this month, French police detained three people on suspicions they were planning to attack Jewish communities in France and then escape to North Africa to join an IS group affiliate. One of the three had been in touch with suspected US jihadist Jessica Bowie, who was arrested by the FBI last month and charged with plotting an attack on the New York State Capitol.
While Islamist militants lured by jihadist groups remain a threat to the West, the groups’ own priorities have shifted since 9/11, often moving away from the global jihad advocated by Osama bin Laden.
The objectives of the most active organisations are now rooted in their local contexts, said Nasr, noting that the Sahel-based JNIM had ceased to take Western hostages since France had pulled its last troops from the region last year.
Read moreInsurgent alliance strikes at heart of Mali’s junta, exposing limits of Russian protection
“In fact, JNIM is now keen to deny involvement when a Western national is abducted in the region,” he added. “Despite its allegiance to al Qaeda, it operates within the framework of a regional insurgency.”

Syria doctors struck off over abuses under Assad's brutal regime

Breadcrumb
Syria doctors struck off over abuses under Assad's brutal regime
The Damascus branch of Syria's Doctors Syndicate has struck 10 doctors from its register over what it described as involvement in “criminal acts that have nothing to do with humanity”.
The decision also cancelled their membership of the syndicate’s co-operation fund and cited violations of professional rules, doctors’ duties and medical ethics, according to Syria TV.
The syndicate said further decisions would be issued against other doctors accused of breaching its regulations and professional standards.
The action follows an investigation by the Association of Detainees and Missing Persons of Sednaya Prison into alleged abuses at Tishreen Military Hospital under the former Syrian government.
The report, Buried in Silence: Mechanisms of Homicide and Disappearance at Tishreen Military Hospital, documented the alleged role of military intelligence, military police, medical teams and administrative staff in the treatment and disappearance of detainees.
It found that detainees transferred from prisons and security branches to the hospital were subjected to torture and other abuse, while some whose health had severely deteriorated were killed.
The investigation also documented how detainees who died in the hospital or other detention centres were registered, how bodies were processed and transferred, and how false or misleading death records were prepared.
The report was based on 154 interviews with 32 people, including former detainees transferred to Tishreen Military Hospital, doctors and nurses who had worked there, and former personnel from Military Intelligence, the Military Police, Political Security and the Military Judiciary.
The interviews were conducted between August 2022 and July 2023.
The report said medical and administrative personnel at Tishreen Military Hospital were part of a wider system involving intelligence agencies, military police and forensic authorities.
It also examined the procedures used by the hospital, the Forensic Medicine Department and the Military Police to record detainees who died either in hospital or in detention.
The ADMSP investigation said the hospital played a central role in a broader system of deaths and enforced disappearances under the former Syrian authorities.
The Doctors Syndicate decision, dated 30 June 2026, is one of the latest measures taken against medical professionals accused of involvement in abuses committed under the former government of Bashar al-Assad.
The move also comes as Syria pursues wider accountability efforts against former regime figures accused of torture, killings and other crimes against detainees.

Russia could lose 30% of oil refining capacity for 18 months – IEA report
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
17:24:00 EEST
23:24:00 KST

Russia could lose 30% of oil refining capacity for 18 months – IEA report
The International Energy Agency (IEA) has cut its baseline forecast for Russian oil refining over the next 18 months to approximately 4 million barrels per day – 30% below the level before the invasion of Ukraine.
Source: IEA's monthly oil market report, as reported by Bloomberg
Quote: "Risks remain that even this more cautious assessment may yet understate the problems that Russia's refining complex faces.
Longer lead-times to source replacement parts and the approach of colder weather could compound the stress placed on the Russian system."
Details: According to the IEA, Russia's oil refining industry is deteriorating as sanctions prevent the sector from recovering from intensive and precise Ukrainian drone strikes.
"It now appears likely that the persistent drone strikes and the patchwork nature of repairs are having a cumulative negative effect and degrading the refining system," the organisation said.
In August, Russian oil refineries were hit at least 22 times – the highest monthly figure since the beginning of the full-scale war.
"Ukrainian forces are using multiple drone waves against single sites, overwhelming protective netting and air defences," the report said. "The targeting also appears more precise," the report says.
Drones are now hitting secondary processing units at Russian oil refineries, whose replacement could take around six to eight months, according to the IEA.
Meanwhile, sanctions against Russia's energy sector are restricting its access to replacement equipment, making repairs even more difficult.
The agency also cut its forecast for Russian oil supply in 2026 by 125,000 barrels per day, to 8.7 million barrels per day.
Background: In its May report, the IEA wrote that Russian crude oil production had fallen by around 5% compared with the same period in 2025, to 8.7 million barrels per day – 10% below the monthly target.

🔴 Follow live Trump’s speech at Pentagon’s 9/11 ceremony

'That's why we fight': The US marks 25 years since 9/11 attacks
New York on Friday marked the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 attacks, with US President Donald Trump attending a ceremony at the Pentagon while Vice President JD Vance and four former presidents joined commemorations at Ground Zero, where victims’ relatives will read the names of those killed.
Twenty-five years after the deadliest attack on US soil, Americans paused on Friday to commemorate the nearly 3,000 people killed when hijacked planes slammed into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a field in Pennsylvania – and to wrestle with the consequences of September 11 that reverberate to this day.
Read more9/11 then and now: Do September 2001 attacks still shape our world?
In New York, family members of the victims joined Vice President JD Vance and four former US presidents at Ground Zero in lower Manhattan. The ceremony began, as always, at 8:46am with a moment of silence to remember the shocking instant when American Airlines Flight 11 struck the World Trade Center’s North Tower.
Shortly after, victims’ family members began reading aloud the names of all 2,977 people who died on September 11, as well as the six people killed in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing, a sombre recitation that will last for hours.
Other moments of silence, marking when the other three airplanes crashed and the two towers collapsed, followed. For the first time, a seventh silence was observed to honour the thousands who have died since 2001 from illnesses tied to the toxic dust that poisoned the air for months afterward.
Read moreNew York City releases post-9/11 air toxicity information kept secret for 25 years
In Arlington, Virginia, senior military leaders gathered amid heavy rain early on Friday to watch the unfurling of an American flag at the west side of the Pentagon where American Airlines Flight 77 hit, killing 184 people in all. President Donald Trump spoke at a ceremony there.
"Today we renew the sacred oath that we first swore in their names a quarter of a century ago. We will never, ever forget. That's why we fight today," said Trump, who opted to skip commemorations in New York.
"We don't have a choice. There can only be victory. We fight hard. We fight to win."

Mourners also held ceremony in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, at the crash site where passengers brought down one of the four hijacked jetliners, United Airlines Flight 93, that had been headed for Washington.
The attacks shaped generations of Americans who lived through the day or grew up in its aftermath, influencing US foreign policy, domestic politics and public attitudes toward security.
But for many whom the attacks directly affected – the victims’ families, first responders and rescue workers – the anniversary is a tribute to the lives lost on a clear blue day a quarter century ago and the heartbreak that followed.
Caroline Ogonowski’s father, John, was the captain of Flight 11, which took off from Boston 47 minutes before striking the North Tower.
Ogonowski, now 39, had her first baby this year and named him after her father. She brought him her father’s grave last week and was attending a memorial ceremony in Boston on Friday.
"This year, there’s this new sadness in knowing that they won’t ever get to know each other," Ogonowski, who has worked in disaster relief and humanitarian assistance, said in a phone interview. "My father will never know his grandson. And my son will never know his grandfather."

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
"We owe it to my father and all the others that we lost on that day to make sure that we continue to teach future generations about what happened, about who these people were, who these heroes were, how our country came together and became stronger because of it," she added.
Generational Pain
A generation of Americans has grown up since 2001 who are too young to remember the attacks but whose lives were fundamentally altered by them.
The attacks initiated the "War on Terror", which led to the creation of the Department of Homeland Security and the US invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq that lasted years. The resulting public backlash helped fuel Trump’s rise a decade ago, when he vowed not to start new foreign entanglements — a promise being tested by the current Iran war.
At home, Americans expressed deep solidarity and patriotism, as well as sorrow, in the immediate wake of the attacks.
At the same time, however, Muslim Americans and immigrants from Muslim-majority countries faced a rise in prejudice and hate crimes. Public polls have found 9/11 colours Americans’ perceptions of Muslims to this day. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the city’s first Muslim mayor, has faced calls from some Republicans to skip Friday’s ceremony, which he rejected.

Casualties were not limited to those who perished on September 11. Many rescue workers who spent weeks or months at the site afterward, as well as nearby residents and others, were sickened by toxins in the air and eventually died.
Patrick Whalen’s father, also named Patrick, was a New York City firefighter who responded to the attacks and continued working at Ground Zero for months amid the dust and rubble. In 2020, he was diagnosed with cholangiocarcinoma, a rare cancer linked to exposure to toxic carcinogens, and died in 2021.
"The government told him it was safe to breathe, and, obviously, it was not true," the younger Whalen said after a New York City Fire Department memorial service this week.
Information that the air at Ground Zero was safe to breathe came from the US Environmental Protection Agency. Its former administrator, Christine Todd Whitman, apologized in a 2016 interview with The Guardian, saying the agency did its best with the knowledge it had.
The New York City Fire Department lost 343 members on September 11. More than 600 additional firefighters, including some retired members who took part in the rescue effort, have died of 9/11-related illnesses since then, department figures show.
Twenty-six have died this year alone.

UK condemns “settler terrorists”, Sudan’s chemical weapons exposed, and Yemen’s war escalates: The Cheat Sheet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:23:02 UTC
23:23:02 KST

Share & more
Our editors’ weekly take on humanitarian news, trends, and developments from around the globe.
On our radar
UK leads 12 countries in announcing major shift on Israeli settlements
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced a major shift in UK policy toward Israel, recognising Israel’s occupation of the West Bank as illegal, and condemning the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians by “settler terrorists”. In a speech to parliament on 8 September, Miliband said the UK would ban goods from Israeli settlements, sanction companies and individuals involved in settlement expansion, and refuse to export weapons to Israel that support the occupation. Eleven other countries – including Canada, France, Ireland, Spain, and Sweden – joined the UK in announcing similar moves. Some Palestinians in the West Bank – where settlement expansion and violence have spiralled – cautiously welcomed the announcement as a good though belated step. Others preferred to reserve judgement to gauge its real impact. The UK and other Western governments have long been accused of inertia, if not complicity, when it comes to Israel’s actions in the West Bank and the war on Gaza. Miliband did touch on Gaza, stating the UK’s support for the case brought by South Africa at the International Court of Justice that accused Israel of genocide. But there were few other specifics, other than calling for the full implementation of US President Donald Trump’s stalled 20-point peace plan.
Sudan’s chemical weapons programme revealed
The Sudanese military ran an alleged chemical weapons programme in 2024 for use against the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), according to an intelligence dossier reviewed by the New York Times and Washington Post. Chlorine gas cylinders were reportedly sourced from global markets and from a water treatment plant in a Sudanese city, where they had been donated by aid groups to stem cholera outbreaks. It is unclear how often the munitions were deployed, though the alleged programme appears to have ended last year after the US determined that chemical weapons had been used and imposed sanctions. France 24 also reported their use. The New York Times and Washington Post received the dossier from an unnamed Middle Eastern intelligence agency, which Le Monde and Middle East Eye reported was Israeli. Israel is an ally of the UAE, the RSF’s main backer, and has held meetings with senior RSF officials during the war. Both the RSF and the Israeli government have carried out genocide crimes, according to human rights investigators.
Lebanon civilians killed as Israel escalates bombing
Israel says it has destroyed a network of Hezbollah tunnels in south Lebanon, in a blast so heavy it triggered a 4.1 magnitude tremor. While Defence Minister Israel Katz said the move “completes the achievement of operational control” over the area, the escalation in attacks has destroyed homes and killed civilians. On 7 September alone, 12 people were reportedly killed in strikes on a residential building and a vehicle. The recent wave of attacks has forced around 20,000 people to flee the district of Nabatieh, including people who were able to return home after a June agreement between Lebanon and Israel that led to a decrease in fighting and bombing – but certainly not an end. “The last few days are a devastating reminder that a reduction in widespread attacks is not the same as safety,” Maureen Philippon, Lebanon country director for the Norwegian Refugee Council said in a statement. “Children are being killed in their homes, health facilities are being hit, and communities that have already endured months of displacement remain exposed to near-daily hostilities.”
Yemenis forced to flee as battles rage
Yemen’s Houthi rebels have seized the Red Sea port city of Mokha and an island in the Bab al-Mandeb strait, consolidating their control over the shipping route to the Red Sea. The Houthis, who control much of north Yemen, say they only plan to target ships coming from Saudi Arabia. The kingdom has relied heavily on the Bab al-Mandeb strait to export oil since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The strategic port is not the only place in Yemen where the Houthis and government-allied forces are fighting anew. There are battles in al-Jawf, which lies between Houthi and government-controlled regions, as well as in Taiz. Aid groups have pointed out that the renewed violence has displaced 46,000 people in just a week, with entire villages emptying and Yemen’s already strained health system coming under serious pressure.
The state we’re in: a humanitarian system in retreat
What a difference four years makes. When research outfit ALNAP issued its last State of the Humanitarian System report in 2022, the COVID-19 pandemic was easing, organisations were expanding, and aid budgets were peaking. Fast forward to today, and the mood has turned dire. A “generational funding collapse” has forced the system into retreat, states the latest version of the landmark report, published on 10 September. The indicators are stark: 64 million fewer people are receiving aid, there’s no safety net for those left behind, and funding has plummeted by at least 30%. The process of picking and choosing who gets help – often called “prioritisation” in the UN-coordinated system – means people have to be increasingly desperate before aid can step in, yet the aid they receive is often not what they want. Despite the tectonic shift forced on today’s sector, some things sound achingly similar. Years-old promises to shift power, both reports highlight, are happening far too slowly. In 2022, it was a warning to improve amid rising costs, soaring needs, and worsening access. In 2026, it’s a missed opportunity for a system at the breaking point.
Opening the door to the benefits of migration in Africa
Migration stirs populist sentiments worldwide. In Africa, that’s currently playing out in Kenya (see below) and South Africa, with xenophobia usually a proxy for domestic policy failure. In South Africa, where GDP per capita has not increased for over 20 years, it’s easier to scapegoat migrants than fix the problem. Yet the evidence shows migration delivers economic growth, and the continent’s future will be shaped, in part, by the movement of people, skills, and labour, a recent Out of Africa podcast by CSIS-Africa suggests. Harnessing the benefits will take vision and policy commitment. Twelve million young Africans enter the labour market each year, but only three million formal jobs are created. The kneejerk reaction is to shut the door to “foreigners”. Yet the development potential of migration can be leveraged by: upskilling; matching those skills to local opportunities; and clearing away the obstacles to legal employment. Much is being made of the African Continental Free Trade Area and the push for deeper regional integration. But that shouldn’t just be about the free movement of goods but also a more liberal regime for people.
Weekend read
And finally…
A new lens on the Strait of Hormuz
While much reporting on the Strait of Hormuz has focused on air strikes, diplomacy, and oil prices, these photos by Morteza Niknahad focus on the people who actually live there. Niknahad grew up in the Iranian coastal city of Bandar Abbas, and this feature in Huck magazine shows how his work has long focused on the diverse communities who live and work near the sea. His new series, “Southern Winds,” is a combination of archival shots and family portraits combined with photos he has taken – on a mobile phone due to new restrictions – of people in Bandar Abbas during the war. “What made me leave the house was seeing something new and bitter,” says Nikhnahad. “Ships burning at sea and the sky over the city turning black with smoke. I thought I had to document these historic moments so I could look back at them later and tell their story.”

Estonian drone maker hires former Bank of Estonia Governor Madis Müller
Defense industry company Krattworks has hired former Bank of Estonia Governor Madis Müller as a financial adviser.
Drone manufacturer Krattworks said on social media that Müller's role will be to strengthen the company's financial and management capabilities as it enters a new phase of growth.
Commenting on his new role, Müller said he was looking forward to the opportunity to contribute to a rapidly developing company, particularly because it operates in the defense sector, which is currently of critical importance in both Estonia and Europe.
Madis Müller served as governor of the Bank of Estonia from 2019 to 2026, having previously served as its deputy governor. From 2006 to 2011, Müller was a portfolio manager at the International Finance Corporation (IFC) where he worked on equity investments.
He has also worked at the World Bank as an adviser and senior adviser to the executive director representing the Nordic and Baltic countries, as an economic adviser to Estonia's prime minister and finance minister and as a consultant.
Müller earned a master's degree in finance from George Washington University in the United States in 2006. In 1999, he graduated from Estonian Business School with a degree in international business administration, banking and finance.
Krattworks was founded in 2018 by Tõnis Voitka and Mattias Luha. Äripäev reported that the company's revenue increased nearly 28-fold in a year: from around €500,000 in 2024 to €19.5 million last year. The company plans to increase its revenue to hundreds of millions of euros in the coming years. Its operating profit was €8 million last year, compared with a loss of €500,000 the year before.
Recent examples of high-ranking public servants moving to the defense industry after leaving office include former EDF commander Martin Herem, former EDF Division commander Veiko-Vello Palm and former Ministry of Defense Permanent Secretary Kusti Salm.

The plant is used by the Russian defense industry to manufacture military-grade products, including components for aircraft engines.
The extent of the damage is being assessed.

European Commission allows Ukraine to buy Patriot missiles with EU loan originally restricted to European-made weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:17:23 UTC
23:17:23 KST

European Commission allows Ukraine to buy Patriot missiles with EU loan originally restricted to European-made weapons
The European Commission has approved a 6.1 billion euro transfer to Ukraine under the Ukraine Support Loan program to buy air defense systems, missiles, and drones, EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said. Kyiv can now use the European loan to purchase PAC-3 interceptor missiles for its Patriot systems.
EU authorities cleared the 90 billion euro Ukraine Support Loan for 2026–2027 in April, with 30 billion euros earmarked for budget support and the remaining 60 billion for defense procurement. Under the loan’s rules, Ukraine can only buy weapons with at least 65% of their components made in Europe or Ukraine. Anything that falls short requires separate authorization.
The Commission had already carved out one exception, for Chinese-made drone components. It has now agreed to five more: three for Ukrainian-made drones and components whose cost exceeds the allowed threshold, and two for American weapons, including PAC-3.
Clearing PAC-3 purchases for European funding doesn’t mean Ukraine will get the missiles quickly, the Ukrainian news outlet Kyiv Independent reported. Kyiv is currently contracting for roughly 1,000 Patriot missiles, but much of that order won’t be filled for years.
Kubilius also said the EU and NATO are discussing a swap arrangement: countries would hand Ukraine missiles from their own stockpiles now and receive interceptors in return once Kyiv’s 2027 batches arrive. Germany had already promised days earlier to send Ukraine missiles from its own reserves.
A shortage of Patriot missiles remains one of the most serious threats to Ukraine’s air defenses. Without these interceptors, Ukrainian forces have essentially no way to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles.
That shortage will become especially critical as winter sets in. Analysts believe Moscow plans to escalate attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure during the cold months to strengthen its position at the negotiating table.

Bab el-Mandeb traffic falls sharply to around 26 vessels a day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:17:23 UTC
23:17:23 KST

Commercial shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has fallen to around 26 vessels a day in recent days, compared with a pre-Red Sea crisis average of about 70, ship-tracking data showed, raising concerns about the prolonged impact of security risks on one of the world's most important maritime corridors.
Data compiled from maritime tracking systems showed that 25 commodity vessels crossed the strait on Tuesday, with 11 entering the Red Sea and 14 exiting.
Traffic increased to 28 vessels on Wednesday, including 16 inbound and 12 outbound ships, before easing to 26 on Thursday, with 10 entering and 16 leaving.
A total of 79 vessels therefore crossed Bab el-Mandeb over the three days, producing a daily average of around 26 vessels.
Kpler data put the broader 10-day average at around 27 vessels per day.
The latest figures represent the continuation of a sharp, multistage decline in traffic through the waterway since late 2023.
From 2022 to 2026
World Bank Data Lab calculations based on IMF PortWatch satellite AIS data show that Bab el-Mandeb handled an average of around 71 cargo and tanker vessels per day from January 2022 to October 2023, immediately preceding the outbreak of the Gaza war.
Traffic initially increased after Oct. 7. Between Oct. 7 and Nov. 16, 2023, average daily transits climbed to over 77 vessels.
After Houthi attacks on commercial shipping began in November 2023, the number of vessels decreased. For the period from Nov. 17, 2023, to Feb. 19, 2024, the daily average dropped to 43 vessels, about 39% below the pre-crisis reference level.
World Bank analysis shows that the physical diversion of ships away from the Red Sea became clearly visible in early to mid-December 2023 and intensified in the following months as major shipping companies began rerouting vessels around the Cape of Good Hope.
By March 2024, traffic through Bab el-Mandeb had roughly halved compared with pre-crisis levels, while research by the International Institute for Strategic Studies found that transits between February and October 2024 remained around 60% below pre-crisis levels.
The lower traffic environment subsequently became persistent rather than temporary.
IMF PortWatch-derived data show daily traffic averaging roughly 33.5 vessels during 2025, less than half the 71-vessel pre-crisis reference level.
Traffic remained broadly within the mid-30s during the first half of 2026, with average daily transits at 34 in January, 37 in February, 36 in March and 37 in April.
The average stood at 36 vessels per day in May and 37 in June, before declining to 34 in July and 28 in August.
The July-August decline marked a second important deterioration in the route.
On July 20, the Houthis announced a naval blockade targeting Saudi Arabian port traffic and warned that vessels calling at Saudi terminals could be targeted.
Kpler said commodity-related Bab el-Mandeb transits had averaged 34 vessels per day before the latest Saudi-Houthi escalation, but the seven-day moving average fell to 24 per day by July 29.
The monthly PortWatch data show the impact extending into August, when average daily traffic fell to 28 vessels, the lowest monthly level in the recent series.
The latest Kpler figures suggest traffic has remained around those depressed levels in September.
The 25, 28 and 26 vessels recorded from Tuesday through Thursday produced an average of just over 26 per day, while the 10-day average stood at about 27.
AIS-based figures may also underestimate actual movements because some vessels transit with their transponders switched off to reduce their visibility amid heightened security risks.
Hormuz traffic falls even further
Conditions at the Strait of Hormuz are considerably more severe.
Only seven commodity vessels crossed Hormuz on Thursday, down from 11 a day earlier and well below the 10-day average of 15 vessels, according to Kpler data.
Before the Iran war began on Feb. 28, the Strait of Hormuz typically handled around 125 large commercial vessels per day, including tankers, gas carriers, bulk carriers and container ships.
The contrast has increased the strategic importance of Bab el-Mandeb as Gulf producers seek alternative export routes through Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast.
However, the latest Houthi advance along Yemen's western coast has added another layer of risk.
Houthi fighters seized the strategic Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the city of Dhubab in western Taiz province on Friday, a Yemeni government military source told Anadolu.

France Télévisions removes Adèle Haenel show over Israel remarks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:14:23 UTC
23:14:23 KST

Breadcrumb
France Télévisions removes Adèle Haenel show over Israel remarks
French public broadcaster France Télévisions has removed an episode of one of the country's best-known literary programmes from its streaming platform after actor Adèle Haenel accused Israel of genocide in Palestine and France of complicity.
Haenel, a two-time César winner and prominent figure in France's MeToo movement, made the remarks during Wednesday night's edition of La Grande Librairie on France 5.
Her comments lasted about a minute and came during a regular closing segment in which a guest is invited to read a personal text without interruption.
“Israel is committing genocide in Palestine, and France is complicit in it,” Haenel said, before calling for “sanctions on Israel and the liberation of Palestine”.
France Télévisions removed the full episode from its France.tv platform on Thursday, saying the remarks had been broadcast without an opposing point of view.
The decision prompted a debate in France over the broadcaster's handling of the programme, with conservative and far-right figures criticising Haenel's comments and politicians on the left condemning the removal of the episode.
Haenel had appeared on the programme to promote her first book, Viser juste, which deals with sexual violence and the silence surrounding it.
Presenter Augustin Trapenard gave her the floor during the programme's traditional closing segment, allowing her to read a prepared text without interruption.
Haenel initially spoke about victims of sexual violence and what she described as media silence surrounding some cases in France before turning to Palestine.
Her comments drew immediate criticism from conservative media.
Le Journal du Dimanche accused her of turning a literary segment into a “political platform”, while CNews devoted part of a programme on Thursday to discussing her intervention.
During the CNews discussion, journalist Yoann Usaï said Haenel “doesn't understand what she is saying” and “doesn't understand the world she lives in”, adding that she “has a serious problem”.
Julien Odoul, an MP for Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally, criticised France Télévisions for providing a platform for what he called “the antisemitic ravings of the far left”.
Muriel Ouaknine-Melki, president of the European Jewish Organisation, said she had referred the broadcast to French media regulator Arcom, arguing that France 5 had failed to challenge Haenel's remarks or provide an alternative view.
France Télévisions said the absence of a counter-view was the reason the episode had been removed.
However, the part of the programme in which Haenel spoke is designed as a personal “carte blanche” for a guest and does not normally involve a debate or response from other participants.
The decision was criticised by politicians from the left-wing France Unbowed party.
MP Sarah Legrain praised Haenel for “resisting all forms of domination” and said she was speaking out amid what she described as widespread silence over Palestine.
Fellow MP Danielle Obono called the removal of the episode a “scandal” and urged people to circulate the deleted clip widely on social media.
Haenel responded to the controversy in a video posted on Instagram overnight on Thursday.
She said France Télévisions' decision supported her argument that certain voices were being silenced and some issues, including Palestine, were being pushed out of public debate.
She sarcastically thanked the broadcaster for providing evidence for her argument.
The controversy comes amid a broader debate over restrictions on pro-Palestine speech in France, where activists and campaigners have repeatedly complained of censorship and political pressure.
Pro-Palestine voices in France have continued to grow louder despite restrictions on demonstrations, legal action against activists and accusations that solidarity with Palestine is being criminalised.
French media coverage of Israel's war on Gaza has also faced scrutiny, with critics accusing some outlets of giving disproportionate weight to the Israeli narrative.
Haenel, 37, is one of the best-known figures associated with the MeToo movement in French cinema.
In 2019, she publicly accused film director Christophe Ruggia of sexually assaulting her when she was a child.
In April this year, the Paris Court of Appeal found Ruggia guilty of sexual assaults committed against Haenel when she was aged between 12 and 14 and sentenced him to five years in prison, including two years to be served under electronic monitoring.
Haenel announced in 2023 that she was leaving the film industry, accusing the French cinema establishment of complacency towards sexual abusers.
Her appearance on La Grande Librairie was part of the promotion of Viser juste, her first published book, released by L'Arche in August.

UK MPs reject bill legalizing assisted dying bill despite previous support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:13:24 UTC
23:13:24 KST

Assisted dying is currently illegal in the U.K. and assisting someone to end their life is punishable by up to 14 years in prison in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. | an landscape. (Photo by Stéphane Rouillard/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
LONDON — British MPs threw out a bill legalizing assisted dying for terminally ill adults in England and Wales Friday.
In a narrow vote, MPs rejected the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill's second reading by 286 to 270.
The decision was a marked contrast to a near identical bill by Labour MP Kim Leadbeater, which received two votes of support from MPs in 2024 and 2025. The legislation failed to become law after running out of time in the unelected House of Lords earlier this year.
Advertisement
The bill, introduced by backbench Labour MP Lauren Edwards, would have legalized assisted dying for adults aged 18 or over who are judged by two doctors as expected to die within six months.
It will now make no further progress and follows members of the Scottish Parliament rejecting similar legislation in March and a previous vote by MPs against assisted dying in 2015.
Assisted dying is currently illegal in the U.K. and assisting someone to end their life is punishable by up to 14 years in prison in England, Wales and Northern Ireland.
The vote was a matter of conscience, meaning parties did not whip their MPs who could vote as they wished.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was not an MP when Leadbeater's bill was previously debated, deliberately abstained to avoid swaying the views of MPs.
Nonetheless, Burnham argued soon after becoming PM that fixing palliative and social care should come before legalizing assisted dying.
“It is very challenging to introduce that wider debate in a context of people not receiving that care and having the peace of mind about that care,” he said in July.

Military personnel who went AWOL and are abroad can return to service under a simplified procedure, says the Ministry of Defence
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
17:12:52 EEST
23:12:52 KST

Military personnel who went AWOL and are abroad can return to service under a simplified procedure, says the Ministry of Defence
Kyiv • UNN
Military personnel who went AWOL and are abroad can submit a report via "Army+" by June 12, 2026. They must arrive at their unit within five days.
Ukrainian service members who committed unauthorized absence from their unit while abroad may use a simplified procedure for returning to service. The Ministry of Defense of Ukraine explains what needs to be done, UNN writes.
A service member’s departure abroad and the legal consequences of failing to return
As noted, service members may travel abroad during the period of martial law, for example, for medical treatment, education, a business trip, or another duly documented reason.
However, this does not exempt them from liability for unauthorized absence from a unit committed abroad. Article 407 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine provides for liability for unauthorized absence from a military unit or place of service by a conscript, as well as for failure to report for duty on time without valid reasons upon dismissal from the unit.
Thus, what matters is not the country in which the service member is located, but their legal status, as well as the established return deadline and the reasons for failing to report.
How a service member absent without authorization abroad can return to service
The Ministry of Defense said that service members who committed unauthorized absence, including abroad, by June 12, 2026, inclusive, may use the simplified program for returning to the military. It operates until September 20 of this year and allows them to independently choose a new military unit from a list of more than 70 units within their structure.
To do this, a service member absent without authorization abroad must submit a report through the "Army+" application.
Representatives of the selected unit verify the information and contact the service member to clarify the details of their service.
For the Armed Forces of Ukraine and the State Special Transport Service, the report is considered within up to seven days; for the National Guard of Ukraine, within up to four days. After the report is approved, the "On the way" status appears in "Army+", confirming the return to the place of service under the approved report.
It is emphasized that a service member absent without authorization abroad must still physically arrive at the selected unit—and do so within five days. Therefore, the report is the beginning of the return procedure, not a remote "reinstatement in service."
Likewise, approval of the report is not a separate permit to cross the state border and does not automatically terminate criminal proceedings or possible procedural measures.
Regardless of whether the service member has "Army+", an appropriate document—a foreign passport—is required to cross the border. If they do not have one, they can contact the embassy.
If the police, a Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center, or the Military Law and Order Service nevertheless stops the service member on the way to the unit, the "On the way" status confirms voluntary return through "Army+". In the event of detention, we recommend calling the hotline at 1519.
After returning and being added to the personnel lists, the service member’s pay, food supplies, and other types of support are restored.

Türkiye, Azerbaijan pursue new power links to Europe

2026-09-11
14:12:47 UTC
23:12:47 KST

Türkiye and Azerbaijan are working on three electricity transmission projects, including a four-country green energy corridor, Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said on Sept. 11.
Speaking at the fifth Türkiye-Azerbaijan Energy Forum in Baku, Bayraktar outlined plans for a line reaching Türkiye through Azerbaijan’s Nakhchivan exclave and a green electricity corridor linking Azerbaijan, Georgia, Türkiye and Bulgaria.
He also said Türkiye could join a separate project to transmit electricity beneath the Black Sea to Europe, reaching Romania and Hungary.
Bayraktar described the four-country corridor as an electricity counterpart to the Trans-Anatolian Natural Gas Pipeline (TANAP), saying Ankara wanted the project to advance to its next stage as soon as possible.
“As a first step, we want to start by using existing infrastructure,” he said, adding that the aim was to develop the project and increase capacity gradually.
Connecting the corridor with Azerbaijan’s agreements with Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan could extend electricity links across the Turkic world, he said.
Bayraktar said he hoped to see agreements signed on the corridor at COP31, the U.N. climate conference to be held in Antalya on Nov. 9-20.
He also said Türkiye would seek joint decisions at the summit on a goal of raising electricity’s share of global final energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035.
Bayraktar said cooperation between Türkiye and Azerbaijan now extended beyond oil and natural gas to mining, renewable energy, energy efficiency and electricity infrastructure.
Azerbaijani Energy Minister Parviz Shahbazov, who hosted the forum, said the countries wanted to build on their existing energy partnership.
“We want to extend our successful cooperation in oil and natural gas to electrification,” Shahbazov said. He added that discussions covered both electricity generation and the connections needed to link a wider Eurasian region through Azerbaijan and Türkiye.
The two ministers signed an updated forum protocol, agreeing that one of the forum’s working groups would focus specifically on electricity interconnections.

Money, not engineering, is what stands between Ukraine and Russia’s fastest drones, Zelenskyy says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:12:36 UTC
23:12:36 KST

Ukraine has not had enough of the right weapons to shoot down Russia's jet-powered drones, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said at a press conference with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in Calgary on 10 September. He put the remaining obstacles at time and money rather than engineering, and used the appearance to press partners for joint production. Russia attacks Ukrainian cities with drones every night, and the defense against the fastest of them is still being built.
"We did not have enough means"
Zelenskyy was answering a question about the Russian drone found at Leipzig airport in Germany and the drone that delayed his own flight out of Moldova.
"We have to be very frank: we did not have enough means to destroy all these fast drones," he said. "Yes, we are on the way, more than 60 companies are already working on this. Yes, we will get a result, but it takes time."
Three days earlier, he noted that only three to five of the firms show real results.
Germany blames Moscow for Leipzig drone attack, closes consulate and cultural center among sweeping diplomatic measures
The bottleneck is money
He then went past the engineering.The problem is not only technology, he said, but the funding to build thousands of interceptors every single day.
That arithmetic sends Ukraine abroad with its blueprints.
"That is why we talk about joint production, about production lines in one country or another," Zelenskyy said.
Russia now builds about 3,000 jet-powered drones a month, by Ukrainian military intelligence's count, and fired some 800 of them in four days at the end of August. They fly faster than propeller Shaheds and are harder to bring down, which has stretched air raid alerts nationwide. Ukraine's Air Force cannot yet rely on usual interceptor drones against them.
One drone, of the kind that turned up at Leipzig or crossed Moldova, is not a problem for Ukraine, Zelenskyy said. Thousands of fast drones a day are.
One Russian drone held up seven flights in Moldova, Zelenskyy’s trip to Norway for King Harald V’s funeral among them
What a night without enough interceptors looks like
The same night, Russia sent 161 long-range attack drones at Ukraine, decoys among them, along with a cruise missile.That is an ordinary night now, and its damage spreads thin across the map instead of landing in one place.
A Russian strike set a nine-story apartment block alight in Kyiv, burning the facade up to the fifth floor and a flat on the second. Firefighters carried seven people out and handed seven more to medics. Russian drones injured eight people in the capital overnight.
North of the city, Russia burned warehouses in the Bucha district, then struck the same site again while the crews were still dousing the flames.
In Dnipro, the drones kept coming back, more than ten times from the evening on, damaging a plant and a row of garages and injuring seven people.
Farther out, Russia injured a mother and her son in Zaporizhzhia and damaged a plant in Zhytomyr Oblast, and the waves ran west far enough that NATO jets went up over Romania.

American woman allegedly smuggled drugs for free trip to Japan

U.S. women arrested for allegedly smuggling $1 million worth of drugs to Japan, one claims she was motivated by free trip
Tokyo police arrested two American women for allegedly smuggling $1 million worth of cannabis into the country, with one suspect claiming she was motivated by a free trip to Japan, an official and media reports said Friday.
The pair, both 25, arrived at Tokyo's Haneda airport from New York last Saturday with two suitcases in which "cannabis-like dried plants were secretly stored," a police spokesman told AFP.
Nippon TV aired images of the drug seizure, showing more than a dozen packages containing the alleged cannabis.
Japan has some of the world's strictest drug laws and smuggling or possession of illegal narcotics can result in a lengthy jail term.
The dried cannabis weighed around 30 kilograms (66 pounds) and is valued at about 150 million yen ($970,000), media reported.
One of the women told police she took the job for the money and because, "I was attracted by the fact I could go to Japan for free," Nippon TV reported.
The other suspect denies the allegation, telling police she "didn't know that cannabis was inside" the suitcase, the Tokyo Shimbun reported, citing unnamed police sources.
The women "conspired with someone else whose name is unknown," the police spokesman told AFP. They claimed they received instructions from a man they met on social media but never met in person, according to local media.
The pair were arrested "on suspicion of violating the drugs and psychotropics control law, or, smuggling to gain profit," the spokesman said.
They also breached two other unnamed laws, he added.
Smuggling cannabis for the purpose of making profit carries up to 10 years in prison and a fine of up to 3 million yen ($19,500).
Last December, prominent American playwright Jeremy O. Harris was arrested in Japan on suspicion of smuggling the psychedelic drug ecstasy. He was released three weeks later.

Giotto's Stories of Saint Francis return to former glory at Santa Croce in Florence
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:10:26 CEST
23:10:26 KST

Giotto's Stories of Saint Francis
have returned to their former glory at the church of Santa Croce
in Florence after a loving restoration lasting four years.
                                    
                                       
				After four years of work, the restoration of the Stories of
Saint Francis frescoes by Giotto in the Bardi Chapel at Santa
Croce in Florence has been completed.
                                    
                                       
				The project has provided a clearer reading of Giotto's painting,
bringing to light its expressive intensity and revolutionary
conception of painted space.
                                    
                                       
				The research and restoration project was promoted by the Opera
di Santa Croce in collaboration with the Opificio delle Pietre
Dure and funded by the Ministry of Culture, the Fondazione CR
Firenze, Arpai, and private donors.
                                    
                                       
				In the year marking the eighth centenary of the 'Transitus'
(death) of Francis of Assisi, the chapel's six scenes depict
crucial moments in his life: the renunciation of his father's
wealth, the approval of the Rule, the apparition at the Chapter
of Arles, the trial by fire before the Sultan, his death, and
the apparition to Friar Augustine and Bishop Guido.
                                    
                                       
				The restoration now clarifies the technical and stylistic
differences among the painters who worked in the chapel under
Giotto's coordination.
                                    
                                       
				It also confirms Giotto's ability to adapt techniques to his own
expressive and operational needs; while working on a "buon
fresco" (wet plaster) base, he made extensive use of "a secco"
(dry) techniques to utilize a wider range of pigments, thereby
varying chromatic and spatial effects.
                                    
                                       
				The resulting image offers a better understanding of Giotto's
figurative and spatial invention, while keeping visible the
chequered history that has marked the cycle over the centuries:
the application of a lime whitewash in the early 18th century,
the rediscovery in 1851—accompanied by Gaetano Bianchi's
restoration—and the subsequent work carried out by Leonetto
Tintori between 1957 and 1959.
                                    
                                       
				During the first phase of the restoration, the most fragile
areas were consolidated, dangerous forms of deterioration were
mitigated, deposits and altered materials were removed, and many
of the old synthetic fills from the previous restoration were
replaced with mixtures more compatible with the original
plaster.
                                    
                                       
				The second phase involved defining the final image through the
delicate filling of losses and interventions aimed at restoring
immediate legibility to Giotto's spatial composition—a crucial
element of his pictorial revolution.

‘Majority do not welcome him’: Trump heads to Ireland amid fury over Gaza
Protests set to erupt across Ireland, where President Connolly has long regarded the US as an untrustworthy power.
Donald Trump is set to arrive in Ireland on Saturday, but most Irish people aren’t happy about it.
A recent poll by the Sunday Independent and Ireland Thinks reported that 69 percent do not support the US president’s visit.

“Thousands of us will march on Saturday because we refuse to normalise a man who has facilitated genocide,” Sean Radcliffe, an economics undergraduate student at Trinity College Dublin, told Al Jazeera.
Taoiseach Micheal Martin “should say it clearly, firmly, and publicly: the United States is facilitating genocide,” added Radcliffe, who is a leader of the student body’s Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions campaign.
Sean Corcoran, an environmental artist based on the Copper Coast in Waterford, spent five hours with three others carving “No Kings” – a nod to anti-Trump protests under the same name in the US, along with “Gaza, Iran, Ice,” into the sand of Dublin Bay Beach.
“As an Irish artist and citizen, I believe it is important for me to use my voice to share my opinion about the Trump administration,” he told Al Jazeera. “Despite the diplomatic and security welcome that Mr Trump will receive when he lands in Ireland, the majority of Irish do not welcome him to Ireland.”
Trump is expected to meet with several figures in Ireland’s leadership, including Martin and antiwar President Catherine Connolly, who has previously said the US is, along with France and England, a nation Ireland “certainly cannot trust”.
Protests are planned throughout Ireland, including in Dublin’s Garden of Remembrance. Many are themed against Trump’s role in supporting Israel’s actions in Palestine.
Ireland, one of the West’s most vocal critics of Israel, was the first European Union country to ban imports from illegal Israeli settlements.
Roughly 4,000 security personnel will be enlisted to protect the US leader from protests and other risks during his visit, including roughly 1,000 US Secret Service agents and “anti-drone weaponry”.
Following his visits with Ireland’s political elites and the US ambassador to Ireland, resulting in the temporary shutdown of Phoenix Park, one of Europe’s largest parks, he is expected to visit the Irish Open golf tournament in Doonbeg, where Trump owns a resort.
Connolly, whose role is largely ceremonial, has said that she is “not afraid to stand against the consensus”. She secured a landslide victory in October 2025.
During her campaign, Connolly said she would meet the US president in her official capacity, but added that “I doubt that [genocide] would be the discussion, I doubt that [Gaza] would be on the agenda”.
“People expect a slightly more activist president who might speak out,” Johan Dornschneider-Elkink, professor of Computational Political Science at University College Dublin, told Al Jazeera. “The high level of consensus in the Irish population means that the president can also feel a bit comfortable pushing it a bit.”
Still, the limitations of Connolly’s role, and the economic obligations of the taoiseach are expected to overshadow the issue of Palestine during high-level conversations.
‘Ireland is very much aligned in spirit’
“I think [the protest] shows that Ireland is very much aligned in spirit and policy-wise with the Palestinian people; they very much identify with Palestine,” Stephanie Dornschneider-Elkink, associate professor of Political Science at University College Dublin, told Al Jazeera.
“But there’s also only so much space to be critical. Ireland depends on the US, and there’s an economic relationship at stake.”
Johan added that the visit is more an opportunity for Irish people who want to make known their stance on both Palestine and the Trump administration.
“There’s an understanding that Trump is one president among many, and there will be another president. There’s a longer history of the Irish-US relationship which nobody wants to see damaged.”
Leader of the Opposition Mary Lou McDonald of Sinn Fein, told journalists this week that she hoped Connolly would raise issues like “ongoing facilitation of a genocide in Gaza,” adding that the party will take part in Saturday’s protests.
The party’s spokesperson on foreign affairs, trade, and defence, Donnchadh O Laoghaire TD, shared on his Instagram that he would join the protest in the Garden of Remembrance, asking others to join him “to stand up against genocide and against war”.
The demonstration is organised by the Irish Neutrality League, in coalition with the Irish Anti-War Movement and social justice movement Tonn na Cle, and has received endorsements from the Social Democrats, Labour, People Before Profit-Solidarity, and the Green Party, in addition to Sinn Fein.
Student groups in Ireland have been among the loudest voices of pro-Palestine organising in the country, with Trinity College Dublin becoming the first university in the world to officially sever ties with Israel.
Radcliffe said there is no generational divide “of any significance” over the Israel-Palestine conflict in Ireland.
“Some of the best [pro-Palestine] activists I know in Ireland are pensioners,” he said.

Exclusive: UK Greens' Zack Polanski vows to champion local issues, global justice if elected MP
UK Green Party leader Zack Polanski has vowed to champion the concerns of local constituents as well as peace and justice around the world if elected to parliament, in exclusive comments to The New Arab on Friday.
Polanski was selected as the party’s candidate for the Holborn and St Pancras by-election following a local party vote the night before, in which he ran against Camden councillor Hamza Chowdhury.
Speaking to The New Arab after the announcement, Polanski underscored the “obvious” issues the people of Holborn and St Pancras care about, including lowering bills and rent controls, but also making sure they were aware they “can and absolutely care about what’s happening around the world”.
“Our government has not just been complicit in the genocide, we've been active participants in it,” Polanski told The New Arab, referring to Israel's war on Gaza.

Since being elected as Green leader in 2025, Polanski has made the Palestinian cause a key plank of the party's platform, which has seen the party pose a significant challenge to Labour from the left.

Mali surgeons perform landmark conjoined-twin operation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

14:07:55 UTC
23:07:55 KST

Mali surgeons perform landmark conjoined-twin operation
Malian doctors have successfully separated conjoined twin girls in what the government described as the first operation of its kind in the West African country.
The procedure was performed on Wednesday by a multidisciplinary team at Gabriel Toure University Hospital in the capital, Bamako, the Health Ministry announced the next day. The twins were born by cesarean section on August 29 following a full-term pregnancy in which congenital abnormalities had already been detected. They were joined through parts of their urinary and digestive systems and shared a bladder and colon, according to an official account reported by local outlet Maliweb.
Health Minister Assa Badiallo Toure visited the newborns and praised the medical team. “Such an operation is truly a feat,” she said, describing it as an important milestone for specialized medicine in Mali.
Hospital director Professor Thierno Madani Diop assembled a team of pediatric surgeons, anesthesiologists, intensive-care specialists, cardiologists, radiologists, pharmacists, and laboratory and operating-room personnel to carry out the procedure.
Conjoined twins develop when a single embryo does not divide completely during the early stages of pregnancy. The condition occurs in an estimated one in 50,000 to 200,000 births, and the viability of separation depends largely on which organs the twins share, according to the US National Library of Medicine.
The operation in Mali follows another rare medical success in Africa in March, when doctors at Mankweng Hospital, a rural public facility in South Africa, separated conjoined newborns. The babies were reported to be in stable condition in neonatal intensive care after the procedure, according to the South African government.

Why Algeria finally broke with the UAE
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:07:45 UTC
23:07:45 KST

Breadcrumb
Why Algeria finally broke with the UAE
Algeria’s decision to sever diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates did not come out of nowhere.
It was the culmination of years of growing suspicion in Algiers that Abu Dhabi was not simply pursuing a different regional policy, but actively backing forces and movements that Algeria regards as threats to its security.
The immediate announcement was stark. Algeria’s Foreign Ministry said it had exhausted attempts to preserve the relationship and accused the UAE of increasingly "provocative or hostile" behaviour.
"After exhausting all avenues capable of preserving bilateral relations, the Algerian government decided, this day, to sever diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates," the ministry said.
The UAE ambassador was summoned and given 48 hours to comply with the decision.
But the ministry did not identify a single incident that triggered the rupture.
That omission matters, because the break appears less about one diplomatic confrontation than about a much wider struggle over influence across North Africa and the Sahel.
For Algeria, the central issue is national security.
Algiers has increasingly viewed the UAE’s regional role through the prism of Libya, Tunisia, the Sahel and Algeria’s rivalry with Morocco. It believes Emirati influence in these arenas has repeatedly worked against Algerian interests.
President Abdelmadjid Tebboune had already made clear that relations were close to breaking point.
In an interview broadcast by state television, he said Algeria had delayed severing ties because it did not want to deepen divisions in the Arab world.
"The Arab world has many cracks and divisions, and we do not want to make matters worse, otherwise we would have cut relations with this mini-state a long time ago," he said.
The reference to a "mini-state" was widely understood to mean the UAE.
The tensions go back several years.
After Algeria’s 2019 presidential election, accusations circulated that Abu Dhabi had tried to influence the contest in favour of former culture minister Azzedine Mihoubi.
Tebboune later made that allegation publicly.
In February 2026, he said: "A state, indeed I call it a mini-state [meaning the UAE], wanted to interfere in the first presidential election, and then the second."
Another major fault line was Israel.
Tebboune strongly criticised the UAE, Bahrain and Morocco for normalising relations with Israel under the Abraham Accords, describing the process as "rushing".
For Algeria, Morocco’s role made the issue particularly sensitive.
The two North African neighbours are locked in a deep strategic rivalry, and any Emirati policy seen as strengthening Rabat or weakening Algeria’s regional position has been viewed in Algiers with suspicion.
The disagreement then widened beyond diplomacy.
In January 2025, a newspaper close to Algeria’s presidency accused the UAE of supporting efforts to destabilise the country and of financing the Movement for the Self-Determination of Kabylie, or MAK.
Algeria did not publicly provide detailed evidence for the accusation, but the allegation touched one of the most sensitive issues in the country: territorial unity.
By then, the dispute had begun to affect practical relations.
Algeria moved to cancel its air services agreement with the UAE, with measures barring Emirati airlines from Algerian airspace coming into force on 29 August.
But the regional dimension remains the most important.
The Libyan nexus
Algeria has long regarded developments in Libya and the Sahel as direct security concerns.
The UAE’s support for eastern Libyan commander Khalifa Haftar has therefore been especially contentious.
Faisal Azghdaren, a researcher at the Centre for Political Studies in Paris, told The New Arab: "In addition to the contentious issues related to bilateral matters such as economic issues and others, I believe that the role of factors connected to certain geographical, political and security issues in Algeria's surroundings should not be overlooked. These played an important role in gradually shaping the Algerian position towards the UAE, bringing it first to the stage of rupture, and then to the severing of diplomatic relations."
He added: "Algeria believes that the UAE has played a prominent role in attempts to disrupt the political and security architecture in Algeria's neighbourhood, through supporting [Khalifa] Haftar in Libya, and in Tunisia and the Sahel in particular. It sees this as a direct targeting of its national security and harm to its national interests, which prompted it to take the step of sending an air force contingent from the army to Niger as a warning, particularly since Niger's transitional authorities spoke of official allegations of Emirati involvement [according to the confessions of an army officer, Captain Gabriel] in the latest coup attempt that took place in Niamey on 29 August."
This is the core of the Algerian argument: that the UAE is not merely a difficult bilateral partner, but a regional actor whose policies are increasingly colliding with Algeria’s own security doctrine.
Abu Dhabi has so far offered a much less detailed public account.
Anwar Gargash, an adviser to the UAE president, appeared to respond indirectly to the rupture on X without naming Algeria.
He said "diplomatic relations are managed through reason, communication and clarity of interests, not through riddles and signals that need to be decoded".
Relations, he added, "cannot be hostage to internal tension or an inability to explain interests and define priorities".
"Ambiguity is not policy, and noise does not compensate for the absence of vision. Successful diplomacy is based on clarity of positions and the sound management of interests and differences," he wrote, adding that "anything else is merely an expression of shortcomings in vision and management".
The comments suggest the UAE rejects Algeria’s framing of the crisis, but they do not directly answer the accusations raised by Algiers.
That leaves one side of the dispute much more fully articulated than the other.
Abdullah Bandar Al-Otaibi, an assistant professor in the Department of International Affairs at Qatar University, told The New Arab that any assessment needed to account for that imbalance.
"A balanced reading of the crisis requires not being satisfied with the Algerian narrative, but also listening to the Emirati position and understanding its motives and background. Every political decision, however severe, has its context and calculations, and relations between states cannot be read from one side alone."
Why now?
The larger question now is why Algeria chose to act at this moment.
The decision itself had been heavily signalled. Algerian media close to the presidency had already reported that a rupture was approaching, while Tebboune had openly said it had been delayed rather than ruled out.
What is less clear is whether a new development pushed Algiers to finally act.
Al-Otaibi said the answer may lie in the accumulation of crises stretching across Libya, Sudan, Niger, the Horn of Africa, the Red Sea and Yemen.
"The decision comes at an extremely sensitive regional and African moment, in which multiple crises and conflicts intersect. Therefore, the fundamental question that should be the focus over the coming hours is: why now? And why at this particular time?"
He added: "Here arises the possibility that there were developments or accumulated disagreements that reached a decisive point, or that there was a straw that broke the camel's back and pushed Algeria to take the decision at this moment. Therefore, understanding the background to the timing may be more important than the decision itself, because it may reveal the true nature of the disagreements and the extent of their connection to broader regional and African issues."
For now, the diplomatic break formalises a deterioration that had been under way for years.
But its significance goes beyond the closure of embassies.
If Algeria and the UAE increasingly see each other as rival actors in North Africa and the Sahel, the dispute could become another layer in a wider regional contest over influence, alliances and security across an already unstable part of the continent.

Why Pakistan is talking to Iran as the Houthi-Saudi fight escalates
Pakistan faces growing pressure to honour its Saudi defence commitments while keeping diplomatic channel to Iran open.
