The calls capped the most dramatic week yet in the Houthi-Saudi war.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Houthis, Yemeni forces engaged in fierce battles: Why each front matters
- list 2 of 4Houthis capture Yemeni town of Mocha: Why it’s important
- list 3 of 4UN envoy warns Security Council Yemen’s war has entered ‘dangerous phase’
- list 4 of 4Houthis control key shipping route after gains along Yemen’s Red Sea coast
Houthi drones and missiles wounded 73 people and set oil facilities ablaze in four Saudi cities on Tuesday, among the heaviest strikes of the war, according to the Saudi-led coalition.
Iran-backed Houthi fighters reached the coastal town of Mocha at dawn on Thursday and pushed offshore to seize nearby islands. By Friday morning, they had grabbed control of all of Yemen’s Red Sea coast. Yemeni government officials said fighters also reached Dhubab, on the Bab al-Mandeb coast, while boats carrying Houthi fighters reached Mayyun Island, at the heart of the strait, after government forces withdrew.
There has been no official announcement by Houthi authorities confirming control of the strait.
Brent crude surpassed $107 a barrel on Friday, as the advance raised fears that both of Saudi Arabia’s main export routes, the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb, could come under pressure at once — one by Iran directly, the other by Tehran’s ally, the Houthis.
Satellite images on Thursday appeared to show a fire along the East-West pipeline, Saudi Arabia’s main Hormuz-bypass route, which carries close to seven million barrels a day over 1,200km (746 miles) to Yanbu.
Riyadh has not confirmed a pipeline strike.
Earlier this week, Pakistan’s Defence Minister, Khawaja Asif, warned that the mutual defence pact between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye “will definitely“ be activated if the fighting spills further into the kingdom.
But with Munir calling Tehran on Thursday night, analysts say the question is not whether Pakistan is preparing to act, but whether diplomacy is the course Islamabad has already chosen.
A briefing full of non-denials
At the Pakistani Foreign Office’s weekly briefing on Thursday, spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan declined to confirm recent reports that Islamabad had passed a Saudi warning to Iran to rein in the Houthis, calling them “unsubstantiated”.
He was equally dismissive of a claim that Saudi Arabia had asked Pakistan to strike Houthi positions in Yemen, calling it “hypothetical” with “no discussion of this kind”.
But when asked whether Pakistan was reaching out to the Houthis through Iran, Khan did not deny it.
Pakistan would “continue to pursue dialogue and diplomacy for peace and stability in the broader region”, Khan said.
Jauhar Saleem, Pakistan’s former foreign secretary and president of the Islamabad-based Institute of Regional Studies, called the phrasing deliberate.
“In diplomacy, what is deliberately not said is as important as what is stated,” he told Al Jazeera, describing Islamabad’s language on the pact as emphasising “deterrence and de-escalation”.
Four trips to Tehran and counting
Pakistan’s military chief Munir has travelled to Tehran four times since April. The latest visit came last month, days after a phone call from US President Donald Trump asking Islamabad to lean on Tehran.
An Iranian source familiar with the diplomatic contacts told Al Jazeera that telephone diplomacy has intensified since the escalation began.
“Over the past week to ten days, there have likely been three to four telephone conversations between the Pakistani field marshal and the Iranian foreign minister,” the source said.
“Only two were made public, by the Iranian side,” the source added, describing the rest as in keeping with Islamabad’s preference for “silent diplomacy”.
Al Jazeera received no response from Pakistani officials to questions on the unannounced contacts.
Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister, Ishaq Dar, has been speaking separately with his Saudi and Turkish counterparts in recent days.
“The role [as mediator between Saudi Arabia and Iran] fits with the pattern, but with much higher stakes,” Saleem said, arguing that Pakistan’s commitments to Riyadh carry greater risk than its US-Iran mediation ever did.
An old script
Pakistan has been here before.
In April 2015, its parliament unanimously rejected a Saudi request for troops, ships and warplanes to combat the Houthis, resolving that “Pakistan should maintain neutrality in the Yemen conflict so as to be able to play a proactive diplomatic role to end the crisis”.
Saleem said now “could pose again the dilemma faced by Pakistan’s foreign policy strategists a decade ago, in this very context”.
A closer precedent came this year.
When Iran struck Saudi Arabia directly in February and March, the kingdom in April announced the arrival of Pakistani forces in Saudi Arabia, even though Islamabad did not directly enter the conflict.
“This shows that the meaning of the mutual-defence principle in the bilateral pact, or the Mecca pact, is a matter calculated by the parties and does not mean the automatic entry of the parties if an attack occurs against the other,” Javad Heiran-Nia, an Iranian analyst on regional security, told Al Jazeera.
How far can Pakistan go?
The specifics of what Munir and Araghchi spoke about on Thursday night remain unclear.
But analyst Heiran-Nia said Pakistan’s role was clear. “Pakistan has recently conveyed Saudi Arabia’s warning message to Iran and asked Tehran to restrain its Houthi allies,” he told Al Jazeera. “This action demonstrates Pakistan’s active and operational role as a communication channel between the two sides.”
On Tehran’s leverage over the group, he was equally direct.
“Iran has significant influence over the Houthis, although this influence is not absolute and unlimited,” he said. “It is true that the Houthis may in some cases make their decisions independently of Iran, but their strategic interests align with Tehran.”
On Friday, after the Houthis gained control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, Iranian leaders were quick to show where their loyalties lay.
Iran’s First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref welcomed the “victories of the heroic nation of Yemen,” in a post on X.
Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, was even more direct in claiming influence over the Houthis, as a part of Tehran’s so-called Axis of Resistance.
“Congratulations on this resounding victory, Ansar Allah,” Mokhber posted on X, referring to the Houthis by their formal name. “Iran’s might in the Strait of Hormuz and the homegrown resolve of the resistance have driven the US and its allies into a tactical and strategic impasse.”
What comes next
Asif Durrani, Pakistan’s former ambassador to Iran and one-time special representative for Afghanistan, framed Pakistan’s position differently.
Under the Mecca pact, he told Al Jazeera, “the major issue is threat perception”, where member states raise concerns and partners respond at the request of the threatened state.
Pakistan, he said, “has the capacity to partner with Saudi Arabia in countering the Houthi threat”.
For the moment, former ambassador Saleem said, “Riyadh does not need Pakistan to fight any battles”. Pakistan could help Saudi Arabia better “by preventing any regional wars,” pointing to Islamabad’s strong ties across the Gulf Cooperation Council and its channels to Tehran.
But Umer Karim, an analyst at Riyadh’s King Faisal Center for Research and Islamic Studies, suggested a moment of reckoning for the Pakistan-Saudi relationship might be approaching.
“The cost of inaction is certainly increasing,” Karim added, “and eventually Pakistan will be pushed to react and fulfil its commitments” under both a bilateral mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia and the trilateral agreement that also includes Turkiye.
“Riyadh is probably for now reevaluating the situation and figuring out what’s the best outcome.”

Britain looks to AI to advance clean energy transition
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
22:06:31 CST
23:06:31 KST

LONDON, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- With renewables generating more than half of its electricity, Britain is looking to artificial intelligence (AI) to make its expanding clean energy system more efficient and affordable.
Renewables produced a record 153 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, accounting for 52.1 percent of Britain's electricity generation, according to statistics from Britain's Department for Energy Security and Net Zero. Output increased by 5.9 percent from 2024, with offshore wind, solar and bioenergy reaching record levels.
Progress across the wider energy system remains uneven. Government statistics put renewables' share of gross final energy consumption, which extends beyond electricity, at 16.8 percent in 2025.
However, energy affordability remains a pressing concern. Simon Cran-McGreehin, head of analysis at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU), argued in a statement that moving away from oil and gas would reduce exposure to volatile fossil fuel markets. He advocated continued adoption of electric vehicles and heat pumps powered by British wind and solar generation.
Meanwhile, growing reliance on weather-dependent electricity generation and flexible electricity demand is making grid management more complex, according to an independent review, The Grid We Need Now, released in September.
To boost the development of a clean homegrown power system, the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has recently opened a call for evidence on how AI can transform the energy system to inform policy development.
"AI could enable renewable power sources, electric vehicles, heat pumps, batteries and smart appliances to work together more effectively. It could help us identify faults before they happen, forecast demand more accurately, make better investment decisions and accelerate the development of new energy technologies," said Martin McCluskey, Britain's Minister for Local Energy and Jobs.
In a document titled Vision for an AI-enabled Clean Energy System, the government says AI could help manage batteries, electric vehicles, heat pumps and smart appliances to shift electricity use to times when power is cheaper and cleaner. Better forecasting and planning could reduce waste and avoid building excess capacity as a precaution.
Some applications are already producing results. The independent review reports that British startup Open Climate Fix combined weather forecasts, satellite imagery and live solar-generation readings to halve solar forecasting errors for the National Energy System Operator (NESO), saving 30 million pounds (40.6 million U.S. dollars) annually in reserve costs.
Other work focuses on coordinating decisions across the grid. In an August 2025 explanation of its Volta program, NESO said its Grand Optimiser project aimed to improve how the grid directs power plants and batteries to supply electricity. The project envisages multiple digital models working together across different operational timescales. NESO said this could streamline control-room processes and potentially reduce electricity system operating costs.
Looking further ahead, the independent review, led by the British government's AI Champion for Clean Energy Lucy Yu, recommends using ongoing assessments of the likelihood and impact of potential disruptions to guide grid operations by 2035 and grid planning by 2036. This could reduce the cost of preparing for fixed worst-case scenarios while maintaining or improving reliability.
However, the review says existing approaches to running the grid and difficulties putting new technologies into widespread use are holding back progress. It recommends setting up a national center to help test AI tools and introduce them across the electricity network.
"While much of it can and must begin immediately, we should prepare for a decade of delivery," Yu wrote in the review's foreword.
The British government also identifies fragmented data, incompatible standards, weak investment incentives and shortages of digital skills as barriers. Existing systems can be difficult to integrate, while unclear regulatory expectations may discourage adoption.
"Just as was true for other technologies in the past, the opportunity from AI comes not just from what it can do in the system as it is, but from its potential to change the system itself," said Yu. ■

Feature: Combining acrobatics and ballet, Chinese drama Swan captivates Athens audience
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
22:06:28 CST
23:06:28 KST

by Liu Baiyun, Chen Gang, Maria Spiliopoulou
ATHENS, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- "Mom, I want to do that too." Eight-year-old Sofia had just watched a female acrobat rise onto her male partner's shoulder, stand en pointe and spin before holding a poised final position on stage at Athens' Christmas Theater.
The scene, known as "Shoulder Ballet," was one of the defining moments of Swan, an original Chinese acrobatic drama by Guangzhou Acrobatic Arts Theatre performed in Athens on Thursday night. As the breathtaking sequence came to an end, the theater exploded with cheering and applause.
Sofia, who practices rhythmic gymnastics, was particularly drawn to the moments when acrobatic movements combined with the grace and balance of ballet.
"It's a bit like ballet, acrobatic," Sofia's mom, Christina Sotiriou, said. Sofia's reaction offered a glimpse of the enthusiasm surrounding Swan at its Athens premiere. The performance, staged as part of the China-Greece International Theatre Festival, drew nearly 2,000 people to the Christmas Theater.
After the finale, the cast had to make two curtain calls, and many audience members waited to take photos with the performers.
For 10-year-old Athena, who studies ballet, it was the first time she had seen an acrobatic performance. Her interest was sparked by her aunt Bella, who teaches in Beijing and had told her that a performance incorporating elements of ballet into Chinese acrobatics would be coming to Greece.
Athena's younger sister Dora, who is eight and learning Chinese martial arts, was equally enthusiastic. "The show was perfect. The dancers were amazing," she said.
"What I saw was truly unique," said another spectator, Markos Kantzios, praising "the acrobatic artistry of the Chinese, who excel at it and are ranked number one in the world."
He also highlighted the effort involved in bringing the troupe all the way from China to Greece.
"It's quite an undertaking to come all the way from China to Thessaloniki and Athens to present this unique performance to Greek audiences," he said.
Rather than retelling the story of the classical ballet Swan Lake, the production draws on the real-life experiences of Chinese acrobats and follows a young performer's pursuit of her dream of becoming a "swan."
The protagonist undertakes demanding training, injuries, setbacks and moments of self-doubt before gradually finding her way forward.
The signature scene "Shoulder Ballet" combines the physical strength, balance and precision of Chinese acrobatics with the lightness and elegance associated with ballet. The play also features acrobatic techniques such as diabolo, rolling-ring acrobatics and hat manipulation.
Using scrim, projections, lighting and stage machinery, the production shifts between the performers' physical and inner worlds.
For artistic director Wu Zhengdan, who is also the real-life inspiration for the production, the story's emotional appeal lies in its connection with the performers' own experiences.
"This work can resonate with audiences in different countries because it tells a real story," Wu said. "It tells the experiences and challenges that every acrobat has truly gone through."
For Wang Wanping, founder of the Sino-Hellenic International Theatre Festival, the Greece tour is also about creating connections through performance.
"We always believe aesthetics is a universal language," as music, body movement, and stage images can transcend borders and cultural differences, creating connections between people with different life experiences, Wang said.
For Sofia, the young rhythmic gymnast, Swan's spectacle of strength, balance and movement had planted a seed--a simple desire to try it herself one day. ■

Displacement in Yemen alarmingly surges past 46,000 amid escalating fighting: IOM chief
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
22:06:23 CST
23:06:23 KST

GENEVA, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- At least 46,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since fighting escalated last week, and the number is alarmingly rising by the hour, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said Friday.
"Families are being forced to flee for the second or third time in this conflict, with almost nothing left," said IOM Director General Amy Pope in a press release. "As fighting spreads, reaching people with lifesaving assistance is becoming harder. We urgently need safe, unimpeded access."
She called on all parties to the conflict to guarantee safe humanitarian access and to protect civilians, aid workers and assets on the ground.
The figure spans the West Coast and Taiz governorates recently, and continues to climb. Overnight, large numbers of people were reportedly seen leaving Mokha city with their belongings. IOM's Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) team is working to establish updated figures to inform the humanitarian system and its lifesaving response, though communication with affected areas remains highly challenging due to widespread telecommunications disruptions.
New arrivals are being reported in Lahj and Aden governorates; reports also indicate people are moving north towards Ibb. Entire villages are reported to have emptied in Maqbanah, Jabal Habashi and Al Ma'afer as clashes moved closer to populated areas. The Mokha-Taiz road, a key supply route, has reportedly been cut, and host communities in the region are under growing strain.
Yemen's conflict began in late 2014 when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting the Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.
The latest advances mark a major battlefield shift along Yemen's western coast amid one of the sharpest escalations since a UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted major hostilities. ■

Ethiopian logistics center expanded by Chinese company to boost capacity, efficiency
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
22:05:58 CST
23:05:58 KST

ADDIS ABABA, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- The expansion project of Mojo Dry Port, contracted by Chinese construction giant China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation (CCECC), was inaugurated Thursday by Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed in Mojo of the country's Oromia regional state.
Speaking at the inauguration ceremony, the PM said that Ethiopia has registered rapid socio-economic growth over the past few years, in which logistics has played a vital role. However, for Ethiopia, a landlocked country, the logistical cost of imported products remains relatively high, resulting in the high price of goods in the market.
He commended the completion of the expansion project, which will greatly boost the capacity and operation efficiency of the logistics hub. "With capacity for up to 1 million 20-foot containers a year, it enables domestic packaging of dry bulk cargo, saving foreign currency and creating jobs for our citizens," Abiy said.
For his part, Sun Mingxi, charge d'affaires at the Chinese Embassy in Ethiopia, noted that the Ethio-Djibouti railway is a flagship project of the Belt and Road Initiative, as well as an excellent example of China-Ethiopia bilateral cooperation, and the Mojo Dry Port is an important facility affiliated to the railway.
"China and Ethiopia are working closely to advance this 'Prosperity Belt' along the railway. The expansion and modernization of this dry port will contribute to the future development of the railway and Ethiopia's export industry," Sun said.
Located about 70 km southeast of Addis Ababa, Ethiopia's capital, this project is an expansion and upgrade of the Mojo Dry Port, covering an area of approximately 67.8 hectares. The average cargo detention time at the port will be significantly reduced from a previous maximum of 60 days to about eight days now, according to CCECC.
As the largest inland port in Ethiopia, Mojo Dry Port handles the storage and transportation of most of the country's imported goods. The expansion of this port costs approximately 110 million U.S. dollars, and all the financing was provided by the World Bank, it was noted. ■

China calls for closer global cooperation on human rights governance

Unknown Publisher

GENEVA, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- China called on all countries to revitalize global cooperation and accelerate the improvement of global human rights governance under the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights at a UN panel discussion here Wednesday.
This meeting was held on the sidelines of the 63rd session of the UN Human Rights Council on promoting and protecting economic, social and cultural rights in a bid to address inequalities. Jia Guide, China's permanent representative to the UN Office at Geneva and other international organizations in Switzerland, delivered a keynote speech.
Amid the ongoing UN fiscal strains, resource allocation for economic, social and cultural rights remains inadequate, so the international community should give these rights higher priority on the multilateral human rights agenda, Jia said.

The panel was held pursuant to the Human Rights Council resolution on promoting and protecting economic, social and cultural rights in the context of addressing inequalities, which was sponsored by China.
The Knowledge Hub for Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, established by the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights as mandated by the resolution, has become the primary UN platform for technical assistance and capacity-building in the field of economic, social and cultural rights. ■

Why is the Kremlin staging Russia’s most boring election ever?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:03:33 UTC
23:03:33 KST

Hello and welcome to Vlast! This time, we focus on the Kremlin’s strategy for next week’s parliamentary elections.
We also analyze why the Kremlin is forcing companies to fund air defense; a 100,000-strong Orthodox religious procession in Moscow; and the closure of the Goethe-Institut in Russia amid deteriorating relations with Berlin.
⏳ This newsletter contains 1,826 words and will take about 10 minutes to read.
Why parliamentary elections resemble presidential elections
Russia’s parliamentary elections next week look set to be the most uneventful in the country’s modern history. Candidates are not campaigning, the major political parties are silent, and there is no criticism of the authorities. The only visible politician is President Vladimir Putin. Notably, the most prominent news story in recent weeks in state-owned media has been speculation about whether a concert by rapper Kanye West will take place in St. Petersburg.
Of course, in Russia’s closely controlled public politics, a lack of drama is no accident. It’s deliberate. The Kremlin believes that suppressing voter turnout by minimizing coverage and campaigning is the best way to increase support for the ruling United Russia party. Particularly given that the war in Ukraine means there is no cash for populist pre-election handouts.
It’s possible that candidates may become more visible in the final week of campaigning (the vote takes place over three days from September 18), but this will not alter the dynamic. After the authorities last month barred the liberal, anti-war Yabloko party from participating, there has been no debate or controversy. Politics has disappeared from the airwaves.
Many candidates do not attend pre-election debates, with empty studios becoming a social media meme. It’s obvious that none of the parties taking part in the elections are trying to attract attention: they do not criticize the authorities, and refrain from discussing topical issues. Televised campaign ads tend to be cheap, make heavy use of AI, and be devoid of substance. None of the parties that are—at least on paper—competing against United Russia have funded their candidates in single-mandate districts.
At the same time, United Russia, which traditionally absorbs public anger directed at the authorities, is pretending it does not exist. The main public figures representing the party in these elections—Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin, war correspondent Yevgeny Poddubny, Children’s Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova, and Ukraine war veteran Vladislav Golovin—have each given one interview to state-owned TASS. That essentially marks the extent of United Russia’s campaign.
Instead, the only political figure visible to voters in recent weeks has been Putin. The result is that parliamentary elections have begun to look a lot like presidential elections—again, a deliberate Kremlin strategy.
On state-owned television, Putin has been doing most of the campaigning for United Russia. Putin has always been involved in boosting support for United Russia, and he “shares” his approval rating with the party. But the absence of United Russia and its candidates in these elections have made his involvement particularly glaring.
In his campaigning, Putin appears to have been aiming to reassure people on key issues. Last week, he twice dismissed the possibility of another imminent round of mobilization. He also said the government would not be confiscating the bank deposits of ordinary people—another major worry for Russians. Data published by Kremlin polling organization FOM on Thursday showed that general anxiety levels have fallen almost 10 percentage points from a multi-year high at the end of July, perhaps as a result of Putin’s interventions.

Yemen’s Houthi group claimed Friday that its forces had taken control of six districts in the western provinces of Taiz and Al-Hudaydah, covering a total area of 5,400 square kilometers, during a military operation launched on Sept. 3.
The claim came in a video statement by the group’s military spokesman, Yahya Saree.
Saree said the Houthis launched a large-scale military operation on Sept. 3 from several directions to drive out forces opposed to the group from parts of Yemen’s western coast.
He said the operation resulted in the “expulsion” of those forces from “six districts in Taiz and Al-Hudaydah provinces, with a total area of 5,400 square kilometers.”
He did not name the districts but claimed they had become “safe and stable.”
Saree also claimed Houthi forces targeted seven military divisions comprising 38 brigades, killing, wounding and capturing hundreds of their members.
He further claimed that the operation led to the release of a number of Houthi prisoners who had been held for years on the western coast.
The spokesman also said Houthi forces carried out 32 operations against warplanes and shot down nine aircraft.
On maritime navigation, Saree said: “We confirm that maritime navigation is safe for all companies except Saudi vessels.”
In his statement, the Houthi spokesman described the forces confronted in the six districts as “Saudi,” a label the group has increasingly used for Yemeni government forces.
Saudi Arabia denies having ground forces in Yemen and says its role is limited to supporting the internationally recognized government and securing its borders.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia or Yemeni government forces on the Houthi claims.
The western coast holds strategic importance because it extends along the Red Sea and lies near the Bab el-Mandab Strait, one of the world’s most important international maritime routes.
Territorial control in Yemen has shifted in recent days as confrontations between government forces and the Houthis have intensified since early July following years of relative calm.

The restoration of external electricity to Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant has reduced the immediate risk of a station blackout, but the facility's electricity supply remains fragile, the UN nuclear watchdog warned Friday.
International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi said in a statement that further measures were needed to stabilize electricity supplies and replenish depleted diesel fuel reserves.
The plant lost its sole remaining external power line on Aug. 20 following military activity and relied on emergency diesel generators for nearly three weeks to maintain essential safety functions, including cooling its six reactors and their spent fuel.

The IAEA also reported continued military activity around the plant, including explosions, drone activity and gunfire.

====================================================================================================

A clever psychological test reveals the subtle detail that makes us want to work harder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:00:46 UTC
23:00:46 KST

A recent study published in Psychological Science suggests that human beings have a deep-seated need to feel their actions matter, a drive that emerges as early as age four. The research indicates that even the tiniest amount of lasting meaning, such as knowing a small piece of artwork will be saved rather than thrown away, is enough to motivate both children and adults to choose productive effort over easy tasks. These findings hint that the desire for meaningful work is a fundamental part of human nature rather than an abstract adult concept.
In psychology, a sense of mattering refers to the feeling that one’s life and activities have lasting worth across time and space, rather than being trivial or fleeting. This feeling is considered a core component of what gives human life meaning. To understand how this need affects human behavior, a 2008 laboratory experiment showed that adults tend to work much less when their creations, such as assembled Lego figures, are immediately broken apart rather than saved. Building on this idea, a 2020 study demonstrated that feeling like one’s actions truly matter is the biggest contributor to experiencing a sense of meaning in life.
The desire to matter is not limited to adults. For instance, research covered by PsyPost in 2024 indicated that a sense of meaning in daily life is associated with better mental health and fewer behavioral problems during childhood. Together, these earlier studies formed a research progression leading to the question of whether the drive to create something lasting is a basic psychological need present from a young age or a complex desire that only develops later in life.
The research, led by Yilin Liu, a doctoral student in developmental psychology at The University of Texas at Dallas, and Fan Yang, a research associate professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Chicago, builds on this foundation by showing that the drive for even tiny amounts of lasting meaning emerges in early childhood.
“When I tell people that I study meaning, they often react as if it is a very big, abstract topic—almost a luxury reserved for certain people or certain moments in life,” Yang, who also directs the Human Nature and Potentials Lab, told PsyPost. “But I have always felt that meaning is much more fundamental than that. We wanted to ask whether meaning matters even for small, seemingly inconsequential actions in everyday life, whether this sensitivity to meaning emerges very early in development, and whether even a small amount of meaning can shape people’s motivation.”
“A lot of research on meaning focuses on relatively big things, such as having a sense of purpose, contributing to something larger than oneself, or seeing an activity as personally important,” Liu added. “We were interested in a more basic question: how much meaning does something actually need to have before it starts to matter for motivation? We wanted to know whether even a very small signal that what someone does matters in some way could influence what they choose to do and how much effort they put into it, and whether this sensitivity is already present in childhood.”
To investigate this, the researchers conducted four related experiments. The first experiment involved 81 children between the ages of four and nine, alongside a comparison group of 80 adults. Participants were asked to use puzzle pieces to create heart shapes. They were introduced to two games: a “no meaning” game where their created shapes would be immediately put into a shredder, and a “minimal meaning” game where their shapes would simply be saved in a box.
The researchers found that most adults and children evaluated the game where their work was saved more positively, regardless of whether they were playing the game once or repeatedly. In a follow-up test with 138 children and 141 adults, participants were asked which game they would actually prefer to play. The vast majority of adults (up to 90 percent) and children (up to 80 percent) actively chose to participate in the game where their work was saved.
A second experiment involving 129 children and 121 adults was designed to see if people simply like seeing items saved, or if they specifically care about the fate of their own creations. Participants were assigned to either a “create” condition, where they made art from puzzle pieces, or a “watch” condition, where they simply watched puzzle pieces move on a screen. They were then given a choice between a free activity where the objects would be dismantled, and an activity that required them to give up a sticker in order to have the objects saved.
In the watch condition, both children and adults preferred the free activity. However, in the create condition, participants were much more willing to pay the sticker cost just to ensure their own artwork was preserved. This suggests that people are uniquely attached to the lasting existence of the things they put effort into making.
The strength of this early-emerging preference stood out to the researchers. “What surprised me most was how little significance seemed to be necessary,” Liu noted. “We deliberately designed the difference between conditions to be minimal, so there were many reasons to expect that participants might simply ignore it. Seeing children respond to such a subtle distinction was especially striking because it suggests that sensitivity to whether something matters may emerge quite early.”
The third experiment, involving 124 children and 121 adults, tested whether the fate of their work would motivate participants to choose a challenging task over an effortless one. Participants were given the option to either use puzzle pieces to create a specific shape or take the easy route of simply moving the pieces into a box without building anything.
When participants knew their completed artwork would be saved, 83 percent of adults and over 80 percent of children chose to put in the effort to create the artwork. When they were told their artwork would be taken apart, only 34 percent of adults and about 50 percent of children chose the effortful option.
The final experiment explored what happens when actions have no lasting consequence, testing 132 children and 119 adults to see if simply focusing on having fun could compensate. Some participants were guided through the same choices as the previous experiment, while others were placed in a “fun” condition where an experimenter pointed to a smiling emoji and emphasized that the main point of the activity was to enjoy themselves.
The researchers observed that emphasizing enjoyment did increase motivation to create the artwork, even when participants knew it would be taken apart. However, the prospect of having the work saved still provided an additional motivational boost, indicating that enjoyment compensates partially but not entirely for a lack of lasting meaning.
“Study 4 was especially surprising to me,” Yang explained. “We had expected that focusing on enjoyment might largely compensate for a lack of significance. Instead, enjoyment only partially made up for it. That suggests that enjoying an activity and feeling that it matters may play distinct roles in motivation, and that pleasure alone may not fully substitute for a sense of significance.”
These results stand in slight tension with research covered by PsyPost earlier this year, which found that long-term goal success is driven more by the intrinsic enjoyment of the process than the perceived importance of the outcome. The new research, however, examined immediate task persistence and tiny amounts of consequence in short laboratory settings, rather than tracking adherence to real-world personal goals over long periods.
“Meaning is not a luxury concern for people who already have everything else,” Yang said. “It may be more like air: it is everywhere, and we do not always notice it, but it is difficult to replace when it is missing. Our findings suggest that even in very small, everyday actions, people are more motivated when they can see some meaning in what they are doing. Meaning may therefore be a much more fundamental psychological need, and a more basic part of human motivation, than we often assume.”
There are a few things to keep in mind regarding these findings. First, the researchers defined a meaningful outcome simply as putting the finished artwork in a box to save it. In the real world, people find meaning in many small ways, such as taking a picture of their work or showing it to a friend, and the psychological impact of these different actions is still not fully understood. Also, objectively saving an item does not guarantee that a person will subjectively feel their action mattered.
“I would not want readers to conclude that any small attempt to make something seem meaningful will automatically motivate people, or that meaning overrides other factors such as difficulty, interest, rewards, or personal circumstances,” Liu added. “These were controlled experimental tasks in which we isolated a very specific form of minimal significance. The broader question of when these subtle signals matter, and when they do not, is something we still have a lot to learn about.”
Another detail to consider is that the participants strongly valued the survival of objects they personally created. It remains unknown whether this protective motivation extends to items created by other people, or if cultural differences in how people view their own identity might shift these behaviors.
“One misinterpretation I would want to preempt is that, although our findings show that even a minimal amount of significance matters for motivation, this does not mean that minimal significance is sufficient for full motivation,” Yang emphasized. “In other words, our findings do not imply that giving children or adults only minimal significance is enough, or that greater significance would not matter more. An important next step is to study whether more substantial forms of significance have stronger motivational effects in certain situations, such as when circumstances are difficult or tasks are not intrinsically enjoyable.”
Finally, the laboratory tasks focused on physical objects. In an increasingly digital world where many daily interactions leave no physical trace, it is possible that the need to create something lasting is even stronger than these simple experiments capture.
Looking ahead, the researchers hope to explore how these subtle signals shape early development. “One direction I’m especially interested in is understanding how children come to recognize that activities, objects, and experiences are meaningful in the first place,” Liu said. “I’d also like to examine different kinds of meaning, such as whether something feels important, useful, connected to a larger purpose, or valued by other people, and how those different signals shape children’s motivation and learning. Ultimately, I hope this work can help us better understand how everyday environments communicate to children that what they are doing matters.”
Yang shares a similar goal regarding human potential. “My broader question is whether some psychological needs and experiences we often think of as ‘higher-level,’ such as meaning, awe, and transcendence, are actually much more fundamental and accessible to human beings than we typically assume,” she told PsyPost. “That’s why my lab has been exploring these topics in children. I want to understand when these capacities first emerge and how they can remain part of our lives over time. Ultimately, I hope this work can help us better understand our experiential potential and, in turn, give better answers to the question of how we can not only function in life, but live well.”
The study, “Moved by the lightest touch of meaning: Even minimal significance matters for motivation from childhood,” was authored by Yilin Liu and Fan Yang.

US consumer prices pick up in August, bolstering chances of interest rate increase
In the 12 months through August, consumer inflation advanced 3.4 per cent after rising by the same margin in July
US consumer prices accelerated in August as the cost of petrol rebounded after two straight monthly declines, bolstering financial market expectations that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates next week.
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) increased 0.4 per cent last month after edging up 0.1 per cent in July, the Labour Department’s Bureau of Labour Statistics said on Friday. In the 12 months through August, consumer inflation advanced 3.4 per cent after rising by the same margin in July.
Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the CPI increasing 0.4 per cent over the month and climbing 3.4 per cent year on year. Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the CPI rose 0.3 per cent last month after gaining 0.2 per cent in July. The so-called core CPI increased 2.4 per cent year-on-year in August after rising 2.5 per cent in July.
The US central bank tracks the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price indexes for its 2 per cent inflation target.
The government reported on Thursday an increase in the Producer Price Index in August, with strong rises in several key components that feed into the calculation of PCE inflation. That added to last week’s robust employment report for August in boosting rate increase prospects next week.
The odds of a rate increase had diminished following comments by Fed Governor Christopher Waller last week that he was inclined to argue in favour of keeping rates steady if data confirmed inflation pressures were cooling.
Oil prices climbed back above US$100 a barrel on Thursday, while diesel costs are at record highs, suggesting inflation was set to remain elevated and broaden out.

Study reveals link between Tibetan Plateau heat and record rain in California
The discovery could transform winter forecasting and explains why severe floods hit the US west coast when dry weather was expected
In the winters of 2016-2017 and 2022-2023, record-breaking rain swept across the US state and surrounding areas, causing billions of dollars in damage and several deaths during years when drier weather was expected in the region.
A study led by researchers from the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) found that these rain events happened shortly after periods of unusually high land surface temperatures on the Tibetan Plateau in early winter.
The record rain caused “extraordinary damage and severe societal impacts”, according to the paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Science Advances on Wednesday.
Rainfall in the winter of 2016-2017 effectively ended California’s five-year drought, with property damage reaching around US$2 billion. Heavy precipitation in the winter of 2022-2023 brought severe flooding, killing several people and causing around US$4.6 billion in damage.

Shock, confusion and uncertainty for expat teachers in Kuwait
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:59:13 UTC
22:59:13 KST

Breadcrumb
Shock, confusion and uncertainty for expat teachers in Kuwait after thousands dismissed
In testimonies to The New Arab, expatriate teachers whose services Kuwait recently terminated describe the shock and confusion they are experiencing as the new academic year approaches and the impact of the Education Ministry's decision on their futures and obligations.
As preparations were underway for the start of the current academic year, Kuwait's decision to terminate the services of more than 7,000 expatriate teachers from Arab and other nationalities came as a "real shock", leaving the teachers and their families confused amid official efforts to gradually "Kuwaitise" specialisations.
The Kuwaiti Education Ministry justified its decision by saying it falls within the first phase of a plan to address the surplus in the education sector, estimated at 33,268 teachers, including female teachers.
However, several teachers affected by the decision told The New Arab about the negative repercussions on every aspect of their lives, as well as the uncertainty surrounding their futures.
Yasmin, an Egyptian primary school mathematics teacher, described the moment she received a notification through the government Sahel app informing her of the Education Ministry's decision to terminate her services.
"It is truly a shock. Just as I was enthusiastically preparing for the start of the new academic year, I was surprised by the Kuwaiti Education Ministry's decision to terminate my services," she told The New Arab.
"On 6 September, we returned to work in preparation for receiving the students in the coming days. The following day, I read the news about the termination of the services of 7,019 expatriate teachers, but I did not imagine that I would be among them. On the third day, I received an official notification that my services had been terminated, something that was not part of my plans," she said.
"I indeed have three months before my services officially end, but I am completely unprepared for the next step, and I do not know what I will do after the deadline expires," Yasmin added.
While stressing that the Education Ministry has every right to terminate contracts with teachers it considers surplus to requirements, or even for other reasons, she said, "I wish we had been informed of such a life-changing decision at a different time.
"If, for example, it had been at the end of the previous academic year, things would have been completely different for me and for hundreds and thousands of teachers. We could have settled our affairs during the summer holiday and determined our options without time pressure, especially since teaching is the only profession we know and we cannot act easily at the beginning of the academic year, bearing in mind that we have financial and family obligations and others," Yasmin concluded.
The Kuwaiti Education Ministry announced on 7 September that Minister Sayed Jalal Al-Tabtabaei directed the relevant sectors to begin implementing a gradual plan to address the surplus in several specialisations, improve the efficiency of human and financial resource management, achieve optimal use of personnel, and maintain the stability of the educational process.
The ministry said the move was part of its approach to balancing the distribution of educational staff, empowering national talent, and aligning the number of teaching staff with schools' actual needs.
Mohamed Ibrahim, a secondary school history teacher and one of the Egyptian teachers whose services were recently terminated, described the decision as "confusing" in terms of its timing.
"I returned about two weeks ago from my summer holiday in my country. It is an annual holiday that I have been accustomed to taking for more than 10 years after the end of the academic year, and then I return before the start of the new academic year," Ibrahim described.
"But today we are facing a new reality. I knew that I would leave my profession one day, but I imagined that moment would come at the end of a particular academic year, when I would be informed, as had previously happened with many colleagues whom we used to hold farewell parties for," he said.
"I live in Kuwait with my wife and three children, and I have monthly obligations like every head of a household, foremost among them the monthly rent for the apartment and an outstanding loan from one of the local banks, which is what worries me most because I do not know what opportunities are available to me to find work, especially since more than 7,000 colleagues are now without work," he added. "I do not want to spend my end-of-service benefit paying off that loan. At the same time, leaving the country without repaying it is obviously not an option."
"I know many people who have bank loans worth several times the value of mine, which have not been fully repaid, as well as others who are committed to different monthly instalments for household and electrical appliances," he further said.
Meanwhile, Ahood Saad, a Kuwaiti mathematics teacher, described the impact of the Education Ministry's latest decision.
"After the decision to dismiss my expatriate colleagues, only three female teachers remain in the department where I work. This is not enough to keep up with the classes, which means our teaching workload will increase unless this shortage is addressed. Some school departments are now facing shortages, such as the computer department, which has been reduced to only two teachers," she told TNA.
"The loss is not only about numbers. We have also lost skills and capabilities, as my departing colleagues have diverse experience in their fields of specialisation, and we benefited from them throughout the years we worked alongside them in the department," she described.
"I remember among the colleagues in other departments one music education teacher who was distinguished by her competence and also played a prominent role in school activities and the educational field, alongside another teacher specialising in physical education who led the morning activities and the school radio programme every day," she added.
While the Education Ministry has not specified the nationalities of the teachers whose services it decided to terminate, previous reports on its replacement policy indicate that Kuwait's public education sector has historically relied on expatriate teachers from Egypt, Palestine, Jordan, Syria, Tunisia, Yemen and other Arab countries.
Sources told TNA that the largest proportion affected were Egyptian teachers, as they constitute the largest community in the education sector, particularly during the period following Kuwait's liberation from the Iraqi invasion in 1991.
The ministry has previously terminated the services of expatriate teachers in recent years, particularly in 2023, when the services of more than 2,000 expatriate workers in the education sector were terminated.
They included 1,815 teachers and 209 female teachers who held department head positions, which it said at the time was part of a "policy of replacing and Kuwaitising educational jobs".
The Kuwaiti Education Ministry said the total number of teaching staff is about 91,761 teachers and female teachers, excluding those in supervisory positions.
National staff account for about 70.6 per cent of them, while Gulf teachers and those classified as illegally residing account for about 10.1 per cent.
Teachers residing in Kuwait from Arab and other nationalities account for about 19.3 per cent.
It said the results of the study showed an actual surplus estimated at 33,268 teachers and female teachers among citizens, contracted Gulf nationals and those classified as illegally residing (bidoon), in addition to teachers residing in Kuwait from Arab and other nationalities.
The surplus was found in several specialisations in which staffing levels exceed the actual needs of schools.
As part of its general budget, Kuwait allocates more than 2 billion Kuwaiti dinars (about $6.52 billion) annually to the Education Ministry.
More than 95 per cent of this is spent on salaries alone, making it the government body with the highest expenditure from the state budget, which has continued to increase year after year.
The Education Ministry also accounted for more than 13 billion dinars (about $42.4 billion) between 2018 and 2023.

Yabloko List Candidates Disqualified in Tomsk Regional Elections

2026-09-11

A judge in western Siberia’s Tomsk region has disqualified the liberal Yabloko party’s list of candidates from the upcoming regional assembly elections, the party said Friday, though candidates running in single-member districts remain on the ballot.
Authorities have now invalidated or denied registration for Yabloko candidate lists in seven regions across Russia. The northwestern Novgorod region is the only remaining region where list candidates can still run for office.
A judge from the Tomsk Regional Court sided with the right-wing Liberal Democratic Party of Russia (LDPR), which accused Yabloko of copyright violations, exceeding campaign spending limits and using banned social media websites.
Yabloko, which accused LDPR of filing a “copycat” lawsuit amid widespread pressure on the party ahead of next week’s elections, said it would appeal the decision.
Seven Yabloko candidates running in single-member constituencies in Tomsk remain on the ballot.
At the national level, Yabloko candidates campaigning in single-member districts are still allowed to run for office after Russia’s Supreme Court last month ruled to cancel the registration of the party’s federal slate of candidates for the State Duma.
But Yabloko candidates competing in single-member districts are also beginning to see their campaigns cut short due to disqualification.
On Wednesday, the party said courts across several regions received last-minute lawsuits seeking to bar its members from running in the State Duma elections.
Yabloko said 17 of its single-member district candidates could be stripped of their registration if the court rulings are upheld, leaving the party represented in 104 single-member races nationwide.
The party also faces the risk of being stripped of its official registration due to legal requirements to field candidates in at least 20% of regional assembly elections or 10% of gubernatorial races every seven years.
Yabloko is Russia’s oldest liberal party and is the only registered party campaigning on a pro-peace platform.

Prosecutor seeks sentencing for pro-Kremlin Lithuanian activists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:59:00 UTC
22:59:00 KST

Prosecutor Redas Savickas on Friday made sentencing recommendations to the Vilnius Regional Court hearing the case of Erika Švenčionienė, Valery Ivanov, and Kazimieras Juraitis, accused of aiding another state in actions against Lithuania and of publicly denying Soviet crimes.
The prosecutor recommended a two-year prison sentence for Švenčionienė, an 18-month prison sentence for Juraitis, and a fine of 15,000 euros for Ivanov. In his closing argument, the prosecutor stated that the defendants acted in the interests of Russia and Belarus.
Švenčionienė and Ivanov, the former leader of the pro-Soviet organisation Yedinstvo, are accused of denying Soviet crimes, while Švenčionienė and Juraitis are accused of aiding another state in actions against Lithuania.
Before the hearing began, Švenčionienė spoke about friendship with Belarus and “vatniks”, recited a poem about Vytautas Landsbergis, and claimed that the September 11 terrorist attack in the United States was orchestrated by the American government.
“This is a crime against Lithuania’s statehood and sovereignty,” Prosecutor Savickas said in his closing argument regarding the charges against Švenčionienė and Juraitis for aiding another state in actions against Lithuania.
According to him, the defendants repeatedly disseminated false and defamatory information about Lithuania and Ukraine when appearing in Russian and Belarusian propaganda broadcasts.
Švenčionienė sought out individuals willing to fight on Russia’s side in Ukraine. The defendants’ ties to Belarusian authorities and the KGB were confirmed by data from the State Security Department (VSD) included in the case file.
According to Savickas, the defendants aided Russia’s information war against Lithuania.
When appearing in Russian television propaganda broadcasts, Švenčionienė urged the Russians to defeat Ukraine as quickly as possible and "rid it of Nazis". She also claimed that Lithuania intended to attack Russia and stated that “your victory is our victory”.
In his closing argument, the prosecutor also mentioned public statements by Ivanov and Švenčionienė in which they denied Soviet crimes committed during the January 1991 events.
This case has been pending in court for nearly three years. The proceedings have been prolonged due to Švenčionienė’s recurring illnesses and the defendants’ endless motions, which the court is required to consider.
During the trial, the defendants claimed that there had been no occupation of Lithuania, that it was not Soviet soldiers who killed people on January 13, and that Loreta Asanaviciute was not run over by a tank.
The Prosecutor General's Office said in December 2023 that the pre-trial investigation had gathered evidence proving that Švenčionienė and Juraitis, acting in a group of accomplices, helped Russia and Belarus and their organisations act against Lithuania on more than one occasion in 2022.
Švenčionienė and Juraitis are members of the International Forum of Good Neighbourhood – a now-dissolved organization founded by Algirdas Paleckis, a controversial former politician and diplomat convicted of spying for Russia.
Under the Criminal Code, a conviction for aiding a foreign state in acting against Lithuania carries a prison sentence of two to seven years.
Denial or gross trivialisation of Soviet crimes is punishable by community service, a fine, restriction of liberty, arrest, or imprisonment for up to two years.
Last June, Švenčionienė was convicted in another case, which saw her sentenced to 1.5 years of restriction of liberty for publicly denying Soviet crimes.
To date, Juraitis has been convicted twice, and Ivanov – four times.
In 2023, Ivanov, a Russian citizen, had his residence permit in Lithuania revoked. Once the guilty verdict is announced and takes effect, he will be required to leave Lithuania.

The Perekop last called at Sihanoukville in November 2019.
The Perekop’s navigational voyage began in July and will last until mid-December. In total, the ship is expected to cover about 30,000 nautical miles. Its route passes through the Northern Sea Route, four oceans, 14 seas, 23 straits, and nine gulfs. According to the voyage plan, the ship will visit 20 ports, including 12 foreign ones. Among the Russian ports are Severomorsk, Arkhangelsk, Nikolskoye, Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky, and Vladivostok. The foreign ports include Cam Ranh (Vietnam), Sihanoukville (Cambodia), Maputo (Mozambique), Pointe-Noire (Republic of the Congo), Lome (Togo), and Conakry (Guinea).

“I already said it in plain language: the army needs to be shaken up. The time has come. The whole army. We will check everyone,” Lukashenko said.

“We are doing everything as it would be in war,” he said, adding that the exercises incorporated lessons from modern military conflicts.
“We could not win such a conflict”
In separate remarks during the military visit, Lukashenko claimed Belarus had no plans to attack its neighbors.
“We are pragmatists. We understand that if we attacked someone, one of our neighbors, for example, it would be tantamount to death,” he said, according to remarks published by the Pul Pervogo Telegram channel and reported by RBC-Ukraine.

Same Appeasement, Same Mistakes

The Belarusian leader also asked Defense Minister Viktor Khrenin whether the military command system could be deployed if war broke out.
“What if there is a war?” Lukashenko asked.

The defense minister said the system could manage the armed forces, government agencies, and the civilian sector during a conflict.
“What we have now, we could only dream about five years ago,” Khrenin said.
Belarus and Russia’s war
Despite Lukashenko’s assurances, Belarus remains Russia’s closest regional ally and has played a significant supporting role in Moscow’s war against Ukraine.
Minsk allowed Russia to use Belarusian territory and military infrastructure to launch its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Russian troops, aircraft, and weapons have continued operating from the country, although Belarus has not formally deployed its forces to fight in Ukraine.
Belarus also borders three NATO members – Poland, Lithuania, and Latvia – and frequently conducts joint military exercises with Russia, fueling security concerns along the alliance’s eastern flank.

Cabinet to stop employers docking foreign workers’ pay for rent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:54:02 UTC
22:54:02 KST

Cabinet to stop employers docking foreign workers’ pay for rent
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Employers will no longer be allowed to deduct rent from foreign workers’ minimum wage from July 2028, social affairs minister Hans Vijlbrief has told parliament.
Under current rules, employers and agencies can withhold up to 25% of the minimum wage – around €144 a week – to cover accommodation, provided the housing is certified.
The scheme is used mainly for the estimated 600,000 to 900,000 foreign workers in the Netherlands, most of them from Poland, Romania, Hungary and Ukraine, who work in meat processing, distribution centres and greenhouses.
Research by the ministry found employers regularly deduct the full 25% even when the quality of the housing does not justify it, Vijlbrief wrote in a letter to parliament on Thursday.
He said employers are using the deductions as a “business model” and told Nieuwsuur that too many people are being exploited.
Employers will still be able to provide housing, but will have to charge for it separately and at a fair price, the minister said. Ending deductions will also make it easier for inspectors to check whether workers are actually being paid minimum wage, he said.
The decision is the cabinet’s third on the issue in little over a year. Eddy van Hijum, former social affairs minister, proposed phasing out the deductions from January 2026, but his successor Mariëlle Paul of the VVD reversed that decision, arguing that workers would struggle to find housing without employer involvement.
Trade union federation FNV called the move a “perverse profit model at the expense of migrant workers”, and parliament has twice voted for the deductions to go.
Vijlbrief acknowledged that the ban will mean foreign workers will have to find their own accommodation amid the housing crisis. As a result, the ban will come with a rent protection bill, which has yet to reach parliament. Both are scheduled for July 1, 2028.
The measure is part of a wider package to tackle the exploitation of foreign workers, including a ban on temp agency staff in the meat industry, also from mid-2028. A long-delayed licensing system for staffing agencies is set to take effect in 2027.

Same Appeasement, Same Mistakes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:54:00 UTC
22:54:00 KST

This past weekend, Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner (who negotiates on behalf of the US with no official government role) traveled to Russia and Ukraine to restart peace negotiations for Europe’s largest war.
According to reporting, proposals floated by Russian negotiators were focused on the “root causes” of the conflict and included the withdrawal of Ukrainian forces from parts of Donetsk and Ukraine’s abandonment of future NATO membership, In total, the proposal differs little from those advanced a year ago.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
We’ve seen this all before: representatives of the second Trump administration visit Russia in search of a potential peace process, Putin delivers a maximalist vision as a starting point to his American audience, and Trump’s emissaries take this at face value and report this ploy for conquest and subjugation as a breakthrough in the peace process. When Ukraine questions the proposal and tries to rationalize compromises, President Volodymyr Zelensky will be framed as a spoiler. Rinse and repeat. See you six months from now.
At least this time Kushner and Witkoff managed to visit both Moscow and Kyiv, rather than just focusing on Russia and Putin’s circle of advisers. Nevertheless, Trump’s envoys still managed to carry Putin’s water, pushing a deal that makes less sense today than it did even a year ago when Russia’s military prospects seemed brighter.
‘Russia Will Feel It Firsthand’: Budanov Warns of Deeper Ukrainian Strikes
Kushner, once again showing both naivete and willful ignorance, referenced a potential “win-win” resolution to the war. Trump and his representatives are still approaching this war like a transaction and a real-estate deal without any comprehension of the geopolitical stakes embodied in this clash between democracies and authoritarian regimes.
The bizarre reference to all the “incredible memories” the American side would have from their negotiations with Putin further underscores that Kushner and Witkoff are completely out of their depth.
There is nothing we will learn from this round of diplomacy that we didn’t already know, and the failure of this round of talks was prescribed before the envoys left the United States. That being said, there are two elements that observers should focus on when viewing this exchange in the context of the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war and the parade of Trump’s foreign policy failures.
The first is that, under Trump, the United States’ aura of indispensability has been absolutely shattered. The Russians know it. The Chinese know it. The Iranians know it. And America’s allies know it.
Trump has rendered the US irrelevant and much of the world view this moment an era to be suffered through. Trump’s closest allies can be played like a fiddle, and by this point the Ukrainians have no expectations for any serious American-led efforts to end the war. In 2022 and 2023 our decisions shaped the direction and outcome of the conflict. Now, we’re a sideshow that can be safely ignored by Kyiv and Moscow, as well as by other great and middle powers.
The second crucial element of this visit that observers should consider is how this display of doomed diplomacy fits in with the recent visit by CIA Director Ratcliffe to Moscow. Not only does the presence of Witkoff and Kushner soften the impact of whatever warning Ratcliffe delivered to Putin’s inner circle, but it also shows that the American government is divided in its own objectives and strategic vision for approaching Russia.
Voices like Ratcliffe and Rubio, who have historically been hawkish on Russia, must now contend with the short-sighted diplomatic initiatives of Trump’s son-in-law and a real estate investor. The Washington Post reported that Ratcliffe warned Russian officials that continuing the war could backfire and that Russia’s position would deteriorate further.
This isn’t a strategy for peace. It’s a recipe for chaos.

Nearly half of world’s migratory bird species in decline, report warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:52:51 UTC
22:52:51 KST

Nearly half of the world’s migratory bird species are experiencing population declines, while one in nine is threatened with extinction, according to a global assessment released Friday.
BirdLife International’s State of the World’s Birds 2026 report found that 45% of the 1,843 migratory species assessed had declining global populations. Thirty percent were considered stable, 14% were increasing and the trends of the remaining 11% were unknown.
The sixth edition of the report, which focuses on migratory species and the routes they follow, combines BirdLife’s data with findings from broader scientific research.
It identified 200 migratory species, or 11%, as threatened with extinction. Of those, 32 were classified as critically endangered, 57 as endangered and 111 as vulnerable.
A further 111 species were listed as near threatened, meaning around 17% of all migratory birds are considered to be of significant conservation concern.
The report found particularly severe declines among birds that depend on marine and coastal wetlands. Some 54% of migratory shorebird species and 49% of migratory seabirds are declining, as are between 47% and 51% of species associated with marine habitats, forests and coastal wetlands.
The East Asian-Australasian Flyway had the highest proportion of declining species among the four major land-based flyway systems, at 53%. Half of the species using the world’s six marine flyways were also in decline.
Regional monitoring indicated that long-distance migratory birds traveling between Europe and Africa had declined by around 35% since 1980. In North America, 419 migratory species experienced a net loss of approximately 2.5 billion birds between 1970 and 2017, according to studies cited in the report.
Migratory shorebirds have been among the most severely affected. In North America, 26 of the 28 shorebird species monitored between 1980 and 2019 experienced declines, with more than half losing over 50% of their populations.
The slender-billed curlew, a migratory shorebird last reliably recorded in Morocco in 1995, has been declared extinct. Researchers described it as the first known global bird extinction of a species native to mainland Europe, North Africa and West Asia.
Worldwide, seven migratory bird species have been confirmed or are suspected to have become extinct over the past 150 years.
The assessment showed that the extinction risk facing migratory birds continues to increase. A total of 102 species moved into a higher-risk category because of a genuine deterioration in their status, compared with 34 that moved to a lower risk category following improvements.
Human activity was responsible for nearly all the principal pressures identified in the report. Invasive species and diseases affected 139 threatened migratory species, while agriculture and climate change each affected 103.
Hunting and trapping affected 99 threatened species, followed by pollution at 96, urban development at 71, human disturbance at 65, fisheries at 62, energy infrastructure at 55 and logging at 39.
“Migratory birds are sentinels, and their declines reveal growing pressure on the natural systems that sustain us,” said Stuart Butchart, BirdLife International’s chief scientist.
Butchart said coordinated conservation efforts had prevented extinctions and helped some populations recover, but action needed to be implemented across entire flyways rather than in individual countries.
Flyways are migration corridors connecting birds’ breeding, feeding and wintering grounds across countries and continents. The loss of a single important wetland, forest or coastal resting site can therefore affect populations across a species’ entire range.
The report called for stronger international cooperation to protect and restore habitats, prevent illegal killing, reduce seabird deaths caused by fishing, control invasive species and make agriculture, forestry and infrastructure safer for wildlife.
It warned that progress toward biodiversity targets adopted by 196 countries for 2030 remained “far too slow.”
The report was launched during the Global Flyways Summit in Nairobi, Kenya, where governments, conservation groups, scientists and financial institutions adopted the Nairobi Flyways Declaration, pledging greater cooperation along migratory routes.
The declaration was accompanied by plans involving the Asian Development Bank, the Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean, and the World Bank to integrate flyway protection into development financing and mobilize about $6 billion for habitat conservation and restoration.

Opposition split on defense official's dismissal and snap election call
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:51:00 UTC
22:51:00 KST

Opposition split on defense official's dismissal and snap election call
The four opposition parties have differing opinions both on the recent dismissal of a top defense ministry official and the wisdom of holding snap elections.
The Riigikogu returns after its summer recess on Monday, and the opposition is positioning itself ahead of that. Former Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur (Reform) resigned on September 2 over a defense procurement scandal but remains in office until his successor is appointed.
The Social Democrats (SDE) and Isamaa have both questioned the legality of Kaimo Kuusk's dismissal as defense ministry permanent secretary; the Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE) disagrees with their line.
SDE chair Lauri Läänemets sent an inquiry to the Chancellor of Justice asking whether Kuusk's dismissal had been lawful and whether party‑political interests may have been involved. The implication is that Kuusk's continuation in the post would have been a sticking point for former Estonian Defense Forces commander Martin Herem agreeing to be the next defense minister.
"Party‑political interests mean that Martin Herem obviously would not have said 'yes' if the Reform Party had not dismissed the secretary general," Läänemets stated.
The prime minister is to formally offer Herem the position of defense minister, it was announced earlier this week.
Kuusk's departure from office was prompted by the imminent change of minister. Herem set as one of his conditions for taking the post that Kuusk would leave, so that the new minister would have freer hands in personnel decisions.
A secretary general (Estonian: Kantsler – the defense ministry refers to the position as permanent secretary – ed.) may be dismissed at the relevant minister's proposal within the first six months in office, if cooperation is not working out. Isamaa chairman Urmas Reinsalu said it is unclear whether that cooperation had failed with the outgoing defense minister, Pevkur, or the incoming one, Herem.
"There is reason to examine the materials setting out the legal grounds on which the government based its decision. Do they say that cooperation with Mr Pevkur was not working, or were there some other reasons?" Reinsalu said.
EKRE leader Martin Helme, however, said no law was broken by dismissing Kuusk, given Pevkur is still in office. "He can do everything with exactly the same authority as any minister. He had the power to submit the paperwork to the government, and the government decided to dismiss the secretary general. That is exactly how it works, and there is certainly no need for anyone here to shed crocodile tears over Kuusk," Helme said.
Kuusk, 50, is a former Foreign Intelligence Service head of department and former ambassador to Ukraine. He became defense ministry permanent secretary in 2024.
Mihhail Kõlvart, leader of the fourth opposition party, Center, meanwhile has said the opposition should decide to submit a motion of no confidence in Kristen Michal (Reform) as prime minister, and trigger an early election, ahead of the Riigikogu election due in March 2027.
Kõlvart was optimistic about the chances of this happening, with the government now being a minority administration with 50 seats at the 101‑seat Riigikogu. "What matters above all is reaching an agreement in substance. If the opposition has the votes, then it is done," Kõlvart said.
A total of 21 MPs' signatures are required to submit a motion of no confidence. If and when signatures will start to be collected will become clear at a meeting of the opposition parties.
Helme said meetings were going ahead. "For the past couple of weeks, there has been intensive communication between the leaders of all the opposition parties. Including the Social Democrats. The next meeting is on Monday next week, and it will cover more than just the no‑confidence issue."
On the early election issue, however, it is SDE's turn to be the dissenting party. SDE argues that with less than six months to go until the scheduled election, there would not be enough time for a proper election debate. Without that, a no‑confidence motion cannot pass, they argue.
Reinsalu said SDE should rethink its position. "Given their extremely critical rhetoric towards the government, they should also demonstrate it through their actions," Reinsalu said.
Läänemets said much the same about Reinsalu, noting the calls for elections on an extraordinary basis were not a new thing. "He has been talking about an early election for two years. Not a single member of the governing coalition has joined Isamaa, and Urmas Reinsalu has not managed to make a single move," Läänemets added.
