IDF releases footage of Hezbollah infrastructure below Ali al-Taher ridge after destroying tunnels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:01:55 UTC
21:01:55 KST

The IDF released new footage and details on Friday from its latest operation in southern Lebanon, in which it secured and destroyed Hezbollah's underground infrastructure on the Ali al-Taher ridge.
Among the items released by the military was a clip from the body camera of a Yahalom Unit soldier inside one of the underground tunnels, as well as drone footage from inside the tunnels, and a video of two terrorists being killed.
Hezbollah attempted to build a heroic myth around the fighting on the Ali al-Taher ridge, portraying it in the style of the “Battle of Karbala.” However, at the conclusion of a determined military operation by fighters from the IDF’s 36th Division, the Commando Brigade, and the Yahalom special engineering unit, Hezbollah was defeated, and Israel captured and destroyed the organization’s most important facility in southern Lebanon.
The IDF said on Friday morning that what remains of the Ali al-Taher ridge, beneath which Iran spent two decades building Hezbollah’s last and most significant line of defense in southern Lebanon, is “nothing more than a sandbox.” Hezbollah and Iran suffered a major blow overnight. The operation to capture the ridge lasted months, as dozens of terrorists, estimated to number around 50, were entrenched inside the tunnels.
The destruction of the 14 tunnel routes on the ridge, stretching about 5.4 kilometers in total, was given the IDF codename “Chisel of Flames.”
The commander of the 36th Division, Brig.-Gen. Yiftach Norkin, told troops shortly before the tunnels were detonated on Thursday, “The Commando Brigade and the Yahalom Unit, together with the Fire Brigade, Golani, and Brigade 7 forces, led one of the most complex operations we have ever carried out, under the command of the Northern Command. We operated above and below ground, facing threats from near and far, with determination and while maintaining strict protection of our forces. Along the way, we dealt with obstacles and collapses, but continued to strive to complete the mission, the destruction of the underground tunnels on the Ali al-Taher ridge and the enemy infrastructure in the area.”
For months, IDF forces fought against dozens of Hezbollah terrorists who had fortified themselves inside a massive underground system on the Ali al-Taher ridge, in what the military described as one of the most complex operations in recent years. Now, after the tunnels were destroyed using 1,100 tons of explosives, a senior military official said the strategic infrastructure built over more than 20 years had been eliminated and that Hezbollah’s ability to command and control the area had been dramatically damaged.
“You have to be there to understand the scale of the event and its significance, both psychologically and physically, for Hezbollah,” the senior military official said. According to him, the compound served as a “nerve center” for the Badr Unit, and north of it Hezbollah does not have infrastructure of a similar scale until reaching the Dahiyeh neighborhood of Beirut, where the terror group’s facilities were also severely damaged.
IDF surprised Hezbollah after crossing Litani River
According to the official, the operation began with the crossing of the Litani River and an attempt to surprise Hezbollah. The IDF carried out deception operations designed to make the organization believe that forces were preparing to cross in another area, while at the same time opening a hidden, bypass route over several days. The Golani Reconnaissance Battalion and the Egoz Unit began clearing the area, with additional forces joining later.
When the forces reached the rear of Hezbollah’s defensive network, the official said, the surprise among the organization’s operatives was evident. “We saw their kitbags, their weapons thrown along the roads and in the orchards,” he said. However, as the forces advanced toward the central infrastructure, resistance intensified.
According to the senior official, around 50 terrorists were inside the underground system at the start of the operation. “The organization fought for this ridge like it did not fight for other places,” he said. He added that most of the terrorists were killed, some inside the tunnels and others while attempting to flee. In some cases, clashes developed between Egoz fighters and terrorists at distances of only a few meters.
At the same time, Hezbollah attempted to transfer supplies to the terrorists entrenched underground and send additional operatives to rescue and reinforce them. According to the official, at least 10 terrorists who attempted to reach the ridge for these purposes were hit. Supplies that were delivered included communication equipment, food, water, cigarettes, and chocolate.
The official said the terrorists entrenched at the site were given the option to surrender and leave with a white flag, but they refused, and some fled in violation of the organization’s orders. The IDF emphasized that, contrary to some reports, no Iranians were found at the site.
After ground control was established, the center of gravity shifted to the tunnel system. The underground network included more than 5.4 kilometers of routes, into which Yahalom fighters from the Combat Engineering Corps inserted approximately 1,100 tons of explosives in a lengthy and complex process. “The entire work of more than 20 years of building such a significant infrastructure collapsed into nothing,” the official said.
Hezbollah called for Iranian assistance, received cold response
The IDF said the operation was also conducted while attempting to prevent a broader escalation. According to the official, Hezbollah repeatedly called on Iran to assist it. “Desperate calls, including publicly and secretly: come help us, do something, at least make a statement,” he said.
The latest appeal by Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem to Iran last week received a cold response from Tehran. Reactions in Lebanon toward Hezbollah have described the organization’s loss of the ridge as a humiliation in domestic discourse.
According to a military source, the IDF has not identified an operational Iranian move in response at this stage, but is not taking risks. “Anything can happen. We do not see anything operational here, but you cannot know.” The military is preparing accordingly with defensive systems against both Iran and Hezbollah.
Despite completing the destruction of the infrastructure, the IDF clarified that it does not intend to leave the area of the Yellow Line. Forces will redeploy to positions that allow control of the territory, and the military emphasized that it will continue enforcing the line and preventing Hezbollah from returning to it.
“We are not leaving it,” the senior official said.

The surprising link between prosocial motivation and dark creativity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:00:43 UTC
21:00:43 KST

Being actively rejected and being silently ignored both cause social pain, but they trigger entirely different forms of dark creativity. A recent series of psychological experiments reveals that people who feel ignored generate highly malicious ideas, while those who feel rejected come up with a higher volume of creative ideas that are less harmful. The research was published in the journal Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts.
Creativity is usually viewed as a positive trait that drives innovation and problem solving. When people use divergent thinking to materially, mentally, or physically harm others, psychologists refer to this as malevolent creativity. The products of this dark imagination combine harmful intent with novelty, making them dangerous, difficult to detect, and hard to anticipate.
People often resort to malevolent creativity when they face threatening or unfair situations in their daily lives. Social exclusion is one common trigger, causing emotional pain that can lead to antisocial reactions. Psychologists have found that individuals use malevolent creativity as a defense mechanism to cope with social threats.
Not all forms of social exclusion are the same. Explicit rejection is a direct action that threatens a person’s fundamental need to belong to a group. In contrast, being ignored or given the silent treatment is more indirect. This implicit exclusion threatens a person’s sense of control and efficacy. According to psychological models of social behavior, people adjust their responses based on which specific psychological need is threatened.
Psychologist Junsheng Wu and a research team from Ningbo University in China wanted to understand how these distinct social threats shape dark creativity. The researchers suspected that the two types of exclusion would alter a person’s desire to help others, known as prosocial motivation, in entirely different ways. They designed a series of independent experiments to test how this motivation bridges the gap between social pain and creative revenge.
The research team conducted three distinct experiments to establish a chain of cause and effect. In the first experiment, the researchers randomly assigned 120 college students to one of three groups. They asked the participants to spend five minutes writing a detailed account of a specific memory. One group wrote about a time they felt intensely rejected and were told they were not wanted. A second group wrote about a time they were ignored, but not explicitly told they were disliked. A third control group recalled a mundane event from the previous day.
After the writing exercise, the participants completed a test designed to measure malevolent creativity. The prompt asked the students to imagine a scenario involving a romantic rival who made them angry. They were instructed to generate as many creative ideas for revenge as possible, regardless of how immoral the ideas might be.
Independent raters scored the anonymous written responses based on three distinct metrics. They measured fluency by counting the number of appropriate ideas generated. They measured originality by looking at the statistical rarity of the ideas compared to the rest of the group. Finally, they assigned a score based on the sheer malevolence or harmfulness of the proposed revenge.
The researchers observed distinct responses from the two socially excluded groups. The rejected group produced a higher quantity of unique ideas, but those ideas were relatively low in actual malice. The ignored group generated fewer ideas with less originality, but their responses scored much higher on the malevolence scale.
A second experiment investigated whether these differences stemmed from a shift in prosocial motivation. The researchers recruited 110 students and used the same memory writing exercise to prime feelings of explicit rejection, being ignored, or a neutral baseline state.
Instead of brainstorming revenge tactics, the participants rated their willingness to donate to a hypothetical curbside fundraiser on a scale from one to seven. This rating served as a proxy for their prosocial motivation. People with higher scores exhibited a stronger drive to act positively toward others.
The results showed that the rejected group reported the highest willingness to donate. The ignored group reported the lowest willingness to donate, falling well below the baseline of the control group. The authors suggest that explicit rejection prompts a desire to reconnect and regain social approval, whereas being ignored triggers self-protective and antisocial tendencies.
The third experiment tested whether prosocial motivation directly alters malevolent creativity. The researchers randomly assigned 67 students to either a control group or a priming group. The priming group wrote a detailed account of a past event where they helped someone, which elevated their prosocial motivation. The control group did not complete a memory writing task.
All participants then completed the same revenge-based brainstorming task used in the first experiment. The researchers scored the answers using the identical three metrics of fluency, originality, and malevolence.
Participants primed with prosocial motivation generated a higher volume of creative ideas, and those ideas were highly original. However, the actual harm intended in their ideas was measurably lower than the ideas produced by the control group.
The researchers concluded that a desire to help others plays a dual role in shaping behavior. A prosocial drive provides the mental energy and persistence needed for creative tasks, elevating fluency and novelty. At the same time, this motivation actively restrains the urge to cause severe harm, leading to a drop in actual malevolence.
The researchers note a few limitations to the experimental design. Measuring malevolent creativity by separating it into distinct facets of fluency, novelty, and malevolence might not fully capture the combined nature of the concept. A single composite score that fuses novelty and harm might provide a more accurate picture of real-world dark creativity.
The experiments also did not directly measure the emotional arousal levels of the participants. Heightened negative emotions might fuel the cognitive persistence needed for creative brainstorming, entirely separate from prosocial motivation. Future studies will need to track multiple emotional and motivational pathways simultaneously to map exactly how social threats translate into aggressive innovation.
The study, “The Impact of Social Exclusion on Malevolent Creativity: The Mediating Role of Prosocial Motivation,” was authored by Junsheng Wu, Xiao Rao, Jiabin Liu, Shuaijun You, Yang Cao, and Lan Jiao.

They drive toward tornadoes. We went with them to see how their work could save lives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:00:05 UTC
21:00:05 KST

On a narrow road in southern Iowa, my phone shrieked.
Tornado warning. Take shelter now in a basement or an interior room on the lowest floor of a sturdy building.
Again, the alert sounded. Then again. As if shelter were a choice.
I peered through a peephole of scratched glass, wedged into the lead storm-chasing truck with tornado researchers Josh Wurman and Karen Kosiba.
On either side of us, only fields. No houses. No basements. No sturdy buildings. The dark belly of a storm dragged across a horizon gone an eerie green.
For tornado chasers, it was a near perfect sky.
My son Cheney, a photojournalist, was somewhere behind us in a rental car alongside two other research vehicles. The convoy was strung out across miles of highway. He had been tracking my location, but now I had lost cell service.
I couldn’t reach him. I kept dialing. No answer.
When a call finally went through, Cheney told me the wind was driving the rain so hard the road had disappeared.
“I’m scared,” he said.
Blinded, he had turned one way, then the other. Finally, he stopped. Either direction, he feared, could put him in a tornado’s path.
Cheney was no stranger to danger. He has covered Ukraine during wartime, spent a New Year’s Eve alone in a car reporting on Chicago homicides, and crisscrossed the country documenting violent weather, including the devastating 2021 tornado in Mayfield, Kentucky.
I hadn’t heard him express fear since childhood.
Then he said it again. “I’m scared. I don’t know what to do.”
About 1,200 tornadoes strike the United States every year. Between 2020 and 2025, they killed roughly 410 people, injured nearly 3,800 and caused about $8.5bn in reported property damage.
The tornado map is changing too. A 2024 study found 25% fewer moderate-or-stronger tornadoes in the western US and 12% more in the east, where mobile homes are more prevalent, basements to get to safety are scarcer, and twisters more likely to strike at night.
Sometimes the change from ordinary to deadly takes only minutes. Several months earlier, physician Jason Persoff had told me about chasing near Joplin, Missouri, in May 2011. A little after 5pm, he and his partner began looking for hotel rooms, figuring they were done for the day.
“Suddenly, it was as if someone vomited on the radar,” Persoff remembered. “It was incredible.”
A violent tornado seemed to emerge from the sky almost fully formed. Its sound lodged deep in Persoff’s body. “I felt irrational fear,” he said. “Like a primal warning.”
They pulled over to help stranded truckers as police arrived. Persoff told one officer he was a physician.
“I hope you don’t work at St John’s,” the officer told him. “That hospital’s been destroyed.”
“That’s still one of the most terrifying things I’ve ever heard,” Persoff said.
More than 150 people were killed in that tornado.
Wurman, whose team I traveled with, is among the researchers trying to understand why some storms produce tornadoes while others do not, and what tornado winds do close to the ground – knowledge that could improve warnings and help engineers design buildings to withstand them.
But the systems built to study and forecast tornadoes are under strain.
In the first four months of 2025, the National Weather Service lost roughly 13% of its workforce – more than 560 employees – to firings, retirements, resignations and attrition.
By the 2026 storm season, the agency was hiring again, but staffing gaps remained, and some stations were unable to maintain the twice-daily weather-balloon launches on which forecasters and researchers rely.
Scientists I spoke with said they had lost confidence in forecast guidance. Chris Weiss of Texas Tech, who led a parallel chase team with the National Severe Storms Laboratory, was blunt: “I don’t remember when a suite of models has performed as poorly as this year.”
Frustrated by the blurred, distant view from fixed-site radar, Wurman invented the Doppler on Wheels – mobile radar laboratories known as DOWs – three decades ago. Filling one with diesel costs about $1,000, and that is the inexpensive part: the greater investment lies in the trucks, trained graduate students and experienced crews that take years to build.
But funding has become more uncertain. By the end of this field season, neither Wurman’s team nor Weiss’s could count on support for the next one.
Cessily Skinner, whose family has lost two homes to tornadoes in west-central Georgia, closely monitors every approaching storm. Now the cuts give her another reason to fear: “As someone who lived through a storm with all the data in place,” she said, “it’s terrifying to think, ‘OK, so now we really are guessing.’”
With Cheney still on the line, a team member plotted his location against the storm. The radar could see what he could not. A tornado we were tracking was east of him and moving east. Cheney should be safe, she said, as long as he stayed put and waited it out.
I repeated this to him.
As we spoke, the rain loosened. The sky lifted. The road reappeared. Cheney pressed the gas and began closing the distance between us.
The second radar truck arrived first. Fifteen long minutes later, Cheney’s rental car came into view.
Relief and disappointment arrived together. The convoy was whole again. But the day had yielded none of the data the scientists had come for.
Several tornadoes touched down across the region that afternoon. None crossed the roads where our instruments were waiting.
The storms left behind a sky ribboned with dark clouds. Some team members stood outside the trucks and applauded its beauty, lifting their phones for photographs. Wurman and Kosiba were not among them. They were already studying the models, deciding where the team should spend the night to be best positioned for morning.
Tornadoes offer enough spectacle to draw film-makers, thrill-seekers, and carloads of chasers with cameras. But scientists who chase for data need more than drama. They need geometry: an open horizon, a road in and a road out, a storm that forms where the instruments can reach it.
Even when everything lines up, a mobile radar crew can spend weeks following one promising storm after another, only to watch each weaken and dissolve before the instruments capture the measurements they came for.
Why do they keep doing it?
For data analyst Paul Robinson, the pull started with an image on television: Dorothy clutching Toto, calling for Auntie Em as a black twister writhed in the distance.
“The Wizard of Oz is still my favorite movie tornado,” he said. “For me, it captures the feeling.” Growing up in West Virginia, he began keeping a notebook, recording the weather whenever it turned severe.
But 31 May 1985, turned that interest into purpose.
Everyone on this team seems to carry a storm they cannot forget. Robinson’s was not a single tornado but an outbreak: 43 twisters tearing across Ohio, Pennsylvania, New York and Ontario, killing 89 people.
“That convinced me that maybe I could do some good by going into tornado research,” Robinson said.
Research scientist Trevor White’s defining storm came later, on 24 May 2016, near Dodge City, Kansas.
“Every chaser and their mother came out,” he recalled. “We were on it from the time it was a small cumulus cloud. I had never seen a storm that could effortlessly produce tornadoes. I counted three on the ground at the same time.”
In two hours, a dozen tornadoes formed beneath the supercell. It was nearly perfect in the way that mattered most: no one died, and the tornadoes remained mostly over open country.
But even experienced researchers cannot always remain beyond a tornado’s reach.
In 2013, veteran tornado researcher Tim Samaras was killed near El Reno, Oklahoma, along with his son Paul and colleague Carl Young. Samaras was Wurman’s friend. Wurman’s team was tracking the same tornado that day.
Asked by a reporter whether the deaths made him reconsider his work, Wurman noted that covering extreme weather “isn’t dangerous statistically”. Samaras, he said, was among the most responsible chasers he knew. Wurman would not speculate about what had gone wrong but said his own team would review its procedures.
Wurman and his colleagues then returned to the data, reconstructing the motion of the nearly impossible-to-see subvortex that had overtaken Samaras and his team.
He pursues the sky at its most theatrical without surrendering to drama himself. He would rather leave a question open than force an answer the data cannot support.
“I wish this research were more of a eureka thing,” Wurman said, “but it’s not. We can’t do laboratory-type experiments. We can’t put 10,000 patients into a study. Meteorology is horrible that way. We’re trying to understand what’s special about the circumstances where tornadoes form and what it looks like when they do. But we can’t control the environment.”
“Every time we’re in a disaster area, I carry with me the trauma of people who survive it,” White told me. “I don’t know if we can do anything to ease the impact of that experience, but I’ll never stop searching. The only thing worse than a human tragedy is a human tragedy where you can’t learn anything.”
A mile outside Good Hope, Illinois, the deployment order came. Our truck slid to a halt on the shoulder of a two-lane road slick with rain.
Robinson jumped out to unleash the radar dish. It began sweeping the sky, each rotation shuddering through the vehicle.
Back in the driver’s seat, he talked to himself – “c’mon, c’mon” – as he worked the controls to lower a stabilizing pad into the mud, trying to keep the vehicle’s right side from sinking. He kept the left wheels on the pavement, he told me later, in case we needed to move fast toward – or away from – a tornado.
In the back, White balanced one keyboard on his lap and kept several others within reach. Four screens glowed in front of him.
“Frustrating,” Robinson murmured. “We’re getting data, but I want to see it; I want to see the fury.”
The horizon closed around us. From the front passenger seat, I watched a low shelf of black clouds over the cornfields, its ragged underside reaching down in unfinished gestures.
The walkie-talkie crackled, then Wurman’s voice came through. “What do you see?”
No one answered immediately. White and Robinson studied the screens and conferred quietly in technical shorthand. They were looking for a hook curling in the rain, a couplet tightening in the wind field, some sign that the atmosphere had made up its mind.
The clouds kept darkening. The dish kept turning. The truck kept shuddering. Robinson waited through one scan, then another, watching new data appear on the screens over White’s shoulder.
Finally he spoke, his voice tight. “It’s falling apart, isn’t it?”
After a few more minutes, Wurman confirmed he saw the same. He called out a new waypoint and then we were speeding again down a country road, pursuing the uneasy hope at the center of this work: a storm dangerous enough to teach but merciful enough to spare.
When things align, the value of a single intercept can endure for years. On 18 May 2013, the team captured data from an EF4 tornado near Rozel, Kansas. It remained on the ground for about 30 minutes, long enough for the researchers to hold position and gather unusually rich measurements.
“That gave us a chance to dig in deep,” Kosiba said. “And that data is still being used by engineers today. That’s why you have to keep going out, even with the misses. We’re in it for the long haul.”
A 2024 study co-authored by Wurman and Kosiba analyzed mobile-radar wind profiles from 36 tornadoes. Those findings helped shape new national standards for designing buildings to withstand tornado winds, showing the potential impact of readings collected in the path of storms.
This is the scale on which science advances: one measurement clarifying another, a dataset enduring long after the tornado itself disappears.
Behind every chase is a life forced to accommodate the forecast. We had driven 2,000 miles in three days, from dawn until after dark, crossing and recrossing North Dakota, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa and Illinois. Wurman’s team had gone weeks without the intercept they needed. Weiss’s team had endured an equally disappointing season.
“We put in the same effort for fewer results,” Weiss told me. “We have lives and families, and we’re making a lot of sacrifices. So when it doesn’t work out, it eats at you.”
White has a soft spot for hummingbirds. He keeps several feeders at home, and goes to great lengths to find someone to refill them when he’s gone. His absence is measured out in sugar water. He carries a small stuffed hummingbird on the road.
“I told my wife a week ago we’d be home tomorrow. Instead, we are still out here, and there’s no end in sight,” he said. “But there’s something fundamental about this research that draws me in. The best version of me is the version that does this work.”
Before this trip, I had imagined storm chasing as a form of appetite, the desire to see the most violent thing the sky could make. I hadn’t understood its strange rhythm: tedious hours beneath empty skies, then sudden races down country roads, decisions pressed into seconds, and moments of stark fear.
The work demands patience when nothing happens and clear judgment when everything happens at once. Inside the truck, it looked less like appetite and more like devotion: painstaking, deliberate, largely invisible.
In a culture that rewards quick verdicts and emphatic claims, these scientists let the sky contradict them. They reverse direction and answer to evidence rather than personal conviction. That discipline feels radical.
Years from now, the data they gather may become a stronger roof, an earlier warning, hospital walls that hold. The researchers may never know whose lives their persistence reaches.
That last night with Wurman’s team, I wrote three lines in my notebook:
 We went storm chasing.
Nothing happened.
We learned a lot.

Cocktail of the week: Cometa’s carajillo – recipe | The good mixer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:00:04 UTC
21:00:04 KST

The carajillo is a ubiquitous drink found across Mexico, and it comes in many forms. Some bars simply pour espresso over ice and add a shot of Licor 43, while others shake coffee with the liqueur and serve it straight up. Whatever the variation, the non-negotiables are coffee and Licor 43. Our version takes those two core ingredients and lengthens the drink with a light, delicious cold-brew coffee liqueur. It’s the perfect serve for a warm afternoon, a sweet after-dinner treat or an uplifting nightcap.
Carajillo
Serves 1
25ml coffee liqueur – we like Black Twist
25ml shot brewed espresso, cooled and chilled
25ml Licor 43
   1 pinch flaky sea salt, to taste
Measure all the liquids into a cocktail shaker, add a generous scoop of ice and shake vigorously. Double-strain into your glass of choice, garnish with a light sprinkling of flaky sea salt and serve neat.
- 
  Tom King, head bartender, Cometa, London W1

Surge in displacement following fighting in southwest Yemen
At least 46,000 people have been displaced since renewed fighting last week between Houthi rebels and pro-government forces in southwestern Yemen, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) reported on Friday.
Key points
- At least 46,000 people displaced since renewed fighting began last week in southwest Yemen — the figure is “rising by the hour”, IOM says
- Houthi fighters have seized the strategic Red Sea port of Mokha, triggering mass departures
- At least 14 civilians, including two children, killed or wounded this month, per OCHA; WHO recorded 67 deaths and 288 injuries between 6–24 August
- Only 60 per cent of Yemen's health facilities are fully operational, WHO says, as hospitals face a surge in trauma cases
- IOM is calling for safe humanitarian access and protection of aid workers and infrastructure
The number approaching 50,000, which as of Thursday covered the governorates of West Coast and Taiz, “is alarmingly rising by the hour”, the UN agency warned. The number, which as of Thursday covered the governorates of West Coast and Taiz, “is alarmingly rising by the hour”, the UN agency warned.
Overnight, large numbers of people were reportedly seen leaving Mokha with their possessions, after Houthi fighters took control of the strategically important Red Sea port city earlier this week.
The Houthis and Yemeni Government forces, backed by a Saudi Arabia-led coalition, have been locked in a power struggle since 2014.
After years of relative calm, Yemen plunged back into war in July, drawn into the regional conflict triggered in late February by the US-Israeli offensive against Iran.
The clashes that erupted last week have left hundreds dead on both sides, mainly combatants, according to media reports.
As conflict between the Houthis and Saudi forces increases, pro-government forces reportedly withdrew Friday from an island base in the narrow Bab al-Mandab Strait, with militants vowing to continue to target Saudi shipping there.
On the run again
“Families are being forced to flee for the second or third time since the start of this conflict, with almost nothing left,” said Amy Pope, the IOM Director General.
“As fighting spreads, reaching people with lifesaving assistance is becoming harder.”
New arrivals are being reported in the governorates of Lahj and Aden. There are also reports of people moving north towards Ibb.
Communities under pressure
IOM said entire villages have been emptied in three districts in Taiz – Maqbanah, Jabal Habashi, and Al Ma’afer – as fighting moved closer to populated areas.
The road linking Mokha to Taiz, a vital supply route, has reportedly been cut off and host communities in the region are under increasing pressure.
IOM is calling on all parties to guarantee safe and sustained humanitarian access.
They are also urged to ensure the safety of humanitarian workers, premises, and assets nationwide, and to restore the communication and transport routes necessary for aid delivery.
This is especially critical as emergency stocks are already depleted following recent flood relief efforts. IOM said the most urgent needs are for shelter, food, water, household items, health care and protection support.
Numerous civilian casualties
The escalation is also taking a toll on civilians. At least 14 civilians, including two children, had been killed or wounded since the beginning on the month, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said on Thursday,
For its part, the World Health Organization (WHO) recorded 67 deaths and 288 injuries between 6-24 August in seven governorates.
The victims were reported in several regions, from Marib and Hadramout in the east, to Al-Hodeidah in the west, and Taiz in the southwest, as well as Shabwah, Al-Dhale’a and Lahj in the south.
Health services hit
Beyond the human toll, the resumption of fighting is severely straining Yemen’s already fragile health system.
Hospitals in Marib, Hadramaut, and Taiz are facing an influx of trauma patients, thus increasing pressure on emergency, surgical, and intensive care units that are already overwhelmed.
According to the WHO, only 60 per cent of health facilities in Yemen are fully operational. Hospitals and emergency services across the country are thus simultaneously facing a sharp increase in demand and limited capacity.
At Marib General Hospital, maternity and obstetrics services have been temporarily suspended to free up additional resources for treating the wounded. The number of deaths has also exceeded the morgue’s capacity.
This reallocation of resources toward trauma care is affecting all patients, while facilities are already struggling with shortages of staff, beds, and medical supplies.

Terrorist propaganda is outpacing global efforts to stop it, UN report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Terrorist propaganda is outpacing global efforts to stop it, UN report finds
Terrorist groups are recruiting, raising money and even planning operations through propaganda that is now “embedded” in every stage of their work, a new UN report warns – and governments are struggling to keep pace.
The report by CTED, the secretariat of the Security Council's Counter-Terrorism Committee, tracks how terrorist propaganda has moved far beyond messaging.
It has become part of the operational structure of these groups, shaping how they recruit fighters, raise funds and govern territory.
One especially alarming trend: children and young people are increasingly being targeted, not just on social media but through gaming platforms and online communities built around shared interests.
Rapid evolution
“The speed at which terrorist groups adapt their propaganda strategies has created an “acceleration gap” between their strategies and the legislation and policies of Member States,” the report warned.
Propaganda has long been integral to terrorist strategies but “the deployment and scale have evolved significantly, and its function is now more central, integrated, and adaptive than in earlier phases,” it said.
Whereas groups such as Al Qaeda – which carried out the seismic terror attacks on the US exactly 25 years ago – relied on centralized messaging distributed mainly through physical media, the emergence of ISIL, also known as Da’esh, in the mid-2010s brought a switch to “high-volume, multilingual, digitally distributed propaganda ecosystems.”
AI, gaming and ‘gore’
The report identifies several emerging trends, including use of artificial intelligence as well as exploitation of gaming platforms and alternative online spaces such as Discord, Twitch and Stream.
“Terrorist recruitment has targeted young people through gaming, with many groups designing violent extremist-themed first-person shooter games and modifying existing games to embed violent extremist narratives within familiar entertainment formats,” it said.
Meanwhile, graphic violent content or “gore” – execution footage and images of mass casualties, for example – and nihilistic online subcultures are increasingly important for radicalisation.
Merging narratives, maximising impact
Another trend is the growing convergence of violent extremist ideologies across the digital space. In this case, content produced blends narratives, symbols, and grievances from various contexts to maximise resonance and reach numerous audiences.
Governance activities as propaganda
Among the report’s recurring themes is the growing intersection between propaganda and other core functions of terrorist groups, with focus on Al Qaeda affiliate JNIM in the Sahel, Al‑Shabaab in Somalia, ISIL‑K in Central and South Asia, and TTP in Pakistan.
Analysis shows that these groups use propaganda “to reinforce governance activities, exploit local grievances, build legitimacy, facilitate fundraising and shape perceptions of authority.”
The report noted that while terrorist groups adjust tactics quickly, “policy responses and implementation have longer legislative and operational timelines.”
It stressed that effective responses must address propaganda not only as content, but as a core operational enabler of terrorism, while ensuring that counter-terrorism measures remain in line with international human rights law.

The world just had the hottest August ever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

The world just had the hottest August ever
Earth just had the hottest August on record, according to newly released weather data.
Key points
- Global sea surface temperature reached an all-time observed high
- Global tropical cyclone activity was above average, producing 19 tropical storms
- El Niño conditions fuelled record temperatures across vast areas of the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean
The planetary heat record was documented by monthly reports from the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Service, the United States National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and NASA.
Its effects were felt around the planet, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said on Friday.
The northern hemisphere experienced its warmest summer while the southern hemisphere had a near-record warm winter.
Meanwhile, the Arctic and Antarctic each had below-average sea ice coverage in August.
Heatwaves and drought
Western Europe saw heatwaves in August, continuing an exceptional run of extreme heat that began in May, and severe drought conditions were reported in France, Hungary, Romania, Serbia and the United Kingdom.
Large parts of central and eastern Europe also saw widespread dryness in August, in some cases persisting since May.
Water flow levels were exceptionally low in major European rivers, including the Rhine, Danube, Southern Bug and Dnieper.
Why so hot?
El Niño was one of the drivers of August’s record climate conditions, WMO reported.
The climate pattern influenced global tropical cyclone activity as well as heavy rainfall and floods in some countries.
Other countries were impacted by drought, with El Niño conditions favouring the intensification of seasonal wildfires across Indonesia, as reported by the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS).
What it means
Data indicates that all 10 of the warmest Augusts on record have occurred since 2016.
In terms of heat, the global average surface air temperature in August was 1.65°C higher than the estimated pre-industrial baseline, the latest data revealed.
At the same time, the global surface temperature was 1.32°C above the 20th-century average – the warmest August since records began in 1850, according to the US National Centers for Environmental Information.
Predictions for what El Niño will bring are sobering.
“It is now firmly established and will intensify into a very strong event in the coming months, with big impacts on rainfall and temperature patterns well into 2027,” according to WMO’s latest El Niño Update.
Tracking the global climate
Organizations around the world help track global climate information.
WMO uses datasets from the Copernicus Climate Change Service, NOAA, NASA and others for its State of the Global Climate reports.
The UN weather agency will present an update on this year’s climate at the next UN climate conference, COP31, in Antalya, Turkey, in November.

At Pentagon, Trump Leads 9/11 Commemoration on 25th Anniversary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
21:20:29 UTC
06:20:29 KST

President Donald Trump and government and military leaders past and present paid tribute to the victims, survivors, and heroes of the Sept. 11 terrorist attack on the Pentagon, marking 25 years since a hijacked plane flew into the building, killing 184 victims.
As rain poured down and the sun rose in the East, a massive American flag was unfurled atop the Pentagon wall, its stars and stripes flooding down the concrete facade, reenacting what first responders did on Sept. 12, 2001—and as they have done on every 9/11 anniversary since.
Hours later, Trump, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine, and former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice took turns at the lectern, each vowing to “never forget” the 2,977 American lives that day in New York, Washington, and Shanksville, Pa. In a coordinated attack, four U.S. airliners were hijacked that day. The first two struck the twin World Trade Center towers in New York City, the third slammed into the Pentagon, and the fourth, brought down after passengers stormed the cockpit, crashed in a field in Pennsylvania.
“A Navy airman had just gotten off the phone with his 10-year-old son,” Trump said. “A secretary was celebrating her 46th birthday. … A sergeant major was chatting with some colleagues he had hosted for a dinner party over the weekend. At 9:37 a.m., every single one of those people and every person at that sergeant major’s party was murdered by terrorists who flew Flight 77 straight into this legendary building.”
Rice, who was President Bush’s National Security Advisory in 2001, recounted her experience on 9/11, “the horror and the shock that I felt” as a TV in the White House bunker displayed images of smoke rising from the Pentagon.
Yet in the midst of disaster, she added, military personnel and civilians alike responded with courage. “It is fitting that here at the Pentagon, we reflect not just on what happened here, but what in that moment of crisis, people did here,” she said. “They summoned a will and a spirit, a sense of obligation that our military lives by every day—I will stand between danger and my fellow citizens, I will leave no comrade behind, I will go, I will serve, I will do my duty.”
Caine, who as a young major scrambled in an F-16 to protect Washington D.C. on 9/11, called the anniversary not just a “story of loss” but one of “great American courage, selfless service, and those who’ve made the choice to carry those memories forward.”
More than 40 federal, state, and local agencies responded to the attack on the Pentagon. Rice described how then-Secretary of Defense Donald Rumsfeld pulled people to safety “as his security detail begged him to flee the danger.” Trump described how, on Sept. 12, Army Maj. Gen. James Jackson ordered the American flag to be hung from the side of the Pentagon.
“First responders climbed to top the walls and hung it next to the gaping holes in this building as a symbol of American defiance,” Trump said. “This morning, that same flag is here to my right for the first time since 2001, along with three firefighters who raised it, Joseph Morabito, Scott Morgan, and Carl Solberg.”
Hegseth, who joined the U.S. Army in the years after 9/11, said the attacks “inspired millions to step forward instead and say, ‘send me.’” Now, 25 years later, he acknowledged that many service members “do not remember 9/11; many were not even born yet. And that leaves it to us on this day and others like it to pass down that memory to our kids, to my kids, to yours, to my grandkids, to yours.”
Both Trump and Hegseth made reference to the ongoing conflict with Iran, calling the Iranian government “the world’s number one sponsor of terror” and connecting the response to 9/11 to the ongoing hostilities.
For the most part, though, leaders focused their remarks on the lives lost in the attacks, the bravery of the survivors and first responders, and the national unity forged in the response.
“September 11th reminded us of the terrible power of hate,” Trump said. “The 25 years since have shown us the even greater power of the American spirit to endure and prevail and to win.”

Iran’s Houthi allies capture strategic island on vital oil shipping route
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Yemen’s rampant Houthi forces have captured the strategic island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab strait, expanding their control of the narrow waterway, one of the world’s vital shipping routes.
The Iran-aligned Houthis took control of the volcanic island after forces allied to the UN-backed, Aden-based government left in the latest of a dramatic series of reverses along Yemen’s west coast in recent days, including the loss of the port city of Mocha on Thursday.
Saudi Arabia, which supports and bankrolls the official Yemen government, mounted air raids on Houthi positions in Mocha on Friday.
The Bab al-Mandab strait links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez canal. Perim island, also known as Mayun, divides the waterway in two, close to its narrowest point. The United Arab Emirates, a former Saudi ally in the anti-Houthi coalition, had been building an airbase on the island before ending its active involvement in the conflict in January.
Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab to export its crude since Iran has been targeting vessels in the strait of Hormuz. About 12% of the world’s goods are typically shipped through the strait.
Full Houthi control of shipping in the strait, alongside Iranian control of the strait of Hormuz, would strengthen the chokeholds of anti-western forces over global energy shipments. Oil prices have risen to more than $100 a barrel as the fighting in Yemen has escalated.
Iran hailed the Houthi advances in an official statement on Friday, its first extended comment on the renewed fighting inside Yemen. Iran and the Houthis have been allied since the Houthis rose to power inside Yemen in 2014.
In a statement the Houthis hailed the expulsion of “Saudi enemy” troops from six districts in the Taiz and Hodeidah regions, the capture of 4,500 sq miles, the targeting of “seven military divisions of the Saudi enemy’s forces” and the “killing, capture, and wounding” of hundreds of soldiers. It also claimed to have released hundreds of prisoners “held by the Saudi enemy’s mercenaries for years”.
British diplomatic sources said they did not at present expect Donald Trump to sanction any US bombing of Houthi positions in Yemen, despite requests to do so from Saudi Arabia. The pace of the Houthi advance, and political divisions in the Yemen governorates not controlled by the Houthis, have left western capitals fearful that even the Yemen government capital, Aden, could fall to the Houthis. The UK effectively treated Yemen as a British protectorate until 1967.
The Houthi offensive has cost more than 500 lives and displaced about 46,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Friday.
The Houthi progress down the Red Sea coast from the port of Hodeidah also strengthens Iran’s hand in trying to reach an agreement with other Gulf states on future control of the strait of Hormuz, the central dispute between the US and Iran. Iran has reached an agreement on temporary approved routes with Oman, the country sharing the southern coast of the Hormuz strait. The proposed deal is supposed to be discussed at a meeting of Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) foreign ministers in the Omani coastal city of Salalah on Monday.
The deal, including a temporary approved route for shipping largely under Iranian control, would – if agreed by the GCC – put pressure on the US to lift its highly effective blockade of Iranian oil ports, which is severely damaging the Iranian economy.
The US struck a surprise ceasefire deal with the Houthis in May 2025 after the cost of a bombing campaign escalated, and Houthis gave private assurances that they would not attack US shipping in the Red Sea. The Houthi leadership this week continued to give similar assurances to all shipping except Saudi Arabian oil tankers.
On 14 August Saudi Arabia assembled a 14-country international maritime naval coalition to protect freedom of navigation in the Bab al-Mandab strait and the Gulf of Aden. The coalition, including Bahrain, Pakistan, Somalia, Djibouti, Turkey and Egypt, has so far been invisible, though Riyadh would argue that such a coalition of the willing takes time to assemble.
Recriminations are under way over the fall of Mocha, with the role of Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, the leader of the National Resistance Forces that retreated from the city, under scrutiny. He said the retreat was necessary to regroup his forces.
On her Facebook page, the Yemeni 2011 Nobel peace prize winner, Tawakkol Karman, called on Yemen’s president, Rashad al-Alimi, to dismiss Saleh and to refer him for investigation and trial on charges of conspiracy and high treason.
Amr al-Bidh, the foreign affairs representative of the separatist political organisation the Southern Transitional Council (STC), said he had warned western diplomats repeatedly of the need for a comprehensive national regional and international strategy to defeat the Houthis, adding occasional airstrikes were not enough.
He accused the Saudis of strategic incompetence and of alienating the southern forces most needed to combat the Houthis.
“The position is now very serious,” he said. “The Houthis’ presence in the strait means they will be able to control the waterways without needing to use sophisticated weapons that as a result they can now use elsewhere. The advance is also likely to give them a new income through control of ports along the west coast of the Red Sea.” The Houthis are already offering concessionary rates to draw traffic from ports controlled by the Yemeni government in the Gulf of Aden.
The STC was the dominant political and military force in southern Yemen until this January, when Saudi Arabia bombed its troops, closed its political organisation down and detained as many as 20 of its leaders in Riyadh.
A Saudi promise of a dialogue about the southern question made in January has never been kept, al-Bidh said, adding that Human Rights Watch warned in a March report that some pro-STC protests in Aden were being repressed with undue violence.
“The betrayal of promises had left the southern population unwilling to leave their home territories to fight the Houthis in the north,” he said. “The Saudis for 10 years have been dependent on the people of the south to deter the Houthis, and the STC with as many as 80,000 troops at its disposal, has been the backbone of that force.”
Saudi Arabia is facing a familiar dilemma: whether to reach a negotiated settlement with the Houthis on the future of Yemen or to try to push the highly stretched Houthi forces back.
Although the Houthis operate independently of Tehran’s instructions, it is hugely to Iran’s advantage for them to be fighting Saudi Arabia, as the Saudis are more likely in turn to put pressure on Washington to relent over Iran.
There is also concern in western capitals about the use of western weaponry by the Saudis in Yemen, and whether their activity complies with international humanitarian law, including whether the Saudi strikes can truly be seen as acts of self-defence.

EU foreign policy chief backs ‘principled’ trade ban on illegal Israeli settlements

Necva Taştan Sevinç
11 September 2026•Update: 11 September 2026
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has backed a bloc-wide ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories, calling it a justified “principled stance.”
In an interview with The Irish Times on Thursday, Kallas said there was broad agreement among EU foreign ministers that expanding Israeli settlements violated international law.
“When Crimea was occupied, then it was very clear -- it’s illegal, we don’t recognize this,” she said. “We should have the same principled stance -- you know this is illegal, everybody agrees, so we should stop trading with Occupied (Palestinian) Territories.”
Kallas said an EU ban on imports from Israeli settlements would not require the unanimous backing of all 27 member states.
As the proposed ban could be introduced as a trade measure rather than a foreign policy decision, it would require a qualified majority of at least 15 member states representing roughly two-thirds of the bloc’s population.
The EU has previously struggled to approve sanctions against Israel because foreign policy measures require unanimity.
Kallas said the European Commission was under “very clear” pressure from national governments to propose a settlement trade ban and that EU foreign ministers were waiting for the bloc’s executive body to act.
Although the volume of trade originating from Israeli settlements was limited, a ban would deliver an important symbolic message, she added.
Kallas acknowledged that member states had differing positions on relations with Israel and said there were “pros and cons” to acting before Israel’s parliamentary elections in late October.
She added that EU members agreed on supporting a two-state solution and ensuring that humanitarian aid reached Palestinians without being politicized.

Yemen’s Houthis seize island that controls key Red Sea strait
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:56:39 UTC
20:56:39 KST

- Houthi forces seized Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on September 11, 2026, after Yemeni government forces withdrew.
- The advance follows Thursday's capture of Mocha and gives Houthi forces a position inside the strait itself, not just its approaches.
Yemen’s Houthi movement seized Perim Island, at the narrowest point of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, on September 11, 2026, after Yemeni government forces withdrew from the island a day earlier.
Four Yemeni government sources told Reuters that Houthi fighters reached the island, also known as Mayyun, tightening the group’s grip on one of the world’s most important shipping routes. A local government official told AFP that the Houthis had effectively completed their takeover of the strait itself.
Government forces also lost the mainland town of Dhubab, directly across from the island, Reuters reported. Witnesses told AFP that armed Houthi fighters were patrolling the shoreline in military vehicles after the island fell.
Perim splits Bab el-Mandeb into two shipping channels at the strait’s tightest point and has its own airstrip, making it a long-standing military prize that Saudi-backed forces had worked for years to keep out of Houthi hands. The island’s capture caps a week-long offensive that also took the Red Sea port city of Mocha and the Hanish islands on Thursday, with Houthi forces reportedly seizing Zuqar Island in the southern Red Sea as well.
The Houthis already controlled roughly a third of Yemen’s territory before this week’s advance and have spent years firing missiles and drones at ships passing through Bab el-Mandeb. Combined with Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz since a U.S.-Israeli air campaign against Iran began roughly six months ago, full Houthi control of Bab el-Mandeb would put Iran-aligned forces astride both corridors that together carry more than a quarter of the world’s seaborne crude oil and petroleum trade. Close to a third of global container traffic moves through the Red Sea.
Saudi crude supply fell 2.3 million barrels a day in August to 6 million barrels a day, its lowest level in more than three decades, the International Energy Agency said Friday, pointing partly to Houthi-linked attacks on ships in the strait. Global oil prices were on track to close the week above $100 a barrel for the first time since mid-May.
Satellite imagery verified by Reuters showed smoke near Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline on Thursday, though Saudi authorities and state oil company Aramco did not confirm any incident there. The pipeline has become a critical route for Saudi Arabia to move crude to the Red Sea since the Hormuz closure.
Reuters reported that the advance came with direct guidance from Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, according to Yemeni government, Iranian and regional sources, and that Iran urged the Houthis last week to escalate attacks on Saudi Arabia while promising more funding, weapons and senior officers. Iran has publicly denied directing the group, describing the Houthis as an ally but insisting they are “not a proxy.”
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called President Trump twice on Thursday urging U.S. strikes against the Houthis, Axios reported, citing two U.S. officials. Trump rejected the request, and officials said Washington does not currently intend to take direct military action against the group, though it is stepping up support for Saudi Arabia. Separately, the Financial Times reported that Gulf and Iranian foreign ministers plan to meet Monday in Salalah, Oman, to try to work out a temporary arrangement for shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Yemen’s government forces said they would deploy weapons and aircraft to retake captured territory, including the road to Mocha, and warned civilians to avoid traveling between Taiz and Mocha.

EU can forget about competitiveness at current energy prices – Tusk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:56:30 UTC
20:56:30 KST

EU can forget about competitiveness at current energy prices – Tusk
The EU can forget about competitiveness while energy prices remain prohibitively high, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has warned, urging Brussels to avoid policies that push costs higher.
Tusk spoke on Thursday at a press conference of the Visegrad Four (V4) – Poland, Hungary, Slovakia, and the Czech Republic – a Central European grouping that coordinates regional interests within the EU.
“We can put aside the dream of competing with China or the US as long as energy prices here remain at their current levels,” Tusk said. “The EU cannot afford to remain naive for even one more day when it comes to various ambitious policies. We must protect our industry.”
Tusk mentioned EU energy and climate measures such as carbon-pricing schemes, noting the region pays some of the world’s highest electricity prices despite Brussels making competitiveness a stated priority. “Energy prices in this region… must come down,” he insisted. “Anything that creates a risk of higher energy prices for us should be blocked.”
Where things stand now
With benchmark TTF gas back near €80 per MWh – roughly four times its pre-2022 level – EU industrial electricity prices are still two to three times higher than in the US and nearly 50% above China’s, while gas in Europe can cost up to five times more than across the Atlantic.
Although today’s energy prices are significantly below 2022 peaks, the crisis has shaved off 15-20% from gas demand, which remains depressed, reflecting not only conservation but a contraction of the industrial base. Many energy-intensive operations were rendered unprofitable. Numerous factories curbed production or shut altogether.
Permanent chemical-plant closures alone have surged sixfold from pre-2022 levels, according to Cefic, while auto-making giants such as Volkswagen, Stellantis, and Renault, as well as multiple other manufacturers, have scaled back or closed European operations amid competition from the US and Asia, and corporate insolvencies have risen.
A major contributor to the EU’s gas woes is the abandonment of cheap Russian energy in light of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. Russia previously supplied around 45% of EU gas imports and 27% of its crude oil, but by 2025, Russia’s share of EU gas imports had fallen to 12% and crude imports to around 2%.
Several EU leaders, notably German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron, have acknowledged that the loss of Russian supplies has played a role in the energy crisis.
While Tusk, a strong Ukraine supporter, did not explicitly link high energy prices to EU sanctions on Russia and the cutting off of Russian supplies, he cited the Ukraine conflict and “constant pressure from Russia” among the broader challenges facing the region, saying “the war is a real problem.”
Tusk’s Visegrad peers also warned that Brussels’ policies are squeezing industry amid the decoupling from Russian energy divorce and ongoing defense buildup.
What other leaders had to say
Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar warned that “dozens of Central European companies are going bankrupt because they cannot afford the price of electricity” and “can no longer afford the price of gas.” Magyar challenged Brussels to fund the energy transition it demands.
“If we need to transition away from Russian gas and oil, if we need to completely phase out fossil fuels, the EU should specify in its next seven-year budget how much assistance affected businesses will receive in turn,” he argued.
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico and Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis similarly rejected leaving individual governments to deal with soaring fuel costs and criticized EU policies they said were hurting industry. Fico called for energy-market reforms, while Babis blamed the Green Deal for high costs, refinery closures and declining competitiveness.
EU energy bind deepens
The warnings come as the EU prioritizes two costly undertakings: completing its break with Russian energy, while financing a massive military buildup that envisages mobilizing up to €800 billion in additional defense spending. Russian LNG is due to disappear from the EU market by the end of 2026 and pipeline gas by autumn 2027.
Critics have warned that these two initiatives will be hard to reconcile and that the rejection of Russian energy will further undermine already flagging industrial competitiveness, and leave some member states scrambling for alternative supplies.
Meanwhile, the US war on Iran and disruption of the Strait of Hormuz are exacerbating the crisis. This, combined with Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping and Saudi energy infrastructure, has pushed Brent crude above $106 a barrel this week.
European households have taken a hit as well. An Ipsos-Secours survey of 10,000 people across ten European countries, released earlier this month, found that 29% were living in precarious circumstances and 73% feared being unable to afford fuel costs. More than a third said they had sacrificed essentials such as food or healthcare to pay energy bills over the past year, while 23% had skipped medical appointments, suggesting energy insecurity is becoming a permanent feature of the cost-of-living crisis.
Moscow has long denounced Western energy sanctions as illegal and self-defeating, arguing they merely redirect Russian exports elsewhere while forcing Europeans toward more expensive and harder-to-obtain supplies. Russia has offered to help fill oil shortages caused by the Middle East conflict and resume supplies to Europe, but says it has received no response.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has warned that the Central European Visegrád Group (V4) would seek to block any European Union climate policies that push up energy prices.
Speaking after a meeting with the leaders of the other V4 countries, Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic, Tusk said that they could not accept policies that further weakened competitiveness at a time when they were already facing high electricity costs.

In recent months, Poland and some other member states have been pushing for a softening of the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), a cap-and-trade scheme launched in 2005 that makes polluters pay for carbon emissions in sectors such as power generation and heavy industry.
They have also secured a postponement of the introduction of ETS2, which will cover emissions from road transport and buildings.
“Whether we are talking about ETS1, ETS2, or other proposals, anything that brings a risk of more expensive energy for us will be blocked by us,” said Tusk on Thursday at a press conference alongside the other V4 prime ministers, as well as Ireland’s Micheál Martin.
“Poland and the V4 will not allow any changes or any proposals from European institutions or other countries that could worsen the energy situation in our countries,” he added. “Energy prices in this region, including in Poland, must fall.”
Poland has recorded the EU's third-fastest rise in household electricity prices this year.
The country now also has the bloc’s second-most-expensive electricity, when taking cost of living into account https://t.co/WNLdCfOP16
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2025
Tusk argued that high energy prices pose a threat not only to Central European economies but also to the competitiveness of the EU as a whole. “We can forget about any dreams of competing with China or the United States if our energy prices remain as they are right now,” warned Tusk.
Slovakian Prime Minister Robert Fico likewise said the V4 countries were united in their approach to the emissions trading system.
“We will be very active, and we will also engage in discussions outside the meetings of the European Council and the Council of Europe to discuss what steps to take to bring down these energy prices,” he said.
Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš also expressed frustration with rising energy costs. “All of us in our industrial region pay a lot of money for emissions allowances. And what did the commission tell us in 2020? That the price of this allowance in 2030 will be €26.50. Right now, it’s €80,” he said.
According to the Eurostat data, households in Poland paid €27.09 per 100 kilowatt-hours (kWh), including taxes and levies, for electricity in the second half of 2025. That was the 11th highest figure in the EU and below the figure of €28.96 across the bloc as a whole.
However, when adjusted for purchasing power standards (PPS), which account for differences in costs of living, Polish households faced the second-highest electricity prices in the EU, at 37.15 PPS per 100 kWh, behind only Romania (49.52 PPS) and the Czech Republic (39.16 PPS).
The effects of ETS on electricity bills has moved to the centre of political debate this year after the main opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), called for Poland to unilaterally withdraw from the system, saying it makes “Poles a cash machine for the EU’s absurd leftist climate policy”.
The opposition-aligned conservative president, Karol Nawrocki, has also twice sought to call national referendums on rejecting EU climate policies, including ETS, arguing they are too expensive. Both his efforts were rejected by the government’s majority in parliament.
While the government has rejected the idea of withdrawing from ETS – which it says would result in large, ongoing fines being levied against Poland – it has pushed for reforms to the system.
In July, the European Commission outlined proposals to soften ETS in response to pressure from countries such as Poland, allowing industries to continue emitting CO2 for longer while providing more financial support for investment in clean technologies.
Yet there are also a number of other EU member states that argue against weakening ETS, saying it would penalise those who moved early to cut emissions.

Just before the European Commission unveiled its proposal in July, Poland’s climate minister, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, said she had assembled a coalition of 10 countries calling for ETS reform and a more realistic emissions-reduction path.
They also want ETS funding mechanisms to account for national differences, including energy mixes and GDP per capita, to ensure a fairer transition for lower-income countries starting from a more challenging position.
Poland, for example, has a historical reliance on coal, which it still uses to produce around half of its electricity, helping make it one of the EU’s biggest emitters.
Renewables generated 29.4% of Poland's electricity in 2025, almost exactly the same figure as in 2024, ending a period of strong growth since 2021.
Coal (52.2%) remained the dominant source, though its share declined.

However, the country has made significant progress in expanding renewables in recent years, particularly solar and onshore wind.
In 2025, renewables accounted for just over 29% of Poland’s electricity generation, almost three times the share recorded a decade earlier. Further progress is expected this year, after Poland began to generate electricity from offshore wind farms for the first time.
Under a national energy and climate plan approved by the current government in June, it plans by 2040 for Poland to generate 18-21% of power from offshore wind and 22-27% from onshore wind. A further 15-16% will come from nuclear, 14-18% from solar, 7-8% from gas and 0-5% from coal.

North Savo District Court has acquitted Mika Moring of the manslaughter of Saara Arva and the aggravated deprivation of her liberty.
Arva went missing in 2019, when she was 35 years old. She was last seen in the Vesanto municipality of North Savo in August of that year.
Police tried to locate Arva for years until an ice fisherman found her remains in April 2024 in a remote headland in Vesanto.
Moring was the only suspect in her disappearance, police said.
He had denied all charges.
Second investigation ongoing
Yle has taken the decision to publish Mika Moring's name because he was accused of exceptionally serious crimes and he has several previous convictions for violent and sexual offences.
Yle also publishes Saara Arva's name because her disappearance and suspected killing was a high-profile criminal case, in which tips from the public played a major part in the investigation.
In a separate case, police suspect Moring killed 28-year-old Katja Miinalainen, who disappeared in August 2022 in Southwest Finland.
She was last seen on 14 August 2022 getting into Moring's car in the Kiikala district of Salo.
Police took the unusual step later that year of releasing Moring's name and photograph, as well as pictures of his car, as they asked for assistance from the public. Moring was at that time also a suspect in the disappearance of Saara Arva.
It is believed they travelled to Tammela in Central Finland and on to Finnish Lapland, where they camped in remote areas.
The investigation into Miinalainen's disappearance is still ongoing, as police search for her remains in the municipality of Muonio in Finnish Lapland.

French public broadcaster France Televisions has removed a replay of a television program in which actress Adele Haenel accused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza and France of complicity.
Haenel said in a video posted on Instagram that she appeared live on France 5’s literary program La Grande Librairie on Sept. 9.
She said she spoke at the end of the program during a segment in which guests were given complete freedom of expression, discussing efforts to silence those speaking out about sexual violence and the genocide in Palestine.
Haenel said her team recorded the segment because they expected her remarks to be edited out, but the broadcaster instead removed the program's entire replay from its website.
The decision prompted criticism from lawmakers in the left-wing France Unbowed (LFI) party.
LFI lawmaker Gabrielle Cathala said on the US social media company X that the replay was removed after Haenel denounced Israel’s genocide against the Palestinian people and France’s complicity.
Fellow LFI lawmaker Daniele Obono described the decision as “scandalous,” while fellow lawmaker Aymeric Caron said Haenel’s remarks about Gaza were accurate.
Caron accused the French public broadcaster of failing in its coverage of Gaza over the previous three years and said it must explain who exerted pressure and requested the replay’s removal.
According to French magazine Telerama, France Televisions said it removed the replay because Haenel’s remarks on Palestine had not been counterbalanced by an opposing view during the broadcast.
Speaking at the end of the program, Haenel said, “I have also made a decision: I am going to speak.”
“The State of Israel is committing genocide in Palestine, and France is complicit,” she said. “Do not accept the unacceptable. Therefore, impose sanctions on Israel and free Palestine.”

Ukraine's Ministry of Foreign Affairs has commented on an incident in Poland in which Grzegorz Braun, leader of the Confederation of the Polish Crown party, damaged a monument to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army The UPA was a nationalist paramilitary organisation that fought for Ukrainian independence during and after World War II, primarily against Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union (UPA) in the village of Białystok in Poland, calling on the Polish authorities to give the actions a proper legal assessment and restore the grave.
Source: European Pravda

At a time when a real war is under way, posing an existential threat to both Ukraine and Poland. This is shameful and immoral behaviour that can evoke nothing but shame and condemnation in any normal person."

Quote: "Ukraine consistently supports the same principle on both sides of the border: Ukrainian memorial sites in Poland and Polish memorial sites in Ukraine must be protected. No one has the right to turn memory and respect for the dead into a circus performance for their own political purposes."
Background:
- On 10 September, Braun posted a video showing how he is damaging the UPA monument in the village of Białystok in Hrubieszów County, Lublin Voivodeship.

Fire kills dozens of schoolchildren in rebel-held DR Congo city (VIDEO)

Unknown Publisher

Fire kills dozens of schoolchildren in rebel-held DR Congo city (VIDEO)
At least 26 students have been killed after a fire swept through two schools and hundreds of homes in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) city of Bukavu, the authorities say.
The blaze began in a house in the densely populated Cimpunda neighborhood on Thursday morning before spreading to the adjoining Furaha and Ujamaa schools, according to local officials. Several children reportedly suffocated after becoming trapped, while others were caught in a violent stampede as they tried to escape.
A statement from the South Kivu provincial authorities, cited by AP, put the toll at 19 girls and seven boys and warned that it could rise.
More than 300 homes were reportedly destroyed. The closely packed wooden buildings in the neighborhood contributed to the rapid spread of the flames, while narrow exits caused a crush at the schools, Cimpunda administrator Moise Lubala told AP.
The Congo River Alliance/March 23 Movement (AFC/M23) rebel coalition, which controls Bukavu, earlier reported 24 deaths and 29 injuries. It said 21 patients were in intensive care and that an investigation is ongoing to determine the cause of the fire. DR Congo government spokesman Patrick Muyaya said Kinshasa is following the incident with “deep concern.”
“While the city remains under illegal occupation, we express our solidarity with the students, teachers, parents, and families affected,” he wrote on X.
The Congolese Education Ministry said students and teachers in areas under occupation remain part of the national education system and “at the heart of the nation’s responsibility and solidarity.” It ordered an assessment of the damage and measures to support victims and continue classes. The ministry said the fire was the latest in a series that have damaged schools in Bukavu. The exact cause remains unknown.
Thursday’s disaster came less than a week after a fire at a wedding party in the capital, Kinshasa, killed at least 22 people. More than 700 homes burned in separate fires across Bukavu during the week ending September 6, according to UN-operated broadcaster Radio Okapi.
The AFC/M23 has controlled Bukavu, the capital of South Kivu Province, since February 2025, when its advance forced Congolese and allied Burundian troops to withdraw. The coalition seized Goma, the capital of neighboring North Kivu, a month earlier during clashes with government forces. Kinshasa and several Western governments accuse Rwanda of supporting the rebels, which Kigali denies. The rebels have since established parallel administrations across large areas of eastern DR Congo, where armed groups compete for control of the region’s mineral wealth.

NEW DELHI: The Janata Dal (United) is considering a proposal to rename the more than two-decade-old party as ‘JD(U)-Nitish’, in recognition of its supreme leader and former Bihar chief minister Nitish Kumar.The suggestion was made by JD(U) working president Sanjay Kumar Jha, who was heard in a purportedly recorded video saying the party owed its standing to Kumar and that its ideology was rooted in his political philosophy.
“We should therefore consider renaming the party as JD(U)-Nitish,” Jha was heard saying.The proposal has received backing from senior JD(U) leaders, including Bihar deputy chief minister Bijendra Prasad Yadav and minister Shrawon Kumar.Yadav, a former state president of the JD(U), said, “It is a very good suggestion. Let there be a formal discussion on the matter so that a decision could be taken.”Shrawon Kumar said, “There could not have been a better proposal. I suggest that a formal resolution be brought by the party at the earliest. It is bound to be passed unanimously.”The JD(U) was formed in 2003 through the merger of the Sharad Yadav-led Janata Dal and the Samata Party.
Though Sharad Yadav served as its national president until 2016, Nitish Kumar was widely regarded as its de facto leader. Kumar formally took over as national president in 2016.The development comes days after Jha rejected a separate proposal to rename Bakhtiyarpur, Kumar’s birthplace, as ‘Nitishpur’ on Thursday. Responding to the suggestion by Hindustani Awam Morcha national president Santosh Kumar Suman, Jha said Kumar “has always let his work speak on his behalf” and “has never believed in renaming places”.Jha also said, “Let us bear in mind that merely changing the name of the place will not erase from history the fact that Bakhtiyar Khilji had invaded the land and set Nalanda, the ancient seat of learning, on fire”.The proposal to rename the town had also drawn support from Union minister Chirag Paswan. “This is indeed a good suggestion. Nitish Kumar ji has contributed immensely to the progress of Bihar over a long period of time,” Paswan said.
The RJD, meanwhile, has criticised both proposals. RJD MLA Bhai Virendra claimed the party could split within months, alleging that the developments pointed in that direction.The JD(U) is yet to announce any formal decision on renaming the party.
