Iran war: Saudi-Houthi escalation intensifies Yemen conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:52:00 UTC
20:52:00 KST

Iran war: Saudi-Houthi escalation intensifies Yemen conflict
September 11, 2026
Fighting between the Houthi militia and Yemen's internationally recognized government escalated further this week as the Iran-backed group seized territory and exchanged missile and drone attacks with Saudi Arabia.
On Thursday, the Houthis seized the port city of Mokha and by Friday had taken control of the town of Dhubab and the island of Perim, Yemeni government sources told the news agency Reuters. Mokha, Dhubab and Perim had been held by forces aligned with Yemen's government. All three are strategically located near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
With Iran having blockaded the nearby Strait of Hormuz, the narrow Bab el-Mandeb Strait has become increasingly important as an alternative route for Saudi oil exports. As the Houthis are aligned with Iran, control of and potential attacks on shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait gives Iran additional leverage in its war with the United States.
The government-aligned National Resistance Forces announced on Thursday that troops were reorganizing and consolidating their defenses in Mokha in coordination with other anti-Houthi forces.
The conflict has also spilled into Saudi Arabia, a close US ally and regional rival of Iran's. This week, the Houthis launched dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at four cities in Saudi Arabia. The Houthis said Saudi Arabia responded with dozens of airstrikes across four Yemeni provinces.
"This is actually a full-scale war," Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemen researcher at the London-based think tank Chatham House, told DW. "It hasn't been given that name yet but we are marching there full time," Al-Muslimi said.
Houthis 'much stronger'
The latest escalation, which started in July, ended a period of relative calm after years of war. A Saudi-led coalition intervened to support Yemen's government in 2015 following the 2014 Houthi insurgency. The war between the Houthis — which the United States redesignated as a foreign terrorist organization in March 2025 — and the Saudi-backed government ended in 2022 with a UN-brokered truce. However, the country remains de facto split.
The Houthis control Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and most of the country's north, as well as parts of the center, and now also much of the western coastal stretch, including Mokha, Dhubab and Perim. The internationally recognized government, represented by the Presidential Leadership Council, is based in Aden. Many senior officials operate from Saudi Arabia. Government-aligned forces control parts of the south and east, while tribal groups retain significant influence in parts of the east.
The political landscape was further fragmented in December, when secessionists backed by the Southern Transitional Council (STC), backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE), seized areas in the south and east. The fallout between Saudi Arabia, which aims to keep Yemen united, and the UAE-backed secessionists ended with the termination of Yemen's joint defense pact with the UAE and the withdrawal of Emirati forces from the country. The STC was dissolved in January.
Elham Manea, the director of the Middle Eastern and Gulf Studies Research Competence Area at the Institute of Political Science at the University of Zurich, told DW that the current situation is very different from that of 2015. "The Houthi movement is militarily and institutionally much stronger," Manea said, "while the camp opposing it, that is, the internationally recognized government, remains more fragmented."
What's Pakistan's role?
Manea said Saudi Arabia had changed its approach. In 2015, Riyadh joined the war in support of Yemen's ousted government. "Now, it is providing greater military, technical and logistical support to the internationally recognized government and forces aligned with it," Manea said.
The key question is whether Saudi Arabia is preparing for a war aimed at defeating the Houthi group or seeking to change the military balance, restore deterrence and eventually negotiate from a stronger position.
"At present, I consider the second scenario more likely," Manea said.
Al-Muslimi offered a similar view: "The Saudis would like to avoid war at any cost."
The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, recently signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, has not yet been invoked. Reuters reported on Thursday that Pakistani officials said no military response under the agreement was currently being discussed, but the government would act when the time came.
Alice Gower, director of geopolitics and security at the London-based political consultancy Azure Strategy, told DW that she doubts Pakistan would join the conflict directly. "But the escalation in Yemen will increasingly test its ability to stay out," Gower said. "Islamabad does not want to antagonize neighboring Iran," she added, "and will try to preserve its role as a mediator, while meeting its growing security commitments to Saudi Arabia through intelligence, advice and other forms of military support short of direct participation."
Humanitarian toll rises
Hans Grundberg, the UN envoy to Yemen, said the country was facing the "harsh reality" of a return to war.
The UN Development Programme estimated that 377,000 people had died as a result of Yemen's conflict between 2014 and late 2021. Of these, approximately 154,000 deaths were directly caused by combat and violence.
The current conflict has already killed nearly 200 people, according to the World Health Organization. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) also warnedthat around 18,500 people have been displaced. "Families are arriving with nothing: no shelter, no food, no way to know if it's safe to go back," Abdusattor Esoev, IOM Yemen's chief of mission, said in a statement. "Many of these are people who have already been displaced once, twice, even four times before," he said. "Every time fighting flares up, they lose whatever little they had managed to rebuild."
This view is echoed by Niku Jafarnia, a Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch. "When you have a country in which nearly two-thirds of people are in need of aid, any additional precarity and displacement will have a real civilian cost," she said.
"Thousands of civilians were killed in the fighting between the Saudi-led coalition and the Houthis between 2014 and 2022, and warring parties repeatedly demonstrated extreme disregard for civilian life," she said. "The renewed fighting now threatens to repeat the devastating civilian casualty events of the earlier years of the war," she added.

How Dead Russian Soldiers Still Manage to Vote in Kremlin-Run Elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:51:46 UTC
20:51:46 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
How Dead Russian Soldiers Still Manage to Vote in Kremlin-Run Elections
Russian commanders in occupied southern Ukraine are allegedly using the identities of soldiers killed in action to fabricate votes for the Kremlin’s ruling United Russia party, according to the pro-Ukrainian ATESH partisan movement on September 11.
The alleged scheme is tied to so-called early voting that began on August 29 in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine ahead of Moscow’s State Duma elections.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
ATESH said its agents uncovered the practice within Russia’s 291st Motor Rifle Regiment operating in the Zaporizhzhia sector.
According to the group, the regiment received an unofficial order to deliver a predetermined number of votes for United Russia.
The problem, ATESH said, was that the unit’s actual manpower was too low to meet the assigned quota because of heavy battlefield losses.
To make up the difference, clerical staff and officers allegedly delayed formally registering soldiers as killed or missing, leaving their names active in unit records.
Staff officers then filled out batches of ballots in the names of those troops and personally delivered them to voting sites in occupied Melitopol, Berdiansk and Tokmak, ATESH added.
Among the soldiers whose names were allegedly used after their deaths were reconnaissance soldier Zamir Kazharov, tank commander Senior Sergeant Valentin Aleksandrov and rifleman Corporal Valery Karpenko.
The partisan group said families of some fallen Russian soldiers remain unable to obtain official confirmation of their deaths or receive compensation while commanders continue using their identities for political reporting.
ATESH described the practice as a system of “dead souls,” borrowing the phrase commonly used for fictitious or deceased names kept on official rolls.
The group said the 291st Regiment is unlikely to be the only Russian unit using such methods.
According to ATESH, commanders across the front are under pressure to meet unofficial political targets, creating incentives to conceal personnel losses while simultaneously reporting near-total support for the Kremlin’s ruling party.
The result, the partisans allege, is a system in which the same missing or dead soldiers can serve two purposes at once: keeping battlefield losses off official paperwork and inflating election results for Moscow.
Earlier, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that Ukrainian intelligence has obtained internal Russian documents pointing to a major mobilization drive in Russia this autumn, timed to follow staged parliamentary elections.

Russia Secretly Converts Maternity Wards Into Military Hospitals Amid Growing Battlefield Losses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:51:42 UTC
20:51:42 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Secretly Converts Maternity Wards Into Military Hospitals Amid Growing Battlefield Losses
The Russian government is increasingly repurposing civilian healthcare facilities, including maternity wards, to treat a massive influx of wounded soldiers from the war in Ukraine, according to an investigation by independent outlet Vot-tak, posted on September 10.
This has led to secret military wards and severely degraded care for ordinary citizens.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The collapse of the civilian healthcare system is a consequence of astronomical battlefield attrition suffered by the Russian army in Ukraine. According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Russia’s total military personnel losses—both killed and wounded—surpassed 1.5 million by September 2026. This toll is 100 times greater than Soviet losses during the decade-long war in Afghanistan.
In Rostov-on-Don, Maternity Hospital No. 5 was abruptly converted into a military hospital, with pregnant women discharged early or forced to seek care in neighboring cities, Vot-tak wrote. A similar conversion occurred at Maternity Hospital No. 5 in Omsk, where the facility was transformed into a veterans' hospital despite protests from local medical staff and residents.
With the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) estimating over 611,000 Russian casualties since the full-scale invasion began, the Ministry of Defense’s roughly 58,000 military hospital beds are overwhelmed. Consequently, Vot-tak found that civilian hospitals in St. Petersburg, the Yaroslavl region, and Siberia have established highly classified military wings.
Medical staff in these units are forced to sign non-disclosure agreements, access is restricted by magnetic keycards, and wounded personnel are treated under assigned numbers rather than their names.
The shift has drastically impacted civilian medical access. A recent government decree mandates that soldiers receive priority, queue-jumping outpatient care at civilian clinics. To support this, at least 11 Russian regions have diverted over 3.2 billion rubles ($37.9 million) toward military treatment in civilian facilities, according to the outlet’s analysis.
Simultaneously, 19 regions are cutting their overall public healthcare budgets for 2026, with Vot-tak noting that some areas are slashing funding for civilian clinics and hospitals by up to 39%.
The influx of combatants has also introduced violence into civilian medical settings. Doctors and nurses told Vot-tak that soldiers frequently drink, steal equipment, and initiate brawls with both staff and civilian patients.
In response to the escalating conflicts, the Russian Ministry of Health issued internal guidelines instructing doctors to handle aggressive military patients by speaking softly “as if telling a fairy tale,” hiding scissors or glass objects during appointments, and offering “imaginary confessions of guilt” during disputes.
The mounting number of severely wounded soldiers has also prompted the Kremlin to funnel disabled veterans directly into the domestic workforce.
Russian leader Vladimir Putin had previously ordered government ministries and corporate executives to place returning combatants, including hundreds of thousands with permanent disabilities or amputations, into the defense-industrial complex to offset severe labor shortages and sustain production.

Russia Continues Attacks on Kyiv Gas Stations, Hitting One in Double-Tap Strike
At least two people were injured in a Russian drone attack on Kyiv on the morning of September 11, with strikes reported at gas stations in the city’s Obolonskyi and Dniprovskyi districts.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Explosions were heard across the Ukrainian capital during an air raid alert as Russian drones targeted the city.
The Kyiv City Military Administration reported that, according to preliminary information, two people were injured in the Obolonskyi district as a result of the attack. According to footage circulating online, the drone struck an Ukrnafta gas station.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that gas stations were hit in both the Obolonskyi and Dniprovskyi districts. He later reported a second strike on a gas station in the Obolonskyi district.
In the Dniprovskyi district, the administration reported a suspected drone strike on a gas station, with emergency services dispatched to the scene.
Klitschko also said medical teams were called to a residential building in the Dniprovskyi district following explosions in the Troieshchyna neighborhood.
The latest attack came just a day after another Russian drone struck an Ukrnafta gas station elsewhere in Kyiv. On the morning of September 10, at least four people were injured after a UAV hit the premises of a station in the city’s Holosiivskyi district.
Klitschko reported that emergency crews were dispatched to the site, where the strike sparked a fire and set a vehicle ablaze.

Russia is investing significant resources in information and psychological operations to make Ukraine and Poland perceive each other as enemies — Fire Point CEO
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:51:07 EEST
20:51:07 KST

Russia is investing significant resources in information and psychological operations to make Ukraine and Poland perceive each other as enemies — Fire Point CEO
Kyiv • UNN
Iryna Terekh noted that Fire Point regularly monitors media attacks and in approximately 90% of cases traces their origin to Russia.
Russia is investing significant funds and resources in information operations aimed at making Ukraine and Poland perceive each other as enemies. This was stated by the CEO of the leading Ukrainian defense company Fire Point, Iryna Terekh, during a panel discussion held as part of the MSPO International Defence Industry Exhibition in the Polish city of Kielce, reports UNN correspondent.
We are in Poland today and hear a great deal about disputes in Ukrainian-Polish relations, particularly online. But I do not know a single Pole with whom we are in contact who would be part of this dispute. And from what I see, Russia is investing enormous funds and resources to make Ukraine and Poland perceive each other as enemies. And even worse—to make us feel like enemies ourselves. I really want you to be careful. We are fighting with missiles, drones, and weapons—in various spheres. But we constantly forget about an extremely important psychological dimension
She emphasized that in war it is important to consider not only the military dimension, but also the psychological and cognitive dimensions.
We must be extremely attentive to the information we consume and to who may be interested in having this information circulate in our minds
In addition, at a press conference in Poland, Iryna Terekh noted that Fire Point regularly monitors media attacks, and in approximately 90% of cases their origin can be traced specifically to Russia.
On the one hand, if we look at this positively, it is high praise for our effectiveness and for how we do not let them live in peace. On the other hand, we see that Ukrainians, being tired and emotional, very often pick up these narratives as well. Therefore, here we should be more critical of our information space
According to her, IPSO often have characteristic features: they appeal to strong emotions, cause agitation, and focus attention on an acute problem. At the same time, the problem itself may be real and important, which makes it more difficult to recognize the manipulation.
Iryna Terekh also noted that Russia is significantly ahead of Ukraine and its Western partners in the development of information and psychological operations and propaganda technologies.
We would add
Russia systematically uses information operations and disinformation as one of the tools of waging war against Ukraine. In particular, Russia regularly claims to have shot down Ukrainian long-range drones and missiles, while citing astronomical figures.
At the same time, claims of the almost 100% effectiveness of Russian air defense are inconsistent with the numerous successful strikes against facilities on Russian territory. In just the past few days, the Defense Forces have hit a number of facilities on the territory of the Russian Federation. For example, the long-range FP-1 UAV struck a strategic facility deep in Russia's rear—the Novy Urengoy condensate preparation plant for transportation (ZPKT) in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug of the Russian Federation—covering a record 3,300 km in the process.
In addition, on September 11, the Defense Forces struck the strategic enterprise Volgogradpromproekt in the Russian Federation with FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, after which a fire broke out there.

Iranian president says he does not support continued war, urges strengthening country’s resilience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:50:35 UTC
20:50:35 KST

Ahmet Dursun, Sami Sohta, and Lina Altawell
11 September 2026•Update: 11 September 2026
 Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Friday that he does not support the continuation of war with the US, calling for the country's resilience to be strengthened for the next phase.
His remarks came during a meeting with heads of Iranian universities, according to the local Mehr News Agency.
Addressing the conflict with Washington, Pezeshkian said, “I am not in favor of continuing the war, but we must strengthen the country’s resilience in the face of upcoming developments.”
Strengthening the country’s resilience requires following a path that does not force Iran to negotiate with the “enemy” from a position of weakness, he said, calling on universities to support the government in this regard.
Economic measures must take into account existing social conditions, the Iranian president said, warning that uncalculated steps would be harmful rather than remedial.
“We must benefit even from the contributions of Generation Z students to solve society’s problems, and ensure their participation in presenting solutions instead of engaging in protests,” he said.
Pezeshkian stressed that, as president, he has no political ties to specific groups, saying he is open to cooperation with all political currents and anyone who contributes to addressing the country’s crises.
The US and Israel launched a war on Iran on Feb. 28, prompting Tehran to fire missiles at Israel and attack US targets and bases in several countries in the region.
Iran also announced the closure of the Strait of Hormuz to navigation, causing widespread disruption to global energy and trade flows.
On June 18, Washington and Tehran reached a memorandum of understanding to end military operations, including guarantees for the passage of commercial ships through the Strait of Hormuz and the launch of negotiations to reach a final agreement within 60 days.
However, the understanding later faltered, and confrontations resumed in July, with the US renewing strikes on targets inside Iran and reimposing a naval blockade on Iranian ports.

European Commissioner for Defence and Space Andrius Kubilius notes that the incident involving Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's plane is direct evidence that the consequences of Russian aggression against Ukraine include a threat to civil aviation within European Union airspace.
“As for the incident involving President Zelenskyy, the so-called incident in Moldova: Zelenskyy himself said this was not direct aggression against President Plain, but nevertheless it's very clear that the situation is, as I said, is becoming more and more dangerous also for civilian aviation in neighboring countries,” he told reporters in Brussels on Friday.
According to the European Commissioner, this requires the EU to take even more active measures to strengthen our defense capabilities. “That is what drone alliance [between EU and Ukraine] is about in order to be ready to react, whatever provocations can come,” Kubilius emphasized.

“I remember myself traveling with Commission President Ursula von der Leyen perhaps last year. Electric shock torture and a meeting with Victoria Roshchyna.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:47:28 UTC
20:47:28 KST

From left to right: Victoria Roshchyna, Iryna Levchenko, Olha Kapralova. Collage: Mediazona
This week, the Russia’s Southern District Military Court in Rostov-on-Don handed down its verdict on Gennady and Olha Kapralov. The couple, from occupied Melitopol, were accused of plotting a terrorist attack involving chemical weapons. A day before the trial concluded, at the defence’s request, the court questioned an unexpected witness—Iryna Levchenko, a retired Melitopol journalist who had recently been convicted on espionage charges. She fully corroborated the Kapralovs’ testimony regarding torture in a secret prison in their home city and, furthermore, recounted that in 2023 she had met another Ukrainian journalist there—Viktoria Roshchyna, who later died whilst in Russian captivity. Mediazona publishes Levchenko’s court statement with minor abridgements.
On 10 September 2026, the Southern District Military Court in Rostov-on-Don sentenced 61-year-old Gennady Kapralov and his 53-year-old wife Olha to 20 and 18 years in prison. Russian security forces consider the couple from Melitopol to be members of an underground group that was planning terrorist attacks involving chemical weapons in the occupied city
On the eve of the Kapralovs’ sentencing, the defence filed a motion to question the final witness – 64-year-old Melitopol-based journalist Iryna Levchenko, whom the Zaporizhzhia Regional Court, established by the occupying authorities, had sentenced on 3 September to 15 years’ imprisonment on espionage charges. Levchenko gave evidence via video link from a pre-trial detention centre in Mariupol
On 6 May 2023, Levchenko and her husband Oleksander were abducted on a street in Melitopol. The man was released a year later, but her family did not know where the journalist was until the summer of 2025. And it was only in January 2026, when Levchenko’s case came before the court, that it became known she was accused of espionage. Due to constant transfers between various remand centres (in Donetsk, Mariupol, Simferopol, and Krasnodar), her family were unable to maintain any regular contact with her
In court, Iryna Levchenko recounted that in 2023, Russian security forces held her for several months in the building of a former psychoneurological early treatment clinic in Melitopol. Like other prisoners, she was subjected to electric shock torture. There she met Olha and Gennady Kapralov and Victoria Roshchyna — a Ukrainian journalist who later died in Russian captivity
Levchenko’s description of the secret prison, given in court, matches in detail the testimony of Gennadiy Kapralov. The fact that Roshchyna was held for some time in the “garages” in Melitopol was reported by Slidstvo.Info and iStories, based on the account of her cellmate. In 2024, RIA Melitopol reported on the torture centre “under the bridge on the road to Novy Melitopol, in the premises of the former psychoneurological clinic, and in the garages in the courtyard”
Journalist Victoria Roshchyna went missing in the occupied territories in August 2023 and died in Russian captivity on September 19, 2024. She was 27 years old. Information about where she was held during the first months after her detention is fragmentary and unreliable; it was reported that she already showed signs of torture upon arrival at the Taganrog pretrial detention centre. The circumstances surrounding Roshchyna’s death remain unclear. Her body was returned to Ukraine in such a condition that experts were unable to determine the cause of death. Later, the National Police announced that her occipital bone had been fractured
When establishing the witness’s identity at the beginning of the hearing, Judge Maxim Nikitin, in addition to the usual questions (full name, date of birth, place of employment), asked why Iryna Levchenko was being held in custody.
“Well, they decided I was a spy,” she replied with a wry smile. “On [Spetember] 3rd, they ‘delighted’ me with a sentence: 15 years. Even though I completely debunked all the speculation, but who would listen?”
“Under which article are you charged? Article 275?” the judge asked, implying “treason” charges.
“Article 276! I’m a citizen of Ukraine,” Levchenko replied, stressing she was accused of “espionage,” which is reserved for foreign nationals in Russia. She assured the court that she had no reason to frame the Kapralovs and called the couple “wonderful people.”
After that, attorney Oksana Olgerdt began questioning the witness and asked when and where she had met the Kapralovs.
Levchenko: “Well, I can’t give an exact date, because we met them in what’s called ‘the pit.’ It was in the city of Melitopol, on Dzerzhinsky Street, presumably at number 212. I didn’t look at the sign, but I think that’s right. It’s a one-story building that used to be a psychoneurological clinic. People were taken there unofficially. I ended up there after being detained by the police, following three weeks in a temporary detention facility in the village of Vesele, not far from Melitopol, which wasn’t operational at the time. Then they brought me to this building with a bag over my head and put me in a separate room.
I saw Olha and Gennady around the end of August—I can’t say for sure, but I know we celebrated my birthday, September 16, together. I mean, the guard let us talk. Olha was in another room, and Gennady was with the men—also in another room. At first, they put people in solitary rooms, just as small as the one I’m in here. And it wasn’t until a few days later that we were able to see each other while picking up our dinner.
When I saw [Olha], she was wearing a thin summer sundress in a yellow-green, marsh-like color—and her arms and legs looked exactly the same; she’d been beaten all over. She said her back was the same, but she didn’t want to undress or take off her long, floor-length dress. Our guard, Arsen, had given her some ointment to rub on [the bruises], and so had Gennady—because that ointment had previously been in the men’s room. She had been horribly beaten. As for Gennady, I know that they tried to knock out his teeth there—either with their hands or with something else.
It was from Olha that we first learned that, as it turned out, we hadn’t been officially arrested. By that time, I had already been sitting there since May 29, expecting that, well, they’d sort things out soon and let us go. And it wasn’t until early September or late [August] that we found out we weren’t officially registered anywhere. That this is the so-called ‘pit’—even though it’s as if we’re staying at home.”
Attorney Olgerdt asked whether Levchenko had witnessed any violence against Olha Kapralova while in the “pit.”
Levchenko: “Look… It’s hard to be an eyewitness from a locked room. The fact that I saw signs of beatings on her… She assumes—because she, too, was either in a bag or wearing a mask—she assumes they beat her with a water bottle. She doesn’t know what they used to beat her; she’s just assuming. Those of us who were tortured weren’t witnesses [to the torture of others]. I think we were together until the end of October. About two and a half months, maybe until November. I didn’t think any of this would be necessary. I thought they’d sort things out and let us go, so naturally I didn’t record anything. This is all from memory.
At first, Olha was in a room with another woman, a young woman named Victoria Roshchyna. Victoria died on her way to a prisoner exchange in August 2024, if I recall correctly. Then Olha was moved to another room, right next to ours. As for Gennady, he was with the men—there were about four or five of them there. I know some of them by name, last name, patronymic, and sometimes even their birthdays, because, as a creative person, I made birthday cards for some of them. If I’d known why I was being invited here, I would have brought the foil medal that Gennady, also a creative person, made for me; it says, ‘Ira, Skilled Hands.’ They try to take it away from me every time during searches; they’ve thrown it away before, but I manage to save it.”
Attorney Olgert: “Let’s go back to the events of that time when you were with Olha Kapralova. You saw her in that dress, a sarafane, and she’d been beaten. Did she have any new bruises?”
Levchenko: “I don’t remember. Maybe toward the end, when she disappeared from view for a moment. Nobody told us anything… We lived behind closed doors.”
The attorney then asks the witness to describe the room where she was being held.
Levchenko: “A one-story building. I think it used to be a psychoneurological clinic; there were twelve rooms in total. A very old building, perhaps from the 1950s or 1960s. Our only guard, Arsen—a forty-year-old Dagestani from Makhachkala—lived in one room. Another room served as the kitchen. Olya volunteered [in the kitchen] for a few days—even a week—after the previous volunteer was taken away. But then the FSB officers said, ‘You don’t need to be in the kitchen.’ And during those days, I even managed to sew an apron for Olya. They removed her from the kitchen, [even though] she cooked very well.
There were larger and smaller rooms; on [the inside of the doors] there were no handles. Naturally, they’d all been removed. They locked us in from the other side. There were windows—insulated glass units—but they were barred, and at the end of June, this Arsen painted them black from the inside as much as he could—can you imagine, through the fine bars? So you could still see little bits of light coming through.”
When the lawyer asks whether the clinic’s inmates were allowed to leave their rooms, Iryna laughs.
Levchenko: “What?! What are you talking about? We were all locked up. The only exception: the men were let out once [a day] in the morning so they could use the restroom and wash up—and they carried their own water bottles. It’s easier for the men; everyone here is an adult. Also, when I was admitted on May 29, as a woman 20 years older than [the guard], I asked him: ‘Could you let us go to the bathroom during the day as well, besides in the morning and evening?
That’s when we received our gruel and two slices of bread. In the morning we had tea with cookies, and in the evening—gruel.
And so the guard... well, he’s that kind of person, more or less kind. He would let the women out during the day when we knocked and asked to use the bathroom ourselves. You see, we can’t use a bottle.
There was another woman with me, a little younger than me, also named Iryna—we only had a three-liter jar with a lid in a plastic bag. Olya had another jar in the other room, the one next door. So we could knock [for the guard to let us go to the bathroom], as long as he wasn’t going somewhere—to headquarters or to the market for groceries and cigarettes…
But sometimes he’d just be lying there, watching TV or on his cell phone, and we’d have to knock for a long time. Sorry for going into such detail—it’s the only way I can explain how it really was.”
In response to a question from the attorney, Levchenko said that neither she nor the other detainees at the clinic had been told why they were being held there. A guard himself once let slip that the secret prison was run by FSB officers.
Levchenko: “Arsen mentioned this. Unfortunately, I didn’t catch his last name. When we were cleaning his room at his request, he pointed out a certificate of appreciation from Governor Yevgeny Balitsky hanging on the wall. Back then, I worked first as a journalist for Yevgeny Balitsky at one publication, then at another. And yes, I saw this Arsen’s last name—it’s a Dagestani name—but I didn’t remember it. Later, I also filled out paperwork for him—he was selling his Zhiguli, so it had to be done neatly. So I know, let’s say, his birthday; I know he’s from Makhachkala; I know his mother’s name, that he has a sister, and his daughter’s name—but, alas, I can’t recall his last name.”
In late August 2023, drunk security officers staged a mass beating of prisoners at the clinic just for fun, Levchenko continued.
Levchenko: “It was August 30 or 31; it happened to be a full moon. And suddenly, in the evening, we heard noise, swearing, and screams. Then we could hear the Russian national anthem being sung out of tune from the men’s cells. There were a lot of screams; I can tell you more about it later.
Arsen told us that it was either a professional holiday for the FSB or some other occasion—they’d been drinking and came to have some fun. So they were going from room to room; one of them was wearing a robe—apparently borrowed from some priest—and carrying a shovel, asking, ‘Do you want to receive сommunion?’ Among us was a forty-year-old priest from Tokmak named Konstantin Maksimov; he naively replied, ‘Yes, I do’—and was struck with the shovel. They [struck] my husband on the back—he was being held with me, just in a different room. Some were hit on the back, others on the buttocks. One of the men had two ribs broken. Arsen said, ‘They can do whatever they want. Even if they kill someone, nothing will come of it.’”
However, the women were not harmed during this beating. And it was likely thanks to this guard named Arsen.
Levchenko: “On the 30th or 31st [of August], when these representatives of the FSB—let’s put it this way—were making their rounds, our cells were the last ones. They were coming toward us from the far end, and we could hear the swearing, the screams, and everything else. Iryna and I were sitting there—two adult women, I’m 60 and she’s around that age—hugging each other, and we were terrified that they’d come for us next. Olha was in a tiny little room across the hall. And after what she’d been through—she was alone, while the two of us were together—she was in shock and later told us about it.
When they reached our room and asked who was inside, he replied—with a distinct accent—‘There are women here, and Olya is over there.’ Olya said she nearly fainted because, well, here there were just women, and there was Olya. And she imagined the door would open and that nightmare would start all over again. But Arsen didn’t open it.”
Attorney Olgert: “Were the Kapralovs taken to court for a pretrial hearing?”
Levchenko: “No. If they’d been taken away for a pretrial hearing, they wouldn’t have been brought back. That’s called ‘pulling them out of the pit.’”
Levchenko didn’t see any noticeable signs of beatings on Gennady Kapralov, but she remembered that he was limping. “He’s a man; he wasn’t with us. Second, he was fully clothed. I can’t remember exactly. I know it wasn’t just a tooth.”
Then, at Kapralov’s request, attorney Svetlana Sidorkina asked whether Levchenko had seen bruises on his face. The journalist replied in the affirmative: “There were marks, yes. I can’t say for sure right now whether it was under the right or the left [eye]. Because there were a lot of us there with various bruises. I know that Olha was worried the whole time that Gena was being beaten. I know that the beatings took place.”
Toward the end of the questioning, attorney Sidorkina asked whether Levchenko knew who had beaten the Kapralovs.
Levchenko: “You see, no one reported [any names] to us. When they took me to be tortured with electric shocks, the people [were] wearing masks, without badges or business cards that would state who was torturing us. They don’t introduce themselves, they don’t give their first or last names, and they don’t mention where they’re stationed, their unit, or their rank. Unfortunately. I saw the people, but they were wearing masks.
I recently filed a statement with the Investigative Committee with as detailed a description as possible. If I had to identify one of the two men, I would be able to—he has distinctive eyes. Remember those milky-blue bottles? Well, if you were to break glass like that… His eyes were piercing. He was taller than me. When he came to see us in the ‘pit’ again and my room was open—they’d let me out to use the bathroom at that moment—he recognized me, called me by name, and asked something like, ‘How’s it going?’ Can you guess how I was doing? He wasn’t wearing a hat at the time; his light blond hair was sticking out. You know, when a man takes off his hat—and it was apparently August, so it was hot—his short hair stands on end, and his was exactly one and a half centimeters long.
At one of the hearings, thanks to my lawyer, the judge was forced to record that I had been tortured, and then an ‘investigation’ was supposedly conducted. ‘Supposedly’ means this: they gave me just enough space to write by hand about this torture. In response, I later received three and a half typewritten pages stating that the temporary detention center in Vesele wasn’t yet operational in May and that they didn’t remember my last name. So they never even asked me. They shoved me and my husband in there, stripped us naked, dressed us, and shoved us into a room. And right outside the door, guards were simply taking turns—one after another—and they fed us periodically. [They wrote] that everything is now equipped with cameras everywhere, that an inspector comes every day and practically kisses everyone’s ass. No one remembers Levchenko, and that couldn’t have happened, because the temporary detention center didn’t start operating until September. There is my handwritten statement, three and a half typed pages... So how could that not have [happened]?”
The final question for Levchenko came from the prosecutor. He inquired as to the purpose of her torture: “Did they demand something specific while using violence, or did they just beat me for the sake of beating me?”
Levchenko: “Are you asking me that?”
Prosecutor: “Yes.”
Levchenko: “Look, there was no verbal abuse or humiliation. Thank God, unlike other women, they didn’t undress me or attach electrodes to my private parts. Others went through that. Just my arms and legs. They demanded: ‘Tell the truth.’ I told the whole truth, yet they wrote it down however they saw fit.
My legs were tied to the legs of an office chair—I have one just like it here now—and my arms were tied behind my back with electrodes attached to them. I had a blindfold over my eyes, secured with tape. One of them was sitting across from me—before they blindfolded me, I could see the back of the monitor. The second one was sitting somewhere behind my shoulder.
Being an educated person, I thought they’d actually brought me there [for questioning. On the way,] they told me: ‘We’re here; we’ve brought a polygraph; you’ll be tested on it.’ And I naively went in to tell the whole truth on the polygraph. Instead of a polygraph, there were powerful electric shocks; several times—at least five, I stopped counting after that, let’s just say five—I was literally thrown into the air along with the chair that was strapped to me. After they torture you like that, you’ll sign anything.”
“Thank you, Irina Yuryevna, for giving such detailed testimony. We won’t keep you any longer,” the judge concluded the questioning.
“Can I go home?” Levchenko reacted, immediately.

India welcomes BRICS leaders for summit clouded by wars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:47:00 UTC
20:47:00 KST

Russian and Iranian leaders were in India Friday for talks ahead of a BRICS summit, also to be attended by Chinese President Xi Jinping, that is expected to be dominated by conflict and economic challenges.
The two-day annual summit, opening Saturday, is expected to address Middle East and Ukraine conflicts, global trade turbulence and oil.
Xi arrives Saturday for his first visit to India since 2019. The visit marks the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the nations, six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Himalayan border.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have warmed, with flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually restored.
"China stands ready to work with India ... by strengthening communication, enhancing cooperation, and properly handling differences," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Friday.
Deep mistrust remains, with their contested Himalayan frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.
Dozens of Tibetan exiles protested in New Delhi on Friday, waving placards against Xi's visit. Their Buddhist leader, the Dalai Lama, has lived in India since fleeing a Chinese crackdown in 1959.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi held talks Friday with Russian President Vladimir Putin, who last visited India in December 2021. Moscow is one of New Delhi's most important strategic partners.
"One should engage in debate and friendship only with the virtuous, and nothing whatsoever with the unvirtuous," Modi wrote Friday in a social media message in Sanskrit to welcome leaders to the 11-nation summit.
Posters of a beaming Modi line streets across New Delhi, with heavy deployments of security forces across the capital and widespread traffic restrictions.
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who arrived in New Delhi on Friday and will hold talks with Modi, said "BRICS was established to counter unilateralism," according to Tehran's IRNA news agency.
As well as Iran, BRICS includes Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates – countries with sharply differing positions on the Middle East conflict. All three have been admitted to the group in recent years, joining founding member states that include India, China and Russia.
"The Middle East conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the BRICS summit," said Harsh V. Pant of India's Observer Research Foundation.
"What was seen until last year as an achievement – the expansion of BRICS – today looks like a big constraint on BRICS," Pant said.
Pezeshkian's participation – his first visit to India as Iranian president – will put the Middle East conflict firmly on the agenda.
"The Middle East conflict will provide a stern test of the group's cohesion," said Shilan Shah of Capital Economics, noting the failure of the BRICS foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May.
UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is also expected, as is Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan and Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
New Delhi has navigated the energy crisis sparked by the Middle East conflict in part by turning to Russia for fuel despite Western sanctions as the war against Ukraine drags on.
Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar visited Kyiv this month, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he was "grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war."

Canada provides almost US$29m to support Ukrainian veterans

Canada provides almost US$29m to support Ukrainian veterans

50 CEOs and investors urge Brussels not to dilute the EU Inc law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:46:11 UTC
20:46:11 KST

Founders and investors call EU policymakers to not water down the EU Inc., the legislative proposal which aims to facilitate businesses in Europe to scale up.
Fifty European CEOs and investors have urged EU legislators not to "dilute" the bloc's EU Inc. law, currently under negotiation in Brussels, according to a joint letter sent to policymakers on Thursday.
The law would make it cheaper and easier for businesses to launch and operate across EU borders and is expected to be approved by the end of the year.
However, negotiations in Brussels suggest the final version may fall short of what many startup founders had hoped for.
The EU Inc. law is among the legislative proposals the bloc is pushing to make Europe more competitive.
Firms in Europe struggle to scale up because of legislative fragmentation, which translates into red tape and heavy administrative costs — a real barrier within the single market.
"Policymakers must ensure that the final legislation delivers a genuinely European company form, rather than adding another layer on top of 27 national systems," the signatories argue.
Signatories, who also include investors from Index Ventures, Accel, Balderton, Atomico and EQT, are urging policymakers to decide "whether EU Inc becomes Europe's economic engine or a legal structure so diluted that nobody uses it".
The demands
Signatories are asking policymakers to preserve the "free choice of registered office," allowing founders to choose their company's home without being forced to locate all operations in the same place.
Eligibility for EU Inc should not be limited solely to "innovative" startups, the signatories argue. However, supporters of such restrictions contend that opening the scheme to everyone could overwhelm the system and undermine its effectiveness.
"EU Inc needs a single, authoritative European register — not merely an interface layered over 27 national systems," the signatories say among their demands. That would simplify the consultation of company records, they argue.
They are also calling for employees to be taxed only once they sell company shares and for employment protection to remain tied to the location where employees actually work.

Russia’s Knyaz Vandal drone equipped with microphone to hear, ambush enemies — developer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:45:33 UTC
20:45:33 KST

MOSCOW, September 11. /TASS/. The Knyaz Vandal of Novgorod (KVN) fiber-optic FPV drone has been fitted with a microphone enabling operators to hear movement and carry out ambush operations, Alexey Chadayev, CEO of the Ushkuynik Research and Production Center, told TASS.
"A relatively small number of KVN drones will be shipped with a pre-installed microphone. At the same time, all drones will be equipped with a connector into which a microphone can be installed if necessary. This is a tactic for ambush operations. Let’s say a drone lands somewhere on a road, and the operator watches the camera feed to see if enemy vehicles are approaching. If they are, the drone takes off and strikes. But, first of all, drones are visible on the road. Second, when the camera is positioned low to the ground, its field of view is limited. But if you have a microphone and can hear the sound of the motor, it’s simple. The drone lands in the grass or bushes, where it’s hidden from view. Hears a noise, takes off, spots the target, and strikes," Chadayev said.
The Knyaz Vandal of Novgorod fiber-optic FPV drone, developed by the Ushkuynik Research and Production Center, was first used in August 2024, after the Ukrainian armed forces launched an incursion into Russia’s Kursk Region. The drone can withstand electronic warfare and perform various missions.

Horse meat fraud: three arrested, seven Dutch premises raided
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:45:30 UTC
20:45:30 KST

Horse meat fraud: three arrested, seven Dutch premises raided
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Belgian police have arrested three suspects in an ongoing investigation into an international horse meat fraud ring, and carried out raids at 24 locations, including seven in the Netherlands.
According to the Belgian Federal Police, a horse trader in East Flanders was at the centre of a ring which faked passport and microchip information to export horses used in racing for slaughter.
European regulations stipulate that animals destined for a slaughterhouse must be fitted with a microchip that tracks, among other things, whether or not they have been treated with medication.
An investigation by Belgian authorities revealed a large number of horses exported from Ireland to mainland Europe had modified or manipulated microchips.
During the raids, more than 1,000 horses were checked and many were seized. Police also confiscated electronics and more than €100,000 in cash.
The operation was carried out with the assistance of Europol, together with Dutch, French and Irish authorities.
In 2013, the Netherlands was embroiled in a horse meat scandal after it was found in products said to be 100% beef in Britain, Sweden, Ireland and Poland. The Netherlands is a major processor of horse meat imported from abroad.

President in shelter, and ‘armaggeddon’ on TV: here’s how Lithuania met 9/11 attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:45:00 UTC
20:45:00 KST

It was early morning in the US. President Valdas Adamkus, who was visiting Washington, was hurried to a secure shelter, while in Vilnius, senior officials gathered for an unscheduled meeting to discuss the country’s security situation.
Based on archive reports from Panorama, this article reconstructs the issues that dominated life in Lithuania in September 2001, the country’s response to the terrorist attacks and how Lithuanians assessed the situation.
‘Armageddon’
"It was like a science-fiction film about Armageddon. But this was really happening, in the very heart of the democratic world’s financial centre, next to Wall Street,” Vykintas Pugačiauskas said as he began his dramatic report on September 11, 2001.
“As panic-stricken people tried to escape the area around the World Trade Centre, oil and gold prices rose around the world, while the dollar fell," he added.
The terrorist attacks also caused concern in Lithuania. That same day, Lithuanian officials and heads of the country’s security and law-enforcement institutions gathered for an unscheduled meeting with then Prime Minister Algirdas Mykolas Brazauskas.
Although it was decided not to declare a state of emergency in Lithuania, then parliamentary speaker Artūras Paulauskas told journalists there was "some worrying information", but declined to elaborate. Prime Minister Brazauskas said at the time that the situation was not dangerous, but additional measures would be taken.
Following the meeting, security at strategic sites was increased. The biggest security operation was at the Ignalina Nuclear Power Plant: access to the surrounding area was restricted without special permits, while armed officers carried out regular patrols.
Increased attention was also given to the Port of Klaipėda and the international ferry terminal, while ships patrolled the waters. Following the attacks, additional security measures were also introduced at Vilnius Airport.
The terrorist attacks brought transatlantic air travel to a halt both in Lithuania and around the world. As a result, large numbers of passengers were stranded at airports. Lithuania was no exception – at the time, an average of about 50 people travelled to the US every day on connecting flights.
The terrorist attacks also pushed up fuel prices. According to the report, the price of petrol rose by five cents. A petrol station representative said fuel sales had increased by 25%. However, no major economic shocks were observed in the first few days.
Banks also saw increased demand for European Union currencies and, somewhat surprisingly, the Lithuanian litas. During this period, people were exchanging US dollars for litas.
Adamkus' US visit
In 2001, Lithuania was making major efforts to join NATO. It was therefore not surprising that visits by the country's leaders to the US were frequent. Before the trip, President Valdas Adamkus said he expected his visit to Washington to be one of the most challenging of his entire presidency.
That morning, Adamkus and the Lithuanian delegation attended a working breakfast with representatives of American Jewish organisations, where the threat of terrorism was also discussed. It was during this breakfast that news of the attacks first broke.
The presidential delegation was taken to a shelter in the basement of the hotel. Later, the entire delegation moved to the Lithuanian embassy in Washington, which was considered a safer location.
Because of the situation, the planned visit was cut short by four days. Interestingly, the delegation was also among the first passengers to be allowed to board a transatlantic flight from the US after the attacks.
The delegation became passengers on the first transatlantic flight after the terrorist attacks. The US authorities also provided a military aircraft to fly the delegation to Reykjavik. From there, they transferred to a Lithuanian Airlines aircraft and reached Vilnius Airport at 04:00 on September 13.
After returning to Lithuania, Adamkus said the attacks would not make Lithuania’s path to NATO more difficult and could, on the contrary, make it easier.
The day after his return to Lithuania, the president issued a special address in which he spoke about the events of September 11 and their significance for Lithuania. The president also expressed his full support for US action and spoke about changes in international politics.
"September 11 shook and changed the world. We, the people of Lithuania, also need to fully understand these changes. In a single day, our world became more fragile and vulnerable, as even the most powerful country in the world proved to be vulnerable," Adamkus said in his address to the nation on September 14.
The speech prompted a range of reactions. People interviewed in the streets of Lithuanian cities disagreed with the position expressed by the president and pointed to the theme of revenge in his speech. Many of those interviewed also referred to Lithuania’s small size and limited influence.
"I would say we should refrain from that. We are a small country, and no one will defend us. We will exhaust our own strength for the sake of others, and there will be nothing left for us," one woman told reporters.
Opinions and assessments varied. It is important to remember that at the time, Lithuania’s prospects of joining NATO and the European Union were viewed in very different ways.
While some saw membership as Lithuania’s steady return to the West, others associated it with an increased threat.
Nevertheless, the government at the time continued the integration process and supported the implementation of Article 5 of the Washington Treaty.
But it was the possibility of further attacks that caused the greatest concern. As reports spread about the possible use of biological weapons, Panorama journalists looked into the situation in Lithuania’s laboratories.
What was Lithuania living through before the attacks?
Events often overshadow one another. The scale of the September 11 attacks pushed some of the major stories of the time out of the spotlight.
September 2001 saw teachers in Telšiai and other cities begin a week-long strike. They were unhappy about delays in the payment of salaries to education-sector workers. They were warned that the strikes would continue for as long as their wages remained unpaid.
Teachers interviewed for the report said they earned 350 litas at the time (around 100 euros). School pupils interviewed were unsure whether the protest would achieve anything – some welcomed it, while others worried about their exams.
The sporting world was dealt a painful blow, which people interviewed in the streets described as a tragedy. Lithuania’s run at the 2001 European Basketball Championship in Turkey ended in the last 16 with a defeat by neighbouring Latvia.
"We praised them too much, glorified them too much. The men were flying high, but you need to keep your feet on the ground," one passer-by said.
Following the fiasco, coach Jonas Kazlauskas resigned. This period in Lithuanian basketball came between the euphoria of the 2000 Olympic Games in Sydney and Lithuania’s European championship triumph in 2003.
After the defeat, Adamkus even joked about severing diplomatic relations with Latvia.
Lithuania continued preparing for integration into NATO and the EU. In September 2001, joint exercises involving Lithuanian and NATO forces, called Amber Hope, were held in Rukla. Almost 3,000 troops took part.
Rukla residents welcomed the increased activity in the town, while the commander of the Land Forces, Colonel Valdas Tutkus, cautiously spoke about the positive assessments expected from Lithuania’s future allies.
Local residents were pleased that turnover at shops and cafés had increased tenfold.
Minsk troubles
Meanwhile, Lithuanian journalists and international observers were closely following events in Belarus. The country was preparing for its second presidential election.
The vote was originally due to take place in 1999, but while serving his first term, A. Lukashenko changed the constitution and extended the presidential term to seven years.
"The elections in Belarus confirmed the thesis of the classic of authoritarianism, Joseph Stalin: 'It does not matter who votes how. What matters is who counts the votes and how'," journalist Jolanta Paškevičiūtė said as she began her report from Minsk.
Lukashenko won the election. He was challenged by the opposition, which accused the authorities of holding a fraudulent election and claimed that Vladimir Hancharyk, who came second, had received about 40% of the vote, compared with 46% for Lukashenko.
But international attention shifted from the election to the US the very next day.

India and Russia are building something big in space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:44:44 UTC
20:44:44 KST

India and Russia are building something big in space
Space exploration and satellite navigation are fragile, failure-prone and enormously expensive. Yet they offer something few other fields can match: technological superiority and strategic prestige.
The main players in space remain Russia, the United States, and China, followed by India, the European Union, and Japan. Newer entrants include the United Arab Emirates, Iran, and a range of states in South America and West Asia. Because the sector is so costly and high-risk, cooperation is highly valued – it brings redundancy, speeds up technological progress, and cuts the price of getting there.
Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov earlier this week, in the runup to Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to New Delhi, noted that Russia and India are considering the possibility of cross-flights involving mixed crews to their future national orbital stations. He said that this cooperation could eventually extend to joint scientific experiments and research.
In May this year, Indian National Security Adviser Ajit Doval visited the Roscosmos Joint Industry Information Center, while in August, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar traveled to Moscow to co-chair the 27th session of the India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technological and Cultural Cooperation (IRIGC-TEC).
Increased collaboration between Moscow and New Delhi within the space sector is occurring within the backdrop of three larger yet interlinked trends: first, the United States’ active dismantling of the remaining international order; second, the ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and Iran; and third, the advancement in drones and defense technologies.
The current US administration has upended the established decades-long US foreign policy by targeting longstanding allies with tariffs and sanctions in the attainment of its goals. India has become a target more than once of American tariffs and economic pressure. Attempts to reach a deal with the Trump administration have failed to produce long-term tangible gains.
This, however, has had a deep impact on the Indian populace. Since the normalization of Indo-US ties, the Indian public had forgotten that historically, American interests had been antagonistic to India during the entire Cold War period. These buried emotions have been surfacing lately with public skepticism regarding American intentions. Deepening cooperation with Russia and attempts to normalize ties with China are New Delhi’s way of signaling its displeasure toward American actions.
Recent developments in Indo-Russian cooperation have involved mutual deployment of ground stations, co-production of engines, and development of national orbital stations. These will allow Russia to offset vulnerabilities by outsourcing joint-production capabilities of critical components to India out of Ukraine’s reach.
The astronomical advancements in drone and smart defense technologies have underscored the significance of satellite-based constellations in warfare. A variety of Russian munitions and weapon systems employ GPS/GLONASS and the upcoming Rassvet system in precision guidance and control. UMPK-equipped glide-bombs, cruise missiles such as the Kh-101, drones like the Shahed-136, Geran-3 & -4, and Orlan-10, along with ballistic missiles such as the Iskander-K, witness a significant increase in accuracy and precision with minimal falloff over large distances.
Furthermore, despite the destruction of existing Viasat infrastructure in Ukraine during the conflict’s opening days, the rapid deployment of Starlink prevented the complete collapse of Ukrainian command and control structures. These attributes make the systems vital to any future operational requirements against adversaries with both limited and significant electronic warfare capabilities.
India’s worst-case military scenarios stipulate for a two-front war. The ability to deploy these munitions and weapon systems may provide its forces with definite tactical and strategic advantages in critical sectors along and beyond the lines of engagement. However, all these require the backbone of GPS/GLONASS capabilities and/or the Rassvet/Starlink low-orbit constellations on which these systems rely. Russia is currently in the process of operationalizing its Rassvet constellation to full functionality.
India’s own NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation) is in dire straits. The indigenous satellite navigation system has dropped below the critical threshold of satellites required for accurate geolocation. Simultaneously, the quest for a reliable low-orbit satellite navigation system over the Indian subcontinent has led to multiple contenders, including the French-TATA venture Eutelsat, the American Starlink and Viasat systems, Reliance’s own planned constellation, and possibly the Russian Rassvet system in the near future.
Space-based cooperation need not be limited to the bilateral level. In August 2021, BRICS space agencies signed an agreement for cooperation in remote sensing satellite data sharing. In May of the following year, the BRICS Joint Committee on Space Cooperation was officially launched. This year, BRICS+ engaged in advanced discussions of cooperation with calls for a BRICS Space Economy being made. Whether civilian cooperation in satellite data constellation ultimately advances to include sensitive military collaboration remains to be seen. What is already clear, however, is that low-orbit constellations are set to become a major disruptor in both civilian and military technology, and this is one area in which the Russia-India partnership could deepen further.

LUGANSK, September 11. /TASS/. By liberating Zarubinka, Russian forces have increased pressure on Ukrainian troops trapped in the encirclement in the area of Reznikovo near Volchansk in the Kharkov Region, military expert Andrey Marochko told TASS.

Beijing freezes plant approvals for energy-storage  batteries amid overcapacity fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

11:43:05 UTC
20:43:05 KST

ExclusiveBeijing freezes plant approvals for energy-storage batteries amid overcapacity fears
‘Dozens of new projects in the pipeline sparked policymakers’ fears about redundancies,’ analyst says
Companies had not been allowed to add new capacity since May, as key regulators like the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) stepped in to curb a construction spree that risked creating severe overcapacity despite rising demand from renewable-energy projects around the world, the sources said.
The temporary ban could be lifted if the supply-demand balance changed, they added.
“The decision to suspend construction of new ESS [energy-storage system] battery factories was made because dozens of new projects in the pipeline sparked policymakers’ fears about redundancies,” said Ivan Li, a researcher at Loyal Wealth Management in Shanghai.
“The ministry-level authorities apparently looked to take pre-emptive measures so that sustainable growth could be achieved.”
Energy-storage systems, comprising batteries along with battery management, power conversion and control equipment, store excess energy generated from renewable sources like solar and wind farms while providing backup power during outages and helping stabilise electricity grids.
The MIIT, which is mainland China’s top economic planning agency, the National Development and Reform Commission and provincial-level regional governments are jointly responsible for drafting policies about ESS projects.

U.S. Army orders more of its M110 sniper systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:43:03 UTC
20:43:03 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Knight's Armament Company a five-year contract worth up to $49,997,842 for M110 Semi-Automatic Sniper Systems through September 2031.
- The award continues a sole-source arrangement dating back years, even as the Army has separately fielded the lighter M110A1 as a planned replacement.
The U.S. Army has handed Knight’s Armament Company, run by founder Charles Reed Knight Jr., a new five-year deal worth nearly $50 million to keep building M110 Semi-Automatic Sniper Systems.
The firm-fixed-price contract covers the rifle, its variants, accessories, spare parts, special tools and training, and runs through September 10, 2031.
Only one company bid, and Knight’s Armament won it, a pattern the Army has followed with the M110 for years. Army Contracting Command in Newark, New Jersey, is overseeing the deal. Work locations and funding will be worked out order by order rather than locked in today.
The M110 fires 7.62x51mm NATO ammunition and grew out of Knight’s Armament’s SR-25 design, which the Army picked in 2007 after a competition. Unloaded, it weighs about 6.27 kg (13.8 lb). It sends a 175-grain round downrange at roughly 783 meters per second (2,570 feet per second) and can hit point targets out to about 800 meters (875 yards). Both the Army and Marine Corps have fielded the rifle, and it saw heavy use in Afghanistan and Iraq.
The Army has spent nearly a decade trying to replace the M110 with something lighter. In 2016 it picked Heckler & Koch’s G28-based M110A1 for up to 3,643 rifles, in a deal worth up to $44.5 million, aimed at giving snipers a weapon that doesn’t stick out the way the longer M110 does. That didn’t end M110 purchases. The Army ordered more in 2018 for about $16.5 million, then kept buying under a five-year contract that ran through last September. This week’s award picks that supply line back up rather than closing it out.
The Army has also been buying M110s for Ukraine. In September 2025, it gave Knight’s Armament a separate $21 million contract to build M110 systems for Ukraine’s armed forces, paid for through the Ukraine Security Initiative and Partnership Capacity Building program, with deliveries due by January 30, 2027. Ukrainian special forces, the National Guard and International Legion volunteers have reportedly carried the rifle.

Russia may exhaust its resources for the war against Ukraine by 2028 — HUR
Kyiv • UNN
The HUR estimates that Russia will exhaust its military and economic resources by 2028 at the current rate of losses. Every day, Russia loses up to 1,500 military personnel.
Russia may exhaust its resources for the war in Ukraine by 2028 if the occupiers’ military losses remain at their current level. This was stated by the head of the Main Intelligence Directorate, Oleh Ivashchenko, in his first interview with international media, including The Times, reports UNN.
Russia has military and economic resources for the coming year, but according to our estimates, they will be exhausted in 2028 if military and economic losses continue to increase at the same rate
He noted that Russia recruits around 1,000–1,200 people every day, while its daily losses on the front amount to 1,400–1,500, with about 60% of them killed.
At this rate, the Russian forces will suffer an additional 765,800 losses over 18 months of fighting. This means that almost 10% of Russia’s male population aged 25 to 49 could be affected by the war by 2028.
Ivashchenko emphasized that these figures are causing a lack of support for Putin’s war effort.
The morale of the Russian army is very low because no one wants to fight. Morale among the Russian population is also very low: most people actually do not want the war

The Ministry of Defence of Ukraine has codified the Steppe Wind (Stepovyi Viter) strike unmanned aerial system developed by domestic company Unwave.
Official codification enables government procurement and the delivery of these UAVs to Defense Forces units, the company told Militarnyi.
The mid-range UAV was jointly developed with partners from Sky Composite Engineering to hit stationary targets, armored vehicles, and personnel.

Fact check: Which EU economy is performing the best?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:42:00 UTC
20:42:00 KST

Recent comments by Portugal's prime minister have prompted discussion about which EU country currently has the best-performing economy and employment growth rate.
Portugal's economy and employment growth are the best-performing in Europe, according to the country's Prime Minister Luís Montenegro. But how true is that?
Montenegro made the comments while speaking to the Assembly of the Republic, Portugal's parliament, on 8 September. Here, MPs were debating a motion of no confidence in the government put forward by the far-right Chega party.
The motion came about after Montenegro refused to sack Interior Minister Luís Neves over allegations of misconduct while he was head of Portugal's Judiciary Police between 2018 and 2026.
Other opposition parties came together to support the centre-right minority government and vote down the motion, in an effort to avoid further political instability. The country has, after all, held three elections in three years.
During the debate, the prime minister told MPs that Portugal had the best economic performance and the top rate of employment growth in Europe.
To find out whether his claims held any weight, The Cube, Euronews' fact-checking team, looked at the most recent Eurostat figures on member states' GDP growth.
They reveal that the EU's GDP as a whole was up by 0.7% in the second quarter of 2026, compared to the previous quarter.
Ireland was the main driver of this, with far and away the highest jump in GDP at +10.2%. Analysts say its strong growth, a sharp upward revision from previous estimates, was largely driven by major output surges from global firms, particularly in technology and pharmaceuticals. Because of this, economists view it as an unreliable metric.
Slovenia and Lithuania came in second and third place, with a growth of 1.8% and 1.7%, respectively.
Portugal came in joint seventh place with Cyprus, with both countries' GDP's rising by 0.8%.
So it's fair to say Portugal is ranking among the best of the 27 member states, but it’s not the best, according to Eurostat data.
Austria was the only country that recorded a decline, with its GDP contracting by 0.1%.
When it comes to employment, the same Eurostat dataset shows that employment had gone up by 0.1% in both the Eurozone and the EU in the second quarter of 2026.
Around 221.4 million people were employed in the EU during that time.
In this case, Montenegro would be correct: When broken down by member state, Portugal came in first place with a 1% growth in employment in the second quarter of 2026.
It was followed by the Czech Republic and Malta in joint second place, at 0.9% growth.
Several countries saw a decrease in employment, notably Finland (-0.8%) and Greece (-0.4%).

Sweden's fractured left holds slim lead in polls before Sunday election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:41:04 UTC
20:41:04 KST

Sweden's fractured left holds slim lead in polls before Sunday election
STOCKHOLM, Sept 11 - Sweden's centre-left opposition bloc holds a narrow lead ahead of Sunday's parliamentary election, three opinion polls showed on Friday, two days before what is seen as a referendum on the incumbent right-wing government's alliance with the far-right.
Across Europe, far-right parties have been on the rise, with Alternative for Germany, which opposes immigration and backs closer ties with Russia, winning a state election and Marine Le Pen leading polls for next year's presidential vote in France.
In Sweden, Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson narrowly remains favourite to become prime minister again after four years in opposition and replace Ulf Kristersson of the centre-right Moderates.
Sweden's four left-leaning parties between them have support of between 49.3% and 50.8%, giving them from 175 to 180 seats in the 349-seat parliament, according to the surveys conducted by the Ipsos, Demoskop and Indikator Opinion polling firms.
Backing for the coalition government and its far-right support party, the Sweden Democrats, stands at 47.6% to 49.0%, corresponding to between 169 and 174 seats, the polls released by Swedish Radio and dailies Aftonbladet and DN showed.
Kristersson has overseen a shift in Sweden away from the liberalism for which the country was once known, introducing some of Europe's toughest policies on immigration.
Andersson's bloc, which has pledged higher public spending, has retained a majority in every poll published this year, with most of the recent surveys pointing to a winning margin of around 10 seats.
But one of the surveys on Friday showed a margin of a single seat, mirroring Sweden's close-fought election of 2022.
In mid-August, the centre-left held a 10 percentage point lead in several polls, which political scientists at the time said was a nearly insurmountable gap to bridge before election day.
Kristersson says that if his bloc wins, the Sweden Democrats, which has apologised for its past links with neo-Nazism, would join the government for the first time.
DIVIDED LEFT
The centre-left remains divided over which parties should be included in a government headed by the Social Democrats, with the Centre Party and the Left Party each ruling out taking part if the other is in.
The parties also differ on key policies, from a tax on billionaires to whether Sweden should build new nuclear reactors.
This may in turn lead to lengthy negotiations and the formation of a minority government including some, but not all, opposition parties if the left wins.
The rival blocs both support Ukraine in its fight against Russia's invasion as well as military rearmament at home and relief for households hit by the rising cost of living.
But while the campaign focused on a range of issues including Sweden's welfare state, immigration and crime, there was no single dominant issue, experts said.
"Nothing has really stuck, it's been sort of unsatisfactory in that sense," said Nicholas Aylott, an associate professor at Sodertorn University.
The Social Democrats remain Sweden's biggest single party with support between 27.4% and 29.7%, down from 30.3% in the 2022 vote, the polls show.
The anti-immigration Sweden Democrats party maintained its position as the governing bloc's biggest group with 18.3% to 19.0% support, down from 20.5% since the 2022 election, the polls showed.
The party has been propping up the ruling coalition without being part of the cabinet. REUTERS
