Combat-Proven Robotics Meet AI Swarm Tech in $224 Million Deal Between Swarmer and Ratel Robotics
Texas-based defense technology firm Swarmer is acquiring Ukrainian uncrewed ground vehicle maker Ratel Robotics in a cash-and-stock deal valued at up to $224 million. The company is backed by Blackwater founder Erik Prince and an investment fund linked to former Google CEO Eric Schmidt.
The transaction serves as an early indicator of consolidation within Ukraine’s expansive defense industry. Over 500 companies currently compete for military orders across roughly 1,500 frontline combat units, The Wall Street Journal reports on September 10.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Originally founded in Ukraine and now headquartered in Austin, Texas, Swarmer develops artificial intelligence software that enables groups of drones to autonomously coordinate actions during combat missions.
Ratel Robotics manufactures uncrewed ground vehicles that secured approximately 37% of the Ukrainian Defense Ministry’s ground drone procurement budget during the first four months of this year. Their ground robots have participated in over 112,000 logistics and evacuation missions since the start of the year.
Swarmer created software that powered one of the first known instances of regular swarm technology deployment in combat, allowing drone groups to autonomously decide which unit strikes first and adapt in real time if an asset loses battery power.
First deployed in April 2024, the company's software has now been utilized in over 100,000 combat missions. In July, Swarmer also teamed up with American drone manufacturer Powerus to supply swarm-controlled drones to the Pentagon.
Market consolidation across the sector continues to accelerate as Western investors and defense firms seek combat-tested technologies developed during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Last year, Ukrainian drone producer Vyriy Industries acquired controlling stakes in five local defense technology companies, while US investment firm MITS Capital merged four Ukrainian defense businesses into MITS Industries.
Additionally, a drone manufacturing company owned by Australian executive Francisco Serra-Martins recently acquired a smaller local competitor. Several companies, including Swarmer and firms owned by MITS, are registering corporate entities abroad to access international capital markets and larger defense procurement opportunities.
“From the perspective of Ukrainian companies, most of them cannot develop the infrastructure required to sell products globally. Therefore, they are looking for partners who can provide them with resources and help them enter new markets,” said Swarmer US Chief Executive Officer Alex Fink.
Swarmer Board Chairman Erik Prince stated that the company intends to continue purchasing and forming partnerships with defense technology and security firms that possess battlefield-tested products.
“The entry barrier to start a drone company is low because 1,500 combat commands can purchase what they believe works best,” said MITS Capital Chief Executive Officer Perry Boyle, noting that scaling remains far more difficult due to high financing costs and heavy reliance on large government contracts.
“The United States has the best capital markets in the world. And the largest defense market, so it makes sense for us to be here,” Prince said regarding international registration.
Former US Navy SEAL Prince, together with Swarmer, recently launched Vectus Air Defense Systems, a company designed to provide enterprises, militaries, and governments with services for designing and operating custom air defense systems.
Earlier, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed hope that the US will support implementing the FREYJA anti-ballistic missile program, with the interceptor missile being built based on the Fire Point FP-7 ballistic missile.
“We are preparing our own FREYJA program. We very much hope that the Americans will support this program as well. But nevertheless, with the Europeans we will definitely achieve the desired result,” Zelenskyy said.

Gaza flotilla activists join hunger strike of fellow detainee in Tunisia
Three Gaza flotilla activists have joined the hunger strike of a colleague to protest against their months-long detention by Tunisian authorities.
Ghassan El Henchiri, Ghassan El Boughdiri and Nabil Channoufi joined the hunger strike of Wael Naouar on its 26th day, according to the Global Sumud Flotilla, as a Tunisian court is set to rule on a potential extension of their pre-trial detention.
Global Sumud Flotilla, which organises attempts to break Israel's siege on Gaza, said in a statement that Noauar's condition "has deteriorated significantly, including severe physical weakness, substantial weight loss and kidney complications, and he is now in a potentially life-threatening state".
The group, known as the Sumud 4, are being held in Mornaguia prison and were arrested in March on charges related to suspected fraud, money laundering, and possible misuse of donations.
Tunisia's Economic and Financial Judicial Pole, a body that handles economic and financial cases, ordered the investigation.
The lawyer representing Naouar, Tunisian League for Human Rights President Bassem Trifi, told Al Jazeera that the fundraising activities should not be treated as ordinary financial transactions subject to public procurement and accounting rules, due to their use as part of a solidarity campaign.
A Tunisian court is set to decide on Friday whether the group's pre-trial detention will be extended for a further six months.
The three activists who joined Naouar's hunger strike wrote a letter from the prison explaining their involvement in the flotilla, saying: "We did not step out seeking personal glory, nor in pursuit of false heroism."
"We stepped out because Gaza was, and remains, calling out to the human conscience."
The Global Sumud Flotilla has urged people to contact Tunisian diplomatic representatives and elected officials over the Sumud 4's detention, as well as to organise demonstrations to "bring the demands of the Sumud 4 into universities, workplaces, unions and community spaces".
"Free the Sumud 4. End the criminalisation of solidarity with Palestine. Let them go home," the group added.
The Sumud 4's detention comes as Tunisia cracks down on international NGOs in the country, with Human Rights Watch last week saying that authorities in the country have weaponised financial and criminal investigations against non-profits.
At least 47 people connected to NGOs have been prosecuted, with 14 having been convicted and sentenced to prison in 2025.
The Global Sumud Flotilla, launched in 2025, has made several attempts to break Israel's blockade of Gaza and deliver aid to the enclave, however has been repeatedly intercepted by Israeli forces in international waters.
In May, an attempt to break the siege saw the mass abduction and detention of hundreds of activists by Israeli forces, with many recounting torture, including beatings and sexual assault by Israeli personnel.

PRESS REVIEW: Friday, September 11– 25 years on from 9/11, the international press reflects on the war on terror, its legacy and its failings. In France, the far-right National Rally party tries desperately to distance itself from the overtly racist comments of one of its security officials, made while on duty for his day job as a police officer. Finally, a fossilised feather may give us new insights into why birds survived the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs.
The Washington Post headline reads "the 9/11 response got the most important thing right", despite mistakes – the paper acknowledges – in Iraq and Afghanistan. A similar verdict from the Wall Street Journal: taking the war to terrorists abroad and holding any country harbouring terrorists responsible were two key principles that protected the US against any similar attack in the 25 years that followed. And, finally, The Times brings us news of a piece of fossilised dinosaur dung in which a feather appears to have survived the domestic journey. The feather may offer a rare insight into why almost all bird families went extinct with the dinosaurs: was it a question of feathers? Did the other prehistoric bird families have plumage too thin for the post-asteroid climate?

Pronounced dead at 17, she lived — and her sister delivered her baby
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
09:16:15 UTC
18:16:15 KST

On Sept. 1, Shahar Davidov gave birth to her third child at Rabin Medical Center in Petah Tikva. The midwife who delivered her baby was her older sister, Zohar — an intimate family moment that brought full circle a story of tragedy, hope and renewal.
In 2009, Shahar was seriously injured in a car crash when her former partner veered off the road and struck a tree.
A doctor who arrived at the scene pronounced her dead. But paramedic Muawiya Kabha, who was on his way to another emergency, heard over the radio about a fatal crash involving two teenagers and decided to change course and head to the scene.
Despite Shahar having been declared dead, Kabha continued fighting to save her, performing CPR for 40 minutes until her pulse returned.
She was rushed to Rabin Medical Center and required another round of resuscitation on the way. By then, radio stations were already reporting a fatal crash in which a 17-year-old girl had been killed. Shahar’s sister Zohar arrived at the crash scene and watched as her younger sister was taken away in an ambulance.
“The paramedic was on his way to another call, and the doctor who had pronounced me dead asked him to treat the other person, who was only lightly injured — but he chose to fight for me,” Shahar said.
“We were on vacation in Tiberias when one of Shahar’s friends called us from her phone to tell us about the accident. We immediately packed our things and headed out,” recalled Shahar’s father, Yitzhak “Ika” Kugelmas.
“We were silent. We didn’t talk and we didn’t turn on the radio — and luckily we didn’t, because they were already reporting that someone had been killed in the crash.
“We arrived at Rabin, and the nurse who met us said her condition was extremely serious,” he said. “I went in to see Shahar, and I could barely recognize her.”
After two weeks under sedation and on a ventilator, Shahar regained consciousness and began a long rehabilitation. During her recovery, she managed to complete her high school matriculation exams and later enlisted in the Israeli military.
‘Everything was planned so Zohar would deliver my baby’
Seventeen years have passed since a doctor pronounced Shahar dead on the side of the road. She went on to build a family and have two children.
Zohar, who had stood at the crash scene and watched the ambulance drive away with her younger sister, eventually chose to study nursing. She later became a midwife at Rabin Medical Center — the same hospital where Shahar was taken on the night of the crash.
Earlier this month, the sisters’ story came full circle in the delivery room.
“This was my third delivery, and thank God, after two births that were anything but easy, this one went smoothly,” Shahar said.
“It was incredibly emotional to have my older sister Zohar as my midwife. She gave me a healing experience with an easy, quick delivery, and the recovery has been easy as well. In fact, I waited for her to finish her midwifery training before getting pregnant,” she admitted with a smile.
“When I gave birth for the first time, Zohar was still working in the neonatal intensive care unit where my son was hospitalized for a week. This time, she was part of the birth itself, right there in the delivery room. Everything was planned so that she would be the one to deliver my baby.”

JOHANNESBURG, Sept 11 - South Africa will extradite to the United States six Nigerian nationals suspected of being members of the Black Axe organised crime network involved in romance scams and cyberfraud, police said on Friday.
The men are wanted by U.S. authorities on charges including wire fraud and money laundering.

The extradition comes after other suspected Black Axe members were arrested in Switzerland and Spain earlier this year. ($1 = 16.1633 rand) REUTERS

25 years after 9/11, survivors are still getting sick—here are the numbers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
09:15:58 UTC
18:15:58 KST

Twenty-five years on, Matthew McCauley still remembers the dust. On September 11, 2001, he was working as a law clerk just blocks away from the World Trade Center in lower Manhattan when terrorists flew a pair of planes into its Twin Towers, causing them to collapse in a cloud of debris, ash and fire.
The dust plume—which contained concrete, asbestos, glass, and more—reached more than a kilometer above New York City’s financial district. McCauley, a former police officer in his early 30s, stepped up to help sift through the rubble at the site, which we now know as Ground Zero. At least two feet’s (more than half a meter’s) worth of dirt and dust covered the ground, he recalls. Sediment hung in the air. Fires burned at the site for more than a month.
“Lower Manhattan just smelled,” he says.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Locals reported dust in their homes weeks after the attacks. In McCauley’s office building, the dust kept reappearing on desks and inside windowsills. “Every single day there was dust to be cleaned,” he says, “every day.”
Now, a quarter-century later, McCauley is plagued by a persistent cough and sinus issues. “I wake up every morning, and you’d think that I smoked. I don’t smoke,” he says. “It’s the gift that keeps giving from Ground Zero.”
Still, McCauley says he is one of the lucky ones: He’s lost several close friends to 9/11-related illnesses. And McCauley, now working as a lawyer for the advocacy organization 9/11 Health Watch, says he’s known hundreds who have died in the aftermath of the attacks.
The true health impact of the attacks is impossible to measure, but an estimated 400,000 people were exposed to “toxic contaminants, risk of physical injury, and physically and emotionally stressful conditions” in the days and weeks after 9/11, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Aside from respiratory issues, 9/11 survivors and first responders have developed health conditions such as cancers, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), substance abuse, anxiety, depression, sleep apnea, and more. As of June 30, 2026, the World Trade Center (WTC) Health Program, a research effort that spans multiple clinics, health agencies and universities, has documented more than 139,000 health conditions—and counting—in more than 150,000 survivors and first responders.
Thanks to years of lobbying by 9/11 health advocates, treatment for McCauley’s cough, as well as for dozens of conditions associated with the attacks, is covered for survivors and first responders under the James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Act, which was signed into law in 2011. But many survivors and their families contend that is still not enough to account for the risks they have faced.
Back at Ground Zero all those years ago, McCauley recalls the dangers posed by burning rubble and dust crossing his mind. But, he says, “the focus was to get things done.”
Wearing a paper mask was unwieldy. “It was hot. It was sweaty. You were just constantly moving,” he recalls. Still, he feels that government agencies could have done more to protect first responders and civilians from the dangers posed by hazardous dust.
“The World Trade Center was basically made of every single carcinogen known to man, as most buildings are, and then [it] was micronized in seconds and became airborne,” McCauley says.
Indeed, researchers are still documenting new health conditions—particularly cancers—among survivors and first responders. As of June 30, cancer made up about 71 percent of the conditions in these groups recorded by the WTC Health Program in the past 12 months. Most people who were present during the attacks and their aftermath and are living with cancer today have nonmelanoma skin cancer, followed by prostate cancer and breast cancer, according to the WTC Health Program. But many also have rarer forms of the disease, such as brain cancer, testicular cancer, leukemia, and more.
“We still see new patients, and a lot of our patients that are coming in now are coming in with a diagnosis of cancer or other latent conditions like interstitial lung disease,” says Denise Harrison, clinical director of the New York University Grossman School of Medicine’s WTC Health Program and an associate professor at the school. That’s because many of these conditions take years to develop, she says.
Alongside the rise in long-term illnesses, researchers have also seen an increase in “adjustment disorders”—that is, anxiety, depression and other mental health issues related to other medical conditions, such as a cancer diagnosis, says Peter Haugen, director of mental health for the NYU Grossman School of Medicine’s WTC Health Program.
“You can imagine, people who come in with cancer that’s progressed or newly diagnosed, it, of course, would make sense that they might be experiencing some of those symptoms,” he says. And treatments such as chemotherapy can also take a mental toll, he adds.
Directly linking an environmental exposure to a complex medical condition such as cancer can be fraught. It’s hard to know who was exposed to which pollutants, where and for how long. Survivors and responders haven’t lived in a vacuum for the past 25 years, Harrison says. They’ve experienced wildfire pollution, COVID, daily allergies, and more—this “complicates the picture,” she says. But under the WTC Health Program, covered illnesses only must be associated with 9/11 exposures; causal proof isn’t necessary.
As time goes on, cases are likely to keep climbing.
Just this week, in response to a lawsuit from 9/11 Health Watch, the New York City mayor’s office agreed to release a trove of documents suggesting the city may have downplayed air quality issues in Manhattan in the months after the attacks. That means health issues may be more widespread than previously documented. McCauley hopes the documents could support new research into illnesses that are not currently covered by the WTC Health Program, as well as the effect of 9/11 exposure on pregnancy and fetuses.
McCauley, now age 56, doesn’t plan to “live in fear” of getting sick. But witnessing the death of many close friends over the years has tested his resolve.
One of his closest friends, Brian Payne, was a volunteer firefighter at Ground Zero. He was a “bigger than life” guy who loved the New York Rangers and the Mets, McCauley recalls. “One day, Brian was healthy and playing hockey and being a fireman and going fishing, and next thing you know, he had cancer.”
Payne died in 2022, leaving a wife and four kids.
More than anything else, McCauley worries about how the deaths in his community have affected his own three college-age kids. They have seen some of their friends’ parents lost to 9/11-related illnesses, too. “My kids kind of look at me, and they’re like, ‘Well, what about you, Dad?’” he says.
“We’re surrounded by it,” McCauley adds.

The US and Mexico Announce They’re Teaming Up Against Drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
09:15:00 UTC
18:15:00 KST

Defense agencies of Mexico and the US have announced they are implementing a new collaborative strategy to combat drones used by criminal organizations. The operation, dubbed High Eagle, or Águila Alta, builds on recent tests of anti-drone technologies carried out along the border between the two countries.
The first phase of the strategy took place between August 31 and September 2 along the border between San Diego and Tijuana, Mexico. Initially, both military forces—simultaneously on the ground from their respective territories—tracked commercial drones used by criminal entities. In the second phase, the agencies neutralized the unmanned aerial vehicles, with support from fixed and mobile anti-drone systems. These activities began on September 7 and will continue through September 21.
The information released by Mexico’s Secretariat of National Defense, known as SEDENA, does not specify the kind of technology involved in the mission. However, US Northern Command has suggested that the operation might employ high-energy lasers. These extremely concentrated beams of light can—in various phases—detect, track, illuminate, damage, or destroy drones from a distance.
The US Army has invested in a particular laser system known as the Locust platform, which is designed for mounting on military vehicles. Authorities have had this technology at their disposal since September of last year, when the company that produces the system, AeroVironment, delivered the first two functional prototypes to the Armed Forces.
So far, it has not been confirmed that these systems are being used in Operation High Eagle, though the Mexican authorities have increased access to these state-of-the-art weapons. Last month, SEDENA and the US Department of Defense signed an agreement allowing the Mexican military to access the US Army’s digital marketplace for acquiring anti-drone systems at competitive prices.
Representatives from both countries have stated that the aim of this new operation and recent agreements is to strengthen efforts against organized crime, especially human and drug trafficking. Earlier this month, the US Northern Command announced it had disabled or destroyed approximately 300 drones linked to criminal activity this year, a third of which were taken down in August. Within recent weeks, 11 of the targets were involved with cartels.
The operation stems from the US-Mexico Bilateral Implementation Group. According to SEDENA, it aims to ensure security on both sides of the border, while respecting the national sovereignty of both nations and “prioritizing the interests of the Mexican State at all times.”
The US ambassador to Mexico, Ronald Johnson, stated that the agreement would strengthen both countries’ ability to combat cartels and address bilateral security challenges.

Government plans care insurance as elderly population grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
09:13:00 UTC
18:13:00 KST

(İHA Photo)
The government will roll out long-term care insurance and adapt the social security system to demographic shifts as the elderly population grows.
The Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) reported that citizens aged 65 and older surged 20.5 percent over five years to 9.58 million in 2025, forming 11.1 percent of the population. This figure was 7.95 million, or 9.5 percent, in 2020.
Within this demographic, 62.9 percent are ages 65 to 74, 27.9 percent are 75 to 84, and 7.8 percent are 85 and older. More than 8,000 residents are centenarians.
Authorities added long-term care insurance to the Medium-Term Program for 2027-2029 to ensure financial sustainability against declining fertility rates. Ministries will build infrastructure enhancing home and institutional support for individuals unable to perform daily activities.
Home health and palliative care will become continuous services integrated with telehealth, easing family burdens. The program mandates risk-based audits for reimbursements and value-based payments to optimize expenditures, expecting results in the first quarter.
Officials will widen the Health Market to cover more drugs and medical supplies, while restructuring university hospital management for efficiency in education, research and service.
To secure actuarial balance, regulations will encourage citizens to stay in the workforce longer. The government will adapt laws to flexible working models, bring uninsured groups into the system and improve premium debt collection.
Authorities will upgrade IT systems to expand data sharing and monitor financial indicators. The system faces pressure from an aging demographic. European nations utilize similar schemes to offset massive state care costs.

European leisure travel to Saudi Arabia forecast to grow 130% by 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
09:12:22 UTC
18:12:22 KST

According to new research, Europe was also the fastest-growing long-haul region for Saudi leisure travellers between 2019 and 2025.
The number of European leisure travellers visiting Saudi Arabia is forecast to increase by at least 130% between 2025 and 2030.
According to new research from Tourism Economics, published this week at WTM Spotlight Riyadh, Europe is among the long-haul markets expected to drive the next phase of Saudi Arabia’s tourism growth. Leisure arrivals from Asia Pacific and North America are also predicted to more than double.
As a result, longer-haul markets are expected to account for 54% of Saudi Arabia’s international leisure arrivals by 2030, compared with 47% in 2025.
Germany and Italy are among the standout European markets, with leisure travel from both countries forecast to more than triple by the end of the decade.
Europe is Saudi Arabia's biggest long-haul market
Europe was the fastest-growing long-haul region for Saudi leisure travellers between 2019 and 2025, with visits increasing by 61%.
The continent is also the top longer-haul outbound region, accounting for 10% of Saudi leisure trips in 2025, although the Middle East remains dominant with an 82% share.
Future growth, however, could increasingly shift towards Asia. Tourism Economics forecasts only “modest increases” in Saudi leisure nights in the UK, France and Spain, while Thailand is expected to grow by 46% and Indonesia, Australia and Singapore by at least 50%.
Saudi’s dramatic tourism growth
In “barely half a decade” Saudi Arabia has “moved from the edge of the global tourism map towards its centre”, Tourism Economics said in its report.
Visitor nights have more than doubled since 2019 to 1.1 billion, while projects like the Red Sea and upcoming events including the 2034 FIFA World Cup are “holding the world’s attention for a decade to come”.
International visitor nights increased 177% between 2019 and 2025, compared with global growth of 12%, with Saudi Arabia recording the largest gain in global market share of any destination.
Leisure tourism is growing particularly quickly. The country recorded 7.6 million international overnight leisure arrivals in 2025 – more than six times the 2019 figure – while associated spending increased fivefold to $12.6 billion (€10.86 billion).
Popular tourism destinations
Makkah and Madinah remain Saudi Arabia’s two largest tourism destinations by some margin, while Riyadh and Jeddah have seen visitor numbers surge as the country expands beyond its traditional religious tourism market.
Known for its desert landscapes and ancient heritage sites, AlUla is also emerging as a major destination for leisure travel. It recorded around nine million visitor nights in 2025, with total visitor nights forecast to grow by 11% a year to 2030.
As part of its push to grow international tourism, Saudi Arabia has broadened its visa facilitation network through agreements with countries across Europe, Asia and Central Asia, including Portugal, Türkiye, Spain, Poland, China, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan.
Citizens of all 27 EU member states are eligible to apply for a Saudi tourist eVisa online. Valid for one year, the visa allows multiple entries and allows tourists to spend up to 90 days in the country. It can be used for leisure trips, events, visiting family and relatives, and Umrah, but not Hajj. Travellers must hold a passport valid for at least six months from the date of entry.

EU's largest political group doesn't want confrontation with China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
09:11:59 UTC
18:11:59 KST

The EU's most influential political family is drafting a paper urging tougher use of trade leverage with China, while maintaining dialogue and avoiding a trade escalation.
The centre-right European People's Party (EPP) is preparing to call for a rebalancing of relations with China that stops short of open confrontation or full decoupling.
In the upcoming paper, senior EPP lawmakers are set to argue for a general rebalancing of economic relations by making fuller use of the bloc's existing economic leverage tools, stopping short of a full escalation, according to the early contents seen by Euronews.
The EPP is the largest and most influential political family at EU level, commanding the largest number of MEPs in the European Parliament and 14 out of the 27 commissioners in the European Commission.
Brussels has grown increasingly worried about the bloc's economic imbalances with Beijing, with a widening trade deficit that EU officials attribute to Chinese industrial overcapacity and generous state subsidies undercutting European competitors.
The EU has set October as the deadline to secure concessions from the Chinese government, after which point the European Commission is ready to impose "harsher measures", according to EU Trade Chief Maroš Šefčovič.
In this context, EPP MEPs sitting on the International Trade Committee are preparing a position paper due to be finalised in mid-October, on the heels of the next European Council summit.
The paper focuses on four main areas: rebalancing trade and investment, export control measures, intellectual property rights, and reform of the World Trade Organisation.
An early version argues for a balanced approach: promoting dialogue with China while more forcefully defending Europe's economic interests, notably by using trade defence instruments more decisively and developing new tools to counter unfair competition.
At the same time, EPP lawmakers insist trade measures should be proportionate and temporary, designed to strengthen the EU's bargaining power rather than lock in permanent protectionism.
The need to diversify supply chains and cut dependency on critical raw materials is also cited as a way to reduce China's economic leverage, notably through the ratification and expansion of free trade agreements with partners such as Mercosur, India, Indonesia and Australia.
The paper also calls for tighter customs enforcement and closer oversight of e-commerce platforms, as the Commission plans a major reform to close the enforcement gaps that let illegal goods into the EU market.
Aviation, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals and biotechnology are flagged as sectors the EU should further develop to cut its economic dependence on Beijing.

- list 4 of 4In maps and charts: Russian and Ukrainian attacks on civilian targets
The United States was the only member to oppose it. US representative Yaryna Ferencevych said before the vote that the resolution was “the reason this institution is losing its credibility”.
“Instead of focusing on genuine problems … this body is debating map projects from the 16th century,” she said.
But since the resolution was approved, at least three other countries have voiced concerns about the changes: India, Ukraine and Japan.
None are explicitly opposed to adopting a new projection. However, they are raising concerns about how certain disputed territories should be depicted.
Here’s what we know:
Why is there a new world map?
The UN endorsed a resolution promoting the Equal Earth projection of the world map, rather than the Mercator projection, which is currently widely used.
The resolution does not ban Mercator or impose a particular replacement – it merely encourages nations to adopt the Equal Earth version, which was created by three researchers in 2018.
The Mercator projection, which was produced by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 when the West was busy “conquering” new territories, attempts to show a three-dimensional globe on a two-dimensional surface. That is why countries closer to the poles appear much larger than countries at the equator.
For decades, map experts have pointed out that Mercator’s projection disproportionately shrinks the true size of the African continent and that of other developing regions, while making Europe and the US seem much larger by comparison.
For example, Greenland is shown as roughly the same size as Africa, but, in reality, it could fit into the continent 14 times over. Europe, which is portrayed as bigger than South America, is actually half its size.
Advocates from African countries pointed out that the map is problematic because of the size issues. Importantly, they argued, it reinforces negative perceptions of Africa.
Several cartographers have attempted to develop equal area maps. However, African activists specifically pushed for the Equal Earth projection map, which significantly expands Africa and shrinks Europe and the US.
Experts say while maps are inherently inaccurate because of the constraints of depicting a spherical world on a flat plane, the Equal Earth projection is as close as it gets.
Why is Ukraine worried about the new map?
Ukraine was one of six countries which abstained from the vote at the UNGA, along with Estonia, Georgia, Moldova, Serbia and Lithuania, who voted in solidarity with Ukraine.
Kyiv has complained that the Equal Earth projection depicts the Russian-occupied Crimean peninsula in a distinctly lighter shade than mainland Ukraine.
Russia illegally occupied and annexed Crimea in February 2014, a move the UN has denounced.
Although the peninsula is also shaded differently from mainland Russia on the new map, its yellowish tint appears closer to the Russian shade than Ukraine’s.
“Ukraine does not in principle oppose the core issue addressed in this draft resolution,” Andrii Melnyk, the country’s permanent representative to the UN, said in an address to the assembly.
Melnyk said Kyiv had asked for corrections before the vote but had not received positive responses. The new map, he said, could be tantamount to opening a Pandora’s box, enabling the “abuse and distortion” of the world map.
“It would be a truly fatal mistake for all of us, and for this General Assembly, to seek to correct a historical injustice in the geographical depiction of countries and continents by simultaneously allowing a deeply troubling interpretation of the text of this draft resolution,” he added.
What is Japan demanding?
Meanwhile, on Thursday, Tokyo, which voted in favour of the new map, said it had also asked for corrections to the Equal Earth projection because the map uses the same colours and shades for Russian territory as it does for the disputed Kuril Islands.
Russia and Japan have long fought over control of the four islands, known in Russia as the Southern Kurils and in Japan as the Northern Territories. In 1945, during World War II, the Soviet Union invaded and annexed the islands as part of a pact with Western Allies that stipulated the Soviets would take the disputed territory. The islands’ Japanese inhabitants were removed.
Subsequently, Japan and the US have claimed that the islands were not part of the original pact. The islands, however, remain under Russian administration.
In August this year, Russia’s President Vladimir Putin paid his first-ever visit to the islands, drawing condemnation from Japan. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called the visit “absolutely unacceptable”, saying it “offends the sentiments of the Japanese people”.
This week, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the Japanese embassy in the US has asked Equal Earth’s creators to change the map.
“Displays that contradict the Japanese government’s position are seen [on the map],” Kihara said at a news conference. “We need to prevent incorrect perceptions regarding our country’s territories and geographical names from spreading.”
Why is India uneasy about the map?
India also voted in favour of the Equal Earth projection, but on Sunday, the Ministry of External Affairs published a caveat regarding depictions of the disputed border territory of Kashmir.
Following the Indian partition of 1947, both Pakistan and India lay claim to the former state of Jammu and Kashmir, which had been controlled by the British through indirect rule. The region has subsequently been a flashpoint for tensions between the two rivals and has led to several wars.
Parts of Kashmir are administered by Pakistan, while other parts are administered by India. China, which also disputes some Kashmir territory with India, administers its northeastern portion.
In his statement, spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal noted that the UN vote was in favour of encouraging the use of equal area projections and that it had not made the use of any one map mandatory.
“India’s sovereign territory, including the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, must be depicted in accordance with India’s official map,” he said. “Any inaccurate or misleading depiction is unacceptable.”

UAE revises AI data center plan after Iranian attacks, sources say

UAE revises AI data center plan after Iranian attacks, sources say
Sept 11 - The United Arab Emirates is quietly revising plans for a 5-gigawatt AI data center project – one of the biggest outside the U.S. – after the Iran war prompted a rethink of how and where critical infrastructure should be built, six people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
Originally envisaged as a 10-square-mile (26-square-kilometer) campus in Abu Dhabi, the project will now likely comprise a network of data centers spread across the UAE, according to four of the sources, who all spoke on condition of anonymity.
Authorities are also considering ways to better protect the facilities from drone and missile attacks, including with air defenses and by building some underground, they said. The likely modifications to the project’s blueprint have not previously been reported.
DATA CENTER PROJECT IS CENTRAL TO UAE’S GLOBAL AI AMBITIONS
Plans for the UAE-US AI Campus, which is being built in partnership with American tech companies, were announced during President Donald Trump's visit last year to the wealthy Gulf state.
The project is central to the UAE's ambitions to become a global AI powerhouse as it shifts its economy away from oil. It is led by G42, an AI firm controlled by Sheikh Tahnoun bin Zayed al Nahyan, the UAE national security adviser and brother of its president.
In return for access to Nvidia AI chips and other advanced U.S. technology, the UAE agreed to cut AI ties with China and invest in the Stargate initiative’s American data centers. Stargate is a joint venture between OpenAI, Oracle and SoftBank to build AI infrastructure.
The people who spoke to Reuters included a U.S. official, a Western diplomat and industry executives briefed on the deliberations. The news agency could not determine how close Emirati authorities are to finalizing a new masterplan or the extent to which the proposed changes might affect construction costs and timelines.
Construction on the first phase of the project, a $30-billion, 1-gigawatt compute cluster known as Stargate UAE, began last year with the first 200 megawatts of capacity due to come online this year. When completed, it will have enough capacity to connect every UAE government agency and commercial institution to the world's most advanced AI models, according to Larry Ellison, chairman and chief technology officer at Oracle, which is partnering with G42 on the project.
Responding to Reuters questions about potential revisions to the project, G42 said work on the AI campus was progressing as planned.
“The project's specifics are subject to continuous review in line with the security, resilience and operational standards expected of critical infrastructure at this scale,” the company said without elaborating.
OpenAI said it was working with the UAE to achieve its AI vision and making “good progress on the infrastructure and adoption priorities needed to deliver it."
The Emirati advanced technology ministry and the project’s other American partners – Nvidia, Oracle and Cisco – did not respond to comment requests. Japan’s SoftBank declined to comment.
IRAN TARGETS U.S.-LINKED TECH INFRASTRUCTURE
Emirati officials began reviewing their AI infrastructure plans soon after Tehran started firing missiles and drones at Gulf neighbors that host American forces in retaliation for U.S. and Israeli airstrikes against Iran, the sources told Reuters.
Two Amazon Web Services data centers in the UAE were damaged in the attacks in March along with one in Bahrain. The company’s cloud computing services in the region are still disrupted, according to the latest updates on its website.
In April, Iran’s armed forces issued a video warning that Stargate UAE was also a potential target. The video included a map purporting to show where the complex is being built, with the caption: “Nothing stays hidden from our sight.”
Two people familiar with the matter confirmed the location at a site near Al Dhafra Air Base, which was not publicly known. The base on the outskirts of Abu Dhabi hosts U.S. troops and has been targeted during the war, which began in February.
Daniel Benaim, who served as U.S. deputy assistant secretary of state for Arabian Peninsula affairs under President Joe Biden, said the conflict has been an "economic earthquake" for Gulf states, which had long marketed themselves as safe havens.
“Changes to harden critical infrastructure are vitally necessary,” said Benaim, a fellow at the Middle East Institute, a Washington think tank. “Every country in the region is going to look at what they can do to reduce the risk” and reassure international partners and investors.
The first phase of construction at the UAE’s AI campus is expected to continue as planned, although with some modifications to protect the site from aerial attacks, according to an industry executive and another person briefed on the matter. The rest of the project will likely be spread across multiple locations, they said.
In addition to building underground, officials are considering putting facilities that host the most sensitive data, such as that used by the military, inside mountains, the two said. In the United States, China and Europe, data centers have been built inside disused mines, Cold-war era bunkers or caves.
The UAE, located on the southeastern Arabian Peninsula, is mostly flat, desert terrain. But there are mountain ranges running through parts of the north and northeast in the Ras Al Khaimah and Fujairah emirates.
Air defense systems are being incorporated into the redesign, including drone and missile interceptors and electronic jamming equipment, three sources said. Other likely measures include the use of blast-resistant concrete and the addition of backup power and cooling systems, another said. REUTERS

Cargo shipping costs rise as Rhine water levels drop again
HAMBURG, Sept 11 - Water levels in the Rhine in Germany have fallen again this week after mostly dry weather, the country’s inland navigation agency said on Friday, with commodity traders reporting rising costs for cargo shipping.
• German companies suffered from low Rhine water levels this summer, with the industry facing higher transport costs, logistics bottlenecks and curbed production.
• Mostly dry weather this week in river catchment areas means levels have dropped again, with vessels sailing part-loaded, commodity traders said. More freight has been transferred to road and railway transport, but the river is holding above record-low levels in August.
• Transport prices are rising as vessels are sailing with less cargo and loads must be spread around several ships. Prices for tanker transport from Rotterdam to Karlsruhe jumped to about €165-€170 ($191.43-$197.23) a ton on Friday, up from around €100 last week.
• Inland navigation agency WSV said the navigable water gauge at the chokepoint of Kaub near Koblenz was around 21 cm on Friday, down from 34 cm on Monday and 50 cm last week. The Rhine at Kaub fell below 10 cm in mid-August, below the previous lowest recorded level of 25 centimetres in 2018. The river is about 1 metre deeper than the navigable water gauge.
• The WSV said that no major improvement in river water levels is expected in the coming week but some expected rain could keep the river stable around current levels.
• Germany and several other European countries endured successive heatwaves and scant rainfall this summer, pushing down water levels in waterways such as the Rhine, a vital shipping route for grain, metal ores, coal and refined oil products. REUTERS

Over 60% of new dentists join Department of Health after mandatory internship

About 60 per cent of Hong Kong’s first batch of dental graduates who underwent mandatory internship training have joined the city’s Department of Health, a move that has helped “significantly ease” the manpower crunch.
The development followed a controversial amendment to the Dentists Registration Ordinance in 2024, requiring all dental graduates in Hong Kong to complete a 12-month internship before obtaining a full licence starting in 2025. The measure aimed to enhance hands-on clinical experience in real-life settings.
Dr Kitty Hse Mei-yin, consultant-in-charge of the department’s dental services, said on Friday that the government had recruited 62 per cent, or 46 of the first batch of 75 interns.

“During the internship, they never know what kind of problems will be brought into the room by the next patients, which is different from their clinical training at school … that could enhance their clinical judgment and independent thinking skills.”

Israel's oldest fruit just became its newest spirit: meet the distillery reviving a 2,000-year-old tradition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
09:08:31 UTC
18:08:31 KST

Israel's oldest fruit just became its newest spirit: meet the distillery reviving a 2,000-yr-old tradition
"There's a very large amount of waste of dates that simply aren't beautiful enough to make it to the stores, but their sugar is perfect"
Just ten kilometers from Jordan, in a small community in northern Israel called Revaya, someone is doing something nobody's done here in two thousand years — turning dates into alcohol.
The distillery is called Zoara, a small, locally owned operation tucked into the Valley of Springs — a region long considered one of the most fertile landscapes in the ancient world.
For thousands of years, this stretch of the Jordan River Valley — from the Sea of Galilee down to the Dead Sea — was exactly that: abundant, full of palm trees and flowing water, according to the Bible itself. Dates were its most celebrated fruit, woven so deeply into life here that a nearby city, Zoar, was simply known as the City of Dates.
And today, Zoara, which is named after that very city, is working with the dates that aren't exactly celebrated — the ones farmers throw away because they're considered too "ugly" to sell.
The Backstory Nobody Told You
Every date harvest, farmers sort their crop by quality. Grade A goes to the fancy stores. Grade B, somewhere a step down. And then there's Grade C — dates that are identical in sugar and quality to the export-grade fruit, just not pretty enough to make it to a shelf. For years, they went straight in the trash.
Zoara’s founder Arnon Enoch looked at that waste and saw an opportunity instead.
"We're a distillery that makes alcohol from dates," he told me. "All the drinks we make are based on Medjool dates. We distill the dates and create Date Spirit. There's a very large amount of waste of dates that simply aren't beautiful enough to make it to the stores," he said. "But their sugar is perfect."
One industry's surplus becomes another's raw material — that's the whole business model in a sentence. And there's a lot of surplus to work with.
Israel isn't just a date producer — it's the world's largest exporter of Medjool dates, supplying somewhere between 50 and 60 percent of the entire global Medjool market. Total production runs around 67,000 metric tons, most of it grown along the Syrian-African Rift Valley — the Arava Desert, the Jordan Rift Valley, the Megillot region by the northern Dead Sea, and right here in the Valley of Springs. At that scale, even a small percentage graded "not pretty enough" adds up to an enormous amount of fruit with nowhere to go. That's the gap Zoara stepped into.
And they've done more with it than you'd expect from a single fruit. From one base spirit, Zoara now produces half a dozen different drinks — gin, arak, limoncello, date brandy and a mandarin liqueur among them — each one infused differently with botanicals pulled from the surrounding land.
A History That Vanished — and Came Back
The tradition of making alcohol from dates disappeared almost two thousand years ago.
So what happened? Empires happened. "It was interrupted because there were successive empires here, including the Romans, and then Muslims who grew dates but didn't drink alcohol," Enoch explained.
Long before that, he told me, people across the region — Jews in Babylon, Iraq and Morocco — made their own arak from dates at home. It just never got past the kitchen table. "And now we've arrived in modern Israel, and this is an opportunity to create a historical full circle."
It's the same instinct that turned rice into sake in Japan, or agave into tequila in Mexico — just with a few-thousand-year gap in the middle. Enoch actually founded the company back in 2021 under the name Jordan Spirits, before it became Zoara — years of research and experimentation into how to bring a lost craft back to life. He's been making alcohol for sixteen years total; this particular obsession is five years old.
Inside the Tanks
The process itself: Zoara buys the rejected dates — which, at over 60 percent sugar, are basically nature's sugar capsules — and ferment them with wine yeast to make an elegant date wine. That gets slowly distilled into a crystal-clear eau de vie, smooth and aromatic, carrying the dates' own natural notes of cocoa, caramel and vanilla. What comes off that still is a jaw-dropping 88 percent alcohol. I felt that one in my bones.
By the time it hits the bottle, it's cut down to around 40 percent for the gin and arak. And unlike whiskey or brandy, it doesn't need years in a barrel to get there — this spirit can be shaped while it's still young.
From there, every spirit takes its own path — infused with botanicals pulled straight from the surrounding land. Sage and tarragon from the Jordan riverbanks. Mulberry from the slopes above. Wild herbs foraged from the hills of Gilboa. Heritage mandarin peel from the valley itself. Nothing imported, nothing generic — fourteen different plants go into the gin alone.
That mandarin, by the way, has its own story — a heritage Jaffa variety that's basically extinct in commercial orchards now. Enoch's team knows the handful of surviving trees personally and hand-picks them each season, leaving the peels in the alcohol for their essential oils before distilling.
And people are noticing. The gin won a silver medal at the London Spirits Competition in 2024 — in, Enoch told me, one of the toughest categories there is.
What's Actually in the Glass
I didn't just hear about this — I tasted my way through it. There's a daiquiri built on date brandy and cardamom. A seasonal gin infused with mulberry and grapefruit peel, the mulberries grown in a nearby moshav. A cocktail called Jasmine, mixing the gin with that mandarin liqueur. And, of course, arak — because you can't do a spirit tasting in Israel without it.
Enoch makes the case that arak and dates were always meant to find each other: "It's anise-based, round and oily, and that's exactly what the date alcohol needs. It's very Mediterranean." He's not wrong.
Where It's Headed
Zoara is already making tens of thousands of bottles a year and just started exporting to Japan. Enoch's hoping the United States is next.
What struck me most, though, was something he said almost in passing — that Israel and its Arab neighbors are basically the only places on earth where Medjool dates grow at this scale. And since most of those countries don't produce alcohol, Zoara has, as Enoch put it, "essentially found ourselves sitting on the mother lode of dates."
The Bigger Picture
Zoara isn't a one-off, either. Michal Akerman, Deputy Head of the Valley of Springs Regional Council, told me the idea behind this distillery- turning waste into magic- is exactly the kind of thinking the region is trying to build around — because the old way of farming here isn't going to survive climate change.
The Valley of Springs has been an agricultural region since before the state existed — the kibbutzim here go back to the "Tower and Stockade" period. But it sits on the Syrian-African Rift, one of the most ecologically sensitive stretches of land in the country, and Akerman says climate change is hitting it hard. Traditional farming, done the traditional way, isn't going to cut it.
"We want to bring a new, younger generation into agriculture, because farmers are getting older," she said. "And for that, we need to be very creative."
She pointed to Zoara as the textbook example. "This valley grows a huge amount of dates... there's Grade A, Grade B, Grade C. Grade C usually goes in the trash. What the young people you're about to meet did was take the Grade C dates and turn them into an alcoholic beverage made from dates. That's innovation. That's creativity."
It's not just dates, either. The same region is turning discarded olive pits — which cause real problems in the soil if left to rot — into flour for bread and crackers. Fish farmers who used to raise carp, mullet and tilapia are now growing sea bream, sea bass and the first blue-and-white Israeli salmon. Different products, same logic: stop throwing away what doesn't fit the old model, and find a new one.
And none of it stops at the border. "Agriculture has no borders," Akerman told me. "It's not a country. When there's a pest, it crosses. When there's something good, that can cross too." Farmers here share water and pest data with Jordan constantly — because a date pest doesn't check passports.
So next time someone hands you a gin and tonic, ask where the gin's from. If it says Zoara — you're drinking two thousand years of history, and one region's bet on reinventing itself, dressed up as a night out with friends.

A court in Turku began hearing the details of an extraordinary case on Friday morning.
An 81-year-old man stands accused of two counts of violating the sanctity of a grave after police discovered last year that he had stored the bodies of his parents in freezers for over 30 years.
The prosecutor outlined the charges to the court, noting that the defendant hid the bodies in freezers for three decades instead of burying them.
The defendant, a trained physician who is also listed as an executive at a firm described as offering funeral services, arrived at court without legal representation.
He is also suspected of digging up a family grave last autumn. His 70-year-old brother has been charged with the same offence.
"No crime has occurred at any stage," the elder brother told reporters outside the courtroom. "We deny it [the charges]. I have only acted in accordance with my father's wishes."
He added that their parents' bodies were freeze-dried, an unproven experimental method called promession, which is believed to turn a human corpse into organic soil fertiliser.
Yle understands that the parents died of natural causes in 1994 and 1995 and their bodies were released to the family for burial.
The brothers initially came to the attention of police in October 2025 when workers at a cemetery in Turku reported the pair were digging up a family grave.
They told reporters on Friday morning that they had been tidying the grave and straightening the headstone. They also distributed photos of the grave digging, which was carried out in broad daylight.
They have both denied committing any crimes and one of the brothers told the media that "we don't know exactly what we're being accused of."
Violating the sanctity of a grave can be punished under Finnish law with a fine or a maximum of one year in prison.

MURMANSK, September 11. /TASS/. The first container voyage from China to Murmansk with car spare parts and a return voyage with potash fertilizers along the Northern Sea Route change the status of the city of Murmansk and the Murmansk port, making it the largest transit and logistics hub in the Russian Federation's north-west, Doctor of Economics, head of the Expert Council on Arctic Development at the St. Petersburg Committee on Foreign Relations Alexey Fadeev told TASS.

"This is a very important fact for Murmansk, because Murmansk is now changing its status, it is not just the capital of the Russian Arctic," the expert said. "Thanks to the global events that are taking place now, Murmansk is becoming the largest transit and logistics hub in this country's north-west, and the first voyage of the kind proves this."
Thanks to the development of the Murmansk transport hub, the railway connection between Murmansk and St. Petersburg, and therefore potentially with the North-South logistics corridor, the city and port in the Murmansk Region are now playing an important transport and distribution role related to the global movement of goods, he continued. "We will see how events will develop, but anyway, as of now, the entire situation favors right this development. Murmansk is already gaining the position of the biggest in the world transport and logistics hub in the North."
Breaking southern routes' monopoly
The first container carrier voyage along the Northern Sea Route may also begin the destruction of the southern routes' monopoly by offering possibilities of the Arctic logistics route, he added. "The voyage was still a trial and we are not talking now about major amounts on the global logistics scale, but this is just the first step that will allow us to understand practically how to adjust the route."
Russian Arctic projects have been heavily politicized for a long time, he said. Some foreign critics believed that only Russia needed projects in the Arctic, since they were unprofitable and not competitive. Similar comments were also on the Northern Sea Route. "I believe politicizing Russian projects may be endless, but it's simply impossible to force international businesses to do things they do not want to do. <...> Businesses choose the shortest, most convenient and safest route, which the Northern Sea Route already is as an integral part of the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor," he said.
The Northern Sea Route has a number of advantages that other global logistics routes lack a priori, he noted. In particular, the Northern Sea Route offers twice shorter delivery terms, it is free from pirate attacks, and the route is more predictable and strategically reliable.

Economic Watch: China aims to join ranks of global auto powerhouses by 2030
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
17:05:09 CST
18:05:09 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- China aims to join the ranks of the world's automotive powerhouses by 2030, with stronger advantages across the entire industrial chain of intelligent connected new energy vehicles (NEVs), according to a five-year industry development plan released Friday.
The plan identifies intelligent connected NEVs as a key direction for transforming the auto industry, as China steps up efforts to upgrade its industrial sector and build a modern industrial system.
The plan, jointly released by nine government departments including the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, sets targets for NEVs to account for 70 percent of new passenger vehicle sales and 40 percent of new commercial vehicle sales in the domestic market by 2030.
Vehicles equipped with autonomous driving functions are expected to see large-scale application by 2030, while highly automated driving is expected on expressways, urban express roads and some urban roads.
China has ranked first globally in automobile production and sales for 17 consecutive years. Last year, both auto output and sales exceeded 34 million units. NEV output and sales each topped 16 million units, maintaining the top position globally for the 11th straight year.
Latest industry data showed that NEVs further consolidated their dominant position in China's auto market in August, with sales accounting for a record 60.6 percent of monthly new car sales, according to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers.
The plan calls for further advances in key technologies, setting targets for average passenger vehicle fuel consumption at 3.3 liters per 100 km and average electricity consumption of pure electric passenger vehicles at around 11.5 kilowatt-hours per 100 km by 2030.
The plan also calls for continued optimization of the industry's structure and a relatively high level of digital and intelligent development, with overall labor productivity targeted to rise 15 percent from the 2025 level.
China has established a full industrial chain system for key intelligent connected vehicle technologies, covering smart cockpits, autonomous driving, and cloud-based connectivity and control.
Intelligent driving technologies have seen wider adoption. Since the beginning of 2026, the penetration rate of new passenger cars equipped with combined driver assistance functions in China has reached 70 percent, according to the ministry.
The plan also calls for further international expansion, with companies expected to strengthen global operations, Chinese auto brands to gain greater recognition, and China to have a stronger voice in shaping international standards and regulations by 2030.
China's NEV exports continue to rise. In the first seven months of 2026, China exported 2.91 million NEVs, up 120 percent year on year, accounting for 47.4 percent of the country's total vehicle exports.
China has also stepped up its participation in international rule-making for intelligent vehicles. In June, the world's first global technical regulation on automated driving systems, jointly developed by China and several other parties, was adopted, with China leading the drafting of its core contents.
The plan also targets peak carbon emissions from the auto industry before 2030 and a faster green and low-carbon transition across the supply chain. Vehicles equipped with autonomous driving systems are expected to significantly outperform human drivers in safety. ■

Far-right could join government in Sweden after elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
09:05:06 UTC
18:05:06 KST

On the 13th of September, Swedes will head to the polls for a parliamentary election that will, in a sense, serve as a referendum on whether the far-right Sweden Democrats—once a marginal force—will become part of the government in a country formerly regarded as Europe’s most liberal, writes Reuters.
The party, which has roots in the neo-Nazi movement, currently enjoys 19% voter support; the ruling center-right minority coalition has pledged to include the Sweden Democrats in its bloc to ensure Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson remains in office for a second term. Kristersson told Reuters in late August that an agreement had been reached to form a joint majority government under his leadership.
The election will reveal whether Swedish citizens wish to deepen the political shifts that have already dismantled the long-standing consensus on immigration and national identity, transforming one of Europe’s most open societies into a testing ground for stricter policies regarding integration, citizenship, and border control. Kristersson has pointed out that, thanks to his cooperation with Sweden Democrats leader Jimmie Akesson, the country has seen growth, lower energy and food prices, a reduction in gang-related crime, and a significant drop in the number of asylum grants. The Prime Minister has pledged to strengthen ties with the far-right party after the election and to give the party seats in the government.
Over the past four years, the Swedish government has abolished permanent residence permits for asylum seekers, tightened welfare laws, and expanded the deportation of individuals who have no right to remain in the country. The number of asylum applications has fallen to its lowest level in 40 years, and while Kristersson has indicated that the main focus will now shift to integration, the Sweden Democrats want to go a step further. One of Akesson’s closest allies in the party,
Mattias Karlsson, stated that Swedish culture, language, laws, norms, morals, and traditions prevail in Sweden;
if someone cannot accept this, they should live elsewhere. Despite a consensus on the need for a strict immigration policy, many Swedes view the far-right as dangerous; polls indicate a tight race against the center-left opposition, which holds a narrow lead that is nonetheless shrinking. Birgitta Ohlsson, Sweden’s former Minister for European Affairs, stated that the entry of the Sweden Democrats into government would have a hugely negative impact on the country’s liberal ideals—an impact already visible while the party remains outside the government, but one that could become ten times worse.
The rise of far-right forces to power has already altered the European political landscape; such parties are already part of governments in Finland, Italy, Croatia, and the Czech Republic, and are posing increasing challenges in France and Germany.
Akesson’s party has been a key parliamentary pillar for Kristersson over the past four years, and some analysts suggest the election will not signal a radical shift, but rather an acknowledgment that
Akesson has succeeded in shedding the party’s extremist reputation.
The party apologized for past neo-Nazi and antisemitic views. Political commentator Jan Guillou told Reuters that the election would also serve as a referendum on whether Sweden continues down the far-right path. A policy that Swedes would have perceived as a rejection of the country’s liberal values just a decade ago is now gaining support among voters across the entire political spectrum.
Meanwhile, critics worry that the Sweden Democrats’ pledges to end multiculturalism, restore traditional Swedish values, and ban certain types of Muslim attire could deepen societal divisions and shift the political center of gravity further to the right. Author and anti-racism activist Kurdo Baksi expressed fears that even more people would be deported. He is also concerned about freedom of the press and speech, as well as the right to assemble for protests.

Tarmu Tammerk: When a TV guest suffers a medical emergency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
09:05:00 UTC
18:05:00 KST

Tarmu Tammerk: When a TV guest suffers a medical emergency
A guest on a recent live ETV panel discussion show received adequate medical care and the situation was properly handled, writes ERR media ethics ombudsman Tarmu Tammerk.
The guest's privacy was also protected, and continuing with Wednesday's "Esimene stuudio" broadcast after the medical emergency unfolded breached no journalistic ethics, Tammerk goes on.
ETV's September 9 program "Esimene stuudio" featured a debate on defense between Estonia's Riigikogu parties, during which one of the politicians suffered a medical emergency. The health of Reform Party secretary general and Riigikogu member Kristo Enn Vaga deteriorated during the course of the live broadcast, and he was escorted out of the studio, where an ambulance took him to the ER for examinations. After these examinations, Vaga was allowed to return home during the night, and is recovering.
The medical emergency which occurred live on air and the continuation of the debate with one of the guests absent raise a number of questions concerning journalistic ethics and editorial practices.
As could be seen on the show and as the production team has also explained, the guest himself believed that he was able to continue taking part in the debate despite his health issue. He remained responsive throughout, and even raised his hand to ask for the floor. When his condition then deteriorated, he was quickly helped out of the studio. These sensitive moments were not broadcast to ETV viewers.
The guest was administered first aid in the area outside the studio until the ambulance arrived, after which he was taken to hospital for further examination. It is good to know that he was discharged from hospital that same night, and hopefully he will make a swift recovery.
Interrupting the show was one possible course of action. However, the production team opted to continue because, in their assessment, the situation had been resolved as far as the broadcast was concerned: The guest had been taken out of the studio and placed in the care of medical professionals. During a live broadcast, such decisions inevitably have to be made quickly, and the situation must be assessed on the basis of the information available at that point in time.
At the same time, I think the incident certainly affected the program's coherence and balance. A short break might have provided an opportunity to let tensions ease and helped the presenters, panelists and viewers recalibrate to what had happened. This could have allowed the program to continue more effectively in terms of its content. We will be reviewing with the editorial team once again whether taking a break would have been a better solution in a situation like that.
There is no reason to see the decision not to halt the show altogether in this situation as a breach of journalistic ethics. There have previously been instances during heated live debates when a guest has unexpectedly needed assistance and has been brought a chair, a glass of water or a towel. Such situations have likewise been handled out of the sight of viewers, after which the individual has been able to continue taking part meaningfully in the debate. In such cases, interrupting the show could attract the opposite criticism: Why draw special attention to a person's temporary condition if the situation can be resolved and the person themselves wishes to continue; after all, anyone can experience a moment of weakness from time to time.
The health of the "Esimene stuudio" guest was attended to, and his sensitive situation was handled out of viewers' sight. In this case, there are no grounds for considering the continuation of the program a breach of journalistic ethics. However, we will discuss with the editorial team once again how to be better prepared for such unexpected situations in the future.
Most likely everyone understands that presenters cannot share preliminary medical information live on air on the precise nature of any health issue. Behind the scenes, there was a swift and humane response, not all of which was visible to viewers, nor, given the nature of health information, should it have been.
--

Editor: Andrew Whyte

CPO prices seen firm despite rising inventories in Malaysia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
17:04:53 CST
18:04:53 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- Crude palm oil (CPO) prices are expected to remain firm over the next three months despite rising Malaysian inventories and weak exports, with potential El Niño-related supply disruptions providing support into 2027, research houses said on Friday.
BIMB Securities expects CPO prices to remain at elevated levels, although seasonally stronger production and high inventories could limit sharp near-term gains.
The research house maintained its CPO price forecasts at 4,400 ringgit (1,082 U.S. dollars) per ton for 2026 and 4,500 ringgit per ton for 2027, with an upside bias.
It said key supports for prices include stronger vegetable oil demand from expanding global biodiesel mandates, a potentially tighter global palm oil supply-demand balance and the impact of El Niño on regional output.
The eight-month 2026 average CPO price stood at 4,413 ringgit per ton, broadly in line with BIMB Securities' full-year forecast.
Official data showed Malaysia's palm oil end-stocks rose 7.5 percent month-on-month and 28.3 percent year-on-year to 2.82 million tons in August, as weaker exports outweighed a modest increase in production.
BIMB Securities expects inventories to remain around this level in the coming month amid the seasonal peak-crop cycle before easing somewhat in the fourth quarter on stronger festive and holiday demand.
MBSB Research also expects CPO prices to remain firm in September, with an average price of 4,514 ringgit per ton, up 0.6 percent month-on-month. It maintained its 2026 average CPO price target at 4,400 ringgit per ton.
The research house said renewed U.S.-Iran tensions could keep crude oil prices elevated, providing additional support for CPO, while the probability of a very strong El Niño has risen to about 90 percent, keeping potential supply disruption firmly on the radar.
However, it warned that near-term downside risks remain largely demand-driven. Continued weak exports could push inventories towards the psychological 3-million-ton level, capping price gains.
Maybank Investment Bank similarly warned that weak August exports were a concern, noting that the impact of El Niño on palm oil production typically lags and may only become evident in 2027.
"There is a good chance that Malaysia's stockpile may continue to snowball and touch 3 million tons by October or November 2026," said the research house.
Short-term CPO upside could also be constrained by competing vegetable oils trading around parity with CPO, demand rationing at elevated prices and uncertainty over Indonesia's B50 biodiesel mandate, it added. ■

Xinhua Commentary: Services opening-up unlocks more China opportunities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
17:04:27 CST
18:04:27 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- What makes the Chinese market an opportunity for the world? The answer is increasingly found not only in its sheer size, but also in the country's expanding strengths in services, innovation and cooperation.
Part of that answer lies in the 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS), the first edition in the country's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) period, which opened its doors at Beijing's Shougang Park this week.
With greater international participation, this year's event underscores the growing role of services in global trade and China's resolve and confidence in advancing high-standard opening up.
Today, services have become an increasingly important engine of the global economy, accounting for 65 percent of global GDP and more than a quarter of world trade, according to UN Trade and Development. Services exports are also growing at more than twice the pace of goods exports.
Meanwhile, with services now forming the bedrock of the Chinese economy, China has placed services trade high on its economic agenda. In the first seven months of 2026, China's services trade expanded 8.3 percent year on year to nearly 4.45 trillion yuan (about 656.9 billion U.S. dollars).
Advancing high-quality development of services trade is a key task set out in China's 15th Five-Year Plan, which calls for efforts to ease cross-border restrictions and foster knowledge-intensive services trade.
Digitalization and green development are emerging as key drivers of China's services development, with advanced technologies like AI and big data increasingly integrated into services trade. This year's CIFTIS has put innovation front and center, highlighting the latest breakthroughs and practical applications.
The fair offers more than a marketplace for services. Norway, this year's guest country of honor, presents a 260-square-meter pavilion featuring a wide range of exhibits, providing a platform for Norwegian companies to pursue practical cooperation in China.
For U.S. pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly, the fair means opportunities to tap China's policy and research strengths and become more deeply integrated into the country's pharmaceutical innovation ecosystem, according to Huzur Devletsah, the company's vice president and China general manager.
The opportunities created by China's expanding services market do not come at the expense of others: as the sector opens further, its growing capacity is opening up new avenues for international cooperation and shared growth.
Reflecting this trend, this year's CIFTIS debuts an exhibition of over 140 cases spanning 12 categories of services trade, including those involving AI, large language models and intelligent agents, offering a glimpse of where China's services sector is headed.
The fair also sets up a new roadshow area that provides Chinese companies with one-stop professional support to expand their global footprint in services.
The country's expanding services capacity is also bringing tangible development opportunities to the Global South. According to Zimbabwean Vice President Constantino Chiwenga, the CIFTIS is expected to help his country identify opportunities for trade in services, build export capacity, and attract credible partners in areas of technology, finance, tourism, education and health care.
As services become an increasingly important arena for global economic cooperation, China's continued opening-up is creating more channels for businesses around the world to connect, cooperate and grow. The "China opportunities" offered by a more open services market are becoming part of a broader landscape of shared growth. ■
