Apple’s foldable iPhone poses a $1,999 question: Who is it for?
CUPERTINO, California, Sept 10 - Apple's new foldable iPhone launched on Wednesday with impressive features and a premium price tag, starting at $1,999 in the U.S. market. But some observers in the packed room at the launch event in Cupertino, California, were left questioning its appeal beyond wealthy tech enthusiasts.
Apple executives demonstrated the iPhone Duo running a variety of apps including Zoom, Slack and Netflix on an expanded display, as they showcased its ability to be used for work, content creation and entertainment.
New Apple CEO John Ternus highlighted how the "larger display that feels as natural and intuitive as iPad" would open possibilities for the iPhone Duo to serve as a user’s personal AI hub.
“Apple doesn't usually define who the buyer is, but in this case specifically, they really shied away from it,” said Carolina Milanesi, an analyst at Creative Strategies.
Analysts say that Apple's brand cachet is enough to assure strong initial sales of the iPhone Duo. But once the euphoria fades, they warn the device's high price and Apple's lack of clear vision of its target buyer could confine it to a niche of wealthy early adopters — a pattern that has plagued the category since its launch.
Foldable phones are on track to account for less than 3% of the global smartphone market in 2026, according to research firm IDC, which also does not expect the figure to change much in 2027, even with Apple's entry.
"Definitely there was a little bit of a lapse in positioning,” said Neil Shah, vice president of Counterpoint Research. “From our end, it was not clear whether it’s for work or play, but I think what iPhone has always stood for is being a versatile device."
A QUESTION OF PURPOSE
By choosing a broad marketing strategy, Apple did not articulate the intended audience it envisioned would shell out for a phone that will retail in the U.S. for $3,199 with the highest storage option.
When Apple co-founder Steve Jobs launched the iPad in 2010, he framed the tablet computer as forging a new category as a supercharged media and entertainment consumption device.
By 2015, then-Apple CEO Tim Cook positioned the tablet's new Pro line as a creative professional tool.
Apple Watch, which the company initially pushed to make a fashion item, evolved into a must-have health and fitness companion.
Apple stumbled out of the gate in 2023 with its Vision Pro augmented reality headset, which analysts similarly lauded for its technology but cast doubts on its high price tag and lack of clear use beyond entertainment.
PENT-UP DEMAND
Counterpoint's Shah estimated Apple would still sell close to 6 million units of the iPhone Duo by the end of the year because it had enough pent-up demand from existing iPhone users. Those sales alone would give Apple a quarter share of the global market, Shah said.
Samsung, the incumbent market leader in foldable phones, has been selling its devices since 2019, and other options are available from the likes of Alphabet's Google and China's Huawei.
Samsung overcame a debacle at launch dubbed by some as "foldgate" that saw wide reports of broken screens and peeling components. It now holds 40% of the market, per Counterpoint data, and unveiled a redesigned passport-style foldable phone in July.
That device has outperformed predecessors and added heft to a publicity campaign Samsung launched in response to the iPhone Duo, mocking Apple for "reheating our leftovers."
Still, the market's growth has slowed in recent years after the devices struggled to attract buyers beyond a niche audience.
Apple's entry is expected to provide the biggest year-to-year boon in foldable smartphone shipments since 2021, according to technology research firm Omdia, which has placed its 2026 market forecast at 22.3 million units.
Bob O’Donnell, chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research, said that the iPhone Duo’s high price narrowed the potential audience, especially among youth, but Apple diehards would bolster early sales.
“It’ll be something that’ll be lusted after,” he said. “It’ll be a status symbol, for a while, because I think it’s going to be hard to get.” REUTERS

Iran destroys US spy Saildrone in Hormuz (VIDEO)
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it has destroyed a US Saildrone Explorer reconnaissance vessel at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, releasing footage showing the unmanned craft burning in the water.
The IRGC Navy said on Thursday that the vessel, identified by hull number 5838, was struck while operating near the strategic waterway. Iranian state media described it as an American surveillance drone, but the US military has not confirmed the loss.
“The American terrorist and aggressor army, over the past few days, out of fear of approaching and confronting the fighters of Islam, has dispatched its unmanned vessels to the Strait of Hormuz,” the IRGC said.
The Iranian Navy: We have struck a US unmanned vessel, with hull number 5838, at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz. pic.twitter.com/WyesLWXI47
— IRIB (Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting) (@iribnews_irib) September 10, 2026
The strategic waterway remains under Tehran’s control and “intelligence surveillance,” the IRGC added, warning that “any hostile presence in this strategic strait will be targeted.”
The roughly seven-meter Saildrone Explorer is an unmanned surface vessel equipped with cameras, sensors, and communications systems for maritime surveillance and reconnaissance. The US Navy previously deployed the platform with the Bahrain-based 5th Fleet’s Task Force 59, which integrates unmanned systems and AI into regional operations.
The latest incident comes just two days after the IRGC captured a US underwater drone at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz. Footage released by Tehran shows what appears to be an Anduril-built Dive-LD autonomous underwater vehicle commissioned in 2025. The Pentagon acknowledged that it lost the submersible, but said it was old and broken and carried no sensitive data or classified equipment.
The incidents come amid an escalating maritime standoff between the US and Iran.
The US has destroyed several Iranian oil tankers after accusing the IRGC of firing ballistic missiles at US warships. Iran has attacked US vessels and commercial tankers it accused of violating restrictions regarding the Strait of Hormuz.
The confrontation has severely disrupted traffic through one of the world’s most important energy corridors and pushed Brent crude above $107 a barrel, while farther west, Iran-aligned Houthi forces are tightening their grip on Bab al-Mandeb, another vital chokepoint linking the Red Sea and Indian Ocean.

What’s a Northern Metropolis-like project doing in Malaysia? Lessons for Hong Kong?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10

08:30:06 KST

In FocusWhat’s a Northern Metropolis-like project doing in Malaysia? Lessons for Hong Kong?
Development of Malaysia’s Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone and Hong Kong’s Northern Metropolis offers case study on mutual learning
Deep in the southern border zone of Johor, Malaysia, separated from Singapore by a narrow strait, a steady flow of commuters moves seamlessly between the two sovereign neighbours.
Beyond the immediate checkpoints, a short 30-minute train ride connects visitors to regional hubs such as Kulai, where a vastly different dynamic comes into view – one defined by the rapid expansion of digital infrastructure.
Covering an area more than four times the size of Singapore, the JS-SEZ aims to generate 260 billion Malaysian ringgit (US$63.9 billion) for Johor’s regional economy by 2030 and create more than 20,000 high-skilled jobs, anchored by the coming 4km Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link designed to slash travel times and cement cross-strait integration.
For Malaysia, the early trajectory of Hong Kong and Shenzhen remains the foundational blueprint.
Lee Ting Han, Johor’s state executive councillor for investment and trade, told the South China Morning Post that despite distinct political frameworks, the wealth gap between Singapore and Johor mirrored the historic economic disparity between Hong Kong and Shenzhen.
“Similarly, it is pretty much like the early days of Hong Kong and Shenzhen, where the economic disparity between the two regions was so wide … what we are trying to do now is see whether there’s a way for us from a business standpoint to make it more integrated from trade relationships to investment culture,” Lee said.

OpenAI Wants to Know if an AI Industry Slowdown Would Even Be Legal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
23:28:42 UTC
08:28:42 KST

OpenAI has asked members of Congress in recent weeks for clear guidance about whether orchestrating an industry-wide slowdown on frontier AI development would be legal, people close to the company tell WIRED.
Substantive coordination on safety between AI labs may risk running afoul of antitrust law, the people say, which poses a significant obstacle to bringing major tech giants on board with the effort.
Last weekend, OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, published a blog post arguing that the best path forward for the AI research world includes “coordinating to slow down future development,” which he thinks will be key to ensuring that self-improving AI systems are safe. In the short term, he expects “voluntary slowdowns to become commonplace until shared safety bars are established.”
But some legal scholars say such an effort could conflict with US antitrust laws. Nicholas Felstead, assistant director of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission and a former AI policy fellow at the Center for Law & AI Risk, argued in a March article that a coordinated pause in AI development may amount to companies restricting output, potentially violating the Sherman Antitrust Act. It would depend “entirely on the precise details of any agreement,” Felstead wrote. “But even if most safety collaborations would ultimately survive antitrust scrutiny, legal uncertainty can act as a powerful deterrent.”
OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment ahead of publication.
There are some early signs that Congress is listening. In July, a bipartisan, bicameral group of lawmakers introduced a bill titled “Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act,” which would explicitly permit AI labs to coordinate on security and safety work without the risk of violating antitrust statutes. The House version was referred to the Judiciary Committee but has yet to be taken up.
Caleb Knapp, director of government affairs at the nonprofit AI Policy Network, which endorsed the bill, says it would create legal channels for AI labs to work together to address safety and security incidents. Knapp adds that Congress has a “growing appetite to get something done” on AI safety but says enacting anything into law may have to wait until after the upcoming midterm elections.
While some AI executives may have genuine concerns about antitrust, another camp of AI leaders argue those worries are just convenient cover to avoid discussing the real reasons that AI developers may be wary about collaborating, which go far beyond potential legal liabilities.
For one, AI is a massive business, and these companies are fiercely competing to capture a slice of the nascent market for frontier models. Some executives share the Trump administration’s view that staying ahead of China in AI is crucial for national security. Perhaps most importantly, different AI developers have vastly different opinions about the best way to develop safe artificial intelligence, and therefore may be reluctant to work with one another on the issue.
“First step is for industry leaders OpenAI and Anthropic to stop feuding and work on a pacing proposal together,” John Schulman, an OpenAI cofounder who is now chief scientist at the rival AI lab Thinking Machines, wrote in a post on X earlier this week. “They'll cite antitrust, but that's fake—antitrust prohibits certain agreements, but not from jointly developing a proposal.”
Long-simmering fears about the race among AI companies to build and release ever more powerful models erupted into the national spotlight this summer. This week, former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon added to the growing alarm when he issued a stark public warning that AI developers were putting humanity at risk. In recent months, a number of security incidents, including OpenAI’s agents hacking Hugging Face, highlighted how the industry’s safeguards have failed to keep pace with the rising capabilities of models. The succession of events has led many lawmakers to make urgent calls for AI regulation.
This is an edition of Maxwell Zeff’s Model Behavior newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Ukraine's fortress cities under fire as Russia bids to seize rest of Donbas
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
00:22:11 BST
08:22:11 KST

Civilians told to flee Ukraine's fortress cities as Russia bids to control Donbas
- Published
It is so dangerous now in Slovyansk and Kramatorsk that police say it is time for civilians to get out. These neighbouring cities are the biggest still under full Ukrainian control in the eastern Donbas region.
In the worst affected areas, forced evacuations of families with children have already begun, says Pavlo Dyachenko of Donetsk police.
"This is the only way to save your life," he says, because security has deteriorated so much.
"If you take Slovyansk, it used to be hit by glide bombs roughly once a week, but now it's almost every day."
Slovyansk, Kramatorsk and Kostyantynivka, to the south, form part of what is known as Ukraine's "fortress belt" – a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the east.
However, Kostyantynivka only has a limited presence of Ukrainian troops left, reports say, while Russia claims to be in full control of it.
The full capture of Donbas, made up of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions, is a key objective for Russia. Moscow has often cited the "liberation" and "protection" of the predominantly Russian-speaking Donbas as justification for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The Russian army already controls almost all of Luhansk region, and is now in control of almost 80% of Donetsk region too, where all three fortress cities lie.
For the past few months, the territory near Kramatorsk and Slovyansk has been the main focus of Russian ground assaults. Capturing them would potentially make it much easier for Russia to advance to the west.
The two cities are now facing intense strikes from drones and bombs.
Many civilians have already left, and key streets there are now covered with anti-drone nets, says Viktor Makurin, a volunteer from London.
"There are often [remote-controlled] FPV drones in the air, you can hear them through the window. Driving around the city is lethally dangerous. There are drones lying in ambush on the roads, too," he told the BBC.
"You can always hear explosions in the background, plus there are mobile groups firing at drones."
Over the summer, the number of civilians wounded by Russian attacks on the two cities increased from 70 in June to 212 in August, say Ukrainian police.
Sixteen people died in June, 20 in July and 15 in August.
Residential housing comes under attack as well as infrastructure, says Dyachenko, causing "very significant destruction".
The number of glide bombs launched by Russia jumped from 40 in June to 109 in July and 92 in August, according to data published by Ukrainian police and studied by the BBC.
One morning two weeks ago, on 25 August, nine glide bombs targeted Kramatorsk. Seven hit civilian apartment blocks, wounding 24 people including a two-month-old baby, Ukrainian police say.
Two days later, it was hit again, this time with seven glide bombs, and five bombs targeted Slovyansk.
Fitted with winglets so they can glide to their target rather than fall, glide bombs are considered one of the most effective and lethal weapons in Russia's arsenal.
Usually, they weigh 250 or 500 kg, but there have been cases of Russia deploying bombs that weigh 1,500 kg.
"The devastation they cause is simply incredible," says Dyachenko.
"Glide bombs are the big fear," another British volunteer, John Auckland Abbey, posted on social media.
"They are silent killers, and when you've been abruptly woken by one exploding, you know at least another one will follow. The question you ask yourself as you lie very still in the dark is: will the next one be closer?"
Kramatorsk is currently home to the headquarters of the Donetsk regional administration. The capital city used to be Donetsk, until it was captured in 2014 by Russian-backed separatists.
What happens to the areas of Donbas still under Ukrainian control was reportedly a key issue when US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky last weekend after their talks with Putin.
In the past, Witkoff has appeared to back Russian claims to the region, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is refusing to pull troops out of it.
He says Putin has given his generals until the end of the year to complete their occupation of Donbas.
"Putin's primary objective on the front line remains the same: Kostyantynivka-Slovyansk," Zelensky told journalists last month.
Faced with mounting military pressure, the Ukrainian leader has created two new taskforces headed by experienced generals, Andriy Biletsky and Denys Prokopenko, to defend the portion of Donbas still in Ukrainian hands.
"There isn't just a battle for Donbas there," one unnamed Ukrainian general has said.
"What is probably the main battle of this year and the next is now unfolding."

Packed into the studio alongside a guitarist, drummer, producer and backing vocalists, ONEFOUR members J Emz, Celly and Spenny laid tough rhymes over Phil Collins's classic 1981 song In The Air Tonight.
Jimmy Barnes and Jessica Mauboy complemented them, sliding Collins's soaring melodies between the rappers' hard bars.
Loading...
We have Mahalia Barnes to thank for bringing her legendary father together with the Australian Idol alumni and Samoan Australian drill-rappers.
"When I got asked to do it, Mahalia, my daughter, rang me up and said, 'Do you want to do this?' I said, 'Shit yeah,'" Barnes told triple j's Abby Butler and Tyrone Pynor.
"We come from very similar backgrounds; we both had to fight to get ourselves heard and to have our say, and we still have to fight 'til this day.
"So, it was a match made in heaven. And I got into the rehearsal room with these guys, and it was just … it was full on straight away. We connected straight away. It was great."
ONEFOUR emerged from Western Sydney suburb Mount Druitt in 2019 with their viral single The Message, opening the world up to a very different style of Australian rap.
Influenced by UK drill, which is associated with crime, violence, prejudice and socio-economic hardship, ONEFOUR drew the scrutiny of the NSW Police, which suggested their lyrics depicting the underbelly of Western Sydney would incite violence among fans.

In the Like A Version studio, the new collaboration marks a moment of connection between the group of artists.
Despite coming from very different corners of the musical world, they all share a deep respect and reverence for Phil Collins and his work, whether they first heard it on the car radio or in a TV ad for chocolate.
"We all come from different genres and music and backgrounds," Celly told triple j.
"So just to come together, it was definitely a moment there.
"You've got Jimmy's roaring voice and Jessica's angelic-type voice, and then you've got us," J Emz added.
"In the beginning we were kind of iffy about how the crossover was going to happen, but then it all came together at the end. Like it was meant to be."
Loading...
Coupled with their cover, ONEFOUR performed their latest single HIM, originally written for the Prince of Malaysia Tunku Ismail, who they met when he booked them for a show.

"[HIM] was actually pretty easy to write because we got to spend a bit of time with the prince over there," J Emz said.
"Just being around him and obviously given that opportunity, we're just inspired to create music based on him and what he's been able to expose us to."

A year after Charlie Kirk’s death, are young voters turning on Trump?
Turning Point USA has expanded its campus presence, even as Trump’s support among young men has fallen.
One year after the assassination of right-wing influencer Charlie Kirk, the organisation he co-founded, Turning Point USA (TPUSA), has expanded its presence in schools across the United States, even as young voters show growing dissatisfaction with the Republican Party.
As of Thursday, Turning Point has more than 3,500 high school chapters, up 180 percent since Kirk’s death, according to the organisation.

It also boasts more than 1,500 college chapters, a more than 60 percent increase.
Kirk was a prominent conservative activist and close ally of President Donald Trump at the time of his death on September 10, 2025. He was assassinated while speaking to students at Utah Valley University, in an incident captured on video.
His assassination would inspire the Trump administration to pursue a crackdown on what it called “domestic terrorist organisations”, including the loose-knit antifascist movement known as Antifa.
Kirk built Turning Point USA into a major youth organising force within the Republican Party, helping to mobilise young conservative voters.
But the growth of Turning Point’s political infrastructure comes as Republicans face growing dissatisfaction among young voters over the economy and the US-Israeli war against Iran.
Only 32 percent of men ages 18 to 29 approved of Trump’s performance in August, down from 43 percent in February 2025, according to polling from the news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos.
That slippage comes after gains during the last general election. Trump won 46 percent of young men’s votes in the 2024 election, a seven-point increase from 2020, according to Pew Research Center data.
Cost-of-living pressures are among young voters’ biggest concerns. A Harvard Youth Poll conducted in March and April found that half of Americans ages 18 to 29 said inflation affected them “a lot”, while 45 percent said they were struggling to make ends meet or had little financial security.
Those economic pressures have been compounded by the war in Iran, which has added an average of $750 in household expenses, according to Moody’s Analytics, an economic research firm.
Within TPUSA itself, debates over US support for Israel have grown. A recent poll from the firm YouGov and the publication The Economist found that only 16 percent of young people thought US military action in Iran was the right decision.
Yet the group’s expanding network gives Republicans significant traction to rally younger voters ahead of the November 3 congressional midterm elections.
A memorial will be held by Turning Point USA at Utah Valley University on Thursday, one year after Kirk was fatally shot during a debate on campus. The group will also memorialise Kirk at the Republican Party’s first-ever midterm convention in Dallas, Texas.

====================================================================================================

Can Europe recharge its battery industry?
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
00:05:47 BST
08:05:47 KST

Can Europe recharge its battery industry?
- Published
Europe has taken some big swings in the battery industry in recent years and has made a couple of high-profile misses.
Both Sweden's Northvolt, external and Norway's Morrow, external filed for bankruptcy and there are fears in Europe that the continent has missed another technology shift.
With more transport and industry switching from fossil fuels to electricity, batteries are likely to be a growth business.
But the length of time required to bring new products to market, coupled with brutal competition, especially from China, means taking a substantial risk.
Could the answer lie at an almost unimaginably small scale? An increasing number of investors and researchers think so.
A single nanometre is one-billionth of a metre, but it's at that level that some of the most consequential work is being done.
"If you can make this work, it touches so many industries [but] it's a risky business," says Christian Rood, chief executive of Dutch tech firm LeydenJar.
Named after a 18th century precursor to electric cells, LeydenJar uses a technique known as plasma deposition to make a lighter, more efficient anode – an essential component of all batteries.
Silicon is a highly effective and cheap material to use in anodes, but pure silicon expands and contracts as the battery operates and is recharged, which causes it to crack.
However, using plasma deposition, LeydenJar can - layer by tiny layer - make an ultra-thin pure silicon foil which resists cracking, allowing a significant increase in battery life, charging speed, and energy density (up to 50%, according to LeydenJar).
"Where normally a pure silicon anode would fall apart, [this] remains stable, so it was a very wonderful invention," says Rood.
"We address the bottleneck in the battery."
Commercial-scale production will start at the end of 2026, but it has taken 10 years to get to this point – the very definition of the time and investment required for so-called Deep Tech innovations.
It's no coincidence that LeydenJar's factory is in the Dutch city of Eindhoven - home to ASML and other important players in the computer chip industry.
"A lot of people talk theoretically about ecosystems; I can tell you this is one of our sources of competitive advantage," Rood says.
"It's really the crossover from semiconductors to batteries that makes us different - once you've demonstrated the principle in the lab, industrialization requires you to work with the semiconductor technology and suppliers.
"That means a lot of risk, but also a lot of opportunity in terms of patenting, in terms of securing your whole intellectual property. And that's much more difficult to do in the US or in China."
Across the Netherlands and Europe more widely there are multiple smaller Deep Tech start-ups looking to develop nanotechnology in the battery market.
One of those is Powall, a start-up in the Dutch city of Delft that is developing commercial-scale equipment for nanocoating the powders that are the raw materials of today's batteries.
Again, the scale is tiny, and once again the technique was born in the semiconductor industry.
Individual powder granules are measured in micrometres, the coatings in nanometres - they are applied using a technique known as atomic layer deposition.
Roderik Colen, CEO of Powall, tells me that the system offers multiple opportunities to adjust and improve the performance of today's batteries.
"Your battery works less well than before after using it thousands of times - that degrading or aging can be slowed down when you're using a nanocoating," Colen explains.
"You can have an exciting new material with a higher capacity or fast charging, all these novel developments. They typically have one element which is very good, but they suffer on the durability side."
And that means they will never be a commercial product.
"That's where we then come in, to give them the protective coating to effectively enable these new materials."
The powders and the coating are carried by gas and brought together in a chemical reaction.
It is, says Colen, a precise but flexible process which can be almost endlessly adapted.
"You have great accuracy in how thick you want to have it. And that makes a difference in performance."
Neither LeydenJar nor Powall are trying to build an entire battery, and both have commercial relationships with customers in Asia.
But Christian Rood of LeydenJar says companies like his can fortify Europe's position in what has become a global contest.
"The easy comparison is with semiconductors, where there's really a race for the best chip technology.
"[Dutch tech giant] ASML is not producing chips; it focuses on a critical step in the production of chips, and in that way, has a seat at the table when it comes to the whole semiconductor battle.
"This is our ambition as well – to have a position where our battery anode is so unique that we have an important position in the supply chain."
So, how do these ambitions play into Europe's goals in the battery industry?
Alexander Brown is a senior analyst at the Berlin-based independent think-tank the Mercator Institute for China Studies (Merics).
"I think having one part of the supply chain based in Europe is great and if that can be a very advanced technological part, which offers the opportunity for high margins, that's fantastic," Brown tells me.
But he cautions that while "there can be collaboration as well as competition at the same time", China in particular will continue to work to reduce its dependence on other regions.
"China is working very hard to develop local alternatives for technologies, including these niche technologies.
"It's no secret that China would love to replace ASML - they're working very hard to do that, and it's not unforeseeable that they will achieve that goal eventually.
"So, I think Europe has traditional strengths in developing very exquisite high-quality products, which can find markets all over the world.
"But I also think it's important for that not to be the only strategy [from the continent's policy makers]."
The challenges of working in such a specialised field are not only technological.
LeydenJar has already reached commercial scale, but Rood says that raising funds within Europe is not always easy.
"There is sufficient financing in Europe, but the risk attitude is quite different than in Asia and in the US," says Rood.
"That means for a company like us that you have to work with different sources of funding at the same time," Rood explains.
He lists government grants, debt financing, help from the European Investment Bank and investors willing to buy a share of the business.
"They set a lot of challenging conditions, and they all want to do their own due diligence. It's hard work," Rood says.
Powall's Colen says Europe, and the Netherlands in particular, is an "innovation powerhouse", and battery technology offers a chance for the continent to make an impact, if the appetite for the risk is there.
"It's a relatively young industry where factories are being built left, right and centre. They're searching for the right tech. So that's where you can play a big role, because the volumes are huge."
Perhaps Europe's place in that business lies not in building huge battery gigafactories, but at the other end of the scale altogether.
As Colen puts it, "small changes make big differences."

From JFK to Biden, Trump joins well-trodden path to the Emerald Isle
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
00:01:55 BST
08:01:55 KST

From JFK to Biden, Trump joins well-trodden path to the Emerald Isle
- Published
When Donald Trump lands in Dublin on Saturday, he will be on a well-trodden international path.
In recent decades, Ireland has become a particularly frequent fixture for US presidential trips.
It stands out among small countries as hosting a high number of visits.
The bond between the two nations was forged by emigration, deepened by economic ties, and cemented by the Northern Ireland peace process – in which Washington played a major role.
Historians generally estimate that around five million people left Ireland for the US in the 19th and early 20th centuries.
Dr Peter McLoughlin, who teaches history and politics at Queen's University Belfast, said that created an "enormous ethnic link".
In 2024, census data found that 32.4 million Americans claimed Irish ancestry – almost one in ten of the population.
That means several presidents have seen political advantage in being seen to explore their heritage.
John F Kennedy was the first president to go to Ireland while in office.
In June 1963, he visited his ancestral homestead in County Wexford, from where his great-grandfather had left during the Irish potato famine in 1848.
In his address to the Irish Parliament, he said: "This has never been a rich or powerful country, and yet, since earliest times, its influence on the world has been rich and powerful."
In the years since, Ireland has become rich by many global measures, with some of the US's biggest firms driving its economic growth.
Tech and pharmaceutical firms - such as Apple, Pfizer and Meta - have key European bases in Ireland.
The rapid expansion of US investment in Ireland in the 1990s coincided with the development of the peace process in Northern Ireland.
Bill Clinton's three visits to the island took in both sides of the border, and he was strongly involved in the Good Friday Agreement in 1998, which largely ended the conflict in Northern Ireland after three decades.
McLoughlin, who has researched America's role, said: "It's one of the examples where you can see US power being used in a successful way to get a peaceful settlement.
"After Clinton, George W Bush was maybe not such a hands-on president as regards Northern Ireland, but his White House was important in making sure the Good Friday Agreement was implemented."
St Patrick's Day in Washington
Politicians, civic leaders and business figures from Belfast and Dublin are hosted in Washington each year on Ireland's national holiday, St Patrick's Day.
The taoiseach (Irish prime minister) traditionally presents the president with a bowl of shamrock, the plant which is a symbol of Ireland.
Dan Mulhall, who was Ireland's Ambassador to Washington from 2017-22, said the yearly access to the White House was "pretty unique".
"I remember some of my European colleagues were kind of puzzled as to how Ireland had pulled this off, given that some of them also have large diaspora communities in the US, but they don't seem to have the same impact or lasting connection with their ancestral homeland as the Irish Americans undoubtedly have."
Barack Obama paid homage to his heritage in 2011, when he visited his great-great-great grandfather's home village of Moneygall in County Offaly.
In a speech in Dublin, he joked: "I've come home to find the apostrophe that we lost somewhere along the way."
Joe Biden described Ireland as "part of his soul" on his trip in 2023, which was the last US presidential visit.
He went to his ancestral counties of Mayo and Louth and marked the 25th anniversary of the Good Friday Agreement.
Donald Trump's visit will be different in content and tone.
He has no known Irish ancestry.
His focus will be on golf rather than genealogy, as he will watch the Irish Open played at his resort in Doonbeg in County Clare.
In Dublin, he will meet the Taoiseach Micheàl Martin and the Irish President Catherine Connolly.
Connolly has a largely ceremonial role as head-of-state, but she has previously been a staunch critic of US foreign policy, particularly in the Middle East.
Earlier this year Trump referred to Connolly as "he" when responding to criticisms she made about the US attack on Iran being "a brutal assault on international law".
"He's lucky I exist," Trump said.
The US Embassy in Dublin criticised a law passed by the Irish Parliament this year to ban the importation of goods from Israeli settlements in occupied Palestinian territory.
The Embassy said the legislation "risked real unintended consequences, particularly for nearly 1000 US companies and the hundreds of thousands of Irish jobs tied to them".
US actions abroad will be the focus of protests in Dublin and County Clare this weekend.
On Thursday a large sand artwork appeared on a beach in Dublin Bay.
The campaign group Uplift carved the words 'No kings - Gaza Iran Ice' into the sand.
Washington's trade policy has been another prominent issue in Ireland, as Trump has expressed unhappiness at the scale of US pharmaceutical manufacturing in the country.
However, tariffs have mostly not been imposed on the sector.
Mullhall, the former Ireland Ambassador to Washington said the economic relationship was "as strong as it's ever been".
He thinks the Irish government will approach Trump's visit with "prudent realism".
"It's not possible to expect that a small country, any country in fact, can deflect Donald Trump from any of his purposes or policies.
"Most countries have adopted the strategy of simply trying to ride out the Trump term and hope for more predictable days ahead.
"So I think the government will play it safe and will be above all else, be wanting to avoid any kind of tension or difficulty between themselves and Donald Trump."
McLoughlin, of Queen's University, sees parallels between Trump's visit and that of Ronald Reagan in 1984, when there was opposition over US foreign policy in Latin America.
The Catholic church was very influential in Ireland at that time and McLoughlin pointed out that senior clergy did not meet Reagan.
"This was a time when many people would have members of the family who were in Latin America as a nun or a priest, and were bringing back first-hand reports of how there were controversial associations with US policy, with right-wing paramilitaries who were engaged in the Cold War struggle."
But he said that amidst the criticism of the visit, the Irish government wanted to "court" Reagan, for "economic reasons, and political reasons involving Northern Ireland".
He added that pictures of Reagan exploring his ancestry, in County Tipperary, helped make the visit "successful" from Dublin and Washington's point of view.
Ireland is more used than most countries to hosting the holder of the most powerful office in the world and the diplomatic delicacies around Trump's visit are another episode in a story dating back many decades.

'NAZA': Guardian-produced film sheds light on Israeli system behind Gaza genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
23:00:12 UTC
08:00:12 KST

A new documentary by Oscar-winning Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor has premiered at the Venice International Film Festival, revealing testimony from 24 Israeli military and intelligence insiders about secret systems used to identify, track and attack Palestinians in besieged Gaza despite expected civilian fatalities.
Titled NAZA, the Guardian-produced film was screened on Thursday in the main competition at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival and is the only documentary competing for the Golden Lion this year.
The film takes its title from NAZA, a Hebrew military acronym for "collateral damage," used by Israeli intelligence to refer to the number of civilians expected to be killed in an attack.
The 80-minute documentary was produced by The Guardian and James Wilson of JW Films, with Jonathan Glazer serving as an executive producer. Wilson and Glazer previously worked together on the Oscar-winning film The Zone of Interest.
NAZA builds on investigations published between 2023 and 2025 by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and The Guardian.
AI systems identify targets for attacks at homes
Israeli intelligence officers and soldiers interviewed for the film describe AI-based systems used to identify large numbers of suspected low-ranking Hamas members as potential targets.
According to their testimony, people identified through the systems were bombed in their homes at night despite knowledge that the strikes would also kill members of their families.
The insiders also describe hacking into the phones of people marked for attack to determine their locations.
Intelligence officers covertly listened to conversations between targets and their wives and children, according to the testimony, sometimes until shortly before attacks on their homes.
Speaking at a news conference in Venice, Abraham said the filmmakers asked the officers to explain their work.
"We just told these officers: 'Please describe to us what you did. How do these systems work? Sketch it out for us.' Sometimes, in just asking the questions, you get the answers," he said.
"Some of them did not express remorse, and some did. Some spoke out of indifference, some out of pride."
Systematic destruction of civilian areas
The testimony also includes first-hand accounts of the destruction of neighbourhoods where the Israeli military estimated that as many as 25 percent of residents were still in their homes.
The interviewees describe the systematic burning of civilian homes and the killing of civilians at a food distribution site.
Several interviewees worked in a secret intelligence unit that reports directly to the office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, according to The Guardian. One of them said the unit's mission was to "thwart peace."
Abraham and Szor said the film focuses on military policies and practices rather than misconduct by individual soldiers.
"Our focus is not on sporadic war crimes committed by rogue soldiers," they said.
Instead, the directors said their focus was on "the orders themselves, the policies, the accepted practices, the language and logic that make those practices possible, and the people who operate within them."
"The system and its cogs," they added.
Abraham described the film as an examination of "systems of mass killing" based on testimony from the 24 insiders.
Gaza genocide
Since the start of the genocide in October 2023, Israel has killed over 73,000 Palestinians, mostly women and children, and wounded over 174,000 others.
Analysts say the estimate is an underestimate, and the actual death toll could be approximately 200,000.
Israel which occupies 60 percent of Gaza has reduced most of the blockaded enclave to ruins and displaced the entire population.
Despite an agreed ceasefire deal in October 2025, Israel continues to violate it daily, killing at least 1,359 Palestinians and wounding 4,571 others.

Hong Kong home prices headed for 15% gain this year, Midland forecast says
As the market digests uncertainties, new property launches are accelerating and buyers are returning to the market, executive says
Hong Kong’s home prices will end the year 15 per cent higher than a year earlier, but still 16 per cent below their high-water mark in 2021, according to local property agency Midland Realty.

Dave Ma Tai-yeung, CEO of Midland (Residential), said that as the market gradually digested geopolitical and external economic uncertainties, new property launches were accelerating and buyers were returning to the market.
“With the improved market sentiment, developers will accelerate the launch of new projects, and the residential market is expected to further recover,” Ma said.
First-hand residential property transactions, after falling for two consecutive months to just over 800 units in June and July, rebounded to 1,100 units in August, while second-hand residential transactions were also gradually stabilising, according to Midland’s data.
Ma said that first-hand property transactions in the final quarter would increase by 50 per cent quarter on quarter to 5,100 units, while secondary market transactions would rise by 10 per cent to 12,700.
“With residential rents hitting new highs one after another, there is room for property prices to catch up,” Ma said.

25 Years After 9/11: Whatever Happened to Mass-Effect Terrorism?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

25 Years After 9/11: Whatever Happened to Mass-Effect Terrorism?
One mystery about 9/11 is why no attack of comparable scale has followed. With new motivations, enhanced delivery and AI-devised weapons, there should be no complacency.
9/11 changed everything. It led to two decades when the US and much of Europe became fixated on Islamism. Western strategists became fluent in half-absorbed subjects such as Wahhabism, Pashtun tribal customs, Frontier Crimes Regulations and the Anbar Awakening while giving insufficient attention to Chinese economic dominance and Russian military rearmament. Who knows what that diversion of strategic and intellectual resources (and the chaos it left behind in the region) has cost the West?
9/11 also bookends that remarkable period from the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1989/90 when peace and reconciliation seemed to break out everywhere. The Oslo Accords of 1993 appeared to chart a trajectory towards a two-state solution in Israel/Palestine. One year later the peaceful multiparty elections in South Africa were nothing short of a miracle. For years Afrikaners had insisted they would fight black rule until the last drop of white blood. This was the brief ‘unipolar moment’ under the then-still largely benign supervision of Washington.
‘Both Triumphant and Disastrous’
9/11 ushered in a new world – one with which Thomas Hobbes would be all too familiar. ‘Covenants, without the sword, are but words and of no strength to secure a man at all.’ ‘Force and fraud are in war the two cardinal virtues.’ Almost every quote from Leviathan is applicable.
Of course, first and foremost, 9/11 was a tragedy for the victims and their families. It was an act of appalling savagery. It was not only the largest terrorist attack in history by a country-mile, but it also introduced a new concept of mass-effect terrorism.
From the terrorists’ point of view, it was also an attack of breath-taking scale and ambition. Osama bin Laden had the imagination to view an aircraft full of fuel and passengers as a terror weapon by knitting together two of Al-Qaeda’s (AQ) previous failures: the truck-bomb attack on the World Trade Center in 1993 and the 1995 Operation Bojinka in the Philippines. Both attacks had been planned by Ramzi Yousef, whose uncle, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, was the chief planner for 9/11.
Contrary to widespread opinion, the concept of mass-effect terrorism had been exercising minds in Washington and Whitehall long before 9/11
It was also, from an AQ viewpoint, both triumphant and disastrous. Its success was that a superpower overreacted for two decades and allowed 9/11 to shape the whole of Western foreign policy as a Global War on Terror. Its failure was due to Washington’s largely successful determination to destroy AQ, a success which was only imperilled when President Trump approved the feckless Doha Accords with the Taliban in 2020, opening the way to the return of AQ to Afghanistan the following year. The latest UN report on terrorism confirms that AQ continues to re-establish itself.
‘Terrorist Ambitions Remained High’
As early as 1998, the British government had warned Washington that it was the likely next target in an operation which would involve hijacked aircraft. This story was told in detail by RUSI for the 20th anniversary of 9/11. The intelligence was briefed to both Presidents Clinton and Bush (junior). Contrary to widespread opinion, the concept of mass-effect terrorism had been exercising minds in Washington and Whitehall long before 9/11. If they had not made the intellectual leap of imagining airliners as weapons, they had nonetheless been thinking a great deal about mass-casualty attacks. This was prompted by three convergent factors.
First, in 1995 a doomsday cult known as Aum Shinrikyo released sarin on the Tokyo metro in an attack which (had it been carried out more effectively) could have killed thousands. This led to much discussion of how to react to a similar attack on the London Underground. There was also concern about chemical and biological substances being brought into the country inside the diplomatic mail bags of state sponsors of terrorism (the bags being protected from scrutiny by the Vienna Convention of 1961).
Second, there were fears about AQ getting its hands on nuclear material and producing a dirty bomb (not a nuclear explosion). At the time, it was believed that fissile material was being sold by former employees of the Soviet nuclear programme and finding its way through Central Asia to Pakistan. Most of it was a scam called ‘red mercury’ which was thoroughly investigated at the time, but there were enough more credible reports to create uncertainty.
Finally, it was known that AQ had two scientists working on chemical, biological and nuclear (CBN) experiments out of Derunta camp near the Afghanistan–Pakistan border. Not all the fine detail was available, but one of the scientists, Dr Sultan Bashiruddin Mahmood, had previously worked on Pakistan’s own sovereign nuclear programme. This story was well told a decade later by the veteran journalist Peter Bergen.
‘Herein Lies the Real Mystery’
Thus began a decade-long US fixation with the danger of terrorists obtaining access to Pakistan’s nuclear weapons. President Obama insisted that ‘The single biggest threat to U.S. security, both short term, medium term and long term, would be the possibility of a terrorist organization obtaining a nuclear weapon.’
Once 9/11 had happened, the assumption was that there would be numerous copycat attacks. In London, much focus was devoted to the towers at Canary Wharf, which housed some of the world’s premier financial institutions and which were also close to the flight paths of both Heathrow and London City airports.
In the years immediately after 9/11, terrorist ambitions remained high, including the Bali bombings in 2002 (202 killed), the Madrid train bombings in 2004 (193) and London 2005 (52). There were two dangerous plots foiled in the UK, Crevice in 2003 and Rhyme in 2004 but the only one on the scale of 9/11 was Operation Overt in 2006, AQ’s plan to bring down seven airliners in mid-Atlantic. Fortunately, it was thwarted by MI5.
And herein lies the real mystery. There have been numerous nasty and costly terrorist attacks since, but none on the 9/11 scale. There is a danger of sounding callous when observing that none of Mumbai in 2008 (166 killed), Paris in 2015 (130) and Sri Lanka in 2019 (269) come even close to 9/11 (2,977).
‘There the Comparison Ends’
Two types of terrorism have emerged since Overt in 2006.
The first was ‘urban siege’, ‘swarm’ or ‘rampaging’ terrorism which we first saw at Mumbai in 2008 and the Westgate shopping mall in Nairobi in 2013 (which killed 71). This is an effective form of terrorism because it captures press attention for hours (62 hours in the case of Mumbai) and makes prompt armed response extremely difficult. However, it is also costly for the terrorists, who are nearly always killed or captured, and their supporting organisations and states identified. The Indians were relentless in following up the Mumbai attack although Lashkar-e-Tayyiba still exists and represents a significant threat to regional peace.
The second (and now the most common) is ‘lone wolf’ terrorism usually committed by lone (and lonely) young men who have become self-radicalised online in their bedrooms and take the family car or a kitchen knife and seek to kill as many people as possible. The problem with this second type is that it is almost indistinguishable from wider mental health problems brought about by social isolation. It risks a substantial drain on the precious resources of security services, which need to be focusing on strategic threats (such as those posed by Russia, Iran and China as well as terrorist groups).
In terms of mass casualties, only one is comparable with 9/11: the brutal Hamas incursion into southern Israel on 7 October 2023. As a proportion of Israel’s population, it is probably the most lethal terrorist attack in history. But there the comparison ends. The attack involved guns, knives and grenades – a far cry from the use of aircraft as a weapon against a ground-based target.
'Still Too Early to Say'
Aircraft and their passengers have often been targets before, notably Pan Am Flight 103 at Lockerbie in 1988 (270 deaths), UTA Flight 772 the following year over Niger (170) and the often-forgotten Air India Flight 182 off the Irish coast in 1985 (329). But in each case the aircraft and passengers were the target rather than the means of delivery against an objective on the ground. 25 years after 9/11, one would have expected to see several similar attacks using aircraft against buildings or (even worse) against stadiums full of spectators.
Why has this not happened?
Advances in drone technology in Ukraine since 2022 could provide terrorists with an effective means of delivery at a time when countermeasures are still in their infancy
Precautions taken by airlines should take some credit. Cockpit doors have been strengthened, and protocols have been largely enforced, although there are signs of laxness creeping back in.
Security services have used bulk data to identify suspicious trends and plots early. AI will help here. It is now much harder for terrorists to operate as groups.
And the US military, its intelligence services and allies wreaked considerable damage on both AQ and Islamic State from 2001 through until 2019.
So, was 9/11 a one-off rather than, as was feared, the start of a new trend? It is still too early to say. Motivation for terrorism remains strong (especially following the destruction of Gaza since October 2023). Advances in drone technology in Ukraine since 2022 could provide terrorists with an effective means of delivery at a time when countermeasures are still in their infancy. And AI could enable terrorists to research and develop lethal payloads.
As we remember 9/11, it is still too early to welcome the absence of successful repeat during that costly quarter-century.

Children of 9/11 to finally get a major health study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
22:57:00 UTC
07:57:00 KST

Children of 9/11 to finally get a major health study
- Around 25,000 children were exposed to toxic dust from the 9/11 attacks, but few were included in early health studies tracking long-term illnesses.
- The US Congress and CDC will fund a major study starting in 2027 to track health impacts on children exposed during or before 9/11.
- Experts stress community support is vital for recruitment, and findings may guide prevention for children exposed to similar disasters worldwide.
AI generated
When hijacked planes brought down the World Trade Center’s twin towers on Sept 11, 2001, roughly 25,000 children were living or attending school nearby in Lower Manhattan and thousands more were in surrounding neighbourhoods. Some were infants and toddlers, while others were still in the womb.
Even though they were exposed to the massive toxic cloud and settling dust containing pulverised concrete, glass fibres, asbestos and other pollutants in the days and weeks after the towers fell, very few of these children were enrolled in the government-funded follow-up health studies of 9/11 survivors. Those were mainly for first responders and other adults.
As a result, there were no means of tracking chronic illnesses, including cancers, cardiovascular diseases and reproductive health outcomes, that may only now be emerging as those children reach their 30s and early 40s, scientists say.
Major questions remain about whether exposure to the toxins and the trauma on 9/11 and afterwards increased their long-term health risks, according to scientists.
To address these gaps, the US Congress announced in 2022 that it would fund a study of these individuals to be conducted with oversight by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
In August, the CDC said it will be seeking applications from researchers to set up the World Trade Center Youth Research Coordinating Center and to identify and track a Youth Research Cohort.
The agency has specified that study participants must have been 21 years old or younger, or in utero, and living below 14th Street in Manhattan or anywhere in Brooklyn on and after 9/11.
A cohort of similarly aged but unexposed individuals will be recruited for comparison.
It is not clear how many participants the CDC hopes to recruit, but an agency spokesperson said it expects to spend up to US$50 million (S$63.4 million) in total programme funding. The estimated start date for the project is July 1, 2027, the spokesperson said.
Members of the public can sign up online for updates and register to be notified when enrolment opens to those who are qualified.
The CDC’s World Trade Center Health Program and the New York City Department of Health’s World Trade Center Health Registry both offered services for children in the early years after the attacks.
But most affected youngsters sought care from their own paediatricians, whereas many adult survivors were uninsured and needed the programmes’ services, recalled lung specialist Joan Reibman of NYU Langone Medical Center.
In adult survivors and first responders, dozens of types of cancers and other health issues related to their exposure have been identified. But data on the effects of childhood exposure has so far come only from small studies.
Reibman, founder of the World Trade Center Environmental Health Center, said gathering participants will require a great deal of community support.
“These people are spread across the United States right now. They’re all older. They may not necessarily want to go back to that period of time,” she said. “There’s going to have to be a lot of work with community groups to try to recruit them.”
Reibman and Leigh Wilson, the current medical director of the World Trade Center Environmental Health Center, both acknowledged that children in war zones today may face some of the same long-term consequences as the children of 9/11.
“I would love to prevent every and any adverse effect on these children,” Wilson said.
Studying the children of 9/11 may shed light on preventive and mitigating measures and resources that could be put in place, Wilson added.
“You have to identify and start studying all exposed populations immediately, whether they’re adults or children,” Reibman said, and “unfortunately we haven’t learnt it from the World Trade Center disaster”. REUTERS
