I went into France's prehistoric caves. The world hasn't looked the same since
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
22:55:32 UTC
07:55:32 KST

One Saturday in mid-May, five of us stood inside a cave in the Ariège Valley in southern France, in complete silence and absolute darkness. We were two archaeologists, a Jungian analyst, a painter and me. I opened my eyes wide and saw nothing. I heard someone's stomach rumble, heard my companions breathing, felt them beside me. Water dripped, each drop echoing. Was this what our prehistoric ancestors heard?
Homo sapiens first entered this cave between 14,000 and 17,000 years ago. They ventured into its depths carrying torches and oil lamps to paint animals on its walls. More than 500 human footprints have been discovered here, including those of three small children.
I closed my eyes. I found myself looking into myself and into the eternity before I was born. I had never felt anything like it. Uncontrollable sobs rose from somewhere deep inside me and filled the cave. I stood there and wept, longing for everything we humans had been before we became estranged from the world, and for everything I, too, had been tens of thousands of years ago.
We spent three hours inside Niaux Cave, but had no sense of how much time had passed between entering and leaving. Time inside a cave is different from time outside. We were deeply moved.
Dr. Ella Assaf Shpayer, 39, a researcher and lecturer in the Department of Archaeology at Tel Aviv University, was very quiet inside the cave and remained so after we emerged.
"What did you feel in there?" I asked her.
"A year ago, I dreamed I was swimming inside myself," she replied. "I was consciously searching for quiet. I knew I had to go deeper and deeper to find it. When I reached my diaphragm, I found a long, spiraling seashell. I felt it inside me, along with the quiet I'd been looking for. I knew I'd come to the right place.
"Prehistoric humans had a thing for seashells. In Europe, Neanderthals collected them, painted them red, wore them and buried their loved ones with them. Sometimes they even risked their lives diving deep to find them. The shells must have been more than ornaments. Surely they wouldn't have risked their lives just for decoration. In the cave, I felt I was swimming inside myself, and I felt the quiet I'd experienced in the dream. Standing in that darkness, I felt a profound peace. The darkness was powerful, but also enveloping, soft and deep. It even felt familiar. An ancient familiarity, something the body and soul remember from long ago."
"It made me think of the Ten Plagues of Egypt," added Dr. Guy Perel, 58, a Jungian analyst and poet. "The plague of darkness is described as a tangible darkness, something you can feel with your hands, touch. The darkness in the cave is dense, but not frightening at all. It holds you up. It's amazing, and cold. You feel as though you're flying."
Niaux was the first stop on our journey through seven caves where prehistoric paintings have been discovered. We had come to experience these places together and better understand how creativity, belief, consciousness and human ability had converged here, finding expression in paintings tens of thousands of years old.
We wanted to enter these ancient wombs, the places where prehistoric humans had experienced an expansion of consciousness. We hoped ours might expand, too.
We set out just days after the cease-fire was announced in the 2026 Iran war. We came from the painful reality of our lives, a reality devoid of reason, compassion and love. Perhaps the instinct that had drawn prehistoric humans into the depths of caves had brought us here, too.
But first, the story of how this journey began.
About 10 years ago, Perel came across "Return to Chauvet Cave: Excavating the Birthplace of Art," by the French prehistorian Jean Clottes. Through it, he encountered the 36,000-year-old paintings discovered in Chauvet Cave in 1994.
The cave contained hundreds of paintings of animals: bison, woolly rhinoceroses, mammoths, deer, cave lions, horses, one particularly famous owl and many others. Yet there was only one painting of a human being. Known as "Venus and the Sorcerer," it depicts a woman's lower body with a mysterious figure above her. Many researchers believe the figure combines human characteristics with those of a bison or an aurochs.
Perel was astonished. He had never imagined cave paintings could be "so beautiful, profound and complete." They stirred powerful feelings in him, and he began studying the subject.
"At some point, insights started coming to me," he says.
"They weren't intellectual. They came through experience and a spiritual connection. I felt I was stepping into the shoes of the prehistoric artist."
That was how he began writing the long poem "A Cave," which took him three years to complete.
"I would sit down to write, and the questions and answers would emerge through the poetry. 'Why did you go in? What happened to you there?' I asked the prehistoric artist. Writing was like entering a cave. I felt I'd managed to enter an altered state of consciousness without actually going inside one."
A year after "A Cave" was published, Perel was contacted by Prof. Ran Barkai, 58, a prehistoric archaeologist, researcher and senior lecturer in the Department of Archaeology and Ancient Near Eastern Cultures at Tel Aviv University. For 17 years, Barkai directed excavations at Qesem Cave, an archaeological site near present-day Rosh Ha'ayin. His research focuses on the Paleolithic and Neolithic cultures that existed in our region. His particular interests include stone tools; prehistoric humans' relationships with animals, the world and caves; and the altered states of consciousness experienced by prehistoric artists.
Barkai walks everywhere, whenever he can. He is almost never cold, but he enjoys gathering wood for the fireplace at his home in Pardes Hanna and sitting by the fire in winter, "just like Neanderthals and their predecessors, because gathering wood was a central task throughout the human past," he explains.
"I started playing with ideas about what caves and their paintings meant for human consciousness," Barkai says. "I was looking for things to read outside the mainstream, and that's how I came across Guy's poem. It blew me away."
The two began meeting beneath the royal poinciana tree at the entrance to Tel Aviv University. Their long conversations led to a book they wrote together with the mysterious title "Why Do They Have No Faces?" (in Hebrew, Idra Press, 2025).
In it, they ask why, some 40,000 years ago, our forefathers and foremothers began painting deep inside caves they did not live in. Why did they so rarely depict themselves? And when they did, why did they leave the human figures faceless? Both authors were also preoccupied by how these questions might relate to the disappearance of large animals from the face of the Earth at that very same time.
In their view, cave art served a shamanic rather than an aesthetic purpose: it was a ritual intended to repair a disruption in the world by appealing to what anthropology now calls "the spirit world." Drawing on their respective fields, they offer a complex explanation. They believe the paintings were an attempt to mend a deepening fracture in the world by recreating the animals on cave walls.
Shortly after its publication, the book found its way into the hands of the painter Gideon Rubin. Rubin, 53, who has lived in London for 25 years, is known for paintings in which every human figure is faceless.
The grandson of the painter Reuven Rubin, he did not always paint this way. On September 11, 2001, he stood on a rooftop in New York and watched the Twin Towers burn. He says he will never forget the taste of dust that lingered in his mouth for four days after the disaster. He has not painted a person with a face since.
"Sometimes you come across a work that feels as though it was made just for you. That's how I felt about this book," says Rubin, who became friends with Perel and Barkai after reading it. "I understood not only why I paint without faces, but so many other things, too. It was as though someone had lit little candles along the path I'm walking."
"Ran and Guy's book looks at how human beings cope with crisis," says Dr. Assaf Shpayer, the fourth member of our group. As a child, she was intrigued when her father told her that other human species had once existed and become extinct. When she began studying archaeology at Tel Aviv University, she realized she wanted to investigate these mysterious people. Her research has since focused on two subjects: prehistoric children and the significance of horses to prehistoric humans.
"Children in prehistory have barely been studied," she says. "I'm very interested in how people understood childhood, and how prehistoric humans saw children and their place in the world."
It was the children, and the traces she believes they left in the caves, that drew her to the journey.
My work as a journalist brought Perel and me together, and we became friends. A year and a half ago, I read his and Barkai's book between ayahuasca ceremonies in the Peruvian jungle. It affected me profoundly. In one vision, I was an old woman dying in a cave. A fire burned beside me, and a prehistoric woman sang me a farewell song. I felt a peace I had never known. I was happy.
When the two invited me to join them on a journey through the caves, I agreed immediately. The five of us set out.
Almost all the paintings we saw were made by people researchers now call the Magdalenians, who lived in Western Europe between 20,000 and 13,000 years ago. They take their name from Abri de la Madeleine, an archaeological site in the Dordogne region of southwestern France discovered in the 19th century.
The Magdalenians were hunter-gatherers who lived in small groups, probably of 15 to 30 people. They moved fairly often, depending on the seasons, their neighbors and the availability of food. They were skilled hunters whose main prey were deer, horses, bison and ibex.
"What was life like for the Magdalenians?" I asked Barkai.
"Life was one long picnic. They got up in the morning, hunted, lit a fire, ate, gathered food, chatted, danced, sang and painted, until circumstances told them it was time to move on. They followed a familiar circuit, returning to the same places again and again. At certain times, they gathered with other groups to celebrate, exchange gifts and exchange genes."
How do we know this?
"Objects from distant regions have been found at some archaeological sites, which suggests these encounters took place. Modern hunter-gatherers live this way, so we assume prehistoric humans did, too. We also assume their creative expression went far beyond the evidence that survives, because much of it involved perishable materials or decorations on their bodies."
What happened to them when they entered a cave?
"Entering a deep, dark cave changes the way the senses work. Sight, our dominant sense outside, is completely neutralized, so the other senses sharpen. Consciousness is a sensory response to the world, so it takes on a different character inside a cave. You also need light to find your way through deep, dark caves and paint inside them. There's abundant evidence that prehistoric humans used torches and stone lamps fueled by fat.
"The air in these caves contains about 21 percent oxygen, and fire brings that down to as little as 13 percent, causing oxygen deprivation. This increases dopamine release in the brain, heightening feelings of contentment and euphoria. So that, too, necessarily alters consciousness. We assume people knew fire had this effect and experienced it from an early age. It gave them the expansion of consciousness they were seeking in a space they saw as a portal between worlds."
My heart skipped a beat when the entrance to Niaux Cave came into view. Everything around it was in bloom, and enormous white clouds sailed across the blue sky. I could feel its depths and coolness waiting for me.
"It looks as though it created the whole valley," Perel said.
"Not created it. It's swallowing it," Barkai said.
The cave is two kilometers long. Soon after entering, you encounter graffiti that visitors have been leaving here since the early 17th century. Martin, for example, was here in 1652, and Louise came 34 years later.
The cave is damp, with a constant temperature of 12 degrees Celsius, or 53.6 degrees Fahrenheit. This is one reason the magnificent paintings in its depths have survived so well. In places, the ceiling rises dozens of meters overhead; elsewhere, visitors have to stoop to avoid hitting their heads. Stalactites hang above still pools of water. The cave is vast, spacious, beautiful and regal.
After walking 400 meters, we passed through a narrow passage, and the first paintings appeared: red and black dots, short lines, dashes and stripes, and a line with a loop at one end that resembled a club or a pregnant woman. These symbols also appear in many other caves in the region and in neighboring Spain. Some were painted with tools, others with fingers. A few are so well preserved that fingerprints are still visible.
Sometimes the paintings face one another or appear on either side of a prominent crack in the wall. Perhaps they are waymarkers, a tribal language or even musical notation. Perhaps they prepare visitors to enter a sacred space. There are many interpretations, all conjecture.
The spot where we stood is not part of the regular tour because of an especially fragile work etched into the clay and sand of a small passage: a rare depiction of a fish. A salmon or a trout, rendered in a few precise lines, it has been swimming in place for some 15,000 years.
"Why was this fish etched in that little passage, in that hidden place?" I later asked Barkai.
"I think they chose animals that embodied the ability to pass between worlds and reach places humans cannot," he said. "Deep water is one such world, one that has always had a place in mythology. Just as birds mediate between humans and the heavens, fish may mediate between humans and the depths. There is clay where the fish was etched, and water certainly flowed here. That supports the hypothesis, but it's still only a hypothesis."
We hadn't realized it, but our encounter with the fish and our silence in the darkness had taken place at the entrance to the Salon Noir, the cave's holy of holies. This cathedral of rock, some 20 meters high, contains six panels with dozens of animal paintings, together considered one of the pinnacles of prehistoric art. All the animals are drawn in charcoal, hence the name Salon Noir, or Black Chamber.
Before entering, visitors are asked to turn off their flashlights. For a moment, they stand in darkness while the guide fits a filter that allows her to illuminate the paintings without damaging them. The pause is brief, but the effect is dramatic: when the flashlight comes on, the animals emerge from the darkness. There are dozens of bison, horses, ibex and deer, including one deer particularly celebrated for its elegance.
For decades, researchers thought a single artist had painted them all. The styles are remarkably similar, and the arrangement suggests a carefully planned composition. The cave's curves, protrusions and hollows give the animals volume and life. They seem to spring from the walls. When the guide moved her flashlight to mimic a flickering torch, they actually galloped.
But in the early 1990s, radiocarbon dating revealed that the animals were not the work of one person. Magdalenian artists, men and women, had visited the cave over hundreds of years, each adding a contribution.
For decades, many researchers believed the paintings were a form of hunting magic intended to ensure a successful hunt. The problem is that they contain almost no hunting scenes, and depictions of wounded animals are also rare. Today, most researchers believe we will never know why the paintings were made and are unwilling to endorse any particular theory. Many disagree with Barkai and Perel's interpretation of the art as a shamanic attempt to repair a disruption in the world by recreating the animals' spirits on cave walls.
What does seem clear is that the artists must have spent a great deal of time observing the animals and knew them well. The creatures are majestic, sometimes enormous. Standing before them, you feel awe.
"People sometimes think they painted what they dreamed or imagined," Perel says. "But we argue that they weren't painting imaginary animals. They were bringing the animals' spirits into being on the rock to repair something in the spiritual, archetypal world. The cave is a portal to that world. In the Jungian approach, what emerges from the unconscious isn't considered imaginary or less real than everyday reality. A dream is a way of encountering another layer of reality, one that is usually hidden from us.
"In the encounter with the rock and the painting on it, something from that hidden world took on a body and became visible. By entering a particular psychological and creative state, the person allowed the 'animal spirit' to materialize on the stone. In that sense, the painting doesn't represent another reality. It is that reality appearing within our own."
It was already evening when we sat by the river in the town of Foix, watching swallows fly above the water. We talked and fell silent, laughed and fell silent. We were human beings and we were animals flickering on the cave walls, drawing closer to ourselves and to one another.
That night, I dreamed of my mother.
Months later, each of the caves we visited still returns to me, especially at night, when my consciousness hovers between waking and sleep. The Gargas cave complex left a particularly deep impression. At the foot of the Pyrenees, near the village of Aventignan, it is known for its hand stencils: 231 in all, in different sizes and colors, some belonging to children.
The stencils were made by placing a hand against the rock and spraying pigment from the mouth. Gargas also contains animal paintings, engravings, some 100 square meters of finger tracings on the ceiling, feminine symbols and numerous depictions of what some researchers interpret as female genitalia. Animal bones, placed there by prehistoric humans, are wedged into cracks in the walls.
We had the caves to ourselves with our guide, Nicolas Ferrer, who is in his 50s and lives in Aventignan. His grandmother sold tickets here, his parents were guides, and he has worked here since he was 14. His love for the place, and his wonder at it, come through in every word.
Local people have known of the cave complex since at least the 16th century, and a graffito dated 1587 survives on its walls. No one then understood the significance of the art around them. Its discovery and study began only in the late 19th century. As in many other caves, new finds still come to light from time to time. The art is attributed to the Gravettian culture, which existed between 30,000 and 20,000 years ago, but remains of the Mousterian culture, created by Neanderthals, have also been found.
We entered through a steel door almost concealed by vegetation and moss. The upper cave is small and narrow, vertical and winding. Bats once lived here, and their droppings damaged the paintings. They were not the only ones to cause harm. Scientists once marked and highlighted engravings in ways that would be unthinkable today. People from National Geographic, for example, used a red pen.
"Maybe in 50 years, researchers will look at what we're doing here and lose their minds," Ferrer says.
The temperature inside is about 11 degrees Celsius. Over the past decade, it has risen by half a degree, and the cave has become drier. Seventy sensors collect data every 15 minutes, but global warming is unlikely to be kind to the art within.
Ferrer showed us the hands scattered through the space, tucked into recesses and spread across the walls: black, red, yellow and white. Only 17 show all five fingers. The others are sometimes missing one, two or even three. Ferrer told us that people once thought the stencils had been made by people who had lost fingers, but it later became clear that this was not the case. Those who made them most likely folded their fingers before spraying the pigment. The stencils are thought to represent some kind of code.
"I met a group of deaf people, and when they stood in front of the hands, they cried," Ferrer told us. "They knew nothing about the new hypotheses, but to them it was clearly sign language. The positions of the hands meant something, and so did the colors."
In their book, Perel and Barkai discuss the many hand stencils found in caves. Were these the first selfies in human history? they ask playfully. They then offer a complex explanation: the point of contact with the cave wall expresses an abstract aspect of the self that extends beyond the physical body.
Later, we stood before a panel bearing children's hand stencils.
"Children have something we adults don't, and prehistoric humans recognized it," Assaf Shpayer said. "It's no coincidence they brought them here. They weren't just teaching them or making them part of the community. They also valued their qualities, their flexibility of thought. Children are closer to the other worlds because they haven't been here long, so they were seen as intermediaries between this world and the other."
Very different from how Western societies view children today.
"It couldn't be more different. Today, children are seen as sponges to fill with information. We teach them and turn them into adults like us. I thought about this a lot when I had children. I'm not a hunter-gatherer, and my children go to kindergarten and school, but I try to let them experience things for themselves without constantly telling them what to do or how best to do it. I don't always manage it."
"This is where I realized that what makes caves addictive is going in and coming out," Rubin added. "Your age disappears inside the cave. Once you've been in, you experience the world outside differently. The volume goes up. You take everything in, hear everything. I lie on the grass, listen to the birds, feel the curvature of the Earth. I lie with my eyes closed and see. I open them and see a horse in the clouds. Maybe 30,000 years ago, someone lay there just as I do, saw a horse in the clouds and then went and created it?
"It's an experience of altered consciousness that brings you back to something that was always there, but that you'd lost touch with. I think I'll keep returning to caves all my life. They're where I understand my place in the world better."
"Gargas is another world," Barkai says. "I think people came here looking for answers, performing rituals to solve problems. I think that, for them, caves were places to send messages, to reach wherever they wanted to go."
Reach where?
"Whatever lies beyond the cave, beyond its walls."
Why do you think they put animal bones into cracks in the walls?
"I think they saw the cracks as a connection between the cave and whatever lay beyond its walls, like the cracks between the stones of the Western Wall, where people leave notes with their requests. And what they wanted was animals. The animals were disappearing, and people wanted to send the message that they depended on them."
Two or three days later, we arrived at Rouffignac Cave. This immense cave, situated between two streams, had been known to local people for centuries. The earliest account of its existence appears in the early 17th-century writings of Jean Tarde, a vicar, astronomer, geographer and friend of Galileo Galilei.
In 1929, the industrialist Charles Plassard bought the estate containing the cave. He and his son Louis were curious nature lovers, and on one of their explorations they noticed figures on the ceiling. They invited researchers from the University of Toulouse, who discovered the first engravings: two mammoths facing each other. The cave turned out to contain more than 250 animal figures, including some 160 mammoths, as well as four human figures.
The discovery immediately sparked a heated controversy. Several researchers claimed they had seen some of the paintings as early as the late 1940s and had even reported them, only to be told they were modern scribbles. Others claimed the paintings were forgeries. Defending their authenticity was Abbé Henri Breuil, one of the world's foremost scholars of cave art, known as the "Pope of Prehistory." Breuil examined the paintings and declared them genuine.
We arrived at midday on a very hot day. Waiting at the entrance was Frédéric Plassard, a fourth-generation member of the family with a doctorate specializing in Paleolithic art. His wife is also an archaeologist, as was his father. In 2020, with visitors kept away by the COVID lockdowns, the couple explored the cave and discovered 12 new engravings, including a figure that may represent a woman.
"I'm more of a caveman than prehistoric people were," he says, "because I've spent far more time in here than they did."
The cave extends for more than eight kilometers, roughly five miles. It was the coldest cave we visited and the only one with an electric train, which carries visitors along the first kilometer. Visitors are not allowed to get off at most points along the route, but that rule did not apply to us.
We boarded and headed inside, following the route the prehistoric artist had taken 13,000 years earlier. The ride seemed endless, the outside world receding behind us. Along the way, we saw the beds dug by cave bears that had hibernated here for tens of thousands of years before prehistoric humans arrived. The bears had scratched the walls, and people had extended those marks with their fingers. Plassard believes they were continuing the bears' work in the hope of acquiring their great strength.
Seven hundred meters into the cave, Plassard invited us to get off the train. Before us was the first mammoth. A simple drawing, just an outline and tusks, yet it looked almost alive. It seemed to be looking at something. There was a young mammoth, too, with two short tusks.
"I'm sure whoever drew it had studied a real, living mammoth," Plassard said. "They probably studied carcasses, too, and knew the animals' anatomy well."
One hundred meters farther on, two groups of mammoths faced each other. We asked Plassard whether such an encounter could have happened in real life. Mammoths disappeared long ago, he explained, but we might learn something about them from their living relatives, African elephants.
"An encounter like this between two groups is unusual," he said. "We also have reason to think these mammoths are males, not females, and groups of males like this don't exist."
How do we know they're males?
"Because of the marks near their temples, which may represent secretions from the male's temporal gland during periods of sexual arousal and high testosterone levels. But males don't gather like this, so this isn't a scene from nature. It's a symbolic expression. Even looking at the animals they chose to paint, it's hard to draw a simple connection between the art and the local environment. For some 20,000 years, across different parts of Europe and in different environments, they kept choosing the same small selection of large herbivores."
What do you mean?
"If there were still mammoths in the Dordogne 16,000 years ago, they were probably very rare. The artists may have studied their anatomy and behavior somewhere else, perhaps 300 or 400 kilometers away, then painted them here months later. So it's hard to see this art as a straightforward depiction of the natural world around them."
We ventured deeper and reached a chamber with a low ceiling covered in drawings of 26 mammoths, 12 bison, 11 horses, 12 ibex and three rhinoceroses. Some even seemed to be smiling.
We said goodbye to Plassard and drove to our next destination. A rabbit and an ibex crossed the road, and we saw a statue of the Buddha in the forest. Out of habit, I glanced at my phone and read about the world we had sought to escape: a plane crash, people killed, war with Iran looming once again. The suffering of modern humans, inflicted by modern humans.
I asked my companions whether they thought there had been wicked people and narcissists among prehistoric humans, too. Had there been troubled psyches and personality disorders? They thought so, but fewer. People then, they believed, had experienced themselves as part of a greater whole rather than as separate individuals. Ego was not what drove someone to paint in the darkness. They hadn't gone there to win admiration for their talent, where no one could see their work. Freedom from the ego is the greatest happiness one can know. There is nothing like it.
By then, we all understood: the shift in consciousness that takes place deep inside a cave is the realization that we are part of the universe. It has the power to make us better human beings, humbler, more whole.
On our last day, we sat on a cliff at sunset, looking out over the forest and the river flowing far below. We listened to the birdsong and said nothing. For those few minutes, we were human beings without nationality, without culture, without history. We were blank pages flying through space.

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels seize strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha
Yemen’s Houthis seized the strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha on Thursday as their offensive against Saudi-backed government forces intensified. Saudi Arabia launched dozens of airstrikes over the past 24 hours, the Houthis said, after the Iran-backed group carried out attacks on Saudi territory that wounded dozens of people.
Yemen's Houthis seized control of the strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha on Thursday, with witnesses telling AFP of fighters marching on the area chanting "death to America, death to Israel".
Saudi Arabia meanwhile launched dozens of airstrikes in the last 24 hours, according to the military spokesman for the Houthis, who control large parts of northwest Yemen and launched a large-scale offensive last week against Riyadh-backed Yemeni government forces.
The Houthis launched attacks on Saudi territory that left dozens of people wounded, in a conflict that has reignited during the Middle East war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February.
A Yemeni military source told AFP on Thursday that the Iran-backed Houthis were advancing towards the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait "after having taken control of Mocha".
The waterway, which links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez Canal, has gained importance as a transit route since the start of the wider Middle East war, which saw Iran blockade the Strait of Hormuz.
The regional war has disrupted maritime traffic in the Gulf, causing oil prices to soar.
On Thursday, the US oil contract WTI surpassed $100, after Brent North Sea crude -- the main international benchmark -- already did so on Wednesday.
After Mocha's capture, the leader of Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, said the protection of the country's coasts and restoring state control of them was an "Arab and international interest".
The military source said the Houthis also seized Zuqar Island in the southern Red Sea, "after rocket attacks and a ground assault carried out using boats transporting fighters".
In a statement, Tarek Saleh, who heads the Yemeni National Resistance Forces that controlled Mocha, said he moved his command centre "to a safe location" to regroup.
Government forces have paid "a heavy price in recent days in the face of a Houthi offensive that was planned and supported by Iran", he added.

'Maritime coercion'
Before the offensive, the Houthis already controlled a large part of Yemen's north, including the capital Sanaa, as well as the major port city of Hodeidah on the Red Sea.
But they did not yet hold any areas directly overlooking Bab al-Mandab.
With their drones and missiles, the Houthis have been able to disrupt traffic in the Red Sea.
But "controlling the coast would strengthen Houthi maritime coercion", said Andreas Krieg, a security expert at King's College London.
The advance of the Houthis in Mocha, as well as in the nearby areas of Khokha and Hays, has driven many people to flee to Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based.
Mohamed, 46, who left Mocha in the middle of the night, told AFP there was an "apocalyptic" atmosphere in the port city.

Hundreds dead
Yemen relapsed into war in July after years of relative calm punctured by sporadic violence and deepening poverty.

The government retaliated by striking Sanaa airport, an attack the Houthis blamed on Saudi Arabia.

The Houthis, after seizing Yemen's capital and forcing out the government, fought the Saudi-led coalition from 2015 until a United Nations-brokered ceasefire in 2022.

Trump administration proposes axing grace period for H-1B visa holders after job loss
- The Trump administration proposes ending the 60-day grace period for H-1B visa holders to stay and find new jobs after losing employment, requiring immediate departure instead.
- This change targets skilled workers including H-1B, E-1, E-2, L-1, O-1, TN, H-1B1, and E-3 visa holders, potentially disrupting tech companies reliant on foreign talent.
- The Department of Homeland Security expects companies to hire US workers or reapply for visas, while critics warn the rule would harm immigrant workers and businesses.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The Trump administration has proposed eliminating a 60-day grace period that allows certain immigrants, including skilled workers on H-1B visas, to stay in the US and find a new sponsor after losing their job, according to a government notice posted online on Sept 10.
Under the planned rule change, published in the Federal Register by the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), those with H-1B and certain other temporary work visas would have to leave the country as soon as their employment ends – a potential blow to top American tech companies that rely heavily on foreign workers.
It is the latest step by US President Donald Trump to limit legal immigration since returning to office in January 2025. His administration has also introduced higher visa fees for skilled workers and recently paused immigrant visa appointments at US missions globally while it implements a new training programme.
Companies affected by the change could see some disruption, the DHS wrote in its proposal, but it said the jobs could go to American workers instead. In some situations, immigrant workers who leave could potentially reapply if their employer petitions for them, it added.
“DHS presumes that they will either offer the same jobs to equally qualified US workers or go through the I-129 petition process depending on their workforce requirement,” the notice said.
The 60-day grace period, in place since 2017, allows foreign workers time to find another US job or get their affairs in order – whether selling a home or pulling children out of school – before leaving the country.
“Many H-1B workers have been here for years, and they and their families have established themselves in their communities,” said Gabriel Chin, a professor at the UC Davis School of Law. “I see no legitimate reason to force them to leave because they are changing jobs.”
Visas critical for tech companies
H-1B visas, established by Congress in 1990, are especially critical for tech companies seeking talent from India and China, allowing them to fill roles where there is sometimes a lack of qualified US workers.
Consultancy companies such as Deloitte, PwC and Ernst & Young as well as outsourcing firms such as Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, HCLTech and LTIMindtree are top H-1B sponsors.
Lawyers for Berardi Immigration Law, which specialises in business-related immigration issues, said the move would “sharply compress the timeline HR teams have to manage layoffs and offboarding for foreign national employees”.
“It seems like every week this administration announces a new step to make life more difficult for immigrants in the US and the companies and communities that rely on them,” said Todd Schulte, president of FWD.us, an immigration advocacy group.
If implemented, the change would also apply to E-1 international trader visa holders; E-2 commercial vehicle operator visa holders; L-1 short-term work for executives or managers with international companies; O-1 visas for people “with an extraordinary ability” in science, sports or the arts; and TN professional workers.
It would also affect H-1B1 skilled worker visa holders from Singapore and Chile and E-3 speciality worker visa holders from Australia.
The rule is subject to a two-month public comment period before it can be finalised. REUTERS

A number of people were killed and several others injured after a bus carrying a Dutch tour party flipped over in a remote Alpine region of eastern Switzerland, police said on Sept 10.
Police in the canton of Graubuenden said the accident occurred near to the village of Susch, and images of the scene published online showed the vehicle lying on its side next to the road, surrounded by police and emergency service personnel.
A spokeswoman for the General Dutch Association of Travel Companies (ANVR), acting as spokesperson for tour operator OAD, said a serious accident had taken place involving an OAD bus and that 48 passengers were on board, all Dutch nationals.
Bayeux Tapestry ‘mania’ sweeps UK as exhibition opens
London’s Bayeux Tapestry exhibition opened on Sept 10 to a British public gripped by “mania” over the medieval artwork depicting the Norman conquest of England, on display outside France for the first time.
Excited visitors who had tickets for the first day of the sold-out exhibition queued outside the British Museum ahead of the opening, where some staff had donned period costumes.
“It is back here for the first time in 950 years!” 46-year-old Catherine Pitt told AFP in the queue outside the museum entrance.

U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance spoke directly with American military commanders in the spring and summer to obtain their unbiased assessments of the war with Iran. What he heard caused him serious concern about U.S. strategy and the state of weapons stockpiles, The New York Times reports, writes UNN.
Details
Commanders warned Vance that stocks of Patriot interceptor missiles were being depleted. In one theater of operations, fewer than 100 such missiles remained by the end of spring. The war also significantly reduced stocks of ATACMS and other precision munitions.

Vance became concerned
After these conversations, Vance expressed concern about the prospects for success. The military also warned that Iran's authorities were prepared to endure significant losses in order to preserve the regime.
The private assessments differed markedly from the administration's public statements. Trump continued to claim that the United States had already won the war and that there were no problems with weapons stocks.

Princess Diana’s ‘revenge dress’ up for auction for first time in decades

Princess Diana’s ‘revenge dress’ up for auction for first time in decades
Iconic Christina Stambolian gown is estimated to reach US$300,000 at Sotheby’s sale in New York
The “revenge dress” worn by the late Princess Diana in 1994 is up for auction at Sotheby’s for the first time in nearly three decades.
The black silk evening dress by Greek designer Christina Stambolian is estimated to fetch as much as £220,000 (US$298,110) when it goes on sale on December 9 during Sotheby’s Luxury Week in New York, the auction house said on Thursday.
Diana wore the dress in June 1994 as she arrived at the Serpentine Gallery in London for a fundraising dinner.
It gained notoriety because the then Prince Charles – from whom she had been separated for nearly two years but not yet divorced – was widely expected to say in a national television interview broadcast that same evening that he had been unfaithful to her.
According to a later documentary, her decision to wear the dress was a last-minute one after initially setting aside a more traditional Valentino outfit. “She wanted to look a million dollars,” her former stylist Anna Harvey said on the programme, according to Vogue. “And she did.”
“On her own terms, Princess Diana turned the dress into one of the most powerful messages she ever made, during one of the most scrutinised and emotionally charged episodes of her life,” said Morgane Halimi, head of fashion at Sotheby’s.

The Italian Ambassador to Ecuador, Giovanni Davoli, opened two events in Quito to present the Giorgio Ambrosoli Award. The event was attended by the widows and family members of the Ecuadorian prosecutors Suarez and Vasconez, victims of mafia violence; the President of the National Court of Justice, Marco Rodríguez Ruiz; the Public Defender General, Ricardo Morales; and the Attorney General, Leonardo Alarcón.

Ukrainian officials say five people were killed and 67 others were wounded when a Russian drone hit a shopping mall in Pavlohrad, a city in Dnipropetrovsk region.

Two other shopping malls - in the cities of Zaporizhzhia and Sumy - were targeted by Russian air strikes earlier this week, according to Ukrainian media.

A full-scale war has been raging between Russia and Ukraine since Russian President Vladimir Putin launched an invasion more than four and a half years ago.

Anthropic details bad actors’ efforts to misuse its AI for bioweapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
22:35:16 UTC
07:35:16 KST

Criminals, state-sponsored groups, spyware vendors, scientists and propagandists have attempted to use Anthropic’s powerful artificial intelligence models to design missiles and bombs, create deadly pathogens and surveil dissidents, according to a threat intelligence report the company published on Thursday.
“The cases we share here aren’t typical misuse, but rather examples of the most notable and novel threat activity we’ve identified to date,” Anthropic wrote in its 154-page report. “We’re publishing this work because we believe we have a responsibility to disclose malicious misuse of our services.”
In particular, the company detailed five case studies of scientists using its AI models in biological research. In these examples, Anthropic said the researchers circumvented its safeguards meant to prevent users from “unsupported regions”, as well as worked to hide the purpose of their work.
“Biological misuse is one of the most serious risks of frontier AI models,” Anthropic wrote. “Without the correct safeguards, such capabilities could have catastrophic consequences.”
Anthropic said it banned these accounts. The company did not reveal the names of the research institutions or the countries where the misuse took place, saying it was uncertain of the researchers’ intent.
Anthropic gave dozens of other examples of threat actors using its AI models. Those included cyber operations such as Russian espionage and “smash-and-grab” cyberhacks; surveillance operations, including a China-based program targeting Uyghurs in Syria and another targeting internal dissidents; propaganda campaigns in Russia, Malaysia, Iran and Bangladesh; and the use of its Claude AI model in Yemen, China and Russia to develop software for conventional weapons, including firearms, missiles, armed drones, bombs and other munitions.
In one of the examples of biological research, Anthropic found a scientist using Claude to work on a state-sponsored grant application to study the virus chikungunya. The virus is a mosquito-borne disease, similar to dengue and malaria, that can cause months of severe pain, fever and other debilitating symptoms.
Such research could be used to develop vaccines, but could also be used to create biological weapons. Anthropic told the New York Times this case was especially concerning because it could see the study was to be done at a military research institute.
The report comes just two days after an Anthropic employee, Jacob Coxon, set off a media firestorm with his resignation. He stated that he quit the company because it was not acting responsibly in creating its technology. Coxon said Anthropic and its rival, OpenAI, were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence” that would cause human extinction by 2030. Current Anthropic employees posted public agreements with him.
Many AI experts say the real-world threats, like those detailed in Anthropic’s intelligence report, are far more concerning within the next three years than an apocalypse brought on by an omnipotent intelligence.
“AI accelerationism and AI doomerism are two sides of the same coin: they both enforce the notion that an AGI superbeing will come into existence,” said Heidy Khlaaf, the chief AI scientist at the AI Now Institute. Khlaaf said AI labs creating technology that can be used for cybersecurity exploitation and weapons of war could be exceedingly more deadly.
In its report, Anthropic said that the potential real-world misuse from AI models is not typically in public view, instead, it’s investigated internally and by academics, governments and international organizations.
The company said that the entire AI industry needs to work together, alongside governments, to address these harms and create defenses.
“As models become increasingly capable, their risks will increase, unless AI developers and society’s defenders act to make them safer,” Anthropic wrote.

Israel says it destroyed Hezbollah base in Lebanon’s Ali al-Taher ridge

The Israeli military says it has destroyed Hezbollah’s underground infrastructure at a key site in southern Lebanon, with Israeli government officials adding that the operation consolidated its so-called security zone in the area.

The Ali al-Taher ridge, about 15 km (10 miles) from the Israeli border, has become one of the most contested areas of the war between Israel and Hezbollah. Katz claimed last Friday that Israeli forces had driven Hezbollah fighters out of what he said was a network of tunnels under the disputed highland.
Reuters reported that Hezbollah is believed to have built an underground command centre and weapons stores there in July, quoting unnamed Lebanese security sources.

Hezbollah has yet to respond to the recent Israeli attack.
The Israeli military said its forces had established “operational control” over the ridge, both above and below ground, before dismantling the infrastructure. The network extended for more than 2 km (just over 1 mile) and contained dozens of rockets, missiles and drones, as well as anti-tank missiles, mines and explosive devices, it said.
The military said a central command complex belonging to Hezbollah’s Badr unit was located within the underground infrastructure. The complex contained command centres, weapons storage rooms and living quarters that allowed fighters to remain underground for extended periods, it said.
Iran reportedly warned the United States last month that it would respond forcefully if Israeli attacks on the ridge continued.
Over the last weeks, Israeli strikes and ground operations around the Ali al-Taher ridge continued despite a ceasefire agreed in June, after Israel gained control of nearby Beaufort Castle and part of the higher ground overlooking much of southern Lebanon and northern Israel.
A US-brokered framework agreed after a June ceasefire — between Lebanon and Israel, without negotiating with Hezbollah — called for Israeli forces to gradually withdraw from southern Lebanon while Lebanese troops disarm Hezbollah.
The process has stalled, however, with Hezbollah refusing to give up its weapons and Israel saying it will not withdraw until the group disarms.
Since 2023, Israel has pushed into southern Lebanon and seized several strategic positions, occupying swathes of land, which it now increasingly says it needs to maintain a so-called buffer zone between Israel and Hezbollah positions in Lebanon.

Live: Rivals Rams and 49ers meet for historic first NFL match in Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10

NFL Melbourne: San Francisco 49ers defeat LA Rams 27-7 at MCG
LA Rams coach Sean McVay says his team's decision to arrive in Melbourne the day before the NFL's historic first match in Australia was not the reason his side was comprehensively beaten 27-7 by the San Francisco 49ers in front of 100,021 fans at the MCG.
The 49ers arrived a week ago, while the Rams raised eyebrows by touching down in Melbourne 28 hours before kick-off.
Despite scoring the first touchdown of the game, the Rams were outplayed by their rivals in the NFC West division.
Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford, the reigning NFL MVP, had a tough day in the Melbourne sunshine, completing 15 passes from 25 attempts for 155 yards and one interception.
Stafford did not finish the game, missing the Rams' final drive of the match with his side down by 20 points.
In contrast, 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy shrugged off an early interception to control the game for his side. He completed 25 passes from 34 attempts for 205 yards, with three touchdowns and one interception.
Asked post-match if arriving in Australia the day before kick-off led to his side's sluggish performance, McVay said he did not believe that was why they were heading home with a 20-point defeat.
"They outplayed us in every facet. I didn't do nearly a good enough job. This is a humbling day for us," he said.
"I don't believe [the late arrival] is why we didn't play well enough, I really don't.
"It's easy in hindsight to be able to say it was a miss but those are responsibilities that I'll take, and then you try to be able to look at it."
Just three points were scored in a tight opening quarter, with 49ers kicker Eddy Pineiro nailing a chip shot from 20 metres.
The Rams scored the opening touchdown of the game on the opening play of the second quarter, with running back Kyren Williams converting up the middle from five yards.
Purdy lost two potential throwing targets in the second quarter, with rookie wide receiver De'Zhaun Stribling and tight end Jake Tonges limping off.
The 49ers took a three-point lead into half-time, thanks to a 39-yard deep pass to Demarcus Robinson.
San Francisco received the ball to start the second half and produced a perfect drive down the field, finished with a short pass from Purdy to Mike Evans, playing his first match for the team after a decade with Tampa Bay.
Leading 17-7, it was the 49ers defence that made the defining play of the game, stopping the Rams on the goal line.
On 4th and goal, Stafford tried to sneak over the goal line but was stopped short, after wide Rams receiver Puka Nacua was tackled just centimetres short on the previous play.
The 49ers came onto the field and Purdy orchestrated a clinical 12-play, 99-metre drive that ended with a 15-metre touchdown pass to Deebo Samuel.
Both teams now head back to the United States.
The 49ers host the Miami Dolphins at home on Monday, AEST, while the Rams host the New York Giants in a prime-time match on Tuesday, AEST.

Confusion over protected status leaves employers and Salvadoran immigrants scrambling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
22:29:25 UTC
07:29:25 KST

Confusion over protected status leaves employers and Salvadoran immigrants scrambling
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- With a crucial deadline passed and no clear decision on Temporary Protected Status, 170,000 Salvadoran immigrants nationwide remain in legal limbo, including 36,000 in California.
- Some Salvadoran TPS holders have already been fired, while others were reinstated after the federal government announced that their work authorization continues for now.
- The Trump administration had already ended TPS protections for Haitians and other immigrants.
Thousands of Salvadoran immigrants nationwide faced uncertainty after the federal government failed to decide by a Wednesday deadline whether to extend or terminate their longtime temporary protections against deportation.
Those protections, known as Temporary Protected Status or TPS, allow immigrants to obtain work permits and by Thursday some Salvadorans had already been fired from their jobs. Others who had been let go were reinstated after the Trump administration clarified that an announcement on TPS for Salvadorans would come “at the appropriate time” and that they would retain work authorization in the meantime.
Employers also expressed uncertainty about whether the statement was enough to legally keep Salvadoran employees on their payroll. Those who lost their jobs worked across the U.S. in construction, at hotels and as janitors.
Some took the announcement that work authorizations remained in place — made late Wednesday by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services — as a cause for hope, while others saw it as prolonged mental torture. There are 170,000 Salvadoran TPS holders, including 36,000 living in California.
Asked for further guidance on Thursday, Homeland Security sent a link to the USCIS website.
Advocates with the National TPS Alliance distributed a letter including the administration’s announcement for TPS holders to share with their employers and stating that “any decision to terminate could not take effect for a minimum of 60 days.” The letter seemed to help, as advocates reported that some fired employees had been able to return to work.
Not everyone was reinstated. Jose Ramirez reported to his construction job in Santa Monica for the last time on Wednesday.
The 63-year-old had been legally working in the U.S. since 2001, when TPS was first extended to Salvadoran immigrants.
He had been in the country for six years before that, and constantly struggled to find stable work. The work permit was a lifeline. He’d dedicated the last 25 years to construction, during which he fathered three daughters and set roots in Compton.
Still, his boss said Ramirez could no longer present for work Thursday.
“I’ve worked on buildings that reach the skies of Los Angeles,” Ramirez said. “I’ve contributed economically and lent my labor to this great country.”
The Department of Homeland Security has not yet announced whether it will end or extend Temporary Protected Status for some 170,000 Salvadorans, including 36,000 in California.
Ramirez’s boss said his job would be available to him, but he’d need to show proof of an active work permit. A notice or a letter is not enough, Ramirez said.
The USCIS announcement was “a ray of hope that they will give us an extension,” Ramirez said. “But, it’s just not certain. Anything can happen. We’re just praying to God that the government will make it official.”
Others were luckier. Karina, 42, who has been a custodian at a university in Houston for 18 years, said she panicked when a human resources representative called to say she wouldn’t be able to return to work. Karina asked The Times not to include her last name or the name of the university where she works out of concern for her employment.
She said her job pays for half of her daughter’s college tuition and the health insurance of both of her children. She also pays for her mother’s kidney disease medication in El Salvador.
Given the uncertainty, the university gave Karina one month of unpaid leave, she said. But after the USCIS announcement, the representative called her back Thursday and said she could return to work the next day.
Karina said she owns a house, has always paid taxes and never relied on government assistance. She said she was grateful for the reprieve, albeit momentary.
“I have my whole life here,” she said of the U.S. “Over there, I have nothing.”
Ending TPS would be a shock to El Salvador’s economy, where remittances from Salvadorans in the U.S. make up nearly a quarter of the nation’s GDP — nearly $10 billion last year. In 2019, President Nayib Bukele, an ally of President Trump, publicly called on the U.S. to extend TPS for Salvadoran immigrants.
More recently, Bukele has embraced Trump’s deportation agenda, including by accepting controversial deals to house foreign detainees in the country’s mega-prison. The number of people deported to El Salvador nearly doubled in the first three months of 2026.
The decision by the Department of Homeland Security to extend or terminate TPS typically has been made at least 60 days before the designation was set to expire. DHS can extend the program for a six, 12 or 18-month period or decide to cancel the designation.
But the Trump administration has delayed announcements, including some made days after the designation expired. A Supreme Court ruling in June determined that the Homeland Security secretary has final authority over the program and cut down the ability for advocates to sue.
Rebecca Shi, executive director of the American Business Immigration Coalition, said she spoke on Wednesday with Trump administration and Homeland Security officials. The group represents companies that employ immigrants, including TPS holders.
She said there has been an internal debate within the administration around the economic impact of eliminating work authorization for Salvadorans, who have lived in the U.S. for decades, perform skilled jobs and can’t easily be replaced. That debate escalated last week, she said.
In initial statements to reporters on Wednesday, Homeland Security had said only that until an announcement about TPS, Salvadorans would “retain protection.” Shi said the clarification that evening that Salvadorans would also retain work authorization was a good sign.
“We’re cautiously optimistic,” she said. “DHS yesterday could have said nothing. The fact that they made that change — that had to be a decision because of the pressure.”
For now, though, some employers are stuck waiting for answers.
Lauren Truslow, CEO of 3D Enviro, a Virginia company that does identification and abatement of hazardous materials, said the lack of a decision on TPS has been stressful and costly. Three of her 30 employees are TPS holders from El Salvador. Another, who is married to a Salvadoran TPS holder, told her his family plans to leave the country if the program is canceled.
3D Enviro is a federal contractor, and Truslow said that her employees’ driver’s licenses and federal badges expired on Wednesday.
“How do they continue to work for me?” she said. “No one seems to know the answer to that. They can’t get into federal facilities without valid ID. Them showing a memo from USCIS is not going to cut it.”
During a news conference organized on Thursday by the Central American Resource Center of Los Angeles, other immigrant rights groups and local elected officials, speakers urged TPS holders to form a plan for their families and schedule a legal consultation with a trusted lawyer. They also called on the administration to issue a decision on TPS for El Salvador and a pathway to permanent legal status.
“Salvadoran families deserve clear, timely and trustworthy information from the government,” said Martha Arévalo, CARECEN’s executive director. “As we gather this morning, we don’t have an extension for TPS. … What we have is another waiting game and a renewed limbo for families.”
“We are going to fight this,” vowed Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass.
In a statement, Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) called the USCIS announcement “clear as mud.”
“Once again, the Trump Administration is punishing immigrants who have followed the rules with chaos, uncertainty, and cruelty,” he wrote.
Also in attendance at the news conference was Carmen Sanchez, 49, who works the night janitorial shift cleaning offices in Los Angeles. She said many of her co-workers who were also protected under TPS were told not to return to work after Wednesday.
Sanchez planned to report to work Thursday evening, but was sure she’d suffer the same fate. She said she has three adult children in El Salvador and is helping two of them pay for college.
“If we lose our work permit, we lose our job. We lose our stability. We lose everything,” Sanchez said. “We’re being kept on this thread of extensions, and we don’t know when that thread is going to break.”

China and the Russian Federation are already using Anthropic&apos;s AI for cyberattacks, surveillance, and the development of dangerous technologies
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
01:28:24 EEST

China and the Russian Federation are already using Anthropic's AI for cyberattacks, surveillance, and the development of dangerous technologies
Kyiv • UNN
Anthropic blocked attempts to use Claude for cyberattacks, surveillance, and the development of dangerous technologies. China and Russia are among those involved.
Malicious actors and state-linked groups in China and Russia are already attempting to use Anthropic’s artificial intelligence for cyberattacks, mass surveillance, and other dangerous operations. This is stated in a new company report, Politico reports, writes UNN.
Details
Anthropic said it had detected and blocked a number of cases involving the misuse of Claude models. These included cyber operations, surveillance systems, influence campaigns, as well as attempts to use AI for research that could potentially be linked to the creation of biological weapons.
The company recorded cases in which its models were targeted for use in automating cyberattacks and intelligence operations. Some schemes were linked to government agencies or entities from China and Russia.
Biological Threat
Anthropic was particularly concerned by requests related to biology. In one case, a user attempted to obtain help from AI with research that could have made a dangerous virus more harmful. The company said it had blocked the activity.
Anthropic is also countering attempts to illegally copy Claude’s capabilities to train other models. The company previously reported on a large-scale illegal ecosystem whose participants were attempting to circumvent restrictions and create a large number of accounts to gain access to its technologies.
The company warns that as AI capabilities grow, such systems may increasingly simplify the execution of sophisticated cyberattacks and other dangerous operations that previously required a significant number of specialists and resources.

‘Wherever they set foot, blood flows’: Algeria cuts ties with UAE in dramatic rupture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
22:27:02 UTC
07:27:02 KST

Algeria announced Thursday that it was completely severing diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates. Although relations between the North African country and Abu Dhabi have deteriorated in recent years amid Algerian allegations that the UAE has interfered in its internal affairs, the decision caught Abu Dhabi by surprise, with officials there expressing hope that it would be only temporary. However, on Thursday evening, Algeria announced another severe measure against the UAE, saying that beginning Friday it would close its airspace to all Emirati aircraft, both military and civilian. Direct flights between Algeria and the UAE will be temporarily exempt from the ban until existing contracts expire at the end of 2026.
In a statement, the Algerian Foreign Ministry accused Abu Dhabi of “provocative and hostile actions,” saying that “Algeria spared no effort in drawing the Emirati side’s attention to the serious consequences that could result from its regrettable and unjustified conduct and in warning it of those consequences.”
“Despite the numerous warnings, the United Arab Emirates continued carrying out these actions to the point where they could no longer be regarded as tolerable within the framework of relations between two sovereign states, nor could they be left unanswered,” the ministry said. “After all avenues for preserving relations were exhausted, the Algerian government decided, effective Thursday, to sever diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates. The UAE ambassador was summoned to the Foreign Ministry on Thursday, where he was formally notified of the decision. He was informed that he had 48 hours to act in accordance with the decision.”
The UAE Foreign Ministry expressed hope that the decision would be only temporary but did not respond to Algeria’s serious accusations. “Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MoFA) affirms the UAE’s appreciation for the brotherly Algerian people and its pride in the bonds that unite the two peoples,” it said.
Anwar Gargash, an adviser to the UAE president, also responded on X in remarks that appeared to reflect surprise at the decision. “Diplomatic relations are conducted through logic, communication and clearly defined interests, not through riddles and signals that require deciphering. They should not be held hostage to internal tensions or an inability to articulate interests and set priorities. Ambiguity is not a policy and noise cannot compensate for the absence of vision,” he wrote.
The decision to sever relations follows several years of steadily deteriorating diplomatic ties between the two countries, which have grown apart and found themselves on opposing sides of several regional issues, including the Abraham Accords to normalize relations with Israel. Algeria strongly opposes normalization, while the UAE and Algeria’s archrival Morocco joined the Abraham Accords in 2020.
The two countries are also on opposite sides of the long-running dispute over Western Sahara. The UAE supports Morocco’s claim of sovereignty over the territory and even maintains a consulate there, while Algeria backs the Polisario Front, which seeks to establish an independent state in Western Sahara.
More recently, the interests of Algiers and Abu Dhabi have also clashed in the Sahel, where the UAE has expanded its ties in recent years, while Algeria’s relations with several of its southern neighbors have grown strained following a series of military coups in the region.
Last year, Algerian state television also condemned what it called a “hostile media campaign” after UAE-based Sky News Arabia aired an interview with Algerian historian Mohamed Amine Belghit in which he made controversial remarks questioning the existence of the indigenous Amazigh, or Berber, culture. Belghit was arrested and imprisoned in Algeria but was later pardoned by President Abdelmadjid Tebboune.
Tebboune had already hinted at tensions with Abu Dhabi last year when he said Algeria enjoyed warm relations with every Gulf state except one, which he did not name. He described relations with Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Oman and Qatar as “brotherly,” while accusing the unnamed country of interfering in Algeria’s internal affairs.
In July, Tebboune explicitly attacked the UAE, describing it as a “micro-state” that he claimed was seeking to destabilize several countries in the region, including Libya, Mali and Sudan.
“Wherever they set foot, blood flows,” Tebboune charged in a television interview, saying the UAE had a “very negative influence.”
“We want them to stay far away so that blood is not spilled in our country,” he added.
In the same interview, Tebboune said the severing of diplomatic relations “would have happened long ago,” but said Algeria had hoped to avoid “deepening divisions” in the Arab world.

Algeria cuts diplomatic ties with UAE

Algeria cuts diplomatic ties with UAE
September 11, 2026
Algeria severed diplomatic ties with the United Arab Emirates on Thursday, citing what it described as "provocative and hostile acts."
The Algerian Defense Ministry said the country would close its airspace to the UAE beginning on Friday.
However, commercial flights to and from Algiers will be allowed to continue until the end of 2026.
Relations between the two countries have been strained for years over the UAE's expanding influence in northern and western Africa.
What did Algeria and the UAE say about the decision?
The Algerian Foreign Ministry said that it had made the decision "after exhausting all avenues to preserve bilateral relations" with the Gulf country.
It added that the UAE had "persisted in its actions, reaching a point where they could no longer be considered acceptable or tolerable."
Algiers said it had given the UAE's ambassador 48 hours to comply with the decision to cut ties.
The Emirati Foreign Ministry said that it hoped that the decision would be temporary.
"The UAE expresses hope that this decision will be temporary, in a manner that preserves the fraternal ties between the two brotherly peoples," the ministry said in a statement.
It said that it "affirms the UAE's appreciation for the brotherly Algerian people and its pride in the bonds that unite the two peoples, particularly through the Algerian community residing in the UAE and Algerian visitors."
Following the announcement, Anwar Gargash, the diplomatic advisor to UAE leader Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, said that diplomatic relations should be based on "rationality, communication and clarity of interests" rather than "riddles and signals that require decoding."
He did not explicitly mention Algeria in his post on X.
What are the tensions between Algeria and the UAE?
Algeria has in the past accused Abu Dhabi of working to destabilize countries in northern Africa and the Sahel such as Libya, Mali, and Sudan.
The UAE has been accused of supporting the RSF paramilitary in Sudan's civil war, a charge it denies.
It also backs former warlord Khalifa Haftar's Tobruk-based administration in eastern Libya, a rival to the UN-recognized government in Tripoli.
In July, Algerian President Abdelmajid Tebboune harshly criticized the UAE for its influence in other countries, saying "wherever they set foot, blood flows."
"We want them to stay away, so that blood does not flow in our country."
Algeria also severed its diplomatic ties with neighboring Morocco in 2021, accusing Rabat of supporting Amazigh separatists in the coastal Kabylia region and amid longstanding tensions over the territory of Western Sahara.

Why these big new AI data centres are set to escape new regulations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
22:25:38 UTC
07:25:38 KST

The bigger, hungrier AI data centres set to escape looming water and power restrictions
Dozens of approved but yet-to-be-built AI data centre projects will escape the federal government's proposed restrictions around energy and water use because the new rules are not expected to be retrospective.
ABC analysis of planning records and company documents has revealed this new generation of data centres will be significantly bigger and power hungrier than existing ones.
Earlier this year, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced the federal government would create Australian standards to quell community concerns about the environment, while attracting the investment of major tech companies.
With the government aiming to pass a law to establish these rules by early 2027, the uncertainty has not slowed the breakneck speed of development.
Business has welcomed the tens of billions of dollars being invested in building the physical infrastructure powering the generative AI boom, although not all of the approved data centres will likely be built.
Bigger, hungrier
ABC analysis of upcoming projects includes developments from Amazon Web Services, Microsoft, AirTrunk, CDC and NEXTDC, as well as property groups Goodman and Stockland, each of which was contacted for confirmation.
The list has been verified by analysts from commercial renewable energy project mapper RenewMap and real estate construction analytics firm CBRE.
Advocacy group Data Centre Australia published a report saying Australia had 162 data centres with a combined IT capacity of 1.5 gigawatts as of March of this year.
The combined capacity of the approved, but unbuilt, 27 data centres is at least 3.38 gigawatts, based on each company's statements of computing power and the state planning-approved energy capacity.
One project approved last week is property developer Goodman's five-storey data centre Project Apollo in Sydney's north.
It will take two years to build and be one of Australia's biggest data centres by computing capacity if it existed today, according to the facility's proposal.
While not subject to the federal government's rules, its approval came with conditions from the NSW government relating to water and energy use.
RenewMap co-founder and director Alex Thompson said the development pipeline had accelerated in recent months, with proposed centres generally much larger than those already operating.
He said NSW and Victoria were the main growth areas, particularly western Sydney and Melbourne's outskirts, while developers were also pursuing regional locations alongside wind, solar and battery projects.
Mr Thompson said even though they have been approved, "not all of these data centres will get built".
Environmental concerns
For software engineer and western Sydney resident Jack Tollefsen, the expansion is happening close to home.
He lives in Horsley Park and works down the road from NEXTDC's S4 development, which is under construction and expected to provide 365MW of capacity.
Mr Tollefsen has started a petition opposing the data centre and others being built in suburban areas.
An environmentalist who opposes AI, Mr Tollefsen said he had raised his concerns with local and state representatives.
"My main concerns with this are largely the environmental impact, the impact it has on the ecosystem, the native wildlife in the area,"
Mr Tollefsen said he was disappointed the federal government had not already introduced minimum standards for data centres.
He said he hoped NEXTDC would at least reduce its water usage by designing it with a closed-loop system, a more water-efficient approach that requires more energy.
The proposed national standards are intended to address energy, water and land-use impacts of large data centres, but state and territory governments will retain their planning responsibilities.
The exact details of the proposed legislated standards have not yet been released.
So far, the federal government has said it will require data centres to underwrite new renewable energy to cover their consumption, cover the connection costs, be as water-efficient as possible, and be built in appropriate locations.
Some of the approved data centres may meet these standards, even if they are not legally required to comply.
Australia wants investment on our 'terms'
In July, Mr Albanese delivered a landmark speech detailing how Australia would respond to the opportunity and challenges presented by AI.
The prime minister said Australia had both the desire and capacity to attract investment from major AI companies, including data centres, as long as they met certain requirements.
He said the government would pass a law in early 2027 setting rules to force data centres to minimise water use and maximise energy efficiency.
"We can set the terms, we can determine AI's social licence," he said, claiming the standards would create certainty for investors, too.
But the prime minister later told ABC Radio Sydney the rules would not apply to projects already approved or under construction.
"You can't retrofit. But as well, many of the centres which are under construction tend to be smaller ones," he said.
A Department of Industry, Science and Resources spokesperson said Australia had far fewer large data centres built and in construction than the United States, citing research from S&P Global Ratings.
"Current investment trends suggest the number of large data centres will increase. The Australian government wants this investment to be sustainable and aligned with our national interests," they said.
Call to stop building until rules in place
Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young has been leading calls for a ban on data centre construction until the government establishes minimum standards.
She said communities were already facing pressure from developments being proposed and built, and argued standards introduced after projects were approved would not provide the protections the government was promising.
"In the absence of a moratorium on building and approving new data centres, then these rules must be retrospective because otherwise they're worthless," she said.
Senator Hanson-Young said the government risked losing community support for AI if it did not take concerns about energy, water and local benefits seriously.
Data Centres Australia chief Belinda Dennett said her industry was already taking steps to meet the government's expectations around power and water use.
"Members will continue to meet those requirements until the new rules are in force — but they cannot comply with something that isn't yet established or even articulated."
Investment continues
Kate Muller, a partner in Ashurst Perkins Coie's projects and energy transition practice, said the delay and uncertainty around national standards was not dampening investor interest.
Ms Muller said Australia was attractive to major technology companies because of its security, and a government and policy environment similar to US-headquartered businesses.
She said developers were used to dealing with some regulatory uncertainty.
"The degree of debate, guideline and regulation is unlikely to deter that investment and we certainly haven't seen that in our practice and with the people that we're speaking to around industry,"
Ms Muller said clear expectations could help ensure projects delivered benefits for Australians, while public debate could help address their potential detrimental effects.
"Indeed, we expect to see a genuine drive toward more data centre development in Australia," she said.
Two federal parliamentary inquiries are examining data centres and AI respectively, and will report back later this year.
Editor’s note 11/9/26: This story was updated after publication, adding two data centres to the ABC’s analysis.
